Manchester United (MUFC) is currently on its longest winless run since 1988, its worst start since 1986, and its fewest wins in the first eight games since 1953. However, Michael Carrick still believes his dressing room is in “a good place.”
The team lies one place above the relegation zone after its latest defeat to Chelsea in the Premier League. Red Devils next face Roma at Old Trafford in the UEFA Champions League on Tuesday.
There have been suggestions in the media that Carrick has until the next international break to resurrect the season for MUFC. After two successive defeats in the Champions League, they are placed 20th, and a win against the in-form Roma would help curb the spiral at multiple levels.
When asked if he has just two games to determine his future in the job, Carrick said, “No, not at all. If you look into the future, you never know what’s going to happen. I don’t know what’s going to happen. That doesn’t change the way I feel, how we’re preparing for the game tomorrow.”
“I’m actually really looking forward to the game, can’t wait for the game tomorrow. You might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had and what’s going on, but I genuinely can’t wait,” he added.
ALSO READ: Manchester United can get relegated: Ten Hag
The defeats and the post-match comments of his players, captain Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez, have brought up questions of unity in the dressing room.
“Perception is a funny thing. You can make things look all sorts of different ways and think about all sorts of different things. I’ve said it before, the commitment of the players to the club, to me, to each other, I don’t question that at all. We need to play better, we can make better decisions, but commitment is not a thing at all.” Carrick responded to the rumours.
Martinez, in particular, has been in poor form, and his comments have highlighted his performances, especially after he got sent off against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge
“Things happen in football, sometimes you do things, sometimes you make decisions, sometimes you make mistakes, sometimes it goes well for you, but the commitment is not an issue for sure,” Carrick said, defending Martinez.
Carrick was asked to recall his last encounter against Roma, back in 2007, where he scored a brace to take Man United to a 7-1 win in the quarterfinals. A time when MUFC were constantly successful.
“It was a magical night, I have to say. It was one of the best nights, one of the best games, one of the best atmospheres I’ve been fortunate enough to witness. The fact that I scored a couple, and that was very unusual, gives me great memories, but it was more the emotion of the night. I have to say, it was a special one,” said Carrick

Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh is stepping down from the investment firm after a nearly decade-long stint. In a statement, the venture capital (VC) firm said that Singh would “transition out of the firm”. The consumer-focused fund has so far not named his successor. On his future course of action, Singh said that he now plans to explore the “frontiers of agentic commerce and its implications for the future of consumption”. “... As AI reshapes commerce faster than most of us expected, I want to spend more time exploring the frontiers of agentic commerce and its implications for the future of consumption. I am excited for this next chapter, and deeply grateful to the Fireside family, and to every founder and LP (limited partner) who trusted us on this journey,” said Singh. An alumnus of IIM Bangalore, Singh counts nearly two decades of experience under his belt. He previously worked at companies like Hindustan Unilever and Bankbazaar. He earlier also cofounded car servicing platform Stepni, which was later acquired by Quikr. He eventually cofounded Fireside Ventures alongside Kanwaljit Singh, Kannan Sitaram and Dipanjan Basu in 2017. Over the past decade, the VC firm has emerged as one of India’s biggest consumer-focused venture funds and counts more than 65 startups in its portfolio. It currently claims to oversee more than $650 Mn in assets under management across four funds. The VC firm last closed its fourth fund at about $253 Mn in December last year. The investment firm currently claims to be helmed by a team of 12 principals and vice presidents. The development comes as a host of seasoned fund managers depart major VC firms to set up their own funds. Earlier this year, Ashish Agrawal, Ishaan Mittal and Tejeshwi Sharma quit Peak XV Partners to establish their own fund, Mettle Capital. Private equity (PE) firm L Catterton’s partner and co-head of India investments, Anjana Sasidharan, also stepped down from the company in March this year to set up Asthrum Capital. We often pick up hobbies to add some fun to our lives. We join a book group, take up knitting, or commit to finally learning how to play pickleball. But before long, what started out as leisure can begin to feel like just another obligation to execute and perfect: We fall behind in the reading, can’t stop dropping stitches, or the tournament schedule gets overwhelming.
Are you over-optimizing your hobbies?
Author Jenny Odell explains how to keep your free time fun.
It’s a tale as old as time, or at least as old as the United States. Our obsession with productivity may feel new, especially when it crosses over to our hobbies, but according to Gary Cross, a historian and author of the book Free Time: The History of an Elusive Ideal, Americans have been trying to make the most of our time for a while now. “A lot of it is that old Protestant work ethic that was part of the early migration to the United States,” he told Vox. “They were predominantly Protestant Christians who saw work as a kind of a special calling from God.”
As Cross explains, this attitude kicked into high gear alongside industrialization. “The capitalists really were all about increasing productivity. Time away from work begins to be seen as in some ways wasted time,” Cross said. And when the labor movement helped win workers some free time for hobbies around the turn of the 20th century, the same mentality made the jump into our leisure time.
That time is something that writer Jenny Odell has thought a lot about and explored in her books Saving Time: Discovering a Life Beyond the Clock and How to Do Nothing: Resisting the Attention Economy. “I think both of my books came out of observing the daily experience that I and the people I knew were having, where our relationship to time felt so painful — this unending intensity that was so exhausting,” she said. “There has to be another way.”
Odell says that one of the ways to shift our relationship with time is through cultivating hobbies — without falling into the trap of relentless quantification and optimization. So how do we learn to truly enjoy our leisure time, and why should we all consider failing a little more along the way? We learn that and more on the latest episode of Explain It to Me, Vox’s weekly call-in podcast.
Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Odell, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full episode on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you get your podcasts. If you’d like to submit a question, send an email to askvox@vox.com or call 1-800-618-8545.
How is our pursuit of hobbies connected to how we think about time?
Hobbies are a place where you can see different ways of thinking about time battling each other. There’s a very fine line between someone who pursues a hobby for the sake of doing it versus someone who feels that they need to optimize it, perhaps even make money off of it. There’s nothing wrong with that, but these are different ways of thinking about the activity that you’re doing.
People read the title How to Do Nothing and they think that I’m a person who literally doesn’t do anything. I love to do things and I love to learn things. I think a lot of people start hobbies because they want to learn.
In American culture, a lot of us stop being given opportunities to learn after we’re children or after we’re students. I think it’s really beautiful that adults seek out ways to learn, often leaning into communities where they’re learning with other people. And learning has progress in it. You do get better at things when you learn them.
My feeling is just that that sense of forward movement and learning gets co-opted by this larger culture that we exist in that is also very American: needing to have something to show for your time. What starts out as wanting to learn something turns into something that you’re giving yourself a score on, without your ever having decided to do that.
I spoke with a historian who said part of the reason that we relate to our free time in this particular way in America specifically is the history of the Protestant work ethic. It’s just so ingrained in us. How do you help yourself break out of that mentality?
I have to shout out this book called The Score by C. Thi Nguyen. He talks about this very question. In that book he talks about games and how when you play a game, you take on a whole new set of values, and you do that for whatever couple of hours and then you put it away. It’s kind of this practice in taking values, putting them on, taking them off, putting them away.
For me, either literally playing games or trying to have a more playful, experimental mindset about what it is that I’m doing can break that cycle. When you get closer to [a goal], it gets more and more seductive. Like “I want a higher number.” You just need something to break you out of that and be like, “What is this number even measuring?”
For me, I’m a writer. Words per day are a measure. You think you want more words per day, but all words are not the same. There have been moments where I was trying to optimize words per day. I have to stop myself and think about what other ways I could value the situation. Like, “What were those words? Did I make some sort of breakthrough?”
There’s all these other different ways that you could think about what it is that you’re doing.
Something I think a lot about when it comes to hobbies is failure. For instance, I’m getting back into photography. I did film photography in high school and this year I picked it back up with the goal to shoot a roll of film per month.
The year’s almost over. I’ve done three rolls of film, one of which I must have unloaded incorrectly because it was completely blown out. What role does failure play in our hobbies and how we interact with that?
I love failure. I think it’s so underrated and games are very useful here. A good sports person is open to failure and knows that that’s fun.
I think that along with not having opportunities to learn as adults, we also aren’t given opportunities to fail. That’s probably been the case for a long time, but now with social media and things being more visible for a lot of people, we really are not used to failing. We think we don’t want it.
I feel like I am actively now seeking out things that I’m bad at just so I can have that feeling. I’m a failure addict.
That is true. Once we leave school, what opportunities do we have to safely learn things and fail and try it again?
I don’t know how else to describe it: It’s really fun to be bad at something. Once you accept that you are bad at it, your reason for doing it has to be something else.
I’ve been going to this native plant restoration thing for two and a half years now, so I definitely know my weeds and I am better than the day that I showed up, but I don’t go there to be the best at something.
I showed up on day one and I wasn’t wearing the right clothes. I didn’t have gardening gloves. I had never gardened in my life. I had no idea what I was doing. It was this fascinating feeling. It’s just so different from being an adult who’s specialized in something.
What’s a way to help yourself fall back in love with hobbies if it’s been a while or if you’ve optimized so much, you want to find the joy in it again?
It’s like the equivalent of being right-handed and trying to write with your left hand. Anything you can do to relax the perfectionist grip that you have on this thing.
That means throwing obstacles in your own way or trying to do things in a way you’ve never done them before. Rediscover the same thing from a new angle or in a different context with new people.

‘Nobody will trust you’: SC rejects Centre’s plea against Vedanta arbitration awards
The Supreme Court questioned the government’s approach to arbitration, asking why it was frustrating enforcement of an arbitral award after the dispute had been adjudicated by foreign courts.
The Supreme Court on Monday dismissed the Union government’s appeal against a Delhi High Court order allowing Vedanta Ltd and Ravva Oil (Singapore) Pvt Ltd to enforce foreign arbitration awards involving claims of $99 million, criticising the Centre for resisting enforcement of awards that date back more than two decades and warning that such litigation could undermine confidence in India’s arbitration regime.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and Manmohan questioned the government’s approach to arbitration, asking why it was frustrating enforcement of an arbitral award even after the dispute had been adjudicated by foreign courts. The bench also questioned the Centre’s commitment to promoting arbitration as an effective means of dispute resolution.
“What are these arguments? You are frustrating an arbitral award like this? At the stage of enforcement of it?” remarked the court, expressing concern over the message such litigation would send to international investors and parties choosing India as an arbitration destination.
“And we talk about all of this arbitration and seat and this and that?...Nobody will trust you,” said the court, questioning the government’s continued resistance to the awards.
The bench ultimately found no reason to interfere with the high court’s July 1, 2026 judgment, which had rejected the Centre’s objections to enforcement of the awards passed in 2004 and 2016 by an arbitral tribunal seated in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.
“We are of the view that no error, not to speak of any error of law, could be said to have been committed by the high court in passing the impugned judgment and order,” said the Supreme Court while dismissing the appeal.
The dispute traces its origins to a 1994 production-sharing contract between the government and a consortium comprising ONGC, Videocon Petroleum, Ravva Oil and Cairn Energy (whose interest subsequently passed to Cairn India and later Vedanta) for the development of the Ravva oilfield in the Krishna-Godavari basin.
The dispute centred on the accounting of payments made by the companies towards ONGC’s historical costs while calculating their respective shares of revenue from oil production, an issue referred to as the ONGC Carry dispute. Under the contract, disputes were to be resolved through arbitration in Kuala Lumpur under Malaysian law and the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Arbitration Rules.
In October 2004, the arbitral tribunal delivered a partial award, ruling in favour of the companies on two of six issues while deciding the remaining four in favour of the government. It left the quantification of the ONGC Carry issue unresolved, retaining jurisdiction to determine the amount if the parties failed to reach an agreement.
The government challenged the partial award before Malaysian courts. Although it was initially set aside by the Kuala Lumpur High Court in January 2009, the Malaysian Court of Appeal restored it in September that year, a decision subsequently upheld by the Malaysian Federal Court in October 2011.
In July 2014, the government issued show-cause notices seeking recovery of approximately $64 million from Vedanta and $35 million from Ravva Oil, threatening to adjust the amounts against proceeds payable to the companies from oil sales.
The companies disputed the claims and approached the arbitral tribunal to determine the outstanding amounts. A reconstituted tribunal delivered its final award on October 26, 2016. The Centre again challenged the award before Malaysian courts, but its challenge was rejected, with the Malaysian Federal Court upholding the award on February 28, 2019.
Vedanta and Ravva Oil subsequently approached the Delhi High Court seeking enforcement in India of the two awards. The Centre opposed their plea, raising objections based on limitation, public policy and the tribunal having become functus officio, or having exhausted its authority after delivering the earlier award.
Rejecting these objections, the high court held that the enforcement court could not reopen the merits of the underlying dispute or revisit the arbitral tribunal’s findings merely because the government disagreed with them. It also held that the enforcement proceedings were within limitation and directed the release of bank guarantees furnished by the companies within eight weeks. The Supreme Court’s dismissal of the Centre’s appeal now leaves the high court’s directions undisturbed.

One annoying problem with the iPhone Messages app has an easy fix
Apple's iMessage can be customized to fit your needs however you like
Apple's iMessage has evolved a lot over the years. In recent updates, the Cupertino company has added everything from satellite messaging that can reach out to your emergency contact while in a remote location to aesthetic changes like customizable backgrounds. Keeping abreast of these changes can be difficult, especially when Apple releases a new iOS update every year.
Despite these updates, users often lament the inconvenience of their iMessage app arrangement. Why, for example, are applications you've never used at the top of the dropdown menu, while your most used apps remain buried at the bottom? The answer is that you likely haven't taken the time to customize the menu's layout.
Some of the most impactful changes have come through the introduction of iMessage apps. Since the introduction of iOS 18, several applications have been installed in the messaging app by default. As of the latest update, iOS 27, 14 apps are included by default. These popular applications bring features like sending your location, voice recordings, stickers, GIFs, music, photos and polls. Other applications, like ESPN and Venmo, further expand the functionalities of your messaging app. Luckily, you can keep them all ordered how you want.
Rearranging your iMessage apps
Before customizing your app layout, let's quickly review how to pull up your iMessage dropdown menu. First, make sure that you have downloaded the latest iOS. Once updated, open your Messages and either tap a conversation or hit the compose button, which resembles a pencil touching a white square located at the bottom of righthand corner of your screen.
Once a conversation is pulled up, tap the Plus (+) button beside your messages. Here, you will find a full list of your available iMessage apps . Next, hold down the app you want to move until the icon shrinks, drag it to its desired place on the dropdown menu and let go.
You can also add more apps to your iMessages. Open your phone's App Store for iMessage. Go to Messages, open a conversation, tap the Plus (+) symbol and touch the circular blue App Store icon. Once you open the App Store, you can peruse Apple's list of popular applications or search for something specific. To download a new app, simply tap the Get button next to the app's name. If the app requires purchasing it, you will see the app's price rather than a Get button. To exit the app store, swipe down or tap Close (X).
Further customizing your iMessage apps
You may want to be cautious about which apps you add. In August 2026, for instance, OpenAI caused a stir when it added iMessage integration to its ChatGPT app for Mac. While some found the app useful, others raised privacy and security concerns. Moreover, some free apps require in-app purchases, which can easily ratchet up your monthly phone expenditures. If you are part of a Family Sharing plan, however, you can take advantage of iOS 27's enhanced parental control features by managing your family's in-app purchasing options. One helpful setting is the Ask To Buy feature, in which you can require the children on your plan to get confirmation before making an in-app purchase.
To delete individual apps you've added, or to manage the iMessage functionalities of your downloaded apps, visit your Settings app. From there, tap Apps > Messages > iMessage Apps. Here you can decide whether you want to toggle the application on or off. You can also delete the app altogether on your device's homepage by tapping and holding down on the icon until a dropdown menu appears. Then, tap the red Remove App option at the bottom of the menu.
Apple even lets you customize some of your iMessage app's functionalities, too. For instance, you can adjust how your iPhone's audio recording app functions within iMessage, cycling between voice note and dictation functions.

How infant deaths in Keralam’s Attappady expose a deep-rooted health, social crisis
12 infants, including 10 tribals, have died in Attappady this year, sparking a political row as the State government orders an expert probe. Tribal activists say the crisis demands action beyond healthcare, addressing malnutrition, anaemia and deep-rooted social issues
Published - October 31, 2026 01:25 pm IST - PALAKKAD
In Attappady, maternal health remains a major concern. Anaemia among pregnant women continues to be widespread, while underweight mothers and low birth weight among newborns add to the risks (file image)
| Photo Credit: The Hindu
The deaths of 12 infants, 10 of them from tribal communities, in Attappady in Keralam in recent months have once again cast a spotlight on a child health crisis that has defied solutions for over a decade. While the State government has set an expert assessment in motion, tribal organisations maintain that the roots of the crisis run deeper than healthcare, demanding sustained action on nutrition, maternal health, landlessness and the wider socio-economic conditions of the community.
Figures cited by tribal activists show that 124 infants have died in the region since 2011. Since 2012, Attappady has also recorded around 300 abortions, 90 intrauterine deaths and two dozen stillbirths. The region came under particular scrutiny in 2013, when 47 tribal infants died. Tribal observers estimate that around 10 children have died annually over the years.

The award‑winning author Craig Silvey sent multiple messages about his sexual desire for young boys and was caught with explicit images of children and adults.
The young adult novelist was jailed on Monday for seven months after pleading guilty to distributing and possessing child exploitation material earlier this year.
The 44-year-old was found with numerous category one photos and videos on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his Fremantle home, the Western Australian district court heard.
Silvey, a father of three, also engaged in an online conversation with another user on a pornography website, where his handle was Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy.
In the chat, Silvey described himself as a “Fremantle guy” before telling the user: “You sound amazing … we have very similar interests, would love to chat more; do you have Signal or Session?”
The pair moved to an encrypted messaging app, where he said he was “extremely open-minded and obsessed with taboos” and preferred boys older than five before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.
Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the International Dublin Literary Award, also wrote he was “drooling” over a sexually explicit photo of a naked man and boy together.
Judge Hayley Cormann said it was very serious and very disturbing offending.
“This offending involves children and it is destructive and it is devastating,” she said.
The popular author is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, considered a modern Australian classic and adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb, Honeybee – which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 – and the children’s novel Runt, which was also made into a film.
Publishers Allen & Unwin and Fremantle Press, which released Rhubarb, stopped promoting his books after Silvey was charged and most of his titles were removed from reading lists across the country.
Two charges of producing and possessing further child exploitation material were dropped in May.

'We often try suicide:' The hidden cost of problem gambling in Canada
Canada saw at least 220 gambler suicides in last decade — but no inquests
This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
Dave, a retiree recovering from gambling addiction, says that when he was winning, he felt like a king, hooked by the prospect of wealth and recognition.
But he says like most gamblers, he "inevitably" started losing.
"Not only money — trust, people we care for, spouses, children, we lose the whole gamut. Everything that we built goes crumbling down," he told CBC News during a recent online Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto.
"So we often try suicide, which I did try. I turned out to be an utter failure at that."
CBC reporter Dave Seglins speaks to a Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)
A CBC News investigation has found that at least 220 problem gamblers in Canada have died by suicide in the last decade, which includes a tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022.
But the national numbers are likely higher, as Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Nunavut don’t track gambling-related deaths, citing a lack of obvious indicators in most death investigations.
What’s more, no coroner in Canada has ever held an inquest into the issue — unlike in Australia and the United Kingdom, where inquests are being used to critically examine the gambling industry and the links between addiction and suicide.
'Misery and great harm'
A coroner in Australia delivered a scathing inquest report last month, calling for major industry reforms after investigating the suicide of 22-year-old Kyle Hudson.
Hudson opened online betting accounts after his 18th birthday and over four years, placed more than 10,000 bets, losing a cumulative $47,000 Cdn.
The morning he died, he had placed and lost bets worth $6,200.
Coroner Paul Lowrie concluded that Hudson’s preferred platform, SportsBet, ought to have detected his problem gambling.
"Kyle’s case reveals, in the sharpest relief, the human cost of online gambling," the coroner wrote. "It should be a clear signal that we cannot leave monitoring and intervention solely in the hands of the betting companies."
Kyle Hudson was 'a young man brimming with promise,' according to a coroner's report in Australia. He was working part-time while in his fourth year at university and loved sport. (ABC.net.au)
Hudson’s betting escalated and triggered 37 alerts on SportBet’s internal "Safer Gambling" monitoring system, the inquest heard.
The company sent him automated support emails and on multiple occasions called him to suspend his account, only to receive a call back from Hudson, who convinced them to reinstate it.
SportsBet also sent Hudson hundreds of bonus offers and inducements to continue playing, which the coroner found to be "contrary" to the company’s safer gambling programs.
"These products are carefully designed to keep gamblers engaged and active, and to extract net losses over time," Lowrie wrote.
"They are dangerous and capable of causing misery and great harm, especially for the young or those whose traits may make them more vulnerable."
SportsBet maintained during the inquest that Hudson did not have a gambling problem. That’s despite accounts from Hudson’s family, experts and analysis of the extent of his online gambling activity.
"It is chilling that this is SportsBet’s view," Lowrie concluded.
Inquests examine gambling companies' player data
Charles Ritchie of Sheffield, England, who started the charity Gambling With Lives, says inquests are an important tool to change laws and cast light on the gambling industry.
He became an advocate after his 24-year-old son Jack took his own life in November 2017.
"We realized straight away that it was gambling that had killed him. It was there in his suicide note," Ritchie told CBC News, detailing how Jack had started gambling as a teen and got hooked online after a fluke win of 1,000 pounds ($1,870 Cdn) on an electronic gaming terminal.
Jack Ritchie’s online gambling addiction led to his death, a U.K. coroner found. (Leigh Day law firm)
Ritchie says an inquest into Jack’s death in 2022 validated that it was caused by gambling.
Beyond that, he says inquests have become a valuable tool for grieving families to hold companies accountable if they have failed to intervene in cases of addiction.
After someone’s death, he says inquests can analyze the deceased’s behaviour using player data and banking records.
"When we look at those figures in the raw… Somebody is, at four o'clock in the morning, having hundreds of bets, is losing hundreds of pounds. You as a human being would say, ‘This is wrong. We need to intervene,’" he said.
"Gambling companies don't do that. And that has been found in so many of the inquests."
The U.K. has held inquests into the gambling deaths of, clockwise from top left, Arthur Soames, Jack Ritchie, Oliver Long, Gareth Evans, Luke Ashton, Ellen Mulvey and Lee Adams. (Leigh Day law firm)
No inquests in Canada
The U.K. has held seven gambling-related inquests since Jack Ritchie’s death inquiry in 2022, resulting in numerous recommendations to the government and the gambling industry.
Coroners and medical examiners in Canada have never undertaken a similar investigation.
CBC contacted chief coroners and medical examiners across Canada, who acknowledge not every jurisdiction tracks gambling suicides.
Nor do most coroners consider whether problem gambling was a contributing factor during suicide investigations. It can be hard to detect without an explicit suicide note.
People with gambling addictions tend to hide their problem from family and friends. Coroners don’t routinely probe a suicide victim’s financial records or online history to determine whether they had a gambling problem.
Journalist Rob Csernyik, author of A Losing Hand: The Human Cost of Canada’s Gambling Epidemic, says chief coroners pledged in 2003 to begin tracking the problem nationally. It has never happened.
"It's just something that hasn't been on the radar in many years in Canada, despite the expansion of gambling," Csernyik told CBC News.
Canada lacks data on gambling suicides, despite the expansion of online betting, says author and journalist Rob Csernyik. (Roger Cosman/CBC)
"I think that now with the larger push into legal gambling markets, that it's something we finally need to address."
Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022, the year the province legalized private online betting, worries him that we'll see an epidemic of addiction.
"This is the thing I’ve been fearful for," said Kelly, an adolescent addiction specialist in Ottawa.
He’s calling for much closer monitoring of problem gambling as well as restrictions on gambling advertising to curb gambling’s harms before they get worse.
"To me, it would be much too late to act when we had irrefutable evidence that our changes in gambling legislation have led to an increase in suicide amongst the vulnerable."
Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022 is a warning sign for public health officials. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
CBC asked Ontario’s Ministry of Health to comment on the rise in gambling addiction and related suicides in the province.
The minister’s press secretary deferred to Ontario’s Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming, which oversees the province’s $3-billion-a-year online gambling market.
The Gaming Ministry did not address the rise in suicide rates but said in an email that since 2018, "our government has invested $421 million, including $70.1 million over the last year, in responsible gambling education, research and addiction treatment."
In the meantime, members at Gamblers Anonymous, a peer-to-peer support group with chapters around the world, are hoping more people who are struggling reach out for help.
Dan, who like Dave considered suicide, describes the group as a "big extended family."
"If I didn't find GA (Gamblers Anonymous), there's a very solid chance that either I'd be living on the streets, lost my home, marriage or even dead," he told CBC News. "That came across my mind many times."

Nearly 2 out of 3 teens and tweens use AI chatbots, new research shows
Artificial intelligence chatbots are increasingly becoming a regular part of life for American youth. Two new surveys show that nearly two-thirds of tweens and teens use AI chatbots. While most kids use the technology for help with school work, and for companionship and emotional support, certain uses were linked with worse mental health symptoms.
One survey, done by the online safety advocacy group, Common Sense Media, found that AI use starts early – years before kids hit the minimum age of 13 on most popular chatbots. Nearly half 9-to-12-year-olds have used an AI chatbot or companion. By the time kids are 13 years old, nearly three-quarters of them have used chatbots.
The other survey, done by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, found that 90% of the 5,500 9-to-17-year-olds in schools across the country have used an AI chatbot. Nearly two-thirds use it both for schoolwork and as companions, or when they are stressed, lonely, anxious or overwhelmed.
The findings are "remarkable" in showing how dramatically AI use by children and teens has changed in a short time, says developmental psychologist Anne Maheux at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, who wasn't involved in the surveys.
"It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using" the technology, she says. "And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping."
"I use it to make myself practice sample questions – sample test questions that I will answer with my own work," says 15-year-old Arjun Sharda, in Round Rock, Texas. "I use it to understand concepts outside of the classroom."
He uses both OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini, he says, although he prefers the latter lately.
In Raynham, Mass., McKenzie Craig, 17, has been using chatbots since she was in eighth grade. "I use it typically if I'm overwhelmed with a bunch of tasks I have," she says. "I'll have it help me prioritize the tasks."
She also uses it for help with assignments. "If I write an essay, I'll run it through either Grammarly or ChatGPT and have it graded, so to speak," says Craig. "It gives me feedback, and then I can edit accordingly."
Sharda says he and his friends also turn to chatbots when they are stressed and anxious.
"With tests, for example," he says, "I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT 'Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'"
Some chatbot uses are linked to worse mental health
Researchers at the JED Foundation also surveyed students on symptoms of overall well-being and mental health.
"We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health," says psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation.
"When young people are using AI, when they're in emotional distress," she adds, "they're more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes." They also report a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.
But the data don't suggest a causal link, cautions Anderson.
"It's unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI," she explains.
But preliminary data collected by other researchers suggests that the link between chatbots and poorer mental health symptoms in young people might go both ways, says Maheux.
"So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them," she says. "But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping."
In a soon-to-be-published study of middle schoolers in one state, Maheux and her colleagues at UNC found that students who use chatbots for companionship grew lonelier over time.
They found similar results in another study of young adults. "We see that people who are using AI more for companionship or feeling like they're overreliant on AI to solve various emotional or cognitive problems, are developing worse mental health over time."
One potential explanation for this effect, she says, is that AI is easing people's emotional distress — loneliness, anxiety, stress — in the immediate moment, but that reliance on the technology is preventing young people from developing the skills to tolerate and navigate normal daily stresses.
That, she explains, "can lead to worse mental health."

America has a classic salary milestone: six figures a year. Anthropic's average employee has cost their employer that much every month.
Anthropic's personnel expenses topped $1.7 billion for its 5,300 workers from July through September, according to an amended S-1 filing the AI company released Monday morning ahead of its initial public offering later this month. That means the expenses averaged over $322,000 per worker over the three-month span.
The total indicates how a seat inside Anthropic became one of the 21st century's quickest pathways to extraordinary wealth. Its coming IPO will mint a new cohort of multimillionaires. Even employees who've only been around for a couple of years have seen their stock options multiply in value several times over.
The AI juggernaut has used high salaries and a rapidly growing valuation to recruit skilled engineers, researchers, and other specialists. Over the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic's personnel costs totaled $4.8 billion, according to the S-1.
The last quarter's $1.7 billion tally included cash salaries and bonuses, benefits, and employer payroll taxes. The largest chunk of the total came from Anthropic's stock-based compensation expenses, an accounting measure of the equity it recognized for employees — that came out to $1.1 billion in the three-month span.
Against the high employee expenses, Anthropic's revenue has raced far ahead. Back in 2023, the company spent more than twice as much on personnel as it made in revenue. In the first nine months of 2026, personnel costs tallied just 15% of total revenue.
The numbers could fluctuate. Anthropic wrote in its S-1 that, as of the end of September, it had more than $32 billion in stock-based compensation expenses that it had not yet included in its accounting. A successful listing on the stock market would increase Anthropic's personnel costs in the coming quarters.
Anthropic quintupled in head count from the end of 2024 to the end of September 2026. It's still much smaller than its tech-industry peers. Meta is valued at around $1.6 trillion, a possible target for Anthropic's IPO. The social media giant has around 67,000 employees. Broadcom, worth about the same, has more than 30,000.
This trim size makes Anthropic look especially efficient, as Business Insider reported last week. The company tallied $6.6 million in annual revenue per employee, compared with estimates that put Meta at $3.2 million per employee and Google at $2.5 million.
"Talent density matters more than talent mass," Anthropic wrote in its S-1.

In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.
OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters.
The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center.
Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.”
Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.
OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round:
“Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”
OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

On 01 November 2026, the INDIA bloc organised a mega rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan to protest alleged electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Congress MP Rahul Gandhi led a ‘Chalo Dilli’ march from the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction towards Ramlila Maidan, where the rally witnessed a large gathering of supporters and party workers from several Opposition parties, including the Congress, Samajwadi Party, TMC and RJD (here, here, and here).
Amid this, several videos and Images are being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming to show a massive gathering at the INDIA bloc-led rally held at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi on 01 November 2026. Let’s verify the claims made in these posts in this article.
Claim: The visuals show a massive gathering of supporters at the INDIA bloc-led rally held at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi on 01 November 2026.
Fact: The visuals are unrelated to the INDIA bloc-led rally held at Ramlila Maidan on 1 November 2026. Video 1 predates the event and was shared by Congress leaders in connection with the party’s 14 December 2025 ‘Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod’ rally at the same venue. Video 2 shows celebrations in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on 20 December 2022, following Argentina’s FIFA World Cup victory. The image is AI-generated, as indicated by AI detection tools.Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
During our investigation, we found social media posts dated 14 December 2025 featuring the same video, shared by Congress leaders Deepender Singh Hooda and Harish Rawat. Both posts criticised the Election Commission over allegations of vote theft. This establishes that the video has been circulating online since at least 14 December 2025 and predates the INDIA bloc’s ‘Chalo Dilli’ march held on 01 November 2026.
Notably, the Congress had organised (here, here) a ‘Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod’ rally at Delhi’s Ramlila Maidan on 14 December 2025, protesting alleged vote theft and demanding accountability from the Election Commission.
Video 2
During our investigation, we found that Factly had previously debunked the same video when it went viral. Our earlier investigation established that the video shows celebrations in Buenos Aires, Argentina, on 20 December 2022, when millions of people gathered to welcome the FIFA World Cup-winning Argentine national football team.
Image 1
Upon examining the viral image, we noticed distorted facial features of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi on the posters. Suspecting that the image might have been AI-generated, we analysed it using AI detection tools such as SynthID and AI or Not. Both tools indicated that the viral image was AI-generated.
To sum up, these visuals do not show the INDIA bloc rally held at Ramlila Maidan on 01 November 2026.

Sebastien Pocognoli faces a major test early in his tenure as he prepares on Tuesday to name his second Scotland squad after back-to-back home Nations League defeats.
The Belgian goes into the final two matches of League B1 knowing that his side must take at least four points at home to bottom-placed North Macedonia and away to the table-topping Swiss to have a chance of even finishing second.
Even then, they also need Slovenia to slip up against both those sides if the Scots are to make the promotion play-offs.
Lose the first game at Hampden and the nightmare scenario of finishing bottom - and suffering relegation to League C - is also still a possibility.
So who are the men vying for a place in Pocognoli's rescue squad shaping up?

Who makes way for McTominay?
Scott McTominay was the major miss from the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco head coach's first selection and will surely be the first name on his list this time.
The 29-year-old midfielder immediately scored two doubles for Napoli following his comeback from minor heart surgery.
Billy Gilmour has been less fortunate, having been left unused on the bench while his countryman made his hero's return before coming on as a substitute in their win over Monza and weekend defeat by Juventus.
However, he has become an automatic choice under Pocognoli along with Lewis Ferguson, who is also a mainstay of a Bologna side that has won three successive games in Serie A, while Ryan Christie has started four of Bournemouth's impressive six straight victories without conceding.
Aston Villa's one defeat in nine came against Bournemouth when John McGinn came off the bench instead of starting.
So who might be in danger of missing out in midfield?
A surprise addition to the last squad, uncapped Kristi Montgomery remains a regular starter with Championship rivals Blackburn Rovers.
Lennon Miller made a rare start on Saturday but could not prevent a 5-2 home defeat by Roma that leaves Udinese without a win in eight.
However, Kenny McLean has only played 45 minutes as a substitute for Norwich City since pulling out of the last Scotland squad through injury and the 34-year-old missed Saturday's win over Watford and is a doubt to face Derby County on Tuesday.
Who will replace McKenna?
One likely absentee is Scott McKenna, who has missed Dinamo Zagreb's past two games and has been ruled out for the next two weeks by the Croatian champions.
Fellow centre-back Luis Binks played 64 minutes of Brondby's win over Aarhus after missing their previous two games.
However, Al-Ettifaq's Jack Hendry, Swansea City's Stephen Welsh and Stoke City's Luke Graham are all regular starters, with the latter helping his Championship side to three unbeaten games without conceding as he pushes for a first Scotland start.
Kieran Tierney dropped out the last squad through injury but is back playing regularly with Celtic, albeit in a defence looking increasingly vulnerable.
Left-back rival Andy Robertson has started Tottenham Hotspur's three straight wins, albeit the 32-year-old national captain does not finish too many games these days.
Josh Doig's chances of displacing either and adding to his two caps was not helped by a 6-2 thrashing for Sassuolo at home to Lazio on his return to the starting line-up.
Right-back continues to be the main worry for Pocognoli, with Celtic's Colby Donovan the one regular starter and with Aaron Hickey and Nathan Patterson used mainly as substitutes for Brentford and Torino, respectively.
Will Falkirk form be Bain of Gunn?
Scott Bain's heroics in Falkirk's first win over Scottish champions Celtic in 19 years was timely, although the 34-year-old was almost always likely to retain his place in the squad given Scotland's lack of back-up in goal.
However, it is even more opportune given established number one Angus Gunn was left on the bench for San Jose Earthquakes's win over Real Salt Lake on Saturday after some criticism of recent performances.
Adams return as Oli burns it up?
While Rangers' Lawrence Shankland is still missing through injury, fit again Che Adams should be in line for a recall after two goals in four games for Torino.
Oli McBurnie has staked his claim for another starting place after scoring his first two goals of the season in Hull City's latest two Premier League games, albeit they are now eight games without a win.
Kieron Bowie had pushed his case to be Scotland's main striker with the opening goal in last month's win over North Macedonia but the 24-year-old has not found the net in five games since and was on the bench for Sassuolo's weekend thrashing.
Robbie Ure has scored his first two Sevilla goals since the last international break, although he was back on the bench for Sunday's defeat by Getafe, while James Wilson has gone eight games without a goal for Heart of Midlothian.
Should Pocognoli's formation allow for wingers, although unused on the bench at the weekend, Ben Gannon-Doak started for Bournemouth in fine wins over Villa and AC Milan, Josh McPake continues to impress with Hearts, while Findlay Curtis makes some impactful cameos for Rangers.
Decisions, decisions but the starting line-up is probably more difficult than a squad that almost picks itself.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Quick Answer
Apple’s new iPad mini features IP67 water resistance, an Acoustic Display with no grilles, a lighter body, and an 8.5-inch 60Hz OLED display with nano-texture options. Powered by the A20 Pro chip, it adds a landscape front camera, fast charging, and Pencil support. However, it lacks ProMotion, starts at $699/Rs 82,990, and comes in only two colors.
Apple has taken the wraps off a new iPad. This one is an iPad mini, and it comes with perhaps the most radical overhaul of Apple’s smaller tablet. The new iPad mini – which is being referred to as the iPad mini (A20 Pro) – comes with a truckload of new features, some of which have never been seen on any other iPad (including the Pros). Of course, it is also more expensive than ever before (such are the expensive memory times we live in), but is it worth sinking bucks in? Here are twelve things we think you should know about Apple’s new smaller iPad:
Table of Contents
First iPad with IP67 rating
Dust and water resistance have finally – FINALLY – come to the iPad. The new iPad mini comes with IP67 dust and water resistance, making this the first Apple tablet that can survive a spell in the rain or even a fall in the water. The iPad just got pool and beach friendly!
First iPad with an “Acoustic Display”: Look ma, no speaker grilles!
The new iPad mini is also the first to come with no speaker grilles at all. Apple says that its latest tablet has an Acoustic Display, which has specially designed woofers that are “paired through the display” for better bass and volume. There are also tweeters between the glass and aluminum enclosure for better highs. That’s some very impressive audio tech right there. What’s more, it comes with a sealed enclosure that enables the iPad mini to be dust- and water-resistant. Not many openings on this one!
The biggest display on an iPad mini – and the first OLED display on a non-Pro iPad
The new iPad mini comes with an 8.5-inch display, which is the largest seen on an iPad mini. The earlier generations of the tablet had 7.9-inch displays, while more recent ones had larger, 8.3-inch displays. It also comes with a higher resolution, 2316 x 1512, as compared to 2266 x 1488 of the previous iPad mini, although both have the same pixel density (326 ppi). The new iPad mini is also the first non-Pro iPad to sport an OLED display. In the past, the iPad Pros had what Apple calls a Tandem OLED display. That said, the display on the iPad mini is different from those on the Pros – the iPad Pros have an Ultra Retina XDR display, while the new iPad mini has what Apple has termed a Super Retina XDR display.
First iPad mini with TWO display options (and a “polishing cloth” in the box too!)
The new iPad mini actually gives consumers two display options. While the base 128 GB storage option has a “regular” display, the 256 GB and 512 GB variants also come with a “nano texture display glass” option, similar to those seen on the iPad Pro models. What’s more, those who go with this option will also get a “polishing cloth”. Such perks.
Not ProMoted to ProMotion: Bigger, brighter display…but STILL with a 60 Hz refresh rate
The iPad mini comes with a larger and brighter (600 nits) display than on the previous iPad mini (500 nits) and even the iPad Air M4 (500 nits), but, surprisingly, comes with the same 60 Hz refresh rate display that is seen in most non-Pro iPads. The new iPad mini does not come with a ProMotion display, which enables higher and lower refresh rates. No ProMotion for the new tablet in this regard. Pun intended.
Bigger display, but still smaller and lighter than the previous iPad mini (only slightly heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max)
Rather remarkably, even though the new iPad mini comes with a larger display than the previous iPad mini, it is actually more compact and even lighter as compared to its predecessor. It is slightly shorter (195.3 mm vs 195.4 mm), less wide (132.6 mm vs 134.8 mm) and slimmer (5.4 mm vs 6.3 mm) as compared to the previous iPad mini. Making this possible are incredibly thin bezels – 24 percent thinner than on its predecessor. At 255 grams, the new iPad mini is also the lightest iPad ever (the previous mini was 293 grams) and is only a feather heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (249 grams) and even the iPhone Duo (255 grams). This is the easiest iPad to carry, by a mile, for miles (pun intended).
Driven by the latest iPhone chip, with differences across storage models
The iPad mini runs on the same processor that we have seen on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Duo – the A20 Pro. Interestingly, however, there are subtle differences between the processors on different storage variants. The 128 GB and 256 GB storage variants come with a chip with a 5-core CPU and 3 efficiency cores, while the 512 GB variant has a 6-core CPU and 4 efficiency cores. The processor on the 128 GB and 256 GB variants also has a 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512 GB one has a dual 16-core Neural Engine. We are not too sure what difference those make in everyday performance, but if you are a spec and high-performance chaser, then the 512 GB iPad mini might be the one for you.
A better front camera, and now on the landscape side
The new iPad mini has a similar rear camera to that of the previous one – a 12-megapixel camera with f/1.8 aperture – but the front-facing camera, or “selfie and video call” camera, is very different. While it has the same megapixel count (12) as its predecessor, it has a larger aperture (f/2.0 as compared to f/2.4) and, most interestingly of all, is now on the landscape edge rather than the portrait one. Apple has almost always shown the iPad mini being used in portrait mode (apart from when gaming), so this is a significant change.
Compatible with both Apple Pencils
The new iPad mini plays fine with both Apple Pencils, the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro, making this pretty much a proper sketching, scribbling tab.
No smart connector, so don’t expect Apple keyboard covers
The new iPad mini has no smart connectors (those tiny metallic dots) on its side or back, so in spite of the bigger display and powerful specs, we do not expect to see keyboard covers from Apple for this one.
Fast charging comes to a non-Pro iPad (but the bundled adapter is a slow one)
While its battery life remains at the classic “up to 10 hours of surfing the web on Wi-Fi or watching video”– that is an iPad standard, the new iPad mini comes with support for fast charging. This enables it to get charged up to 50 percent in about half an hour with a 35W or higher adapter. Mind you, you will need to shell out extra bucks for that adapter, as the one that comes in the box is a 20W USB-C Power Adapter.
Also Read: Apple iPad mini (A20 Pro) vs Apple iPad mini (A17 Pro)
Kinda pricey: Priced close to the iPad Air 11 (M4)
The new iPad mini is the most expensive iPad mini ever released by Apple. The iPad mini (A17 Pro) started at USD 499 (Rs 49,900 in India), but the new iPad mini starts at a much higher USD 699 (Rs 82,900 in India). That places it incredibly close to the iPad Air (M4), which comes with a bigger display, a desktop-level processor, and an official price tag of USD 749 ( Rs 89,900 in India), but which is often available at lower prices.
And one more thing…ONLY TWO COLORS
The iPad Mini has generally had a wide range of color options. The 2021 iPad mini and the iPad mini (A17 Pro) had four color options each – space grey, blue and starlight, as well as blue for the A17 Pro and pink for the 2021 edition. The new iPad mini has, however, trimmed the product color palette – it is available in just two shades: midnight and starlight. Hopefully more colors will come along soon!

‘She is upstairs’: Panchkula school boy who attacked 6-year-old led her father to bloodied classroom
The incident took place between 3 pm and 4 pm at the school in Sector 20 on October 28.
The eight-year-old boy who allegedly attacked a six-year-old girl inside a government school in Haryana’s Panchkula later led her father to the classroom where she lay unconscious in a pool of blood.
The boy told the father, “Uncle, I will take you upstairs. She is there,” the girl’s uncle told The Indian Express.
The incident took place between 3 pm and 4 pm at the school in Sector 20 on October 28. A video purportedly showing the assault surfaced on social media on Saturday and was widely circulated.
Deep Dive
The footage appears to show the boy pulling the girl by her hair and repeatedly banging her head against a desk. After she falls to the ground, he allegedly kicks her and hits her with an object that appears to be a brick.
However, Hindustan Times could not independently verify the authenticity of the video.
Also Read: Panchkula school assault case: Two suspended, child rights panel seeks report
Girl lured into empty classroom
The girl’s uncle said that the boy lured her into another classroom by telling her that her father was coming to the school.
“She went upstairs to her classroom at around 3.15 pm. The assault probably took place between 4.15 pm and 4.30 pm. The boy told her, ‘Tere papa aa rahe hain school’ (your father is coming to school), and took her to another classroom," he said.
The boy allegedly hit the girl seven to eight times with a brick, banged her head against a bench and struck her with an aluminium dustbin, the uncle alleged. He then left the room but returned around half an hour later and assaulted her again.
The uncle said the girl went missing when the auto-rickshaw driver arrived to pick her up after school. Unable to find her, the driver immediately informed her father, who rushed to the school.
The boy then approached the father and offered to take him to the classroom where the girl was lying, the uncle said.
School management booked
The Education Department of Haryana has suspended two Junior Basic Training (JBT) teachers with immediate effect in connection with the case, news agency PTI reported.
An FIR has been registered against the school management for alleged negligence. Preliminary police findings have pointed to lapses in security arrangements and the supervision of students.
