5 reasons why the Democrats might not take control of Congress in U.S. midterms
Even with Donald Trump's deep unpopularity, Democrats face steep climb to flip both House and Senate
Political strategists of both main parties in the U.S. believe it’s almost certain the Democrats will take control of the House of Representatives from the Republicans in Tuesday's midterm elections.
The likelihood of the Democratic Party flipping the Senate, however, is another story.
In the House, non-partisan election-forecast websites such as Cook Political Report rate the Republicans as vulnerable in as many as 30 GOP-held seats. The Democrats need a net gain of merely three to get a majority.
Also, consider that the party of the sitting president has suffered a net loss of House seats in all but two midterm elections since the late 1930s, and that no U.S. president has gone into a midterm with a lower approval rating than what Donald Trump has right now.
But when it comes to the Senate, there are doubts the Democrats have a clear path to flipping the four states they need to reach the majority threshold of 51.
Here are five reasons why the Democrats may not wind up with control of both houses of Congress for the remainder of Trump‘s time in office.
1. The 2026 Senate map is tough for Democrats
Flipping the Senate this year was always going to be a tough haul for the Democrats, simply because of their limited opportunities to gain seats in this particular midterm.
Only one-third of Senate seats are up for grabs each election, because senators are elected to six-year terms.
Nearly all of the Republican-held seats the Democrats are seeking to flip are in states that Trump carried by at least 11 percentage points in 2024. (The only exceptions within easier reach are Maine and North Carolina.)
That means to get a majority, the Democrats must gain at least two states from a list that includes Ohio, Iowa, Texas, Alaska and Kansas.
That will require a giant swing toward the Democrats in states that have long been ruby red.
2. The polls could be off
There's been a well documented history of polling in the Trump era failing to measure the full extent of support for Republicans. On the final weekend before the 2024 presidential election, a poll in Iowa (by a pollster with a sterling reputation) showed Kamala Harris up by three points. Trump won the state by 13.
Polling firms have, over the years, adjusted their methods to try to compensate for the tendency of Democrats to be more likely than Republicans to answer polls.
They weight responses so samples better reflect the full demographics of who actually shows up at the polls, factoring in education, income and ethnicity. They ask respondents who they voted for in the last election to check the sample isn’t torqued toward one party or the other.
Polling is a science, but an inexact one, and it’s important to remember its limitations. One key limitation is that when two candidates are polling within the margin of error — say, a lead of just two percentage points — you really can’t say who’s winning.
Recent polls in the Senate races in Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Kansas have all shown results within the margin of error.
3. So much depends on turnout
Voter turnout in midterm election years has historically lagged behind turnout in presidential election years. The key midterm challenge for each party, whether on the offensive or defensive, is getting their supporters simply to show up.
While polling broadly suggests registered Democrats are more enthusiastic about punishing Trump than the Republican base is defending him, Democratic candidates still need help from independent voters to win in toss-up races.
It's worth noting that the highest turnout for a midterm election since the First World War came in 2018, during Trump's first term.
One factor that could dampen a blue wave is whether the Democratic Party and its candidates made strong enough arguments for why Americans should vote for them, rather than simply relying on their desire to vote against the Republicans.
4. GOP money has flooded the airwaves
Extraordinary amounts of money have gone into campaign advertising this midterm cycle.
In just the competitive Senate races, Republicans and their affiliated political action committees (PACs) have spent some $1.2 billion US, outpacing Democrats by $237 million US, according to a Bloomberg analysis of ad-buying data from the consulting firm AdImpact.
Elon Musk alone has spent the staggering sum of nearly half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates in the midterms ($475 million US, reports the New York Times, $446 million US, according to the Guardian.)
The race to be come the next U.S. senator for Texas — between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico — is poised to become the most expensive non-presidential campaign in history, with spending since the primaries already surpassing $500 million US, according to data compiled by AdImpact.
5. Democrat candidates could underperform
Don’t discount the possibility the Democrats could fall short in a state or two because their particular candidate fails to capture the full extent of the swing away from the Republicans elsewhere in the country.
In Maine, the Democrats had to scramble in July to nominate a candidate to replace Graham Platner, the oysterman who’d attracted national attention for his anti-establishment campaign only to be forced to resign amid allegations he’d sexually assaulted a former partner.
His replacement, Troy Jackson, is a logger who’s been a politician for 20 years and, while equally plain-spoken, lacks much of Platner's charisma.
Jackson is also battling a formidable opponent in Susan Collins, who has held this Senate seat for 30 years despite Maine’s history of voting Democrat for president.
Michigan is another state where the Democrat candidate is potentially at risk. Abdul El-Sayed, one of the most left-leaning Senate candidates the party is fielding this cycle, won the bitter nomination battle this summer to replace the retiring Gary Peters.
Trump has leaned into Islamophobic rhetoric to attack El-Sayed, repeatedly calling him a "jihadist" who's "on the side of the terrorists." The results on Tuesday will give some indication whether those attacks resonated with Michigan voters or repelled them.

Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack
- Published
Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.
The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles – an unfamiliar sight for most residents.
New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".
Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl – were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.
The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".
"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."
But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.
ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.
Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.
The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.
Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.
But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.
The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.
"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.
One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.
His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

Snap settles social media addiction lawsuit to avoid trial
CEO Evan Spiegel was due to testify in the upcoming trial.
Snap CEO Evan Spiegel won't have to testify in a high-profile trial over social media addiction after all. Snap has settled a lawsuit brought by two teens who alleged their use of the app led to self harm and other mental health issues.
Jury selection began last week and the trial was due to start this month. The teens previously settled claims against Meta, YouTube and TikTok. A lawyer for the teens, identified in court documents as K.D.B. and S.J., confirmed a settlement has been reached, though terms of the agreement were not disclosed.
"We are proud to have achieved justice for our bellwether clients so far, including K.D.B. and S.J. Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal," Emily Jeffcott, an attorney for K.D.B said in a statement.
The case was one of several high-profile lawsuits against social platforms over alleged social media addiction and other mental health harms. Earlier this year, Meta, YouTube, Snap and TikTok faced another lawsuit brought by a 20-year-old woman who said the apps had harmed her as a child. Snap and TikTok settled before the trial. The jury in the case ultimately ruled against Meta and YouTube and ordered them to pay $6 million in damages.
After Meta settled in the latest case last week, Snap was the only remaining defendant. Spiegel was expected to testify if the case went to trial, which would have been the first time the Snapchat creator appeared in court during a social media addiction trial. "The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner," the company said in a statement. Snap is "committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community," a spokesperson said.
Both Meta and Snap are still facing numerous other lawsuits over social media addiction and other alleged safety issues.

The US has charged five individuals as part of the first broad federal crackdown on “ghost students”—fraudsters who steal the identities of hundreds of Americans to pose as fake college students and steal student loans.
In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from “a network associated with Kenyan nationals” after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that “this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya,” while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun.
“If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build a future—we will find you,” McDonald said. “Whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.”
At a press conference, McDonald was joined by FBI and Department of Education officials to explain how the scheme works.
It starts with bad actors purchasing personally identifiable information (PII) of Americans—most frequently targeting high school graduates who never attended college and went straight into the workforce.
Once they have that sensitive data, they fill out the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) while seeking to enroll in universities and community colleges. If accepted, student aid is distributed first to schools to cover tuition and fees, but any leftover money is deposited into bank accounts controlled by the fraudsters. Dozens of Americans have opened bank accounts to act as money mules for fraudsters, the DOJ said.
To keep money flowing, bad actors use AI to fill out applications, complete coursework, and even make it appear that a student is attending virtual sessions.
“It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class,” McDonald said at the press conference. “Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester.”
Oblivious Americans stuck with bills
So far, the DOE has “identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens,” officials said at the press conference. If all those accounts are ghost students, total losses come close to $130 million, the DOJ said.
For Americans whose data is stolen, there’s little opportunity to discover the scheme until the government comes collecting on loans years later. In the meantime, victims’ credit can be damaged. Once they detect the scheme, they’re stuck defending against demands to repay inflated student loans, which McDonald admitted is messy.
“The Department of Education does a great job to help unravel that mess, but it is a mess that no one should have to endure,” he said.
In connection with the arrests, officials said they “identified more than $32 million in actual loss tied to these specific subjects” and “we believe that actual total is substantially higher,” with “millions more suspected.”
The DOE’s Office of Inspector General first detected the fraud patterns that brought the alleged scheme to light. The FBI then helped identify how many accounts were impacted, tracing money to US and foreign bank accounts and crypto wallets. In one case, a defendant “used multiple bank accounts across several financial institutions to receive over 700 fraudulently obtained federal student aid refund deposits, totaling approximately $1,439,548,” the DOJ said. In another, “one person received more than $1 million in deposits that were linked to more than 300 fraudulent student accounts,” Inside Higher Ed reported.
At the press conference, First Assistant US Attorney Theophani K. Stamos for the Eastern District of Virginia said that data analysis “identified unusual, suspicious patterns of behavior” that the FBI said indicated “coordinated fraud was happening involving FAFSA.” Those patterns gave investigators “a solid basis and a solid lead to open further inquiries that have led to indictments,” Stamos said.
To keep the crackdown going, his office has sent “approximately 50 referrals to 26 FBI field offices across the country” to hunt down stolen taxpayer funds.
“We are just getting started. Working with partners around the world, we are sending a clear message: student aid belongs to real students, the data always leaves a trail, and we will follow it wherever it leads,” Stamos said.
Automated fraud detection isn’t perfect
The DOJ suspects this scam has been running since at least 2021, growing increasingly sophisticated as AI opens new avenues for loan theft.
“These fraudsters are exploiting Americans who have never been to college before, preventing the Department of Education from cross-checking applicants,” the DOJ said. “Many known victims have reported attaining only high school diplomas—and are shocked by their faked attendance at an institution hundreds of miles away.”
At the press conference, Undersecretary of Education Nicholas Kent accused the Biden administration of leaving Americans unprotected.
“When we walked in the door last January, we were extremely troubled to find that the Biden administration had turned off nearly every fraud detection measure,” Kent said.
Trump’s DOE said it introduced online identity verification requirements that Kent claimed would stop ghost students from ever receiving funds. Relying on automated systems to flag behaviors and reject fraudulent FAFSA applications, Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, vice chair of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, insisted that fraud could be easily stopped without allocating staff and resources or overly burdening the US government.
“The computers help us find it, and we keep the money in the agency,” Ferguson said.
The automated system isn’t perfect, however, and advocates have warned that false flags burden schools, meaning students’ access to aid could be delayed as administrators work through the added identity-verification processes.
Glitches have already affected fraud detection and student applications. In August, the DOE confirmed a technical issue from June 29 to July 6 prevented fraud evaluation results from being shared with certain FAFSA forms. After detecting the glitch, the DOE reprocessed those applications.
Real students may be flagged as fakes
Colleges and universities are also considering adding fees to stop the ghost student fraud.
Some advocates have acknowledged that the fraud deprives real students of funds. But they’re concerned that both the fees and online identity verification could become barriers to access to higher education for low-income students.
To verify their identities through the online FAFSA portal, students are expected to have government-issued IDs on hand in “real time.” They hold the IDs up to their cameras, and automated systems review them. A senior DOE official told Insider Higher Ed that the systems are “similar to the ones used by financial services companies like banks” and that he believed they are the same ones used by rental car companies.
Automated systems then assign a risk rating to the student, and anyone flagged as “high risk” is rejected. Once a student is rejected for aid, it’s up to the university to conduct any follow-up to verify if the application was real.
MorraLee Keller, a senior consultant for the National College Attainment Network, told Inside Higher Ed that “a lot of low-economic kids may not have secured, for example, a driver’s license” and may be set back in the application process while trying to obtain alternative IDs. That could also add fees during the application process.
Students may also be subject to automated fraud detection when seeking to make corrections to their FAFSA, which could delay fund distribution if a false rejection is issued.
“We want to make sure that timing doesn’t interrupt the aid getting credited to their account to pay their bills on time so that they could start classes, get refunds to go get their books, and all those kinds of things,” Keller said.
The Trump administration has said that it expects the number of real students flagged as fraudulent to be low. But the president of the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, Melanie Storey, pushed back “a little bit” on that claim during a podcast from the association recently, asking “the department to quantify the volume of in-person verification that will remain,” Inside Higher Ed reported in April. At the time, Aaron Lemon-Strauss, executive director of the FAFSA program, replied, “I’m not going to be able to give you a number yet.”
Storey noted that many people complete the FAFSA form at in-person events, further narrowing potential false positives as the government expands its ghost student crackdown. For any students who “accidentally get caught in the net,” Lemon-Strauss recommended that universities remain vigilant and take action to ensure support goes to Americans who need it most.

Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests over school conditions and the high cost of living.
The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.
As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end the lycée blockades, which have been running since September and have prompted one of the biggest protest movements and social crises of his presidency.
From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demanding more replacement teachers and repairs to buildings barricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.
University students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities across France to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.
Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.
He said measures offered by the government last week to cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.
He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”
Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.
In Montpellier, the Socialist senator Hussein Bourgi accused the government of “misconduct” and “provocation” after video footage showed a 53-year-old school nurse saying something to police near a school barricade before being forced face-down to the ground, handcuffed and taken into police custody. The local prefect, in charge of police operations, defended the arrest, saying the woman had insulted officers and resisted police.
The education ministry said 41 high schools were blocked across France – around 1% of the nationwide total. Students’ unions put the figure at 150.
Nicolas Bonnet, of the headteachers’ union SNPDEN-UNSA, said: “It’s time for us to return to our job: teaching and supporting pupils.” He warned that coursework, final-year exams and university applications were at risk.
He said he understood why high-school students felt the government had not offered enough to fix problems in schools, but urged more dialogue between the government and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said he would meet school students’ unions again next week.

Crypto giant Binance freezes $2.5bn of assets over suspected hack
- Published
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth more than $2.5bn (£1.87bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue.
The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses".
"It does look like a hack on Binance," said Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao, who remains a majority shareholder of the firm.
Zhao added that two other crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, have also frozen around $1.7bn in stolen assets.
Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said the firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.
Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.
Tether did not immediately respond to queries from the BBC.
Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets.
"We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates," it said, adding that users' funds are safe.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
Bitcoin dropped by around 5% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

The Delhi High Court has given the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the Delhi government’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) two weeks to submit a joint inquiry report on the medical qualifications of two doctors accused of mishandling a child during treatment.
Justice Neena Bansal Krishna passed the order on October 30 while hearing a contempt petition filed by the child’s mother, Sapna Jain, on behalf of her minor son.
According to the petition, the child suffered severe brain damage “after being mishandled by two unqualified doctors (misrepresenting as super-specialists) in the Neonatal ICU of Fortis Hospital, Shalimar Bagh”.
The petition claims that the child is now in a permanent vegetative state and suffers from West Syndrome, epilepsy and cerebral palsy. It also states that he continues to experience severe pain and suffering.
In March 2025, the High Court had called for affidavits clarifying whether the qualifications claimed by the two doctors “are qualifications entitling these Respondents (doctors) to undertake specialisation practice in this country.”
In May 2026, the court further directed the NMC Secretary and the DGHS to conduct a joint inquiry into the doctors’ qualifications and submit a report within eight weeks.
However, the fresh contempt petition alleged that the deadline of July 24, 2026, passed without the authorities submitting the report or seeking an extension from the court.
“The matter concerns the qualifications of doctors treating critically ill newborns. The NMC, being the statutory regulator, is duty-bound to ensure transparency and accountability, and its continued failure to place a clear and conclusive report before this Court raises serious questions regarding its fairness and credibility and that of its officers. The DGHS has likewise failed to discharge the joint duty cast upon it by this Court,” the plea said.
The court has posted the case for hearing on December 16.

Chamber of Trade & Industry (CTI) chairman Brijesh Goyal questioned who would compensate traders for the disruption caused by the INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi on Sunday, claims that the trading sector had suffered losses of around ₹10,000-11,000 crore,
“The question now arises: who will compensate for this loss, or who will make up for it—will the organisers do so?” he said.
Goyal said around 20-25 major markets in the vicinity of the rally venue were affected, with approximately 2.5 lakh shops remaining closed out of nearly three lakh shops across these commercial hubs.
According to the CTI chairman, the closures were largely driven by concerns over the expected arrival of a large number of people and vehicles for the rally. Citing information received through traders' WhatsApp groups, he said around 80% of shops in the affected markets remained shut.
The disruption also reportedly affected the movement of customers, suppliers and dealers from towns surrounding Delhi. Goyal claimed that around 3 lakh to 4 lakh people who usually travel to the capital for business did not arrive on Sunday.
He further said nearly 5,000 vehicles, including small tempos, trucks and larger goods carriers, could not operate, disrupting the transportation of goods from industrial areas and transport hubs to markets in Old Delhi and Central Delhi.
“The movement of goods—loading and unloading—was completely disrupted. During the peak Diwali season, these markets with individual turnovers collectively generate business worth approximately ₹10,000 to ₹12,000 crore. Even where shops remained open, sales were virtually non-existent; there were simply no customers,” Goyal said.
The traders' body said the disruption was particularly significant as the markets were in the peak festive trading season, with Dhanteras shopping scheduled four days after the rally.
Separately, traders across Delhi's major commercial hubs had opposed the INDIA bloc's mega rally, warning that a large political gathering in the heart of the capital during the Diwali shopping season could disrupt wholesale markets, affect daily livelihoods.
The Automotive Parts Merchant Association (APMA), based at Kashmere Gate, also raised concerns over the timing and location of the rally. The association said traffic congestion and apprehensions among buyers travelling from outside Delhi could affect wholesale trade across markets within a three-kilometre radius of Old Delhi.
APMA president Vinay Narang said the association was not opposed to democratic protests but objected to holding the gathering at Ramlila Maidan during the festive shopping period.
“We are not aligned with any political party, nor are we against democratic protests. But the timing and the venue are completely wrong,” Narang said.
He pointed out that major commercial centres, including Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Daryaganj, Mori Gate and Kashmere Gate, are located within a three-kilometre radius of the rally venue.
APMA members urged the administration to intervene, warning that disruption to wholesale trade could push thousands of daily-wage workers into financial distress.
The INDIA bloc held the rally at Ramlila Maidan on Sunday to protest alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
The gathering was attended by several Opposition leaders, including Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, former West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav.

Ireland captain Stirling out of Namibia series
- Published
Ireland captain Paul Stirling will miss the final two games of his side's one-day international series in Namibia after fracturing his finger.
The 36-year-old sustained the injury while fielding during his side's loss in the third ODI on Tuesday, a result that leaves his side trailing their hosts 2-1 in the five-match series.
Tim Tector, brother of middle-order batter Harry Tector, has been called up as a replacement.
The younger Tector sibling is uncapped in ODIs, although he has made eight appearances for the side in T20 cricket, averaging 17 in the shorter format.
Battling to save the series, the injury to Stirling is another blow to head coach Gary Wilson.
The Ireland opener was unable to bat in his side's innings following the injury on Tuesday, but had a pair of half-centuries in the first two games in Windhoek, leading the side with scores of 56 and 77.
Ireland won the opener of the series on 22 October but have suffered losses of 31 and 63 runs in the two games since.
The series, which is being used by Ireland as preparation for next year's World Cup qualifiers, resumes on Friday before a concluding fixture on Sunday.

As BYD and Geely hit sales highs, pressure mounts on China’s smaller carmakers
Sales momentum among leading carmakers contrasts with a domestic market downturn that is accelerating industry consolidation, analysts say
Shenzhen-based electric vehicle (EV) giant BYD handed over 490,168 cars to customers at home and abroad last month, up 11 per cent year on year, while Hangzhou-headquartered Geely delivered 310,183 petrol and electric cars worldwide in the same period, up 1 per cent from a year earlier, according to company statements.
“Top players, banking on their new models and advantages in cost and technology, showed their resilience in sales,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “Their sales rises have ratcheted up pressure on weak carmakers that are struggling to survive [in a fiercely competitive] domestic market.”

'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

Capillary Technologies reported a consolidated net profit of ₹21.9 Cr in Q2 FY27, up from ₹28.8 Lakh a year earlier, while operating revenue grew 51.3% YoY.
Revenue growth outpaced the increase in overall expenses, improving pre-tax profitability, while a ₹2 Cr net tax credit further supported the bottom line.
Capillary returned to profit after a ₹9.6 Cr loss in Q1, when a ₹33.4 Cr exceptional charge linked to banking fraud weighed on earnings.
SaaS company Capillary Technologies reported a consolidated net profit of ₹21.9 Cr in the September quarter of FY27, up over 75X from ₹28.8 Lakh in the year-ago period. Operating revenue rose 51.3% to ₹271.4 Cr from ₹179.3 Cr. Sequentially, revenue increased 5.7% from ₹256.6 Cr, while the company returned to profit from a ₹9.6 Cr net loss in Q1 FY27.
Capillary provides cloud-based customer engagement and loyalty software, helping businesses manage customer relationships and rewards programmes.
Total expenses increased 41.8% YoY to ₹257.5 Cr during the quarter. Other income increased to ₹6.1 Cr from ₹2.2 Cr a year earlier, taking total income to ₹277.4 Cr.

France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
- Published
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

Can Alcaraz's ex-coach help Shelton challenge his former protege?
- Published
Ben Shelton's name rarely cropped up when Juan Carlos Ferrero - the former world number one who nurtured Carlos Alcaraz to stardom - teased he was going to coach a new player.
But there are obvious reasons why it suits both parties.
For US Open runner-up Shelton, it is an opportunity to tap into a mind that knows how to win major titles and has the inside track on the world's very best.
Ferrero started working with Alcaraz when he was 15, turning his fellow Spaniard from a "piece of spaghetti" into a seven-time Grand Slam champion.
Alcaraz is seen as the most naturally gifted player on the ATP Tour, having dominated the biggest tournaments alongside Jannik Sinner before their respective injuries this season.
Guiding world number four Shelton is a different assignment.
With explosive power and supreme athleticism, the 24-year-old American already possesses weapons which can inflict serious damage.
The left-hander has been a fixture inside the world's top 20 for the past four seasons and reached his first Grand Slam final in New York two months ago.
However, he has often fallen short against the very best.
Shelton earned the best win of his career against an undercooked Alcaraz in September's US Open quarter-finals, but could not beat new world number one Alexander Zverev in the championship match.
His New York run was underpinned by an improved backhand and better defensive skills, but not being able to execute his damaging forehand in crucial moments proved costly against Zverev.
Shelton has also suffered blips against opponents he was expected to beat, including a defeat by Swiss world number 222 Jerome Kym in Basel last week.
It acted as a reminder of the work he still has to do and the consistency he needs to find.
Ferrero, who will work alongside Shelton's father and current coach Bryan, is regarded as an astute thinker and tactician.
He demands focus and clarity from his charges so they can thrive in the most intense battles. It means he will want the fiery Shelton to play smarter - and perhaps calmer in certain moments - to maximise his weapons.
"Juan Carlos is one of the great minds in tennis," Shelton said.
"His experience of winning at the highest level and developing champions will be a huge asset to our team."
Ferrero has point to prove with 'extraordinary talent'
Ferrero enjoyed a stellar playing career and won the 2003 French Open, but he has become known to a younger generation as the coach who guided Alcaraz to the pinnacle of the sport.
He has largely kept away from the ATP Tour since their sudden split in December last year - but that does not mean he has kept a low profile.
The 45-year-old used his new book to further promote his reputation as a 'supercoach', but can he achieve success with someone other than Alcaraz?
Ferrero always had an eye on coming back in 2027 and held exploratory conversations with a mixture of top-20 stars and younger talents.
Some talks were more serious than others but he did not discuss terms with anyone other than Shelton, who put Ferrero top of the list when considering bringing in another coach.
The plan is for Ferrero to cover 10-12 tournaments next season, including the four Grand Slams.
The pair will begin formally working together during an off-season training block in the United States, although Ferrero will watch Shelton on site at next week's ATP Finals in Turin.
"Ben has extraordinary talent, power and character," Ferrero said.
"I'm looking forward to contributing my experience and working together with everyone to help Ben achieve his ambitions."
Will the partnership lead to success?
How Ferrero gels with Shelton's dad - a former professional player who won two ATP titles - will be key.
Ferrero previously had a six-month spell coaching Zverev, which ended after a third-round Australian Open exit in 2018.
Ferrero was hired by Zverev as an outside voice coming into a father-son coaching dynamic, but the German fired him after claiming Ferrero was "disrespectful" to his team.
Ferrero later said Zverev lacked the professionalism he expected from a top player.
Shelton, known for having a strong work ethic and insatiable will-to-win, is likely to be receptive to Ferrero's demands - as long as they do not neutralise his raw weapons.
But Rick Macci, the veteran American coach who guided the Williams sisters as teenagers, believes Ferrero will find it harder to improve Shelton's technical deficiencies.
"Shelton can win a few Slams if things break his way," Macci said.
"His backhand groundstroke and return can be technically unpredictable - at the top of the mountain the margins are razor thin.
"Ferrero can help a lot in many areas because [Shelton's] backbone is better than his backhand, but getting to number one is a different landscape to mow."

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.

Trump plans closing election pitch at the Reflecting Pool after troubled revamp

President Donald Trump said Sunday that he plans to deliver a closing midterm election message at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, putting his delayed, costly, and troubled restoration project back into the spotlight as Election Day approaches.
Speaking to reporters after deplaning from Air Force One before a rally in Iowa, Trump said that holding an event at the landmark would "show how beautiful it is."
"We might hold it tomorrow or something," Trump added without offering specific details. In a social media message posted prior to landing, Trump said his Sunday evening rally in Kansas—following his stop in Iowa— "Will be my last stop."
This statement suggests that rather than traveling on Monday to key swing states to energize his "Make America Great Again" base as Republicans attempt to preserve their congressional majorities, Trump could instead choose an event at a Washington renovation site that has proved both contentious and embarrassing.
The decision would represent a shift from Trump's month-long strategy of hosting more than 25 rallies in primarily conservative areas. Republicans are hoping to overcome his low approval ratings alongside polling indicating that the Iran war, elevated energy costs, and rising living expenses could result in significant gains for Democrats on election night.
Throughout his rallies, Trump has frequently spoken about his second-term goal of reshaping the White House and the surrounding nation's capital to mirror his personal aesthetic. His plans have included adding gold touches to the Oval Office, tearing down the East Wing to build a large ballroom, transforming the Rose Garden into a patio reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate, and constructing a large helipad on the South Lawn.
Additionally, he closed the Kennedy Center after failing to append his name to the venue, outlined plans for a massive arch on the city's outskirts, and pushed to renovate a century-old municipal golf course.
Trump has dismissed criticism from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats who argue he spends excessive time on construction projects, maintaining that renovations help him relax and that he executes them quickly without needing lengthy planning periods.
Trump initially asserted that the Reflecting Pool repair would be fast and inexpensive. The project began in April when Trump expressed a desire to change the pool's color, claiming he would hire familiar contractors to complete the work in a matter of days for around $1.5 million before Independence Day.
However, the repairs were completed nearly three months late, with the overall budget expanding to more than ten times Trump's initial estimate—assuming no further work is required in the future.
Trump had declared the project finished in June. Yet shortly after the redesign was unveiled, the pool became filled with algae blooms, and its "American-flag blue" liner started peeling off in sections. The pool was promptly drained again for further repairs in mid-July.
While Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals for the setbacks, the office of the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia—headed by former Fox News host and long-time Trump ally Jeanine Pirro—stated the issues were caused by shoddy workmanship.
In his comments on Sunday, Trump stood by his assertion that the Reflecting Pool "was vandalized badly," adding that security cameras have since been installed to prevent further damage.
The situation was further complicated when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the site, only to drop the case abruptly this summer after determining he was not responsible.
A judge later permanently dismissed the charges.
The outcome led Trump to complain that Pirro "choked," stating he was "disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella"—though he stopped short of removing her from office.

Some of the health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force (2016-2025) than in the previous decade (2006-2015) as climate action fails to keep pace, according to the 10th Lancet Countdown Report on Health and Climate Change.
The report, which was released on Wednesday, said the annual average heat-related deaths rose by nearly 36% globally after the Paris Agreement was introduced.
"In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths with more than 70 per cent of that toll attributable to human-caused climate change," it said.
The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action.
The report highlights that cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, too insufficient, and too inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
"Rising overall energy demand and slow system change means fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024," it said.
The report added that despite gains in some countries, fossil-fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.8 million people a year worldwide.
Moreover, adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed.
According to the report, the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates.
However, only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.
"This substantial financing gap is reflected in countries' ability to translate adaptation priorities into action, with finance and human resourcing identified as the top barriers to implementation of Health National Adaptation Plans," said the report.

The White House has spent several months preparing for a potential Democratic takeover of Congress, formulating plans to advance core elements of President Donald Trump's agenda through executive action while bracing for congressional investigations, according to an administration official and two individuals familiar with the strategy.
Senior aides, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working alongside the White House Counsel's Office since April. Their objective has been to identify executive measures on immigration, tariffs, housing costs, and federal spending that Trump can pursue without legislative approval, three sources told Reuters.
White House counsel Will Scharf and his staff are also assessing "what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court," the White House official noted.
These preparations highlight a key paradox of Tuesday's midterm elections: while capturing Congress would empower Democrats to open inquiries, block legislation, and restrict spending, Trump would maintain sweeping executive authority over trade, foreign policy, and the federal bureaucracy—powers he has drawn on extensively during his second term.
If Republicans lose their majorities, Trump said he expects to issue vetoes for "a month or two" before negotiating agreements with opposition leaders.
"I guess I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump told the New York Post's Pod Force One podcast in an interview excerpt released Sunday. "And then at some point, we'll probably make deals."
Democrats require a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and the US Senate to overturn narrow Republican majorities of 218-214 and 53-47, respectively. Public polling suggests Democrats are favored to capture the House, while the Senate contest remains exceptionally close.
Throughout the past month, Trump has held rallies nationwide to help maintain Republican control of Congress, even as his internal team quietly plans for a starkly different legislative landscape in 2027.
The White House rejected suggestions of potential Republican losses, criticizing media reporting on the subject.
"This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.
Among the executive actions under review are new tariffs on imports of wind turbines and critical minerals, stricter rules on visas for temporary foreign workers and international students, and measures intended to lower construction and housing costs, according to the White House official.
Federal agencies have already submitted policy proposals and legal reviews regarding steps the administration could take unilaterally, one source said.
Vought, who leads the US Office of Management and Budget, is reviewing which initiatives can move forward using funds previously appropriated by Congress, two sources added. He also aims to revise federal grant rules to grant political appointees greater authority over which government programs receive funding, potentially increasing White House oversight of spending without congressional consent.
Trump has been briefed on these preparations and has participated in discussions regarding the strategy, the White House official confirmed.
When asked about Trump's willingness to govern primarily through executive power under a Democratic-controlled Congress, one source noted he would be "very comfortable."
Governing without Congress
Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has routinely tested the boundaries of presidential authority, utilizing executive orders to levy broad tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, reduce the federal workforce, and advance foreign policy goals—including military operations against Iran—without new legislation or congressional consent.
A notable exception was a major package of tax and spending cuts passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.
"President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power," said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. "I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities."
Trump has repeatedly declared national emergencies to broaden his ability to act independently. While Congress can vote to terminate those emergency declarations, Trump could veto any such resolution, requiring a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override him.
However, a Democratic-controlled Congress would still present substantial challenges. A Democratic majority in the Senate would allow the party to block Trump's judicial and executive nominees, including potential Supreme Court appointments.
"I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president's appointments," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.
Democrats could also decline to advance Trump-backed bills. However, Trump could veto any Democratic legislation, and the party is unlikely to secure enough votes in the House to override a presidential veto.
Furthermore, courts could strike down executive actions that exceed statutory authority. To prepare, the White House plans to request formal legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine the limits of Trump's unilateral authority and build defenses against potential legal challenges, one source noted.
Democratic investigations
One major challenge that executive power cannot prevent is congressional oversight.
Previous reports from Reuters noted that senior House Democrats and committee staffers have discussed conducting hearings, issuing subpoenas, and requesting documents to investigate whether Trump has used presidential authority for personal benefit, or to favor allies and donors.
White House aides have been preparing for potential oversight for months, according to all three sources.
White House attorneys have been advising political appointees and agency heads on responding to congressional document requests, subpoenas, and inquiries, instructing officials to exercise caution regarding written records.
Additionally, administration lawyers have sought a Justice Department opinion that could enable Trump to invoke executive privilege to protect communications with private advisers from legislative oversight, one source said.

Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.
While polls suggest that a number of races in deep-red Texas are looking dizzyingly close, Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk has given at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Texas attorney general Ken Paxton’s bid for Senate, and last week Musk explicitly endorsed him in a post on X. “The fate of Texas and America is at stake,” Musk wrote. “Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today.”
Newly released state campaign filings also show that Musk also donated $5,000,000 to Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor.
Abbott’s relationship with Musk has been the subject of public interest for years. State representative Gina Hinojosa, who is running against Abbott, recently sued to view, in full, 1,400 pages of the governor’s correspondences with Musk. Abbott has been trying to block their release for some time; his office has described the communications as too “intimate and embarrassing” to be made public. This week, a judge ruled that Abbott had illegally “obstructed and continues to obstruct” Hinojosa’s right to inspect the documents in her capacity as a state lawmaker and ordered their release to her. Abbott has since appealed; a hearing is scheduled for November 2, one day before the election.
State representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton for Senate, has campaigned on his opponents’ checkered past. As attorney general, Paxton has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges (which he settled without a plea), was accused by whistleblowers of using his office to benefit the financial interests of a political donor, and was impeached (though later acquitted).
And at a campaign event on Monday in El Paso, Talarico raised questions about Paxton and Musk’s relationship. “Ken Paxton has the ultimate megadonor,” Talarico said. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat.”
But Musk’s business dealings in Texas politics didn’t start with the midterms. For years, he has enjoyed lucrative state contacts, tax breaks, and allyship from Texas leaders. In 2021, Musk moved Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Palo Alto, California, to Austin, and SpaceX’s headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas, in 2024.
Musk’s initial relocation to Texas coincided with a shift in operations inside the Texas Attorney General’s office. In the past, lawyers would prepare notices of investigation (administrative subpoenas known as CIDs) based on public complaints or evidence collected, then send them up the chain for approval.
Sources tell WIRED that from about 2021 onward, lawyers were increasingly instructed by Texas’ executive branch—which included Paxton and Abbott—who and what they were going to investigate, despite internal efforts to steer resources toward more “legitimate” issues. For example, in 2022, eyebrows were raised internally when, the same day Musk sent a letter to Twitter threatening to abandon a $44 billion acquisition agreement over Twitter’s alleged misrepresentation of the number of bots on the platform, Paxton’s office issued a statement asserting that his office would be launching its own investigation against Twitter.
A year later, Paxton once again appeared to use his office to benefit Musk. Musk sued the progressive watchdog Media Matters for defamation after it published an investigation showing that X, under Musk’s ownership, had been placing ads from major brands next to white-nationalist content. Moments after he filed his suit, Paxton’s office announced its own investigation into Media Matters. (Media Matters sued Paxton, asserting that his investigation was brought out of retaliation for its coverage of Musk and X.) In 2024, after Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against the World Federation of Advertisers and major brands, accusing them of a conspiracy to pull revenue from X, Paxton announced his own investigation into the organization, accusing them of a “potential anticompetitive scheme to withhold advertising dollars from certain social media platforms.” (He did not mention X by name.)
And when the Department of Justice’s Public Integrity Section wrote a letter to Musk warning that his America PAC million-dollar sweepstakes program ahead of the presidential election could violate federal election law, Paxton intervened by filing a FOIA request, accusing the government of “intimidation of businessman Elon Musk.”
This summer, Musk’s activities in Texas didn’t slow down: Texas legislators called for an audit after the Texas Broadband Development Office allocated $110 million in grants to Musk’s satellite internet company Starlink; Texas’ Office of the Comptroller recently announced that “Terafab,” Musk’s proposed 100-million-square-foot chip manufacturing facility in Grimes County, was the recipient of a $1.66 billion tax break; and SpaceX has also received around $30 million in state grants.
