Can the Carney government's second budget help put Canada on a path to net zero?
This week's budget is an opportunity to fill out a new federal climate agenda
In the spring of 2024, nine months before he formally entered politics, Mark Carney made a couple of public appearances to discuss the state of the Canadian economy and the possible paths forward.
And on at least one specific area of policy Carney suggested he would do things differently than Justin Trudeau.
"Personally, would I swap one battery plant for a million, million-five heat pumps?" Carney asked himself rhetorically during a Q&A in Toronto, referring to a series of deals the Trudeau government signed to attract battery manufacturing facilities to Canada. "Yeah, I would. Because that would deliver — let's deliver stuff for people."
The government, he said, needed to "make choices that deliver for people today as part of a larger change."
- What we know about Ottawa's $2B rebate plan for heat pumps
- Canada facing carbon tariff threat from European Union
Earlier this month, Carney acted on something like that idea, announcing a $2-billion heat pump rebate program that the federal government projects could benefit approximately 820,000 households.
The Carney government hardly invented the idea of helping Canadians retrofit their homes or install heat pumps — the Trudeau government had its own initiatives, including a specific program for households that used oil to heat their homes. But the new program did add something to a Carney climate agenda that has so far been defined by the Trudeau-era policies he has subtracted.
Nonetheless, the Canadian Climate Institute greeted the announcement as a "modest" boost toward greater electrification.
"It's modest in terms of the level of ambition that this government is showing on other public policy files. It's modest in terms of the amount of money that this government is spending on other public policy files. And it's modest in terms of the time frame and the number of homes impacted," says Rick Smith, president of the climate institute.
"I hesitate to use this overused expression, but it's a good first step."
That more needs to be done is fairly indisputable.
Analysis published by the Canadian Climate Institute last month confirmed that Canada is not on track to meet its greenhouse gas emissions target for 2030. The Trudeau government set a goal of reducing emissions by 40 per cent below 2005 levels, but the institute estimates emissions might only fall by 21 per cent.
That Canada would not achieve its target for 2030 was tacitly acknowledged by the prime minister in June when he said the changes made by his government would mean that "our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government's plan."
The Carney government remains committed to aiming for net-zero emissions by 2050, but the institute's projections still show what it calls a "cavernous gap" between Canada's current track and the mid-century goal.
Could this week's federal budget go some way toward filling that gap?
What will the budget mean for climate policy?
Pre-budget submissions from climate-focused groups — the Green Budget Coalition, New Economy Canada, Clean Energy Canada, Efficiency Canada and the Pembina Institute — offered a number of proposals for boosting clean electricity and supporting home and building retrofits. Such initiatives would seem to be in line with where the Carney government would like to focus.
Carney has said Canadians' affordability concerns are weighing on climate policy and he has put clean electricity at the centre of his agenda moving forward.
"The path to net-zero is electrification," the prime minister said earlier this year, announcing the government's new electricity strategy.
That strategy embraced the goal of doubling Canada's electricity grid by 2050. But getting to that goal without overly burdening ratepayers might require significant amounts of federal funding. Carney himself has spoken of "using the government balance sheet" in a way that "spreads out the cost over a long period."
To that end, the climate institute has proposed a new federal fund to help provincial utilities manage the cost of expansion. Tyler Meredith, a former policy adviser in the Trudeau government, has proposed a new federal transfer of $5.4 billion per year contingent on legislated conditions (similar to the way the federal government provides provinces with funding for health care).
"First and foremost [to doubling electricity and getting Canada on track to net-zero] is helping provinces finance the electricity build out and the interconnections that are needed," says Merran Smith of New Economy Canada, a coalition of business and labour organizations.
"I'm not sure they're going to have exactly what the answer is [in the budget], but I'll be looking for progress on identifying how the federal government thinks it can work collaboratively with [provincial utilities]."
That the government chose to put a picture of electricity transmission lines on the cover of the budget might bode well for such hopes. But obviously the details within the budget will matter more than the nice photo on the front.
The future politics of climate policy
In an op-ed published earlier this fall, Rick Smith argued that Carney could now be measured against his own climate commitments, including the target of net-zero by 2050.
The prime minister has, for instance, set ambitious goals for electric-vehicle adoption. Recent changes to vehicle regulations were met with disappointment from climate groups, but the government also promised a new national charging infrastructure strategy.
The Carney government has also talked about improving industrial carbon-pricing systems and perhaps linking provincial carbon markets — a federal-provincial working group is scheduled to offer recommendations on the latter next summer.
"To the extent that the current government has a climate change plan, it is a series of specific commitments that the prime minister has made that the federal government has yet to put the legs under," Smith says.
The Carney government's approach to climate policy so far is no doubt downstream from the political reality of this particular moment.
When the Environics Institute surveyed Canadians in 2019, 24 per cent said climate change was the most important issue facing the country. When Environics asked again this year, just three per cent said the same, putting climate change far behind concerns about Donald Trump and the cost of living.
The Carney government also faces only limited pressure within the House of Commons to take action to reduce emissions — the Conservatives are primarily focused on opposing existing federal climate policies.
But as Abacus Data laid out earlier this year, the fact that Canadians are prioritizing other issues right now does not mean Canadians aren't worried about climate change. As of this spring, 80 per cent of Canadians said they were at least moderately concerned about climate change.
Abacus also detected a certain amount of uncertainty about the direction and effectiveness of the Carney government's approach to climate policy. And such doubts have at least the potential to become a problem in the future.
"The Carney government's challenge … is to ensure that if climate becomes a bigger issue, Canadians believe it has a credible plan to respond," Abacus Data's researchers wrote.
This week's budget is another opportunity to fill both the political credibility and the practical emissions gaps.

It's ACA open enrollment time. Here are the changes for health insurance shoppers
Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.
Shoppers need to plan accordingly.
Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts started earlier, and some states have been allowing "window shopping" to check premium rates.
A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.
But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.
Have your ID ready
One of the biggest changes for people shopping for their 2027 coverage will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents. The requirements are aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.
The new rules, outlined by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.
For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.
Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed "high-risk" must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as "high-risk" first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.
Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because "someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer."
The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.
The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned "that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing" and may just give up and not get insured.
Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian's help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver's license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.
"Some people may have trouble not because they're not real, but because they don't have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names," said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
She said the changes might "be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles."
There may be fewer brokers
CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.
CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of "significant compliance concerns" in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out "hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers" this year.
Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients' coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.
"Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense," he said. However, in the short term, "I don't know if they care about the chaos it will cause."
That's because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he's unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.
He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.
"They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long," Fine said.
Groups representing agents are very unhappy with the directive. One, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, filed a lawsuit on Oct. 15 against the Trump administration over the moratorium, saying it unfairly targets 19,000 agents who may want to sell ACA plans for next year.
"Just because you're a new agent doesn't mean you are fraudulent," said Ronnell Nolan, president of Health Agents for America, another sales agent group, which on Oct. 21 filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order on the moratorium. "All these agencies who have trained new agents and paid thousands of dollars now have people who won't be able to work."
It all leads to an important piece of advice from Georgetown's Pogue: Consumers should not delay making appointments. "If you rely on an agent or broker, and a lot of people do, their slots might fill up faster because there will be fewer of them to help with enrollment. I would reach out early."
Costs will continue to be an issue
This year, after Congress did not renew the expiring enhanced subsidies, most people getting ACA coverage saw what they had to pay increase. Higher earners lost subsidies entirely. Add in double-digit premium increases, and most people had to pay substantially more for their coverage.
Still, most people who buy ACA coverage for next year will receive a subsidy. It will just be less generous than it was before the enhancements expired at the end of 2025.
The subsidies are pegged to the premium costs of benchmark plans, the name given to the second-lowest-price silver-tier plan in an area.
This helps offset premium increases.
"For most folks, overall affordability will stay about the same," said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst forHealthInsurance.org. "That's not to say it's great, but if you were able to manage the premiums this year, it should be similar to that."
But there are other factors at work, too.
Last year'saverage premium increase of 26% was the largest in years. It was driven in part by insurers' fear that the expiration of subsidies would cause healthier people to drop out of the marketplace. Other drivers often cited for such increases include a rise in overall medical care costs and general inflation, and labor shortages.
For the upcoming year, those dynamics remain a concern, with premiums slated for double-digit increases, although, at 15%, slightly lower than last year.
Subsidies are income-based and cut off for households earning more than four times the federal poverty rate. During this open enrollment season, that amount is $63,840 for a single person, $86,560 for a couple, and $109,280 for a family of three, for example.
"The biggest issue we will face is affordability," said Anne Petry, who, with her father, owns Jaggi Petry Insurance & Investments in Forsyth, Illinois, and helps customers purchase health insurance, including ACA plans. "There definitely will come a breaking point for people."
Agents and other experts say consumers should not allow their plans to automatically renew and should instead go online to compare premiums and coverage, which can change each year even for the same plan. There may be less expensive alternatives, including plans from new insurers, so they suggest looking at not just premiums, but also deductibles and other costs. At the same time, several insurers, including Cigna, have dropped all or part of their ACA coverage areas.
"If you just sit on the sidelines and let the policy auto-renew, you might miss out on what could be a better opportunity," Norris said. She said it is important to check options because the cap on out-of-pocket maximums for ACA plans is also increasing.
That amount, which represents the most a consumer must pay toward deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance before the policy is expected to cover remaining in-network medical costs, was $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family plan this year. In 2027, it will grow by 13% to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for family coverage. Lower caps on out-of-pocket maximums are set for households earning up to 2.5 times the federal poverty level.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed last year, also strips subsidy eligibility from many lawfully present immigrants, including people holding temporary H-1B work visas, refugees, asylees, people with temporary protected status, and those with pending green-card applications.
Three immigrant groups can still get ACA subsidies: green-card holders, who have permanent legal status; certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants; and citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, or Palau.

How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?
Older Apple TVs have received up to a decade of updates, but Apple doesn't promise that.
At $299, the new Apple TV 4K is a lot to pay for a little black box that sits under your TV waiting for you to pick a show to watch. The fourth-generation model will be available November 13 with an A19 chip, an improved Siri Remote and hands-free Siri controls. For that price, how many years can you expect it to last before the next upgrade beckons?
Apple doesn't guarantee how many updates will be available for tvOS or how long its streaming boxes will be supported. But its history is a pretty good indication. Older Apple TVs have received major software updates for eight to 10 years, with security patches continuing beyond that. The hardware may continue to function long after it exits official support, with software and app compatibility concerns the most likely reasons for replacing one.
How long does Apple support an Apple TV for?
While the Apple TV HD was introduced in 2015, and the first Apple TV 4K in 2017, both were updated to tvOS 26 in 2025. Plus, security patches were provided in tvOS 26.6 in July 2026. That's about 10 years of major software updates for the HD and eight for the original 4K, plus some security support.
The impressive streak came to an end in September 2026 with tvOS 27. Apple's new tvOS compatibility list begins with the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021, which means the 2015 and 2017 models can't get the latest operating system. Apple has not yet confirmed whether those older boxes will get additional security patches. It's not a guarantee that the new Apple TV 4K will get 10 years of support. Apple hasn't provided an estimate of how many years of tvOS updates to expect, so the best indication is its track record.
In contrast, Amazon promises at least four years of security updates for Fire TV devices bought new directly from the company, or through the model's published support date (if later). That's not the same as a major OS upgrade, but at least Fire TV customers have a minimum support deadline in writing.
When should you actually replace your Apple TV?
Not being able to update to the latest version of tvOS doesn't make your Apple TV an expensive brick. Netflix still supports the Apple TV HD and first-generation Apple TV 4K, even though neither is eligible for tvOS 27. That could change as developers raise their minimum software requirements, potentially leaving older devices unable to install or update certain apps.
A better way to think about your Apple TV is to consider its performance, not its age. When menus start to become painfully slow, apps begin to crash or a service that you care about stops working, an upgrade makes more sense. Security is also a factor, especially if your Apple TV is used as a smart home hub and no longer gets patched.
Upgrading is a tougher pill to swallow with the newest release costing $299. Apple's Siri AI beta will also be available on the second-generation Apple TV 4K and newer (if the Home admin has an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad), so you don't have to buy the latest box just for Siri AI. The 2026 Apple TV 4K does have some significant improvements over the 2022 version, such as a faster A19 processor and built-in microphones for hands-free control. But it's a significant amount to pay if you're already happy with your current Apple TV.
Then there's the Siri Remote, which frequently finds itself in the sofa. If yours is lost or breaks down, you can use your iPhone as a TV remote instead of replacing the whole setup. Apple's latest Siri Remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K models and even the 2015 Apple TV HD, and a replacement costs $59.

India bagged four gold, two silver and eight bronze to finish top of the medal tally at the prestigious 46th International Tammer Boxing tournament in Tampere, Finland, on Sunday.
Aarti Dhariyal (women’s 54kg), Ankushita Boro (women’s 65kg), Arundhati Choudhary (women’s 70kg) and Pawan Bartwal (men’s 55kg) clinched gold while Hussam Mohammed (men’s 60kg) and Jaismine Lamboria (women’s 57kg) finished with silver medals.
Organised by the Tampere Boxing Association, the tournament has been held annually since 1977 and is an established event on the international boxing calendar.
India fielded a 14-member squad with a focus on providing international exposure to boxers ranked third in the country’s Olympic weight-category bench strength, along with top-ranked pugilists in Olympic weight categories that are not part of the Asian Games programme.
In the women’s 54kg, Aarti convincingly beat Kernachan Stephen of Scotland 5:0 while Commonwealth Games gold medallist Arundhati got the better of Igharo Evelyn Ivi of Ireland 3:2 in the women’s 70kg final.
Later in the day, Ankushita Boro (women’s 65kg) defeated England’s Thompstone Ella 4:1 and Pawan Bartwal (men’s 55 kg) defeated Ireland’s Louis Rooney 5:0.
“The results reflect the progress we are making in building depth across weight categories and give us confidence as we prepare for the LA Olympics qualifying events,” said Boxing Federation of India President Ajay Singh.
Vivek Meena (men’s 65kg), Hitesh (men’s 70kg), Akshay (men’s 80kg), Bobin Chauhan (men’s 90kg), Chetan Choudhary (men’s 90+kg), Tanu (women’s 51kg), Disha Patil (women’s 60kg) and Imroz Khan (women’s 75kg) bagged the bronze medals.

The Indian chef who brought curry to America - then vanished
- Published
One hundred and twenty-five years ago, in 1901, an Indian chef opened what was almost certainly the first Indian restaurant in the US.
Ranji Smile was one of the most colourful and enigmatic figures to shape the American food scene.
In the summer of 1899, Smile sailed from London to New York. We know hardly anything about his origins and early life, not even his real name.
"Ranji" was probably a nod to the Indian cricketing sensation KS Ranjitsinhji, then a star attraction at Test matches in Britain. "Smile" could have been an anglicisation of "Ismail".
Whatever his origins, Smile possessed an uncommon knack for reinvention. Once through the portals of Ellis Island, he appended a new name to his identity, something more in keeping with America's egalitarian promise: Joe.
Joe Ranji Smile arrived in New York to work at Sherry's Restaurant, a glittering new establishment on Fifth Avenue.
In London, he had been a curry cook at the Cecil and Savoy hotels. Here, according to an 1899 profile in Harper's, he was noticed by Sherry's owner, Louis Sherry, who invited him to bring his culinary skills across the Atlantic. Late Victorian London already boasted an Indian dining scene: as early as 1810, Sake Dean Mohamed, a native of Patna, had opened his Hindostanee Coffee House near Portman Square, plying customers with both curry and hookah.
Manhattanite tastebuds lacked much exposure to masala. There was, however, growing curiosity about India and its culture. Swami Vivekananda, the spellbinding orator and exponent of Hindu philosophy, enthralled audiences during his visits to the city in the 1890s. At the same time, more Indian sailors, students and professionals trickled into New York. This was probably why Louis Sherry decided to add a curry cook to his kitchen staff.
At Sherry's Restaurant, Smile joined one of the great culinary institutions of the American Gilded Age. Positioning itself as a rival to Delmonico's, New York's byword for fine dining, Sherry's catered to city plutocrats like the Astors and was famed for over-the-top dining experiences. During one such soiree, patrons marched their horses into a ballroom, saddled up and ate on horseback.
Smile, a skilled showman, thrived in this environment.
Customers soon flocked to taste his preparations of Bombay duck, a glutinous lizardfish that is a delicacy along the western Indian coast, and novel creations like "Lettuce Ceylon".
Cooking and serving became a performance. Dressed in a satin coat and blue silk turban, Smile salaamed in front of customers before enquiring, "Will you have the curry hot or mild, sahib?" Pictures of Sherry's curry chef were soon splashed across newspapers and magazines. One headline said it all: "New York women go wild over him."
As his fame grew, Smile decided in 1901 to leave Sherry's and set up his own establishment, one exclusively devoted to Indian cuisine. For financial backing, he leaned on Roland R Conklin, a prominent financier, external and the inventor of an early version of the motorhome.
Omar Khayyam, Smile's Indian restaurant, opened in late 1901 at 325 Fifth Avenue. This was prime real estate, a block away from the original Waldorf-Astoria Hotel where, 29 years later, the Empire State Building would rise. Smile adorned the restaurant with Indian draperies and hanging lanterns.
As the New York Herald reported, a fleet of Indian waiters in "voluminous turbans" staffed the premises, as did a group of Indian musicians. Now quite the embodiment of the American immigrant success story, Smile eagerly awaited his customers and fans.
Alas, they never materialised. Within a year, Omar Khayyam shuttered. The New York Sun claimed that people had "tired" of Indian fare, dismissing it as a passing fad.
Smile's stardom, which had blazed so brightly in the Big Apple, also began to dim. Unfortunately, his showmanship and flair for theatrics shaded into deceit and criminal activity.
Smile began claiming that he was, after all, not an everyday Joe but rather a prince, the son of the emir of Baluchistan, a fictional title. And, before opening Omar Khayyam, he made a quick visit to Bombay, where he pronounced himself to be a guest at the upcoming coronation of King Edward VII in London and recruited a retinue of staff: valets, a dancing girl, and "mahouts to drive his herds of elephants".
All of this was reported in New York newspapers like the Times because, as a subsequent federal case against him alleged, Smile illegally trafficked this staff into the US to work at his restaurant. Instead of becoming a pioneer outpost of Indian gastronomy, Omar Khayyam nearly got Smile deported.
"Prince" Joe Ranji Smile evaded deportation (many in his retinue were not as lucky) and went on evolving his invented persona, all while wooing and marrying a series of impressionable young American women. He began claiming that Indian food was a secret elixir for female beauty. "The eye will grow lustrous, the complexion will be yet so lovely," Smile promised, displaying his wives as clinching proof.
Meanwhile, he honed his performing skills at Indian cooking demonstrations across the country.
In Washington DC, Smile prepared dishes, including a dubious-sounding dessert called "bungalow", while a juggler and dancing girl entertained him. On his way to Chicago, as one newspaper in remote Idaho reported, he declared himself to be no longer the son of the emir but the brother of an even more fanciful figure, the "great Beglerberg of Baluchistan". If Smile was guilty of being a conman, then his American interlocutors were equally guilty of wide-eyed gullibility.
While Smile's theatrics and good food kept people entertained for a while, the tall tales and outright fabrications soon caught up with him.
Smile retreated from the public gaze, hurt by further brushes with the law which ranged from forcible confinement of one of his dancing girls to refusing to pay a bill at an Italian restaurant in Manhattan. By the 1920s, he apparently abandoned cooking entirely, listing his occupation as a merchant.
The final shred of evidence about Smile dates from 1937, when his fourth or fifth American wife approached the New York Supreme Court and filed for an annulment of her marriage to her now-absconded husband. Ranji Smile's last act of reinvention was to simply disappear.
Despite this inglorious end, Smile and his Indian restaurant did pave the way for the popularisation of Indian cuisine in America. Other immigrants soon tested the waters.
In 1909, Saint Nihal Singh, a peripatetic journalist from Punjab, introduced readers of the Chicago Daily Tribune to recipes for bhajias, puris, halwa, and "Fried Chicken a la Hindoo".
Aware of the unfamiliarity of many Indian ingredients amongst Chicagoans, Singh urged readers to look for them in the city's Chinese grocery stores. On another occasion, which might make contemporary chefs blush, he suggested that hamburger meat was an adequate substitute for preparing gosht pilau (a meat pilaf).
Not long after Ranji Smile was hauled to court for trafficking immigrants, a young man from Ceylon named KY Kira arrived at Ellis Island.
Like Smile, he had a talent for reinvention. Kira joined a troupe of Sinhalese dancers which performed for American circuses like Barnum and Bailey and Ringling Brothers. In 1913, he opened an Indian restaurant in Harlem, eventually called the Ceylon India Inn. Unlike Omar Khayyam, the Ceylon India Inn was a hit.
New York now had a much larger immigrant Indian population and the restaurant attracted expatriate nationalists and revolutionaries. But it also benefited from a burgeoning American interest in Indian culture and food. By the 1920s, Kira's restaurant, now located off Times Square, catered to Broadway and Hollywood stars. The Ceylon India Inn remained in business until the late 1980s, touting itself as the first Indian restaurant in America.
That, of course, was not the case. Ranji Smile might be long forgotten, but 125 years after the brief existence of his Omar Khayyam restaurant, his legacy lives on in the thousands of Indian eateries flourishing across the US.
Dinyar Patel is associate professor of history at SPJIMR in Mumbai

Award-winning actor Patrick Stewart, known for his roles as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the "X-Men" and "Star Trek: The Next Generation" series and films, died on Oct. 28, aged 86.
Posting on Stewart's social media pages the following day, a representative said his death followed "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia (archived).
Numerous public figures have paid their respects to the late actor. Among the tributes is a message fellow thespian Ian McKellen purportedly shared regarding his friend of decades.
Social media users posted screenshots on X and Facebook allegedly showing McKellen's words, in which he appears to describe Stewart as "a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love."
In short, McKellen did post this heartfelt tribute to his late friend Stewart, whom he met "half a century ago." McKellen shared the same text across his social media accounts — X, Facebook and Instagram.
McKellen's 'love' for Stewart
In the tribute, McKellen speaks of his love for Stewart, and recounts details of his friend's Hollywood film career and his time on stage in the U.K.:
McKellen wrote, in part:
Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.
McKellen went on to recount how the pair met 50 years ago as "ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company." He said that when Stewart was cast on the television series "Star Trek," McKellen expressed concern that Stewart was risking his stage career in the United Kingdom. He continued:
Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences, who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes ('X-Men' of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London's West End and on Broadway.
The two actors openly spoke of, and exhibited, their bond. For example, many photographs on reputable image bank Getty Images reveal the pair's years-long friendship.
McKellen also officiated Stewart's marriage to Sunny Ozell, his third and last wife.
In a 2014 conversation hosted by the Screen Actors' Guild, the two touched each other and held hands many times. When McKellen, who is gay, recounted his "coming-out" story (starting around the 1:16:40 mark in the video below), Stewart leaned towards McKellen with evident pride and affection.
Shortly after receiving one of his two Laurence Olivier Awards for playing Claudius in "Hamlet" at London's Novello Theatre, Stewart was knighted for his services to drama in 2010. He is survived by a daughter and a son.
Snopes has examined several rumors about the two actors, including a false claim that McKellen visited Lviv, Ukraine, in 2022.

In September, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fired the two vice chairs of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. This move was both unsurprising and troubling. The task force is a critical advisory body to HHS, reviewing scientific evidence to provide recommendations on whether private health insurers should be required to cover services like cancer screenings at no cost to patients. Congress created the task force as part of the Affordable Care Act and require by law that it be staffed by people with “appropriate expertise,” and “to the extent practicable, not subject to political pressure.”
These firings are the latest chapter in a vast project of eliminating, ignoring, and replacing scientific advisory committees. In 2025, the Trump administration terminated 151 advisory committees at scientific government agencies, including 75 in HHS. It has altered or ignored those that are left. In 2025, Kennedy fired the entire Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which provides public recommendations on vaccines. His replacements are, to varying degrees, sympathetic to his unscientific views, and a majority lack substantial expertise in vaccines and immunology.
At the Food and Drug Administration, agency leadership has largely ignored the standing advisory committees that have historically weighed in on new drug approvals. The FDA convened a record low number of advisory committees in 2025. Instead, it hosted a handful of pseudo-scientific look-alike meetings called “expert panels.” Panelists were handpicked and invited for a single meeting to share their own data, analysis, and conclusions, unmoored from any semblance of collaborative consensus and, too often, scientific rigor.
Expert advisory committees matter for two reasons. The first is obvious: Agency policymakers need high-quality, independent advice to improve the quality, credibility, and legitimacy of agency decision-making. Agencies can’t possibly have the internal expertise to handle every question. This is especially true after staffing cuts to agencies like the EPA, FDA, and CDC.
The other reason is accountability: When a legitimate expert advisory committee makes a recommendation about what an agency should do, it leaves a public record that enables us to hold our government accountable if it declines to follow that advice.
Over the past few decades, courts, Congress, and the public have come to rely on these public recommendations — in congressional oversight, judicial review, and science journalism — to better understand the choices expert agencies make.
This is what happened when the FDA approved the Alzheimer’s drug aducanumab in 2021 despite the near-unanimous vote of the advisory committee (which included one of us) against approval. The committee noted conflicting evidence on the drug’s efficacy and clear safety risks, including brain bleeds, in large numbers of patients.
The negative vote anchored the debate that followed. Critics pointed to it as evidence that the FDA had made a terrible mistake, and payors and hospital systems used it to justify not paying the outlandish price set by the manufacturer. Patients largely avoided drug, with the whole episode culminating in investigations by the media and Congress that demonstrated improper pressure by the manufacturer on the FDA leading to the approval decision.
Advisory committees don’t just provide recommendations to agency policymakers. They enable us to literally hold the agency to account for its decision — to explain why it thinks its advisers were wrong. With no advisory committee to create a record, policymakers can more easily evade hard questions about unscientific or politically motivated decisions.
The dismissals at the USPSTF follow a Supreme Court decision in 2025 stating that the secretary of HHS can remove members at will. The court reasoned that the secretary has the power to appoint them, and “no statute restricts [their] removal.”
But Congress can, and should, change this. It has an array of tools at its disposal. Depending on the circumstance, it could enact for-cause statutory removal protections, staggered terms, formal expertise and qualification requirements, and enforceable conflict of interest rules. It could require that advisers be chosen more transparently and according to stricter criteria. It could even vest the power to choose advisers in another body entirely, akin to how independent redistricting commissions draw state electoral boundaries.
These reforms would likely survive constitutional scrutiny because advisers do not actually make policy. Their advice is nonbinding. The Supreme Court’s recent decision striking down statutory removal protections for agency heads depended on the idea that the agency head was exercising executive authority that must ultimately be accountable to the president. But independent expert scientific advisers do not exercise authority; they merely speak authoritatively. And when they speak, they are heard by those of us — courts, Congress, the press, and through them, the public — to whom public policy must ultimately be accountable.
This evisceration of scientific advice is untenable. If Congress is committed to the idea that evidence, science, and expertise should guide public policy, then it needs to act by insulating expert advice from arbitrary political control.
C. Joseph Ross Daval is a research specialist at the Program On Regulation, Therapeutics, And Law (PORTAL) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School and a former lawyer in the FDA’s Office of the Chief Counsel. Aaron S. Kesselheim is a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, director of PORTAL, and a former member of the FDA’s Peripheral and Central Nervous System Advisory Committee.

India swept the singles titles at the Hylo Open 2026, with P.V. Sindhu and Lakshya Sen crowned women’s and men’s champions, respectively, at the Saarlandhalle in Saarbrücken, Germany, on Sunday.
Sportstar looks back at how each Indian fared at the tournament.
P. V. Sindhu
A particular hush falls when a Sindhu smash lands steep and unreturned, and the Saarlandhalle heard it often during her opening rounds. The No. 2 seed gave UAE’s Prakriti Bharath 10 points in each game of a 21-10, 21-10 win, before France’s Rosy Oktavia Pancasari fared worse, going down 21-9, 21-6.
She continued her commanding run with a 21-12, 21-10 victory over Germany’s Amalie Schulz in the quarterfinals, before beating compatriot Anmol Kharb 21-13, 21-16 in the semifinals to set up a title clash against Denmark’s Line Højmark Kjaersfeldt.
Sindhu came into the tournament having lost the French Open final in Paris the previous week, after letting an early lead slip against An Se-young. This time, she gave her opponent no such opening. She won 21-12, 21-14, and at no point did the match feel as though it might turn.
The Sindhu of Saarbrücken won rallies by pushing opponents deeper and making them pay for every inch of court they gave up, rather than trying to finish them in a flash. The two-time Olympic medallist and 2019 world champion won in a final that lasted just 38 minutes. At 31, she remains a formidable presence on the circuit and the benchmark against which India’s younger women’s singles players are measured.
ALSO READ | PV Sindhu wins Hylo Open - List of BWF tour title wins
Lakshya Sen
Saarbrücken first saw Lakshya as a teenager in 2019, when he came from a game down to beat China’s Weng Hongyang and lift his first big senior trophy. Seven years later, he returned as a Commonwealth Games gold medallist and won another title: the Hylo Open 2026 with a 21-17, 21-10 win over Indonesia’s Jonatan Christie. It was not an easy week. Joakim Oldorff pushed him early, Kiran George tested his legs and patience in an all-Indian clash, and Kalle Koljonen took the quarterfinal opener. Each time, Lakshya tightened his defence, lifted his tempo and waited for the rally to turn his way.
Toma Junior Popov had beaten Lakshya in both of their previous meetings, including a 21-11, 21-10 rout at the China Masters last year. This time Popov’s aggressive baseline game made a late push in the first, but Lakshya held his nerve to close it 21-17, then took the second 21-13.
In the final, Christie started well, and the early exchanges were fast and flat. Lakshya’s court coverage and net touch slowly shifted the balance, and he led 11-9 at the break. When Christie surged late with a flurry of cross-court smashes, Lakshya stayed calm and closed the game 21-17. The second game decided the match. Christie came out swinging, but Lakshya absorbed the pressure, countered cleanly and let the errors pile up on the other side. It was 11-7 at the interval and 21-10 at the end. For a player who spent the week answering questions about his body and form, it was the most complete reply he could have given.
ALSO READ | Lakshya Sen wins Hylo Open 2026 final, beats Jonatan Christie in straight games
Ashmita Chaliha
Ashmita has the left-handed leaping smash and the foot speed to make any first game look promising. Against Bulgaria’s Kaloyana Nalbantova in the first round, she took the opener and the match went the distance, but the decider ended 21-8 to Nalbantova, a sharp fade after a competitive start.
Anmol Kharb
Anmol reached the semifinals the hard way, twice over. She got past Sri Lanka’s Ranithma Liyanage in the first round, then came the No. 3 seed, Denmark’s Line Christophersen, who flattened her in the first game. Anmol hit back to take the second and then the decider 25-23. The nerve she showed in India’s Badminton Asia Team Championships gold run in 2024 was on display again, and it earned her a quarterfinal against compatriot Unnati Hooda, which she won in three games, before Sindhu stopped her in the last four.
H. S. Prannoy
If any Indian match had the makings of a classic, it was Prannoy’s first-round match against France’s sixth seed, Toma Junior Popov. The 2023 World bronze medallist pushed the opener to tiebreak, but it slipped away 21-23, and that single game decided the match. Popov took control of the pace and closed out the second.
For a player of Prannoy’s explosiveness, with the jump smashes and deceptive net dribbles, it was a bruising early exit.
ALSO READ | India at the French Open 2026: Sindhu’s final, Ashmita’s upset and a doubles dip
How the others performed
Unnati Hooda: The No. 6 seed’s game is quick hands and quicker feet, a front-court rush designed to make an opponent flinch before the rally begins. She dropped the first game to the Czech Republic’s Tereza Svabilkova, then took the next two comfortably, before losing the all-Indian quarterfinal to Anmol.
Malvika Bansod: Her week began with a compatriot. Devika Sihag took the opening game, but Malvika, the tactician, found her angles and drops and won the next two to move on. Canada’s Wen Yu Zhang then beat her in straight games, and her placement-and-patience game never found the gaps it needed.
Isharani Baruah: A grinder who lives on long rallies and her opponent’s errors, she beat Germany’s Miranda Wilson in straight games. The No. 8 seed, Kjaersfeldt, then beat her in straight games too, the second game close enough to hurt.
Aakarshi Kashyap: She lost to Ukraine’s Polina Buhrova in straight games.
Men’s singles: Kiran George opened with a straight-games win over Malaysia’s Cheam June Wei, but lost to Lakshya in an all-Indian clash, fading in the decider. S. Sankar Muthusamy Subramanian found few openings against Finland’s Kalle Koljonen and went down in straight games, as did Tharun Mannepalli against Taiwan’s Chi Yu Jen.

- The claim that U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was married to her brother is unfounded.
- The latest rumor stems from a New York Post story claiming Omar's father's name was Nur Said Elmi — not Nur Omar Mohamed — and that Omar has a sister in the United Kingdom named Leila Nur Said Elmi who allegedly lived with Omar's ex-husband Ahmed Elmi, suggesting they were all siblings. A legal motion from the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia also referred to Omar as "llhan Nur Said Elmi."
- A recent New York Times report citing unnamed former and current officials said an investigation during former U.S. President Barack Obama's tenure found some evidence that Omar had entered into a fake marriage with a man suspected of being her brother, but the case stalled because the possible crime fell outside the five-year statute of limitations.
- Snopes found that the claims lack evidence because they appear to be entirely circumstantial and unsubstantiated. Having possibly similar names does not prove that Omar is related to Leila Nur Said or Ahmed Elmi. Additionally, the claims did not confirm Ahmed Elmi's parentage or his relationship to Leila Nur Said. The claims also ignore Somali naming conventions in which children receive first names tied to their paternal lineage.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Omar, the U.S. attorney's office and an individual believed to be Ahmed Elmi, and are waiting for responses.
For years, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has been the subject of claims that she committed immigration fraud by marrying her brother, which Snopes has determined were unfounded. In October, President Donald Trump's administration reopened an investigation against Omar in which it claimed to have more evidence about her family history and alleged she had committed identity fraud, leading to federal agents raiding her home in Washington, D.C.
Following this development, Snopes readers asked us to once again determine whether Omar married her brother to commit immigration fraud and whether the U.S. government had DNA evidence to substantiate that claim.
The accusations continued to claim that Omar had married her brother, a man named Ahmed Elmi. New reporting from The New York Post claimed Omar's father's name was actually Nur Said Elmi, not Nur Omar Mohamed. According to the Post, Omar's ex-husband lived in London with a woman named Leila Nur Said, who was believed to be Omar's sister and whose father's name was also Nur Said Elmi, according to a U.K. marriage certificate.
A Fox News story, citing anonymous sources, claimed Omar's real name is Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Motions filed by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, related to the search warrant also referred to Omar as "Congresswoman Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar."
In an X post, responding to allegations about her name, Omar wrote: "So let's make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar."
A NewsNation report claimed the federal agents went through Omar's garbage in the hopes of obtaining DNA samples during the raid on her house. Omar told MSNOW that she did not believe they had taken DNA samples, nor was she asked to provide any. Without DNA testing Elmi and Omar, there is no definitive proof they are siblings.
In an interview with MSNOW, asked directly whether she was related to Elmi in any way, Omar said, "Not to my knowledge."
On Oct. 29, 2026, The New York Times published an article citing unnamed former and current officials. The report says an investigation during former President Barack Obama's tenure found some evidence Omar had entered into a fake marriage with a man suspected of being her brother, but the case stalled because the possible crime fell outside the five-year statute of limitations.
In sum, we found that this was not evidence enough to support the claim she married her brother or committed immigration fraud. We have reached out to Omar's office for a response to the above allegations, as well as to Pirro's office, and will update this report accordingly.
Below, we break down all the claims about Omar's past marriages, her father's name and her alleged sister:
What is the timeline of Omar's marriages?
As we have reported previously, Omar was married twice before her current marriage to Tim Mynett: to Ahmed Hirsi (who was Ahmed Aden before he gained U.S. citizenship) and to a U.K. citizen, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — the subject of the above claims.
According to a statement Omar released in 2016, she and Hirsi applied for a marriage license in 2002. The couple married in an Islamic ceremony but never completed the process for a civil marriage, according to Hirsi. By 2008, Hirsi and Omar had separated (per Islamic custom). After that relationship ended, Omar had a civil marriage with Elmi in 2009. When that relationship ended, Elmi moved to England and they divorced per Islamic practice in 2011, but without receiving a legal divorce.
Omar and Hirsi reconciled in 2011 and remarried in an Islamic ceremony, according to her statement. In 2017, Omar formally petitioned for divorce from Elmi, and legally wed Hirsi in 2018. Citing a State of Minnesota campaign finance inquiry (Page 6), The New York Times reported on Oct. 29, 2026, that Hirsi and Omar filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 while Omar was still legally married to Elmi. Minnesota court records show Omar and Elmi's marriage was legally dissolved on Dec. 4, 2017. Minnesota court records show Hirsi and Omar legally divorced on Nov. 22, 2019. Hirsi and Omar have three children together, according to court documents.
The Times reported that even though Omar is an observant Muslim, her marriage certificate to Elmi was signed by a Christian pastor, not an imam.
Who is Omar's father?
Nur Omar Mohamed died in 2020 from COVID-19 complications, according to a report in Sahan Journal, a Minnesotan news organization focusing on immigrant communities. The obituary described him as a prominent Somali military officer during the late-1970s Somalia-Ethiopia war.
The report noted Mohamed was a colonel during the dictatorship of Mohammed Siad Barre, who was removed from power in 1991, after which the country descended into civil war. Mohamed and his family subsequently became refugees.
In a statement announcing his death, Omar referred to her father as Nur Omar Mohamed. However, in a deleted 2013 tweet about Father's Day, Omar referred to her father as "Nur Said." Many jumped on this as evidence that Omar's father could also be the father of her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi.
In 2019, after Omar's account deleted the tweet about her father, Omar's spokesperson said (archived):
When people write vile things on posts about people she loves—including posting disturbing doctored images of her father—she takes them down. Nur Said means 'Happy Light' and it's been her dad's nickname since he was a kid. He has a public page with the same name. She isn't deleting it for the disturbing and hateful reasons that are being implied by conspiracy theorists.
According to the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center, part of the Defense Department, Somalis have names with three or more components and don't commonly use hereditary surnames. A Somali often receives a personal first name at birth, followed by their father's first name, and then their grandfather's first name. So most children, male or female, share their father's and grandfather's first names. However, many Somalis also have additional names based on their lineages or clans. The institute noted, "Because all three names come from a shared pool of personal names, many Somalis have names that are the same or similar."
Omar's tweet referring to her father as "Nur Said" on its own does not establish that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was her brother. The names Said, Nur, and Elmi are extremely common among Somali Muslims. Further, according to a 2016 profile of Omar, her paternal grandfather's name was Abukar.
Snopes was unable to find Mohamed's original Facebook account. It is likely the account has been deleted.
Is Omar related to Leila Nur Said?
The New York Post connected Omar's father's Facebook account to Leila Nur Said, saying she frequently left "hearts" on his pictures. Snopes was unable to locate either account and thus cannot independently verify this connection.
The Post's pool of evidence that established these connections is flimsy. A U.K. marriage certificate obtained by the Post for Leila Nur Said lists Nur Said Elmi, a military officer, as her father. Ahmed Elmi is not mentioned on this certificate. The Post reported: "Elmi's parentage is not known, but he lived in London with Leila Nur Said, a Somali woman who is thought to be Omar's sister, who possibly raised him."
Neither the Facebook connection to Omar's father, nor the marriage certificate, can effectively establish Ahmed Elmi's relationship with Leila Nur Said.
The New York Times' Oct. 29, 2026, article about the Obama-era investigation into Omar notes that it is unclear what evidence prosecutors had that Elmi is Omar's brother.
Media reports claim Elmi is a doctoral researcher at the University of Bristol. We reached out through an email listed on the university website and will update this post accordingly.
Our previous coverage
As we reported before, Omar showed a reporter from the Minnesota Star Tribune photos of documents from her family's entry into the U.S. after fleeing the civil war. She did not provide the reporter with copies of these papers but showed that they listed her father and showed her as the youngest of seven children. There was no one named Ahmed Nur Said Elmi listed in the documents.
We previously noted that Omar and her siblings all arrived in U.S. with refugee statuses. Omar was a minor when she became a naturalized U.S. citizen. How one sibling could end up with a completely different immigration status from the others remains unexplained by the claims.
According to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services policy, immigrants can apply for permanent residency status (opening the pathway to naturalization) if they are siblings of a U.S. citizen, or if they are married to a citizen. Any sibling of Omar would not have to marry her in order to secure a path to citizenship.
If Elmi desperately wanted U.S. citizenship, he would not have immediately returned to England after his split with Omar. However, the Times reported that Elmi initially received a provisional two-year green card. When he sought a permanent green card and was asked to provide additional evidence of the validity of his marriage, he reportedly abandoned the petition and left for the U.K.
In sum …
There is not enough evidence establishing familial ties between Elmi and Omar. Media reports are relying on similar names to establish connections — disregarding Somali naming conventions in which unrelated people can share common names. Until we know more, we leave this claim unrated.
For further reading, we are have reported on numerous rumors about Omar, including that she allegedly fled to Morocco after the raid on her home and that she changed her birth year in official records.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader
- Published
Joseph Kabila was a commander in the rebel alliance that brought his father to power in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1997, went on to succeed him as president and now, at the age of 55, he is a rebel leader once again.
In an even stranger twist, the man he has sworn to topple is the very man he handed power to after 18 years at the helm, and with whom he had formed a coalition government after stepping down. While one of the rebel groups he had fought against as president is part of his new alliance.
His career reflects the ever-shifting nature of politics in DR Congo, where alliances are ephemeral, with the use of force a constant threat.
When Kabila was named leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), earlier this month, it confirmed what many Congolese had long believed – that the former president was working with the M23 rebels, who last year seized much of eastern DR Congo, including the region's main cities of Goma and Bukavu.
Nevertheless, the confirmation sent shockwaves through DR Congo – a vast country two-thirds the size of western Europe, with huge deposits of gold, diamonds and even more importantly minerals used to make everything from the mobile phones to batteries for electric vehicles.
For Kabila, the alliance offers a possible route back to the power he had lost.
For the M23 rebels, his involvement brings the experience and networks of a former head of state to a movement whose military advances have yet to translate into broad national legitimacy.
But it is far from certain that they can achieve their stated goal of ousting President Félix Tshisekedi.
Policy analyst Henry-Pacifique Mayala told the BBC that Kabila had been left with few options for regaining political influence.
"He actually was left with no other choice," he said.
Facing a death sentence after being convicted in absentia of treason, as well as US sanctions over his alleged support for the M23, Kabila may have sought assurances that the partnership could serve his interests, Mayala suggested.
"I'm not sure that he is making this huge leap in the dark without having received considerable assurance," Mayala said, adding that the M23's military strength could give Kabila greater leverage in any future negotiations with the Congolese government.
Kabila's involvement also raises questions about whether the conflict could spread beyond the east.
The M23's territorial gains have been concentrated in the country's eastern provinces, some 1,500km (1,000 miles) from the capital, Kinshasa.
Kabila's political networks could give the rebellion a broader reach, but that does not necessarily mean it has the capacity to extend its military campaign across the country.
And it is not clear how far Kabila's national reach extends.
While he was in power, after being named following the mysterious assassination of his father Laurent in 2001, he was often seen as something of an outsider in Kinshasa. He was far more at home speaking Swahili, the lingua franca of eastern DR Congo, as well as east Africa, rather than the Lingala spoken in Kinshasa.
His father's rebel group actually walked across the country to Kinshasa, also starting in the east, over a period of seven months, before eventually seizing power in May 1996 and ousting long-time ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who had governed the country as his own personal property for more than 30 years.
There is little suggestion that Joseph Kabila's FRN would try to repeat that feat but earlier this week, he likened Tshisekedi to Mobutu.
"You have a tyrant who wants to impose and dictate what he thinks is right and not necessarily follow the constitution, which is the supreme law of the land," he told Conspiracy Trackers Great Lakes (CTGL), a pro-M23 research group.
Kabila accused the government of using the death penalty, ending the moratorium introduced during his own presidency, to intimidate civilians, politicians and members of the military, as well as himself.
"This is personal," he said.
He framed his confrontation with Tshisekedi as a fight against authoritarianism, invoking Section 64 of the constitution, which calls on citizens to resist anyone who seizes power or exercises it in violation of constitutional provisions.
Tshisekedi is rumoured to be planning to change the constitution to allow him to seek a third term in office, with the C64 coalition of opposition parties named after that same section of the constitution, campaigning against such a move.
But in a sign that he may not get everything his own way, the C64 coalition this week refused to back Kabila's rebellion, saying that Congo's multiple security crises cannot be resolved by military means alone. Instead, it announced plans to seek direct talks with both Tshisekedi and Kabila in pursuit of what it called a "genuine and inclusive national dialogue".
Richard Moncrieff, a Great Lakes analyst with the International Crisis Group think-tank, said President Tshisekedi retained substantial advantages.
"Tshisekedi has strong American backing. He has a lot of money. And he generally controls the political system and, as far as we can see, the military system," Moncrieff said.
In his first public reaction to Kabila being named FRN leader, Tshisekedi was damning: "In my view, it's simply proof that he has never loved this country, and even less its inhabitants," he said last week.
And yet Kabila is widely believed to have helped ensure that Tshisekedi succeeded him, rather than Martin Fayulu, who was the true winner of the 2018 elections, according to leaked results provided by the Catholic Church, which had observers around the country.
Indeed, the former head of the electoral commission who announced Tshisekedi as the winner, Corneille Nangaa, has said as much.
Now one of Kabila's deputies in the FRN, he claimed that Kabila and Tshisekedi had reached a political agreement before the final election results were announced.
"I can confirm that I helped draft the deal," Nangaa told France 24 in September 2023. "Tshisekedi is a liar. He knows there was an agreement and he knows what was contained in the deal."
Tshisekedi has maintained that he won the election legitimately.

  - Published5 December 2025
- How Trump wants the US to cash in on mineral-rich DR Congo's peace deal 
  - Published28 July 2025
After the disputed election, Kabila and Tshisekedi entered a power-sharing arrangement that allowed Kabila's coalition to retain control of parliament even after Tshisekedi took office in January 2019.
The arrangement unravelled in December 2020, when Tshisekedi moved to break Kabila's parliamentary dominance and build his own majority. The former allies became rivals, and Kabila went into self-imposed exile in South Africa.
From exile, Kabila's criticism of Tshisekedi grew louder.
He returned to DR Congo in 2025 and appeared in rebel-held Goma. In September that year, a military court sentenced him to death in absentia on charges including treason and financing violence in eastern Congo.
At the time, he rejected the accusations.
Yet another intriguing sub-plot to the announcement is Kabila's relationship with Rwanda's President Paul Kagame.
In the early years of his presidency, ties were strained between DR Congo and Rwanda, which accused its giant neighbour of not doing enough to remove ethnic Hutu militias involved in the 1994 Rwandan genocide from its territory. Their presence in what is now DR Congo has been used to justify Rwanda's repeated military involvement in its giant neighbour, going back to its backing of Laurent Kabila's rebellion.
The M23 was formed in 2012, vowing to stand up for the rights of ethnic Tutsis and to protect them against these militias, but also battling the Congolese army, under the control of Joseph Kabila.
From the start Rwanda was accused of backing them. It has always denied these allegations, as it still does despite overwhelming evidence.
However, relations later improved and Kabila's government worked with Rwanda against the Hutu militias.
Alex Adams, Africa programme director at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said Kabila's appointment as rebel leader could bring his interests into alignment with those of Rwanda's president, even though their objectives differ.
"Kabila wants to recover political influence nationally, while Kagame is primarily concerned with Rwanda's security and strategic position in eastern Congo. This is an alignment of convenience rather than a partnership built on deep trust," he said.
Policy analyst Mayala said Kabila's involvement could help Rwanda counter accusations that it was interfering in Congo's internal affairs.
"This is a former president. It's finally a Congolese rebellion," he said.
Even before the announcement of Kabila as the rebellion's leader, fighting was continuing despite a peace accord overseen by Donald Trump last year.
Part of that deal saw the US sign an agreement to extract DR Congo's mineral wealth and the US has since seemed to side with Tshisekedi by imposing sanctions on various Rwandan officials and bodies, accusing them of prolonging the violence.
Elections are scheduled for 2028, but Tshisekedi has warned that fighting in the east could delay voting.
Against this backdrop, Kabila has questioned whether elections alone can resolve the country's political crisis.
"Does Congo need elections or a revolution?" he asked, arguing that lasting peace required a fundamental overhaul of the country's executive and legislature.
International security analyst Ovigwe Eguegu argues that Kabila is banking on military force to regain political influence, while Tshisekedi seems to be trying to extend his time in office beyond what the constitution allows.
"It looks like the Congolese people are going to lose either way, because neither of these two sides present a credible economic transformation plan for both the eastern Congo and the entirety of the country," Eguegu said.

- Sony's PS5 firmware update 26.07 - 14.22.00 introduces security fixes on November 2.
- The release arrives amid growing PS5 jailbreak research and homebrew.
- GTA 6 launches November 19, but its minimum firmware requirements and jailbreak compatibility remain unconfirmed.
Sony has released a fresh PS5 firmware update with security fixes, and its timing is raising questions as the console’s jailbreak scene continues to make progress before the GTA 6 launch. The new system software version 26.07-14.22.00 arrived on November 2, thereby giving the console an opportunity to reinforce its security.
The latest PS5 firmware update is approximately 1.267 GB in size and is available to download now. Interestingly, the description of the patch notes is quite small, and Sony states the following change:
We’ve made some security fixes to the system software.
This is practically everything Sony has revealed about this release, and there is no mention of new features, performance improvements, interface changes, or any specific bugs addressed. What catches the eye of gamers is the security-focused nature of the update and that it arrives right after the recent developments surrounding the PS5 jailbreaks.
This update follows firmware version 14.20 that arrived on October 21. The homebrew community has been actively exploring the vulnerabilities in Sony’s console and previously released a jailbreak that supports firmware versions 7.00 through 13.60.
Naturally, with few days left till GTA 6, this development is more interesting. Some speculation has emerged that the minimum firmware required to run GTA 6 would be at least version 14.10. Following the latest release, online reports suggest that version 14.22 is required to run the game.
However, there is no official confirmation from Rockstar Games yet, so these claims should be treated as speculation.
A successful jailbreak might potentially allow users to modify their consoles and create opportunities for piracy. Being such a high-profile game and with GTA 6 launching on PlayStation and Xbox consoles first, this news is really concerning.
With the GTA 6 release date approaching, Sony might introduce some additional security updates in the upcoming weeks. So, are you excited to check out the brand-new activities in GTA 6? Let us know in the comments below.

Kimi Antonelli’s race at the 2026 Mexico Grand Prix paves the way for the 20-year-old to enter a short list of Italian drivers to win the Formula One World Drivers’ Championship. So far, only two Italians had topped the standings and Kimi Antonelli is not only the third but also is the youngest amongst the Italian winners.
Giuseppe Farina clinched the title during the inaugural edition of Formula 1 in 1950, while driving for Alfa Romeo. He remains the only driver to win the championship in his first season.
Ferrari’s Alberto Ascari won both the 1952 and 1953 Formula One titles, making him the second Italian to win the Championship. He was also the first driver to win back-to-back titles in the sport.
This makes Kimi Antonelli the first Italian winner in 73 years.
Italian drivers to win the F1 World Championship:
Giuseppe Farina
Alberto Ascari
Kimi Antonelli

Indian drug regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical Industries to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in its quality management system, documents reviewed by Reuters showed.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on August 20 after a joint federal-state inspection of the facility identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma’s move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands.
India’s drug quality standards have come under increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally made cough syrups were linked to the deaths of children in India and also in countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan.
The regulatory agencies’ move marks an escalation of the action against Sun Pharma, India’s biggest pharmaceutical firm, which will be unable to continue ophthalmic drug production at the Assam factory until it submits a satisfactory compliance report. Sun Pharma said previously the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver.
The regulator sought more information on the recall of 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products — liquids used to treat eye conditions — the documents showed.
In an internal notice sent to stockists at the time, the company said it was withdrawing the products as a “precautionary measure.” It remains unclear whether all of the recalled products were contaminated.
Sun Pharma did not publicly disclose details of the recall.
The company has submitted a compliance report in response to the order, which is being reviewed by the regulator, an official familiar with the matter told Reuters on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
“We voluntarily initiated a temporary cessation of manufacturing activities and informed the regulators,” Sun Pharma said in a statement on Friday (October 30, 2026), adding that remedial measures have been put in place.
It did not respond to a request for comment on the recall. The company says on its website it follows a single global quality standard.
Recall could involve hundreds of thousands of bottles
Some of the recalled products included Lotepred 1% 5ml eye drops, Nepalact OD eye drops, Nepalact-Z, Brinzotim eye drops 5ml and Depopred 2ml. The eye drops are used to treat eye inflammation, infections and chronic eye diseases, according to doctors.
It is unclear whether these eye products were exported from India or whether any patients reported any adverse effects.
Reuters found that, based on the product packaging, most of the recalled products were manufactured at the Assam state facility in Kokjhar village. Reuters could not independently verify whether the 332 batches cited by regulators were related only to the 11 identified brands in the recall notice or included additional brands.
The affected batches could translate into hundreds of thousands of eye-drop bottles, according to industry experts, who declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
Ophthalmology contributes about 3% of Sun Pharma’s domestic revenue, according to its 2025-26 annual report. It is also one of its key areas for the U.S.
The company reported a drop in second-quarter profit on Friday (October 30) weighed down by a one-time charge related to its acquisition of U.S.-based Organon.
The eye product recall coincided with a patient-safety advisory issued in June by the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS), an independent body of eye specialists, warning that certain batches of Predmet eye drops appeared to be contaminated.
“There were some adverse cases of infections reported in patients who used Predmet and we got sealed bottles investigated and found it was contaminated,” Santosh Honavar, a doctor and secretary of AIOS, told Reuters, adding that Sun Pharma had also recalled those Predmet drops.
Sun Pharma did not respond a request for comment on the AIOS advisory.
The regulators issued a show-cause notice to Sun Pharma on August 10, citing the quality management system failures, the documents showed.
Dissatisfied with the company’s response, the regulators ordered a halt to the manufacturing, sale and distribution of all ophthalmic products from the facility.
Indian regulators did not respond to requests for comment. The agency did not issue a public health alert after the recall.
It is not the first time Sun Pharma’s sterile manufacturing facilities have faced regulatory scrutiny. Last year, the U.S. FDA halted the company’s shipments from Gujarat’s Halol plant after inspectors cited shortcomings in contamination controls.
