Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

'Crazy' Carrick looks forward to Roma game
- Published
Michael Carrick accepts it might sound "crazy" but the beleaguered Manchester United boss says he is looking forward to the Champions League showdown with Roma at Old Trafford.
United go into Tuesday's game without a win in nine matches in all competitions.
It is their worst run since 1988-89. They have not gone 10 without a win in a single campaign since 1977-78 and there is a growing feeling Carrick will lose his job during the forthcoming international break.
Roma's only defeat so far this season was at home to Real Madrid in the Champions League last month, when they led 3-1 with seven minutes left.
United are 17th in the Premier League and after defeats by Atletico Madrid and Como have slumped to 21st in the Champions League table after three games, with only the top 24 making it through.
It is a bleak backdrop, but rather than fret over what lies ahead, Carrick is viewing it as a chance to change the narrative of the season.
"You might think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on, but genuinely, I really can't wait for the game," said Carrick. "I'm really looking forward to it.
"Listen, I can't look into the future, you never know what's going to happen. That doesn't change the way I feel. Whatever happens is going to happen in whatever direction it goes in, but we want to make it a big night tomorrow."
Carrick watched over a lively open session of pre-match training at Carrington.
Striker Bryan Mbeumo and midfielder Carlos Baleba were particularly vocal, with Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez also fully engaged despite his red card at Chelsea, which triggered such a negative reaction.
While there have been calls for Martinez to be dropped for the Roma game, Carrick was more philosophical.
"Things happen in football," he said.
"Sometimes you do things; you make a decision, you make mistakes. Sometimes it goes well for you."
He also dismissed concerns both about Martinez's commitment, and that of his entire squad.
"Perceptions are a funny thing," he said.
"They can make things look all sorts of different ways. The dressing room is a good place.
"I've said it before, I don't question the commitment of the players, to the club and to me and to each other. We need to play better. We can make better decisions. But commitment's not a thing at all."
Just need a win - Mainoo
England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo sat alongside Carrick at the media conference and also stressed the strength of the group.
Mainoo returned from a four-match absence with a muscular issue as a second-half substitute at Chelsea.
At 21, Mainoo is one of the youngest players in Carrick's squad. However, given he joined the club as a seven-year-old, he is also the longest serving and has a unique insight into the responsibilities that come with life in the Old Trafford spotlight.
"I've been at this club for a long time and know there's always going to be ups and downs," he said. "It's never going to be plain sailing and smooth to the top. You expect bumps.
"Of course it's been a tough season. We've not had the results we've wanted, but I feel like we're one win away from changing that."
United were last relegated in 1973-74. They have not been in the relegation zone after nine games or more since November 1986, when they collected a single point in Sir Alex Ferguson's first two games in charge following Ron Atkinson's dismissal.
Their lowest position after at least nine games of a season since then was 17th in 1989-90. They were 16th under Ruben Amorim after 37 games of the 2024-25 season.
Mainoo says the present position is unacceptable for a club of United's size.
"United's a huge club," he said. "I think a lot of people know the values this club holds and have been passed down through the people who've worked here and played here.
"I feel like I take some responsibility in spreading the word of what Manchester United is, coming up through the academy, and I plan to send that message for as long as I can."

When it comes to election pressure, this year's Georgia or Michigan could be anywhere
There's one big difference, Tina Barton says, between running an election in a battleground state and a non-battleground.
It's what happens when there are mistakes.
"If a human error happens, it's easily explained in the press and it's not a story," Barton says. "You have a human error in a battleground state and all of a sudden it can become a massive conspiracy."
Barton would know.
In 2020, she oversaw elections as city clerk of Rochester Hills, Mich. On election night, her office mistakenly sent an unofficial absentee vote file twice because the first one didn't initially appear to send.
Such mistakes happen every election cycle in a national process run by tens of thousands of human beings. A machine isn't plugged in. A poll worker sleeps through their alarm clock and doesn't open a precinct on time. Someone gets handed the wrong ballot.
In Barton's case, the issue didn't impact actual votes, and it was corrected in the tally the following day.
But it changed her life regardless.
The chairwoman of the Republican National Committee accused her office of improperly giving votes to Democrats, and Barton received a rush of death threats, including a voicemail saying she deserved a "throat to the knife" because she had "frauded out America of a real election."
More than half a decade later, for better or worse, election officials in swing states like Michigan, Georgia and Arizona are more used to that level of pressure and scrutiny.
In this year's midterms, however, because the races that will decide control of the U.S. House and Senate are spread around the country, local officials in places like Iowa, Alaska, New York and Kansas may find themselves in the national spotlight for the first time.
Chris McGinn is executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials. In an interview with NPR earlier this year, he noted that Texas has been a reliable Republican state for the better part of 50 years, which has meant fewer competitive elections and less pressure on voting officials in federal election cycles.
A huge part of McGinn's job has been preparing clerks for the possibility that could change this year, considering the U.S. Senate race there could decide the balance of power in that chamber. The Republican nominee for that seat sought to help President Trump overturn his 2020 election loss.
"We're still in a state of not thinking it can happen to us — 'That happens in other places,'" McGinn said. "One of the things that I jokingly but realistically preach to our members is we don't want to be Florida in 2000."
On a whole, the threat environment for voting officials seems calmer than it did in the period following 2020.
Wendy Link — the supervisor of elections for Palm Beach County, Fla., a county that includes part of a toss-up congressional district this year — says her office still regularly gets "love letters," as she calls them, but she's not as worried for own safety as she has been at different points in the job.
"We get emails saying, you know, 'We're going to send our army to arrest you, you'll be spending your time in Guantanamo Bay,'" Link told NPR. "So do I love reading some of the emails? No. Do I think some of them are clearly intended to intimidate me? Yes. But am I reaching out and asking for a security detail? No."
But Barton, the former Michigan clerk, worries it could all escalate again if the midterms are close. She's now vice president of the Committee for Safe and Secure Elections, which helps local officials game-plan and prepare for different worst case scenarios.
"It can happen whether you're a red state or a blue state. Controversy can find you," Barton said. "All it takes is some ballot equipment going down, a problem with ballots jamming, a website going down."
Researchers who study election misinformation say most false narratives usually emerge from real events like those Barton mentioned, which are then seized on by influencers or politicians to falsely imply they're happening intentionally or at a wider scale than they actually are.
This year CSSE doubled the number of trainings the organization led when compared to 2024 — a sign of new concerns around the Trump administration's actions in elections but also an expanded understanding of what it means to be in a battleground state.
When Barton talks to officials in competitive districts, her message is simple.
"I've told them all, you better be on your game," Barton said.

Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions. While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions, covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

When Nisha Panwar,30, was diagnosed with lupus in December 2013, she felt relieved. After months of recurrent fever, rashes and worsening symptoms, she finally had an explanation for what was happening to her body. Before the diagnosis, she says, several doctors had told her she had no disease and that it was “all in my head” and was referred to a psychiatrist.
For Tabassum Sultana, 28, a Bengaluru-based content creator, the diagnosis of mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), with features of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), in 2024 was followed by another setback. She developed avascular necrosis of the right hip and underwent surgery in September 2025. Her recovery was slow, she became dependent on her mother for everyday activities and had to stop working. Recurring flare-ups continue to affect her mental health.

It wasn't clear precisely what the exercise was in preparation for, though it appears the conclusions some people drew about an imminent or specific threat originated from social media, not the Army itself. We reached out to the Army for comment and will update this story if we receive a response.
Images purportedly showing U.S. soldiers practicing digging mass battlefield graves circulated on social media in late October.
According to several posts, the purpose of the supposed grave-digging rehearsal was to prepare soldiers for large-scale temporary burial until bodies could be identified and returned home in the case of mass casualties as the U.S. war on Iran stretched on.
"DISTURBING: The U.S. Army is now training soldiers to dig MASS BATTLEFIELD GRAVES for American troops as the war continues," one Facebook post read (archived).
Both the image and the claim were real. The images were originally distributed (archived) on Oct. 22 by the Department of Defense's media distribution service.
According to the photo credit, they were taken by Capt. Thomas McCarty on Oct. 21. The caption called the operation a "simulated temporary interment trench," meaning that soldiers were practicing digging 15-foot-wide trenches for temporary burial of bodies so that they could later be identified and relocated. The full caption read:
A U.S. Army D6 bulldozer, operated by horizontal construction engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, backfills a simulated temporary interment trench during Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant near the St. Mere Eglise Drop Zone, Oct. 21, 2026. The test-of-concept exercise, executed by the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, evaluated the structural impact of heavy earthmoving equipment on remains by placing simulated skeletal models and sealed water containers inside burial bags. Operators practiced casting dirt inward from a 15-foot-wide trench to verify that the gravity fall of displaced soil preserves remains intact for future forensic identification and repatriation, while refining spatial standards for future Army fatality management doctrine. (U.S. Army photo by Capt. Thomas McCarty)
McCarty later wrote a report on the training exercise that both the Defense Department and the Army website published. (The article on the Army website appeared to no longer be available, as of this writing.)
According to McCarty, the exercise was "an operational reality the U.S. Army has not executed at scale since the Korean War."
The report detailed how in a 24-hour period of continuous operations, a crew could bury up to 2,400 bodies.
"Backfilling without desecrating the remains is where the real skill lies," one engineering officer reportedly said.
It wasn't clear precisely what the exercise was in preparation for, though it appears that conclusions drawn about an imminent or specific threat originated on social media, not the Army's report. We reached out to the Army for comment and will update this story if we receive a response.

No Grealish, no cry - the rise of Everton's youngsters
- Published
As Everton prepared to face Newcastle in the fourth round of the EFL Cup at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday, the stakes were high.
A quarter-final tie against League Two opposition in Fleetwood awaited the winner, and a fanbase starved of trophies began to look ahead - albeit, for some, through covered eyes.
Then, in the build-up to the match, it was revealed Jack Grealish had been dropped from the squad over what is understood to have been an unauthorised absence from training.
The unwanted headline threatened to derail preparations for the latest round of a competition that perhaps offers Everton's best chance of winning a trophy for the first time in 31 years.
Instead, the club's younger players came to the fore, led by the influential Hayden Hackney.
A £16.5m summer signing from Middlesbrough, the 24-year-old made light of his inexperience at the highest level against a strong Newcastle XI, assisting James Garner's opening goal before scoring Everton's second with a close-range volley.
Hackney, though, has needed to be patient early in his Everton career.
After starting the opening game of the season - a 2-0 win against Crystal Palace - his only subsequent start prior to Thursday's cup victory was in the third round of the same competition against Wolves.
The central midfielder is not known for being prolific - the fourth-round win was only the second time in his career he had scored and assisted in the same game - but he knitted together phases of possession and carried the ball with the confidence that led to him being named Championship player of the year last season.
David Moyes, though, is a demanding manager and one perfectly prepared to keep young feet on the ground.
"I thought there were bits of his game that were very good," said the Everton boss. "Getting a goal was great. There were other bits where I didn't think it was where it was [supposed to be].
"But I see this as a bit of bringing in Championship players, getting them used to the Premier League. A couple of times he got caught on the ball.
"But I really enjoyed bits. He gave us a bit of an attacking play, getting into the box, and obviously getting the goal was really good. A really good assist from Thierno Barry as well, to be fair."
While Hackney was ably assisted by strong performances from Garner and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall in Everton's midfield, the threadbare nature of the Toffees' squad means the development and contribution of the club's younger players could prove crucial in any success this season.
Of the 10 players signed on permanent deals since Moyes rejoined the club in January 2025, seven are aged 24 or under, including Barry.
The France Under-21 international is playing just a third season in a top-five European league after joining from Villarreal in July 2025, but his introduction to elite football has been more pressurised because of Everton's lack of options up front.
Barry is the club's only specialist centre-forward, starting every match and playing 918 minutes this season. His tally of seven goals is already just one off his total from last season, despite playing 30 fewer matches.
Everton have recorded 24 big chances, and Barry has been involved in 15 of them (62.5%).
Whiles Moyes' hand has been somewhat forced in giving Barry game time because of a lack of alternatives, there has been a broader indication he is more prepared to back the younger members of his squad this season.
The average age of Everton's starting XI in the Premier League has dropped by almost 18 months this season to 26 years and 216 days.
The departure of veteran midfielder Idrissa Gueye has made a difference but first-team players aged 24 or under are playing a much higher proportion of Premier League minutes than in the previous campaign.
Moyes used just 22 players in the Premier League last season. He has already used 22 in this one.
Even the youngest players in the squad appear to have gained more trust. In 2025-26, players aged 21 or under totalled 1,088 minutes for the Toffees, a figure that has already been exceeded this season (1,206).
At 19, Harrison Armstrong is the youngest regular in Everton's senior squad. In January, he had completed a six-month loan spell at Preston and Moyes considered sending him back to Deepdale for the remainder of last season before slowly integrating him into the first team.
This season, the teenager has started every Premier League match.
Winger Tyler Dibling, 20, initially struggled after a £35m move from Southampton in the summer of 2025 but was positive in getting Everton on to the front foot on against Newcastle on Thursday night.
Tyrique George joined on a permanent deal from Chelsea in the summer after spending the second half of last season on loan at Everton during which he made only one league start.
The 20-year-old has already made five this season, scoring his first goal for the club in the 2-2 draw with Manchester United in September.
George also started the EFL Cup fixture last week and won back possession for the opening goal.
Merlin Rohl broke into the team towards the end of last season and the 24-year-old midfielder, who also signed permanently in the summer following an initial loan spell, has since been trusted to fill Everton's problem position of right-back.
After missing four games because of injury, he was immediately brought back into the starting XI against Chelsea. He was then preferred to the more experienced Ainsley Maitland-Niles at right-back for matches against Arsenal and Newcastle.
When asked if Grealish would return to the squad for Monday's rematch at St James' Park, Moyes said he would not reveal any team news, though there is no doubt that experience still counts among the 63-year-old's most valuable commodities.
Defender James Tarkowksi, 33, has been a standout performer so far this season, while the form of fellow senior players such as Jordan Pickford, 32, and Dewsbury-Hall, 28 remain critical to this Everton side.
But when Everton meet Newcastle for the second time in less than a week on Monday, Grealish could again miss out.
In his absence, younger heads were good enough to win a cup tie. It would be further indication of their growing influence if they were to repeat that result in the Premier League.

You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.
One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.
It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.
Moments Lost
You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.
Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”
The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.
It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.
By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.
Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one. Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.
There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.
Other App Picks
As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.
One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.
Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.
ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.
One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.
Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

India's largest share sale could end cheap mobile internet for millions
- Published
India's biggest telecom giant, the Meta and Google-backed Jio Platforms, is set to make its stock market debut on Wednesday.
Despite a bruising spell for Indian markets, its historic $3.2bn initial public offering (IPO) - the country's largest ever - has drawn overwhelming demand from top global fund managers, domestic institutions and mom-and-pop retail investors.
Bids outstripped the shares on offer within hours of subscriptions opening on 21 October.
Owned by Asia's richest man, Mukesh Ambani, Jio is one of India's most consequential companies, with half a billion people subscribing to its cheap mobile data. But its meteoric rise has also been dogged by controversy.
The company burst onto India's crowded telecom scene in 2016, offering throwaway tariffs that got millions of Indians hooked to the internet.
But its launch led to a huge disruption in the telecom sector. A market once crowded with 17 operators shrunk to an oligopoly of just three, with critics accusing the deep-pocketed company of waging a price war that pushed rivals out of business.
More recently, Elon Musk criticised Ambani, calling him the "real boss of India", suggesting that Jio was trying to thwart Starlink's entry into India. Reliance dismissed the allegations saying it welcomed competition from Musk.
For all the scrutiny it has faced over the last decade, Jio's discounted data plans have been a bedrock of India's digital revolution, spawning a huge digital economy and democratising online payments, food delivery and e-commerce in Asia's third-biggest economy.
Within three years of its launch, customer data usage rose fifty-fold and data prices crashed.
This aggressive discounting helped Jio rapidly amass some 553 million mobile subscribers by 2026. It also cemented its dominance in other segments, capturing 50% of the wireless broadband market and more than 40% of fixed broadband.
Jio also carries 60% of India's wireless data traffic and boasts of the largest 5G subscriber base outside China, according to brokerage Emkay Global, which has described the company as the "digital engine of India".
But analysts say its stock market debut - which will see its promoters dilute their shareholding by about 3% - could mark a turning point in Jio's pricing strategy, potentially bringing an end to years of ultra-cheap tariffs.
"The era of Jio using cheap tariffs as a market-share weapon is drawing to a close," said Nitya Shah, co-founder of KamayaKya Wealth Management.
"A listed Jio must answer to minority shareholders… which structurally reduces its incentive to keep pricing suppressed."
Jio's future growth will no longer be driven primarily by adding subscribers through discounted plans. Instead, it will depend on "earning more per subscriber - through the migration to 5G, successive tariff revisions, and the extension of fixed wireless broadband into homes fibre has never reached", brokerage company Motilal Oswal said in a note.
The listing could also pave the way for Jio's competitors to raise prices, as fears of being undercut by a cheaper rival begin to recede.
"The biggest beneficiary of this shift could be Vodafone Idea," says Shah. "It is a moment the sector's weakest balance sheet gets its strongest tailwind".
For Indian consumers, any further increases would come on the heels of an industry-wide tariff hike a few years ago. Analysts say another round of price rises could trigger a fresh churn in the market as price-sensitive customers switch to the cheapest plans available.
While consumers may have to brace for higher bills, Jio's IPO offers investors a bet on India's seemingly insatiable appetite for data - and the growing ecosystem of digital services the company offers across entertainment, cloud computing, gaming and financial services.
India has emerged as the second-largest consumer of mobile data in the world, driven by lower tariffs and rising penetration of smartphones.
Jio's monthly data use per customer has climbed from 28.7 GB in 2024 to 42.3 GB in 2026 - up by 52% in two years. As per some estimates, usage is expected to surge further to 65GB by the end of this decade as disposable incomes rise.
All of this will give a tailwind for Jio to drive long-term growth in average revenue per user.
"Penetration of most digital services remains well below China and the US, which leaves significant headroom [for growth]," according to Emkay Global.
The listing is also likely to enhance transparency and provide investors with a "clearer market valuation" for the company, according to Moody's rating agency, as Jio is currently part of Reliance Industries, which has businesses spanning oil refining and retail.
But as much as its central and growing role in India's economy has excited investors, the buzz about the IPO also comes from the fact that this is the first share sale from the Reliance conglomerate in over two decades.
The company - which started as a small spice and polyester yarn trading venture in 1958 before expanding into textiles, petrochemicals, refining and eventually to retail, telecom and digital services - is known for its track record of long-term wealth creation, and enjoys legendary status among mom-and-pop investors.
Dhirubhai Ambani, the founder of the Reliance empire, is said to have played a foundational role in popularising equity investing and taking it beyond the preserve of traders and wealthy families in the 1980s and 90s.
In its early years, Reliance built a vast base of individual shareholders by turning its annual general meetings into grand spectacles of big announcements, dividend payouts and celebrations of public share ownership. Over time, this helped forge a fiercely loyal investor base, many of whom developed a deep emotional bond with the company.
And while Reliance Industries' stock has fallen nearly 20% over the past year, its longer-term track record continues to inspire confidence.
"The company has given average annualised returns of around 30% consistently for thirty years," Kranthi Bathini of Mumbai-based WealthMills Securities told the BBC.
"That's why there's anticipation that the same magic can be replicated with the Jio IPO."

Rahul alleges ‘foreign support’
Deep Dive
The Congress leader has alleged that India's financial system was “controlled” and backed by foreign forces, while foreign social media platforms supported the Prime Minister. He challenged Modi to debate the allegations at any venue and time.
“Mr Modi, stop lying to this nation," Rahul Gandhi wrote on X. "You became PM because of foreign help. You remain PM because of foreign help. Your financial system is fully controlled and supported by foreigners. Foreign social media fully backs you.”
“I challenge you to an open debate about this. Any stage, any time. Come if you have the guts. You won't dare, because you are terrified of what I know about you,” he added.
The Opposition leader's open challenge came in response to Modi's comments at the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas celebrations at the Statue of Unity in Ekta Nagar, Gujarat, on Monday. The event marked the birth anniversary of India's first home minister, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.
Addressing the gathering, Modi accused certain forces of trying to divide the country and using social media to spread rumours and damage India's image.
“Certain forces are continuously engaged in conspiracies to divide the country... After more than a decade of frustration and disappointment, these forces have now come out in the open,” the Prime Minister said, as per news agency ANI.
ALSO READ | Rahul Gandhi says Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail, warns BJP of ‘legal action over vote chori’
He also questioned the alleged links between these forces and groups abroad, asking who was meeting whom overseas and which anti-India forces were supporting them. Modi urged people to recognise such activities and confront them together.
The Prime Minister also criticised the Opposition, saying its role in a democracy was to question government policies but that it had instead become an obstructionist force.
“In a democracy, the responsibility of the Opposition is to oppose government policies, but it is our misfortune that the Opposition (virodh paksh) has become an obstructionist force (avrodh paksh),” he said, accusing it of creating hurdles in the country's development and undermining the Constitution.
Rahul Gandhi's Ramlila Maidan attack on Modi, Shah
On Sunday, Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders held a major protest at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan against alleged electoral irregularities and the SIR exercise. The 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' rally on November 1 followed a march from the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction to Ramlila Maidan. Leaders of 21 Opposition parties participated in the mobilisation, demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and alleging large-scale deletion of voters from electoral rolls.
ALSO READ | '40% of Ramlila Maidan vacant': BJP mocks Rahul Gandhi over 10-lakh turnout claim
At the rally, Gandhi accused the Election Commission of facilitating vote theft and alleged that the BJP had benefited from manipulation of electoral rolls. He warned that Modi and home minister Amit Shah would face ‘legal action’ over the alleged irregularities after Kumar's removal.
The Congress leader described the CEC's removal as the first step towards restoring the country's democratic institutions. He also accused the Prime Minister and the home minister of being involved in the alleged electoral wrongdoing.
Other Opposition leaders, including Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Sonia Gandhi, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Trinamool Congress leader Mamata Banerjee and RJD leader Tejashwi Yadav, also addressed the gathering.
The Opposition has maintained that the SIR exercise could deprive eligible voters of their voting rights. The Election Commission, however, has defended the revision process, saying it is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and update electoral rolls.
Amit Shah challenges Rahul Gandhi to debate SIR
Amit Shah on Monday challenged Rahul Gandhi to debate allegations of vote theft, electronic voting machines (EVMs) and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Parliament. Speaking at the BJP's 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' padayatra in Hyderabad, Shah said the government was ready to convene a special session of Parliament for the discussion.
“Rahul ji, you don't allow Parliament to run. Be it EVMs, SIR, infiltrators, I challenge you from Hyderabad. We are ready to convene a special session of Parliament. Come for debate,” Shah said, as per PTI.
He also accused the Congress and other INDIA bloc parties of trying to stop the SIR exercise to protect illegal immigrants from Bangladesh, whom he alleged were part of their vote bank. Shah described the Opposition's rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on Sunday as a 'Ghuspetiya Bachao' (Save Infiltrators) rally.
Rejecting Gandhi's claim that 13 crore voters' names had been deleted from electoral rolls, Shah said 6.15 crore people had shifted, nearly three crore were deceased and around one crore entries were duplicates. He alleged that the remaining three crore entries belonged to infiltrators and said the government would remove them from the electoral rolls.
Shah also questioned the Congress's criticism of EVMs, asking why the party had won assembly elections in states such as Telangana, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh if the machines were faulty.
He accused the Congress of questioning electoral processes only when it lost elections, while taking credit when it won.

Australia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, major bank economists say, as the Reserve Bank is forced to keep interest rates higher to rid the nation of persistent inflationary pressures.
The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, in a move that will push the cash rate to its highest since 2008 amid rising worries the economy could even be tipped into recession.
Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, said the extended Middle East conflict, collapsing house prices and a more aggressive central bank would drive real GDP down to just 1% by the middle of next year, nearly half the previous estimate of 1.8%.
Growth through 2027 would be barely stronger at an estimated 1.1%, according to the updated projections.
Allen said she had expected to see “signs of economic recovery” by the New Year, but now sees the economy “bottoming deeper and later”.
This more pessimistic outlook was “mainly given oil has been a lot higher than we had been expecting,” she said.
“Most people thought we would see a resolution to the Middle East conflict by now and oil [prices] looking more normal. Alas, that has not been the case.”
Instead, Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, has surged from about $US72 a barrel in early July, to back above $US110 in recent days as the conflict broadens and hopes for a peace deal in the near future have all but disappeared.
After Jim Chalmers last month warned the December mid-year budget update would show a more pessimistic economic outlook, analysts at NAB also revealed a major downgrade to their forecasts.
Gareth Spence, the bank’s head of Australian economics, said “unemployment might need to rise higher than we thought” in order to get inflation back under control – a view he said reflected recent comments by top RBA officials.
The economy would grow below trend over 2027 and 2028, Spence said, echoing the forecast of just 1% growth next year.
Spence forecast the key jobless measure would need to rise from 4.7% to as high as 5.4% by the end of next year, as the RBA doubles down on its battle to regain control of inflation.
The CBA forecast was more optimistic, seeing unemployment peak at 5.1% over the same timeframe.
Either way, the RBA’s multi-year strategy of bringing inflation to heel without sacrificing post-Covid employment gains now looks unlikely to be achieved.
As union leaders protested against the anticipated rate hike in front of the RBA’s offices in Sydney on Monday morning, Spence said the risk was that the central bank would have to hike again.
The deteriorating economic outlook comes as new data showed Australia’s property slump remained on track to be one of the deepest on record.
Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said home prices could fall by as much as 15% before levelling off late next year, with Sydney property values already down by 10% from their recent peak.
Drawing from RBA research, Oliver said a property correction of that magnitude could deliver a substantial hit to the economy, as worried homeowners pull back on spending – a phenomenon known as the “wealth effect”.
A weakening property market will also weigh on homebuilding, Oliver said, adding to the multiplying pressures on the economy.
While an economic contraction was not his “base case”, he warned there was a “significant and rising” risk of recession, the chance of which would rise to as high as 45% should the RBA hike as expected on Tuesday.
“We don’t know the tipping point.”

"The race is too hard for women. They are simply not tough enough to do it."
Those are the words of Lazarus Lake, race director of the Barkley Marathons - one of the world's hardest ultramarathons which to date, of the approximate 1,000 people who have started, only 20 have ever completed.
Speaking in 2015 and daring for someone to prove him wrong, it took nine years until a British ultra-runner did just that.
Completing the extreme 100-mile course with just one minute 39 seconds to spare of the 60-hour cut-off, Jasmin Paris from Midlothian made history and cemented her name in the ultra-running history books.
But now, increasingly, she is not alone.
Last summer, there was a female one-two for the first time in the gruelling Montane Summer Spine Race from Derbyshire to Scotland. Rachel Entrekin set a new course record and became the first woman to win the Cocodona 250 in Arizona in May, while last month Sophie Woods smashed the overall record by six days to complete the Via Alpina.
It appears female runners are no longer just taking part in ultra-endurance events, they are competing with their male counterparts, breaking records and in some cases, winning races outright.
All of this has prompted suggestions that they are perhaps better suited to these kinds of challenges.
But is there any scientific proof? Do women really have any physiological or psychological advantages in endurance exercise (anything that takes more than six hours)? And if so, could we see more of these records fall in the future?
In running distances up to the marathon, there is on average a 10-12% performance gap between males and females.
Men are generally stronger and built with a bigger aerobic engine.
But as the distance increases, those physical advantages appear to become less relevant and the gap starts to narrow.
The "gender pace gap" diminishes to 0.25% in 100-mile races, according to a study of more than 20 years of amateur ultra-race data conducted by RunRepeat, in collaboration with the International Association of Ultrarunners,
Anything further than 195 miles and women have the potential to be faster.
So why might this be the case?
For Professor Andy Jones, an expert in endurance performance at the University of Exeter, there are three potential physiological explanations why women could perform better over longer distances or durations.
Fat metabolism – women have higher fat stores and burn it more efficiently, giving them a steady energy source for longer.
Muscles – women have more oxygen-efficient muscle fibres, known as "slow twitch", that are better suited for endurance activities.
Fatigue resistance – women retain more strength over hours of endurance exercise.
However, Jones, who played a key role in Eliud Kipchoge's sub two-hour marathon challenge in 2019, is keen to point out that the science in this area is "behind".
"There isn't as much hard evidence as there would be for shorter distances, which have been studied for a long time in quite some detail," he adds.
That is a view shared by Dr Richard Burden, co-lead of female athlete health and performance at the UK Sports Institute, who feels a lot more information needs to be gathered before conclusions can be made.
"At the moment we are speculating … there are definitely some physiological adaptations that you see more in women than men that are favourable for ultra-type events. But those need to be better established and more studies would need to be done."
Physiology, however, only gets you so far. The realities of ultra-endurance exercise - multi-day events, sleep deprivation, extreme terrain and conditions, to name but a few – mean the journey to the finish line is as much mental as it is physical.
And for Sophie Woods, this is where women have the edge.
"It's not necessarily about being the fastest person at the start," she says. "It is about preparation, it is about mental strength and being able to continue to persevere when things go wrong."
During the New Zealand runner's record-breaking run of the Via Alpina, she was forced to expect the unexpected – from disruption caused by wildfires that made her route longer and more dangerous to swarms of horseflies.
"I was so tired and there were so many of them and I wanted to have a complete meltdown and just cry, but I couldn't because if I stopped moving, they started biting me," she says.
"I think women are really good at adapting and continuing and just knowing that once we start something, you've just got to keep moving until you get to the finish."
That view is echoed by Yngvild Kaspersen, who last month became the first woman to win the prestigious Ultra-Trail Mont Blanc CCC race in the Alps twice. She credits her victory to the "mental game" she puts herself through in training.
The Norwegian, who balances life as a professional runner with her job as a GP, also believes female ultra-runners are so strong because camaraderie in the community is unrivalled.
"We're competitors but we're also motivating each other, inspiring each other, pushing each other to do better in the races," she says. "If you see the podiums for the women this year [at UTMB], how close we are and how we're running together out there - that's very special and I'm very proud to be a part of that community and that group of women."
So can we explain why women might be more resilient?
Sports dietitian Renee McGregor, who specialises in athlete nutrition and hormonal health, believes the answer comes from the female body itself.
"The moment women step into puberty, we are dealing with a fluctuating hormonal system," she says. "We never ever give ourselves credit for that, it's just an accepted part of being female. But actually, it is an endurance in itself and I think that's probably where a big part of our resilience comes from."
McGregor, an ultra-runner herself, points to research that suggests female runners display more disciplined and even pacing strategies than men in distance races, maximising on what she terms the female "brain bank".
"I don't think women go into these races without a lot of thought and contingency planning," McGregor adds.
"For example, if you've been through a pregnancy and you've dealt with nausea, if you've had a baby and dealt with the lack of sleep or if you've gone through fertility treatment, you have to go through so much discomfort, but you know you can get through it. And I think it's that knowledge of 'I can get through this, I can find a solution'."
One of the biggest reasons why we cannot talk with any certainty about the potential physiological and psychological advantages that women may have in this field is because participation numbers are low, with women making up roughly only 20% of those on ultramarathon start lines.
Research by SheRACES, a network set up by British ultra-runner Sophie Power to correct gender disparities in running, suggests the reasons for this range from societal perceptions around women's abilities, to concerns around the time needed for training, or access to the right support at the events themselves.
Slowly but surely, however, things are starting to change.
Earlier this year, a trail race in New Zealand became the first UTMB World Series event to achieve a 50:50 gender split, while a leading UK race provider has launched a new initiative to target gender parity at its events.
And now, according to Dr Burden, society is talking about the limits of human performance in a different way too.
"Historically, the majority of the time it [the limits of the human] will be established from male models or male sports," he says. "Now we're starting to break it up into the limits of male performance and the limits of female performance and that's a distinction that needs to be made … but to make better comparisons, we would need more women taking part in ultra events."

When it comes to participation, visibility is key.
Kaspersen describes Rachel Entrekin's historic victory at Cocodona 250, one of the most demanding ultramarathons in the world, as an "inspiration" among the elites to "dare to try".
And at the amateur level, there are those like Emily Fairs, a 22-year-old ultra-runner who documents the realities of her training and races on social media as part of her mission to get more women of all ages on start lines.
"When it comes to endurance training, there are so many components that come into it and that we are fearful of but by seeing another woman do it you think 'right, if she can do it, if she has the tools, she has the knowledge, she has the ability to do all these crazy difficult challenges, then so do I. I'm no different to her. She's no different to me'," says Fairs.
Fairs says she has received thousands of messages from women about how her content has encouraged them to lace up their trainers, and believes recent trends of female success in ultra-running are just the start.
"When the proportion is so low, we have no clue what women are capable of. We're starting to see more women get faster and enter the sport and push themselves and break records. So, who knows where we'll be 10-15 years later down the line?"

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor known for portraying Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the "X-Men" and "Star Trek: The Next Generation" series and films, died aged 86 on Oct. 28, following "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia.
As tributes poured in following his death, social media users shared a quote (archived) purportedly attributed to the thespian that took aim at Donald Trump. For example, one X user claimed Stewart said of the U.S. president in 2017:
The fact is, when America sneezes, the world catches a cold. America, I think, is on the edge of a very bad flu infection, and it's because of the man who is in the White House.
Patrick Stewart on Trump (2017): "You might say to me, well, you're not an American, what has it got to do with you? The fact is when America sneezes, the world catches a cold. America I think is on the edge of a very bad flu infection and it's because of the man who's in the White House"
— Marco Foster (@MarcoFoster_) October 29, 2026
Other users posted the alleged remark on Instagram and Facebook, while Snopes users contacted us with numerous inquiries about the late actor, including one email asking whether the comment is authentic.
In short, the quote is correctly attributed to Stewart. It originates from a video interview (archived) he gave to The A.V. Club — an online newspaper and entertainment website — that published on Nov. 16, 2017, roughly 10 months into Trump's first presidential term.
The A.V. Club posted several other clips on its website around that time that appeared to be from the same interview with Stewart. The outlet published the videos before generative artificial intelligence was widely available. Therefore, there is no reason to suspect any of the footage is AI-generated.
One clip, titled, "Sir Patrick Stewart is pretty godd*** upset about Donald Trump," features the in-question quote. It shows Stewart saying (emphasis in bold ours):
You might say to me, "Well, you're not an American, what has it got to do with you?" The fact is, when America sneezes, the world catches a cold. And America, I think, is on the edge of a very bad flu infection, and it's because of the man who is in the White House. I do find, as time goes by, I find myself becoming increasingly anxious about where he's heading.
Stewart went on to say that he was "scared" about the political situation in both the United States and Europe. He added (time code 1:01):
There are whole aspects of the country that are not being attended to, I mean, there are still all these jobs that haven't got appointees as yet. And he said, "Well the government was overstaffed anyway, there were too many people."
It probably would be fair if I said that the anxiety that I feel about politics in the United States, and particularly what is going on in the White House, reflect what I feel about Brexit, in Europe, and what a disgraceful mistake that is and how it's being proved to be with every week that goes by.
Aside from his "X Men" and "Star Trek" roles, Stewart was an award-winning stage actor who spent 16 years as a "core member" of the Royal Shakespeare Company. He received one of his two Laurence Olivier Awards for his role as Claudius in "Hamlet" at London's Novello Theatre and starred in a critically acclaimed performance of "Macbeth" on the West End in London and Broadway.
In 2010, he was knighted for his services to drama.
Stewart had been an ambassador for Refuge — a British charity that helps victims of domestic abuse — since 2007, after growing up in an abusive household.
He married American singer and songwriter Sunny Ozell in 2013 in a ceremony officiated by his friend and fellow actor Ian McKellen. He is survived by a daughter and a son.

Australia's Glenn Maxwell announces retirement from international cricket
Glenn Maxwell had already retired from one-day internationals and has now called time on his T20 international career as well; batting all-rounder's last appearance for his country came at 2026 T20 World Cup; Maxwell hit the fastest 50-over World Cup century, from 40 balls, in 2023
Monday 2 November 2026 20:00, UK
Australia all-rounder Glenn Maxwell has announced his retirement from international cricket but will continue to play T20 for Melbourne Stars in the Big Bash League.
The 38-year-old's final appearance for his country came against Oman in the T20 World Cup earlier this year, when he recorded figures of 2-13 from three overs with his off-spin and was not required to bat.
Maxwell scored five T20 international hundreds, a record he shares with India's Rohit Sharma, while he is one of only five Australian men, alongside Shane Watson, David Warner, Josh Inglis and Mitchell Marsh, to score a ton in all three international formats.

Speaking on the Final Word podcast, Maxwell said: "I suppose [I had] a small hope that I might have been able to potentially get a send-off game at the MCG. But I can completely understand the direction they're going with this [T20] squad.
"There's going to be a lot of change over the next 12 to 24 months with the Olympics coming up [in 2028], and they've got to make sure they get their eyeballs on a few young guys coming through, making sure they're getting exposed to international pressure."
Maxwell - who said he had considered trying to get ready for Australia's T20 series at home to England in late November, which includes a match in Melbourne - quit one-day international cricket in June of last year, the format in which he put in his most memorable performance during the 2023 World Cup.
He plundered a match-winning 201 not out from 128 balls against Afghanistan while battling injury as Australia recovered from 91-7 to reach a target of 292.
Maxwell's 128-ball double hundred was the-then second-fastest in all ODIs, behind India star Ishan Kishan's 126-ball effort versus Bangladesh in 2022, but is now fourth.
England white-ball captain Harry Brook smoked the quickest ODI double ton from 114 balls against Sri Lanka in October, after India's Shubman Gill had done so from 117 deliveries versus West Indies less than a month earlier.
Maxwell's heroics against Afghanistan three years ago came in a tournament in which he also hit the fastest 50-over World Cup century, from 40 deliveries against the Netherlands.
The right-hander won the 2023 and 2015 50-over World Cups with Australia, while he also hit the winning runs as his nation claimed the T20 World Cup title in 2021.
Across 286 international matches (149 ODIs, 130 T20Is and seven Tests), Maxwell scored over 7,000 runs and took 136 wickets.

Pernia’s Pop-Up Shop parent Purple Style Labs narrowed its consolidated net loss for the September quarter by 12.9% YoY to ₹68.3 Cr from ₹78.4 Cr loss incurred in the year-ago period. Sequentially, net loss went down by 22.5% from ₹88.1 Cr.
Operating revenue for the quarter grew 30.7% YoY to ₹142.1 Cr from ₹108.7 Cr, and 19% QoQ from ₹119.4 Cr. Including other income of ₹3.9 Cr, it recorded a total income of ₹146 Cr during the quarter.
The company reported an exceptional expense of ₹3.1 Cr during the quarter, resulting in a total comprehensive loss of ₹69.3 Cr.
“Exceptional item pertains to employee compensation expenses towards grant of employee stock options to eligible employees of the group and expense incurred towards fees paid for increase in authorised capital of subsidiary,” the company’s PnL read.
Total expenses jumped 36.9% to ₹211.2 Cr from ₹154.3 Cr in the year-ago period.

For people living with peripheral artery disease (PAD), walking even short distances or doing routine household tasks can become difficult because of leg pain. The condition develops when arteries supplying blood to the legs become narrow, usually because fatty deposits build up along their walls. With less blood reaching the muscles, walking can cause pain, cramps or heaviness that ease with rest. In advanced cases, pain may persist even when a person is sitting or lying down, and poor circulation can lead to wounds that do not heal.
Treatment can be challenging too because movement is an important part of managing PAD, while pain makes it difficult to stay active. Structured exercise, medicines and control of risk factors such as smoking, diabetes and high blood pressure can help manage the condition. When blood flow is severely reduced, procedures may be needed to prevent damage to the feet and legs. PAD can also affect overall cardiovascular health, increasing the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Managing pain
Pain, cramps, heaviness in the calf or thigh that develop during walking and ease with rest are known as intermittent claudication. This happens when narrowed arteries cannot supply enough blood to meet the muscles’ increased needs during activity.
Venu S., consultant vascular surgeon, Prashanth Hospitals, Chennai, says structured walking programmes can help patients gradually increase the distance they can walk. Patients are generally advised to walk until the discomfort becomes moderate, rest until it settles and then resume walking. Sessions commonly last 30 to 45 minutes and take place several times a week, with supervision where possible.
He says patients who follow a structured programme for about three months may be able to walk twice as far, or more, before pain begins. The pace and duration should suit each patient’s ability. Those who find walking difficult may need an adapted exercise programme under medical supervision.
Balaji V., senior consultant, vascular surgery, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai, says quitting smoking, eating a healthy diet, staying physically active and controlling blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol are also important parts of treatment.
Exercise should not mean pushing through severe pain. Pain that does not settle with rest needs medical assessment. Pain in the feet or toes while resting, particularly at night, can indicate a serious reduction in blood flow and requires prompt medical attention.
Diagnosis and treatment
Diagnosis usually begins with a review of symptoms and medical history, followed by an examination of the legs and feet, including checking the pulses. Doctors may measure the ankle-brachial index (ABI), which compares blood pressure at the ankle with that in the arm, to assess blood flow. A Doppler ultrasound scan can help identify narrowed arteries and assess circulation. In patients with severe symptoms or wounds that do not heal, a CT angiogram may be needed to locate the blockage and plan treatment.
Medicines aim to relieve symptoms, slow the progression of arterial disease and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke. Antiplatelet medicines such as aspirin or clopidogrel help prevent blood clots. Statins lower cholesterol and help stabilise fatty deposits in artery walls. Medicines to control blood pressure and diabetes are also important. Cilostazol can help some patients with walking-related pain walk farther before symptoms begin, but it is not suitable for people with heart failure. Select patients may need additional medicines to reduce cardiovascular and limb-related risks.
Experts say treatment often needs to continue long term, even when symptoms improve. Patients should not stop or change prescribed medicines without consulting their doctor.
Diabetes can damage nerves and reduce sensation in the feet, allowing cuts and wounds to go unnoticed. It can also affect smaller arteries, making some blockages harder to treat. High blood pressure and cholesterol contribute to arterial damage and the build-up of fatty deposits. Kidney disease can cause calcium to build up in artery walls and delay wound healing. Heart disease can occur alongside PAD because both may result from the same underlying process.
During follow-up, doctors assess changes in walking distance and symptoms and may repeat ABI measurements or Doppler scans to check blood flow. Blood tests can help monitor cholesterol, blood sugar and kidney function.
Preventing complications
When symptoms remain disabling despite medicines and exercise, doctors may consider a procedure to widen the narrowed artery. The decision depends on the location and extent of the blockage, the severity of symptoms and the patient’s overall health.
Angioplasty uses a small balloon to widen a narrowed artery. A stent may be placed to help keep it open. Experts say newer techniques can also help treat complex blockages.
Intravascular lithotripsy uses shock waves delivered through a specialised balloon to modify heavy calcium deposits in the artery, making it easier to widen the vessel. Atherectomy devices can remove fatty deposits in selected cases, while thrombectomy devices are used to remove blood clots. The appropriate method depends on the type and location of the blockage.
For extensive disease, bypass surgery creates an alternative route for blood to reach the affected part of the leg. The choice between a procedure performed through a blood vessel and surgery depends on the blockage, the patient’s condition and the likely benefits and risks.
Pain at rest, wounds that do not heal or gangrene can indicate that the leg is at risk and require urgent medical assessment. A wound that has not healed within two weeks, a cold or discoloured foot, or a black patch on a toe or heel should not be ignored. Sudden, severe leg pain accompanied by paleness, coldness, numbness or weakness is a medical emergency because it may indicate a sudden blockage of an artery.
Regular foot checks are particularly important for people with diabetes, who may not feel an injury developing. Recognising worsening symptoms and seeking timely care can help preserve mobility and prevent serious damage to the feet and legs.

Vietnam withdrew on Monday a proposal allowing children aged 15 to 17 to donate their organs after death following public criticism in a country where deceased donor transplants remain limited.
The Southeast Asian country began kidney transplants in 1992 and performs the most annual transplants in the region, according to state media.
However, the vast majority of transplants in Vietnam rely on living donors. Transplants in many other nations mostly use organs from deceased donors, expanding their donor pool.
Officials in Vietnam say they are seeking to update a 2006 law on organ and tissue donation, aiming to increase life-saving transplants while safeguarding donors.
A draft submitted to the National Assembly last month proposed allowing 15- to 17-year-olds to donate their tissues, organs or bodies after death, provided the child's parent or legal representative consented.
But, after online backlash, officials removed the under-18 donor provision from a revised draft dated Sunday, with the government saying it had accepted recommendations from lawmakers that only legal adults should be permitted to donate their organs.
Dissent is heavily restricted in communist Vietnam, but opposition centred on whether parental consent could adequately protect child donors from pressure or exploitation.
Criticism also focused on a survey of schoolchildren as young as seven conducted in October to gather feedback on the draft law.
The poll prompted questions about whether minors could understand complex medical, legal and ethical issues, state outlet Tuoi Tre News said.
It said "the provision allowing minors to register as posthumous organ donors prompted considerable controversy and differing opinions among the public".
"Taking these concerns into account, the government has revised the draft," stipulating that only people aged 18 or older may donate their organs, Tuoi Tre said.
National Assembly deputy Pham Khanh Phong Lan urged lawmakers last month to oppose allowing child organ donors, saying: "You cannot sacrifice one child to save another."
One Threads user posted on Monday: "The power of public scrutiny has paid off. It is a relief to see this draft proposal rejected."
The newly revised draft still allows living minors to donate regenerative tissue, for bone marrow or stem cell transplants, to family members when no suitable adult donor is available.
The procedure would require health assessments, counselling and consent from both the child and their legal representative.
A draft law is expected to be approved this month.
