How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
- Published
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.
Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.
The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.
But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.
Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.
A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.
"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - Vučiċ supporters - gathering near voting stations," Péter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.
Orbán in Hungary, Vučiċ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, Vučiċ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.
They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.
The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar Vučiċ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor Orbán did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.
There has been speculation this week that Vučiċ spoke to Orbán twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that Orbán convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
Vučiċ denies that he spoke to Orbán before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor Orbán, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.
An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.
There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number Péter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija Srdanoviċ, said on the eve of the vote.
Srdanoviċ was one of those Péter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
Orbán, 63, and Vučiċ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.
The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.
Hungarian companies close to Orbán were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the Orbán and Vučiċ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Áron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

It is officially the flu season with winter and monsoon seasons creeping in on large parts of the world. There is a need to take precautions and be aware of the risks of the season, particularly at a time when we are hearing of old viruses resurging, or new, never-before heard pathogens rearing their heads, even known microorganisms that cause disease among humans, after a zoonotic spillover.
As in the case of the Shamonda virus. Last week France reported the first human Shamonda virus case, a virus usually circulating amongst livestock. The severely immunocompromised patient died, spurring global public health concerns. While France said there was no health risk as a result of this, there are definitely problems when a new pathogen crosses the barrier. For everything we currently know about the Shamonda virus, read Athira Elssa Johnson’s explainer, here.
She also writes on Melioidosis in India: a potentially deadly infection that may be going undetected. Melioidosis caused by B. pseudomallei which is found in soil and water in tropical and subtropical regions, can cause pneumonia, bloodstream infection, skin and soft-tissue infections, abscesses in organs such as the liver and spleen, septic arthritis and bone infections. It can also affect the kidneys, muscles and prostate.
Meanwhile, as the second patient in Nigeria, a relative of the first case of death from Ebola in the nation, also died of Ebola, some hopeful news came from DR Congo where the Ebola vaccine trial began for the Bundibugyo strain.
In the U.S., where an early U.S. flu season has set in, doctors warned that the current strain may signal a higher risk for younger people; and urged them to get shots.
Talking of the weather, it is also time to discuss pollution and climate-related health effects. Nikhil M. Babu writes that air pollution in Delhi-NCR has come ahead of winter.
In Mumbai, Yohaan Varghese says another crisis is brewing, as attention remains on the northern States. Mumbai recorded 231 days of ‘good’ or ‘satisfactory’ air quality in 2026. The BMC has been forced to unveil a winter pollution action plan.
Geetha Srimathi interprets a global report that claims: Extreme weather, harmful chemicals escalating health risks among food workers.
As a bellwether State for healthcare in the country, what happens in Kerala affects the entire nation, in some way. The Spinal Muscular Atrophy controversy, currently brewing in the southern State too could contain lessons for the nation.
First do read C. Maya’s explainer on what this controversy is all about, here. After the government switched the drug in its SMA programme from branded to generic, parents of children living with SMA have been asking for a switch back to the branded version; meanwhile the label on a drug bottle has sparked concerns, and political parties have now latched on to the issue.
Meanwhile, experts have opined that the Row over SMA drug distribution in Keralam is unwarranted and a hospital rejected charges of ‘clinical trial drugs’ given to children. Further a doctor at SAT Hospital said Parents were actually counselled about the generic drug that was to be used ahead of administration.
We are sure to be following up this story until it reaches its logical conclusion.
Further on the regulation scenario in the health care/medical sector, the issue of prices of drugs was top of the agenda after the recent Supreme Court judgement. Devyanshi Bihani looked at data and found that ₹8,447 crore in medicine overcharging claims remain outstanding as SC seeks wider price controls.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan wrote on the concerns over the National Medical Commission withdrawing the 2023 Rules on medical education standards. While the government claims this has been done to eliminate duplication and multiple overlaps, it has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.
She also recorded the disability lobby’s demand that the Centre classify communication aids as essential products.
Dr. C. Aravinda explained what the National Medical Commission’s new guidelines say about advertising in medicine, while Afshan Yasmeen reported a Lancet review that called for clinical assessment over routine scans for back pain.

This recent UK-Chennai collaborative study showed that good-quality diets are associated with better cholesterol levels even among those with a genetic predisposition.

The Mumbai Crime Branch police arrested a 22-year-old woman from Haryana in connection with the firing involving Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff in Juhu last month, taking the total number of arrests in the case to 13.
According to a press note issued by the Crime Branch on Monday (November 2, 2026), the woman was arrested in Karnal district in Haryana on Sunday (November 1, 2026), with assistance from the local police. Investigators suspect her involvement in the conspiracy behind the shooting.
The incident took place on the evening of October 18, when assailants opened fire near a football ground in Juhu as Mr. Shroff was leaving the area. His driver and a bystander were injured in the incident.
A case was subsequently registered at the Juhu police station under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) and the Arms Act before the investigation was transferred to the Mumbai Crime Branch.
The investigation has since expanded beyond Maharashtra, with the Crime Branch arresting suspects from Kota in Rajasthan, Delhi and Sonipat in Haryana. Two women were among those earlier arrested in Delhi in connection with the alleged weapons supply network, making the latest accused the third woman to be arrested in the case.
The Crime Branch also invoked provisions of the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crime Act (MCOCA) on October 27, following which all 11 accused arrested at that stage were produced before a special MCOCA court. The court permitted the Crime Branch to formally arrest them under the stringent organised crime law.
Investigators are also probing the alleged involvement of absconding gangster Anil Pandit, believed to be associated with the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, in the conspiracy behind the shooting.
The latest arrest follows the apprehension of another accused from Sonipat, who was subsequently remanded in police custody till November 6.
Police have not disclosed the identity of the woman arrested from Karnal or specified her alleged role in the conspiracy. Further investigation is underway to establish her involvement and identify others who may have assisted in planning or executing the attack.

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.
Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.
Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.
Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.
The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).
'Nigerian patient did not travel to Congo'
In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.
The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).
Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.
Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.
The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.
U.S. introduces new protocol for all travellers
United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.
Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

The Supreme Court has allowed the bursting of approved green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR on November 7 and 8, ahead of Diwali 2026, but has imposed strict conditions on manufacturers, sellers and consumers, according to PTI. The court directed authorities to ensure that only certified green crackers are manufactured and sold. Diwaliwill be celebrated on November 8 this year. The temporary relaxation comes after the court expressed concern over the implementation of its earlier directions and measures taken by authorities to control firecracker-related pollution in the national capital region. Quick answers to key questions Green crackers may be burst on November 7 and 8, from 6 am to 7 am and from 8 pm to 10 pm. The complete ban returns on November 9. Manufacturers must hold valid certifications from both CSIR-NEERI and PESO. They may produce only green crackers listed on the CSIR-NEERI website, during the permitted manufacturing window of November 2–6. Buy only approved green crackers with product-specific QR codes. Scanning the code should show details such as the manufacturer’s identity, registrations and licences, formulation, and test certificate. Firecrackers containing barium, products not approved by CSIR-NEERI as green crackers, and crackers joined in series, such as ‘ladis’ or garlands, are prohibited. They cannot be burst within 300 metres of hospitals, health centres, old-age homes, educational institutions, or notified silence zones. These areas are to be marked and publicised as no-cracker zones. A bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale passed the directions in an order dated October 29, which was made available on Monday. It clarified that the complete ban on firecrackers would return from November 9. The Supreme Court has specified that manufacturers must hold valid certifications from the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (CSIR-NEERI) and the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO). Only manufacturers possessing valid certification from both bodies are permitted to produce approved green firecrackers. The manufacturing window has been restricted to November 2-6, 2026, and manufacturers can produce only those green crackers listed on the CSIR-NEERI website. The court has also directed that boxes containing green crackers must remain completely sealed to prevent conventional or unauthorised fireworks from being mixed with certified products. Firecrackers containing Barium, as well as products that have not been approved by CSIR-NEERI as green crackers, cannot be manufactured or used under the court's directions. The manufacture and sale of firecrackers joined in series, commonly known as 'ladis' or garlands, have also been prohibited. The court has permitted the sale of only approved green firecrackers carrying product-specific QR codes. Scanning these codes must display details including the manufacturer's identity, NEERI registration, PESO and district magistrate licence, formulation and test certificate. Traders whose licences were cancelled will receive temporary restoration from November 4 to November 6, to enable them to sell approved green crackers purchased from CSIR-NEERI-certified manufacturers. The bench has also directed authorities to require manufacturers and traders to furnish monetary security deposits. These deposits will be forfeited immediately if they violate the court's directions or applicable regulations. District collectors and commissioners, in consultation with the police, will identify designated locations for the sale of green crackers across the NCR. The sale of fireworks at any other location, including through online platforms, will remain prohibited. Authorities have also been directed to prevent the movement of illegal and conventional firecrackers into Delhi-NCR by checking vehicles entering the region. The Supreme Court has allowed the bursting of green firecrackers only during two specified windows on November 7 and 8: Morning: 6 am to 7 am Evening: 8 pm to 10 pm The permission is subject to restrictions on the location of fireworks. No crackers can be burst within a 300-metre radius of hospitals, nursing homes, primary and district health centres, old-age homes, educational institutions and notified silence zones. Authorities must declare these areas no-cracker zones, mark them on the ground and publicise their locations. The court said, “Though imposition of a blanket ban seems to be the ideal solution, we are of the opinion that this court, at this point in time, is short of adequate data to decide whether or not a complete ban would be the best solution to solve the problem of environmental pollution, caused by bursting firecrackers.” It also observed that the right to follow an individual practice, even if it has a religious association, is subject to constitutional restrictions. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), in consultation with state pollution control boards and their regional offices, has been directed to monitor AQI levels across their respective NCR jurisdictions. Authorities must prepare daily air-quality reports covering November 2-8 and a further set of reports for November 9-30. They will also collect sand and water samples during the period for comparative analysis. The court has asked state education department secretaries in NCR to sensitise schoolchildren about the health and environmental impact of pollution, particularly during festivals. The State government has released ₹9.86 crore for the modernisation of 16 drug de-addiction centres functioning in government hospitals across Andhra Pradesh, with a focus on strengthening medical treatment, counselling and rehabilitation services for people suffering from substance addiction.
The funds have been released by the Prohibition and Excise Department to upgrade infrastructure and provide advanced medical equipment at the centres.
A statement issued on Friday said the initiative aimed to make de-addiction services accessible at the grassroots level while strengthening specialised treatment and rehabilitation facilities at major regional hospitals. The proposed works include renovation of hospital buildings, restructuring of rooms, installation of glass doors, improvement of electrical systems and provision of modern furniture.
The centres will be equipped with advanced medical devices, including biofeedback machines, breath-testing equipment, multiparameter monitors and ECG machines. Digital information technology facilities will also be introduced to improve healthcare delivery.
Modernisation works will be taken up at 10 government teaching and major hospitals under the Medical Education Department. They include Kurnool Government General Hospital, SVRR Government General Hospital in Tirupati, Guntur Government General Hospital, Srikakulam Government General Hospital, Nandyal Government General Hospital, Rajamahendravaram Government General Hospital, Ongole Government General Hospital, Vijayawada Government General Hospital, King George Hospital in Visakhapatnam and the Institute of Mental Health under Kadapa Government General Hospital.
Of these, Vijayawada Government General Hospital, King George Hospital in Visakhapatnam and the Institute of Mental Health in Kadapa will be developed as specialised Centres of Excellence. These three regional centres will provide advanced medical treatment, specialised addiction care and comprehensive rehabilitation support to people struggling with substance abuse.
Infrastructure at six other district and area hospitals will also be upgraded. They are Anakapalli District Hospital, Narsapuram Area Hospital, Narasaraopet Area Hospital, Chittoor District Hospital, Hindupur District Hospital and Bapatla Area Hospital.
The works at these hospitals will focus on improving buildings and electrical infrastructure and installing modern medical equipment to strengthen de-addiction treatment services.

North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.
Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.
North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.
Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.
The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.
The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.
Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.
“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.
North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.
A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.
The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.
The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.
The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.
Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.
The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

Editor’s note, November 1, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary. The one below was originally published in August 2025.
Can’t commit to vegetarianism but want animals to suffer less? You’ve got options.
This doesn’t have to be all-or-nothing.
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here.
I typically eat vegetarian, and have considered going fully vegan out of concern for animal welfare. But lately my on-again, off-again gastrointestinal problems have been acting up, and I’ve had to go back on a more restricted diet to manage my symptoms — no spice, no garlic or onions, nothing acidic, and nothing caffeinated. Sticking to a “bland” diet is hard enough, but doing so while vegetarian is very difficult when things like tomatoes and onions and grapefruits are off the table.
I know a lot of people with these issues eat fish or meat, and some medical professionals recommend drinking chicken bone broth to soothe flare-ups. I don’t want to abandon my commitment to animal welfare while my gut sorts itself out, but my food options are limited right now. How should I approach this?
Dear Would-Be Vegetarian,
You’re not alone in finding it hard to stick to a purely vegetarian diet. Only 5 percent of American adults say they’re vegetarian or vegan. What’s more, one study found that 84 percent of people who adopt those diets actually go back to eating meat at some point. And most of them aren’t even dealing with the gastrointestinal problems you face.
So, it speaks to the depth of your moral commitment that you’re really wrestling with this. I’ll have some concrete suggestions for you in a bit, but first I want to emphasize that how you approach the question of meat-eating will depend on your underlying moral theory.
There’s a classic split in moral philosophy between deontologists and utilitarians. A deontologist is someone who thinks an action is moral if it’s fulfilling a duty — and we have universal duties like, “always treat others as ends in themselves, never as means to an end.” From that perspective, killing an animal for food would be inherently morally wrong, because you’re treating the animal as a means to an end.
Meanwhile, a utilitarian is someone who thinks that an action is moral if it produces good consequences — and behaving morally means producing the most happiness or well-being possible, or reducing the most suffering possible. Utilitarian philosophers like Peter Singer argue that we should be reducing, and ideally eliminating, the suffering that animals endure at our hands.
Deontologists and utilitarians are often pitted against each other, but they actually have one big thing in common: They both believe in a universal moral principle — whether it’s “always treat others as ends in themselves” or “always maximize happiness.”
A lot of people find that comforting, because it offers certainty about how we should act. Even if acting morally requires hard sacrifices, it’s incredibly soothing to think, “If I just do X, then I’ll know for sure that I’m being a good person!”
But these moral theories assume that all the complexity of human life can be reduced to one tidy formula. Can it, really?
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!
Another school of philosophy — pragmatism — says we should be skeptical of fixed moral principles. Human life is so complicated, with many different factors at play in any ethical dilemma, so we should be pluralistic about what makes outcomes valuable instead of acting like the only thing that matters is maximizing a single value (say, happiness). And human society is always evolving, so a moral idea that makes sense in one context may no longer make sense in a different context. To a pragmatist, moral truths are contingent, not universal and unchanging.
I think one pragmatist who can really help you out is the University of Michigan’s Elizabeth Anderson. In a 2005 essay applying pragmatism to the question of eating meat, the philosopher points out that for most of human history, we couldn’t have survived and thrived without killing or exploiting animals for food, transportation, and energy. The social conditions for granting animals moral rights didn’t really exist on a mass scale until recently (although certain non-Western societies did ascribe moral worth to some animals).
“The possibility of moralizing our relations to animals (other than our pets),” Anderson writes, “has come to us only lately, and even then not to us all, and not with respect to all animal species.”
In other words, Anderson doesn’t think there’s some universal rule like “eating animals is inherently morally wrong.” It’s our social and technological circumstances that have made us more able than before to see animals as part of our moral circle. She also doesn’t believe there’s a single yardstick — like sentience or intelligence — by which we can judge how much of our moral concern an animal deserves. That’s because moral evaluation isn’t just about animals’ intrinsic capacities, but also about their relationships to us. It matters whether we’ve made them dependent on us by domesticating them, say, or whether they live independently in the wild.
It also matters whether they’re fundamentally hostile to us. Killing bedbugs? Totally fine! They may be sentient, but, Anderson writes, “We are in a permanent state of war with them, without possibility of negotiating for peace. To one-sidedly accommodate their interests…would amount to surrender.”
Anderson’s point is not that animals’ intelligence and sentience don’t matter. It’s that lots of other things matter, too, including our own ability to thrive.
With this pragmatic approach in mind, you can consider how to balance your concern for animal welfare with your concern for your own welfare. Instead of thinking in terms of a moral absolute that would force you into a “purist” diet no matter the cost to you, you can consider a “reducetarian” diet, which allows you to ease your own struggle while also taking care for animals seriously.
The key thing to realize is that some types of animal consumption cause a lot less suffering than others.
For one thing, if you’re eating meat, try to buy the pasture-raised kind and not the kind that comes from factory farms — the huge industrialized facilities that supply 99 percent of America’s meat. In these facilities, animals are tightly packed together and live under unbelievably harsh and unsanitary conditions. They’re also often mutilated without pain relief: think pigs being castrated, cows being dehorned, and hens being debeaked. Oh, and chickens have been bred to be so big that they’re in constant pain; they live miserable lives from start to finish.
A pasture-raised label doesn’t mean an animal has been spared all of the harms of modern agriculture — it doesn’t guarantee that pain relief is used for painful procedures, and farm animals across different production systems have been bred to maximize production, which can take a toll on their welfare. And of course they’ll ultimately meet the same fate as those raised on factory farms — slaughter. But your goal here is to meaningfully reduce, not 100 percent eliminate, the harms. And at least pasture-raised animals have gotten to roam around in a field and engage in natural behaviors up until the end.
It’s a similar story for fish, by the way. More than half of the fish we eat comes from fish farms, which are basically just underwater factory farms. Wild-caught fish is not perfect — slow, suffocating deaths are common — but it’s better than farmed.
The caveat here is that a lot of the welfare labels you’ll see on animal products are basically a con. And some certification schemes have similar names, so you have to pay close attention. If you see the label “Certified Humane,” that’s genuinely higher-welfare — but don’t mistake it for “American Humane Certified,” which is really not. And be wary of putting much stock in labels like “cage-free” or “free-range.” They’re better than nothing, but because the terms are often ill-defined and unenforced, they’re not as meaningful as you might think. Here’s a good guide to separating the real deal from the advertising spin.
Another classic recommendation among animal welfare advocates is to eat bigger animals — in other words, go for beef rather than chicken. That’s both because of how miserable chickens’ lives are on factory farms and because, as my former colleague Kelsey Piper has written, it just takes way more chicken lives than cow lives to feed people. Cows are huge, producing about 500 pounds of beef apiece, while a chicken yields only a few pounds of meat. So, every year, the average American eats about 23 chickens and just over one-tenth of one cow.
That said, cows take a heavier toll on the climate than chickens do, so you don’t want to eat tons of beef either. The environment is also one of the key values at stake in our consumption choices, so that has to factor in, too.
Of course, another possibility — to the extent that this works with your gastrointestinal issues — is to reach for low-fiber plant-based foods like tofu, seitan, and the smorgasbord of newer products now available (like Beyond and Impossible burgers).
But assuming you’re going to eat meat, it’s a good idea to set some clear parameters and standards around your reducetarian diet. A lot of reducetarians — myself included — have fallen into the trap of saying, “I’ll reduce how much meat I eat,” but forgetting to quantify what that means. That can lead you to eat more meat than you’d intended. So it’s probably better to commit to something like “weekday vegetarian” or “vegan before six” — you can check out the Reducetarian Foundation for suggestions.
At the end of the day, remember that there’s a plurality of values at stake here, and no one of them necessarily trumps all the others. If you feel that eating some meat is important for your well-being right now, and you try to do that in ways that keep suffering for animals to a minimum, I don’t think you need to feel bad about that. That’s because you won’t be shirking your values: You’ll be recognizing that your values are plural, and you’re doing your best to balance between them. That may be the best any of us can really do.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- The blogger Bentham’s Bulldog published a piece titled “How to cause less suffering while eating animals.” It contains some of the same recommendations I mentioned above, but the underlying ethical framework is different and it makes one recommendation I didn’t: “offsetting” your meat consumption by donating to highly effective animal charities. I worry that offsetting might create a moral hazard, as with people offsetting their carbon emissions and then potentially feeling free to fly more. But it’s worth considering, particularly if you pair it with clear parameters around your reducetarian diet.
- This Aeon essay answers a question I’ve often wondered about: Why haven’t other animals — say, birds — developed complex civilizations like we humans have? Why don’t they build rocket ships, argue about economic policy, and play canasta? I’m grateful to the evolutionary biologist who wrote this piece for finally giving me a satisfying answer.
- I can’t stop thinking about this post on how AI companies may have designed chatbots to play an underspecified “helpful assistant” character who, due to being underspecified, looks to the internet for examples of how to play that role, finds tons of science fiction about cheesy robots, and thus starts to behave like a cheesy sci-fi robot (ChatGPT will say things like, “Gee, that really tickles my circuits!”). This post is mega-long, deeply trippy, and worth reading.

Don't be cantankerous.
David Heinemeier Hansson has some advice for engineers as they adjust to AI. Often referred to as DHH, Hansson created the webapp framework Ruby on Rails and has fashioned himself into a software sage.
On Monday, Hansson shared his prediction on X: "The age of agents is going to be amazing for most programmers, but it'll be hard times for the cantankerous ones."
Hansson wrote that special abilities won't save those who are difficult to work with. That would be a dramatic shift in software engineering, where some so-called "cracked" coders can get away with large egos or social awkwardness.
"Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote.
The prediction sparked a conversation among engineers about their social habits and professionalism. One pointed out the irony: agents "don't care how cantankerous you are," but your human coworkers do.
One user wrote a eulogy to the "guy whose whole job security was 'only I know how this works.'"
Dart cofounder Zack Swafford wrote that teams only tolerated bad attitudes because the staffers had "arcane tribal knowledge."
Others questioned how new the change was. People skills have long been valuable, from networking your way into a job to landing that big promotion.
"Been true in every company forever," one X user commented. "Skills get you hired, being easy to work with keeps you around. Agents just make it obvious faster."
Hansson is committed to the future of AI coding. In September, he declared "pencils down" on handwritten code. Hansson explained that writing code was an "exceptional state," performed only when something went wrong with the AI-generated code.
For some engineers, Hansson's post was a vocabulary lesson. "I had to search the definition of 'cantankerous,'" one engineer commented. "First time reading that word."
For the record: cantankerous means bad-tempered and uncooperative.

Seamless failover when power cuts out. Discreet; disappears almost completely behind your fridge. Reasonably mobile; can conceivably be used for other needs in a pinch.
TIRED
Scheduling system is very basic. No logging system to speak of. Installation is tougher than it seems. (Learn from my mistakes!) Very costly; TOU rate-shifting benefits are minimal.
Every part of a power outage is always a massive nuisance, but nothing is quite as aggravating as losing power to your refrigerator and the resultant spoilage of everything inside it.
Homes with a whole-house battery backup can avoid this headache, but the cost for a system like a Tesla Powerwall can easily hit $15,000 after installation. It takes an awful lot of melted ice cream for those numbers to balance out.
BioLite—known for its range of lighting and portable power solutions—is on the cusp of launching an alternative to whole-house batteries. Backup by BioLite is a modular battery system designed specifically with the fridge in mind, offering long-term emergency power at a fraction of the cost of more complex systems and which homeowners can install themselves. I installed it in my home and found it a capable (if limited) way to get a little extra peace of mind.
Smart Cells
Backup by BioLite is hardly a difficult concept to grasp. The massive battery—offering 1526 watt-hours of power with a rated output of 1800 watts (and supporting peak surges up to 3000 watts)—mounts on the wall behind your refrigerator, or it can simply sit on top of it. The power pack measures 29 inches high by 13 inches wide, and a single unit weighs a hefty 40 pounds. No special wiring is required. You simply plug the Backup into a standard 120-volt outlet, then plug your refrigerator into the Backup.
Want more power? Backup’s Core unit can be daisy-chained to a Backup Extend add-on device, an identically sized (but slightly lighter) unit that doubles the power capacity to 3072 Wh.
Depending on your refrigerator, the full “Backup Complete” solution, with two cells, can provide up to 60 hours of running time if the grid goes down. If that’s not enough, additional Backup Extend devices can be added in series, with a total maximum capacity of 10.5 KWh. (Though, at that point, you may as well spring for a whole-house solution.)
DIY Time
One of the biggest selling points of Backup by BioLite is that you can install it yourself, with no electrician. I’ve got no trouble wielding a drill, so I undertook the effort to see if BioLite’s promise of a 30-minute install would pan out. I tested Backup Complete, with two Backup batteries situated side by side.
The process seems straightforward (and is enhanced by a helpful printed manual), but I quickly learned that my refrigerator’s location—tucked into an alcove—would complicate things because of the limited space in which to work. BioLite suggests having an extra pair of hands to hoist the heavy battery packs into place, but there was simply no room for my wife to squeeze into the alcove to help with any of the process. I managed on my own, but I expect this will present a challenge for some.
The batteries mount to metal brackets, and BioLite provides a template to help you position them properly and ensure they are level. It’s essential that the two batteries in a Backup Complete arrangement be located at a specific distance from one another, as the cable that connects the two is limited in length.
I dutifully chose a location for the template, ensuring that the batteries—once attached to the wall—would not block access to the electrical outlet. Since my outlet is placed 3 feet off the ground, that meant hanging the batteries high, with the tops level with my eyeline.
Photograph: Christopher Null
BioLite provides all the hardware you need to mount the units in drywall, including anchors and screws. I tried to find a stud to anchor at least one of the screws, but found none in the spots where I needed them. Oddly, I had to use my own drywall anchors for some of the screws, as BioLite’s screw-in style anchors refused to engage and drive into the wall. (I don’t blame BioLite for this but rather some peculiarity with how that section of wall was constructed.)
With holes drilled and anchors set, I carefully attached the metal brackets to the wall. Everything looked level and sturdy, at which point I heaved the first of the massive batteries into place. Or, at least, I tried to. Turns out, I’d made a massive mistake. My idea was to mount the bracket so the Core battery was flush with the right-hand wall, but unfortunately, the Backup template isn’t designed with enough buffer space on each side of the brackets. The batteries stick out well beyond the sides of the brackets and a bit beyond the template; in my case, with the template flush with the wall, the battery pushed up against the wall and was unable to properly seat atop the bracket. Even if it had, it wouldn’t have mattered: The outlets for the Core battery are on its right side, so you need another few inches to make room to plug things into it (and to scan the QR code printed there during setup).
All of that is a long way of saying that BioLite simply needs to make its template larger to account for the extra room needed on the right side of the device. It’s also a long way for me to say that I then had to disassemble the brackets and redo the entire thing, shifting everything left a few inches.
Photograph: Christopher Null
With my brackets finally repositioned, I was able to mount the batteries on them. The shape of the cells and their lack of handholds makes them a little awkward to wrestle into place—particularly after my earlier mishaps with the misplaced brackets—but once I had them hanging where they were supposed to be, secured with a single screw on the underside of the bracket, everything felt amply secure. The entire process took about 90 minutes.
With all that said, if I had to do it again, I’d strongly consider just dropping the batteries on top of the fridge instead of bothering with the wall mount, a setup fully endorsed by BioLite. This would save a lot of time and headache, and this design would make them far easier to move elsewhere in case of future emergencies.
Energized
After plugging everything in, the batteries begin charging automatically. Some status lights on the left side of each battery indicate charge level, but these were hard to see, especially after pushing the fridge back into place. (I also noted that my fridge is no longer flush with the wall, now sticking out a couple extra inches due to the added hardware behind it.)
Photograph: Christopher Null
Before replacing the fridge, I made sure I had the app setup. As noted earlier, BioLite’s Backup app requires you to scan a QR code on the side of the battery, but after that it’s a fairly quick jog through pairing the units with your phone, then bridging them to connect to your home Wi-Fi network. A firmware update then started, during which my refrigerator was without power, though this only took a few minutes.
While the Backup app is intuitive and easy to use, I was a little surprised by how simplistic it is—perhaps overly so. Front and center, you’ll see some basic stats: Battery charge level, and energy input and output levels—including whether you are drawing from the battery or the grid. If you have solar power (I don’t), this is split from grid power input so you can track usage types. If you have multiple Backup batteries, you can drill down to see the battery life remaining for each.
BioLite has done a generally great job with Backup’s emergency power features. When I cut the input power manually by tripping the circuit breaker, the battery kicked in immediately and without delay. Batteries draw down roughly equally, ensuring that over time they’ll be taxed at about the same rate. (BioLite specs that after 4,000 cycles, total capacity should remain at 80 percent of each battery’s original maximum.)
What’s missing? When the power goes out, there’s no audible alarm or other notification, except for a push notification that’s sent to your app. An alarm option would be helpful, as would a notification when power is restored. As it stands, the only way to know if the power is on is to check the app to see where output to the refrigerator is coming from. It also looks like BioLite’s estimate of my backup time (“a day”) is overly optimistic. Based on my refrigerator’s average draw of 170 watts, I expect I’d have on the order of 18 hours of reserve power, which BioLite’s app should be able to easily calculate. (That said, I have avoided running the batteries down to zero, as I wanted to preserve their longevity.)
ScreenshotBioLite Backup app via Christopher Null
ScreenshotBioLite Backup app via Christopher Null
As with all home batteries, there’s some bonus value in Backup to be found in running the battery when there’s not a power outage. That’s because you can take advantage of Time of Use (TOU) rate billing from your utility, running off of battery power during peak times when rates are high (usually the afternoon and evening), and drawing from the grid and recharging the batteries when rates are low. I had to do some research to find out if my utility provider even offered TOU billing, as I’ve had a conventional, static rate plan since we moved into this house four years ago. Turns out they did, and I promptly switched over to the new one to give this a try.
It’s easy to set up a battery schedule in the Backup app: Just set the time each day you want the battery to kick in and the time for it to switch back to grid power under the Scheduling tab. Charging can be paused during certain times of the day as well, and you can set a lower limit for how far the batteries can drain. Weekends can be excluded from all of this at your discretion.
Unfortunately, that’s it: You can’t set multiple on/off cycles during the day (my provider has two peak disconnected billing times during the winter, so this would have been nice), nor can you set different schedules for different times of year (again, my provider has three different billing schedules, depending on the month). If you’re going to spend thousands of dollars on backup batteries, it would be useful to be able to really fine-tune how they’re used. I did encounter one bug when trying to save the schedule, but a quick force-quit and restart ultimately got everything working fine.
The other missing feature is a log. Power nerds like me would love to see how long the battery ran each day, how much power was used during each run, how much power it required to recharge it, and potentially how much money was saved. Unfortunately, there’s no logging system at all in the Backup app aside from a simple record of when outages happened along with any errors or updates.
It’s easy to do the rough math on how much money I’m now saving. For the fall, I am able to shift four hours (5 to 9 pm) of refrigerator running time that would normally cost 8.6 cents per kWh to the BioLite batteries, which recharge after hours at 4.3 cents per kWh. While the numbers are surely imperfect due to the vagaries of energy loss among these various components, I’m now able to move 680 Wh of usage from the higher rate to the lower rate each day. Total savings: 3 cents per day, or about a dollar a month. That’s admittedly not very impressive, but in the summer months, the peak usage rate here hits 16.2 cents per kWh, moving monthly savings up to three dollars each month.
OK, still not that impressive, but not nothing.
A Costly Life Vest
One final feature of note is that BioLite ships the unit with a power strip, complete with an optional magnetic backing that lets you slap it onto the side of your fridge. This power strip attaches to a second outlet on the Backup and can be used to connect additional devices to your battery backup system. The power strip is totally optional, but it’s a capable product, with three standard outlets, two USB-A, and two USB-C plugs. Ultimately, I didn’t use it because I didn’t have anywhere convenient to place it, and nothing to plug into it anyway, but it’s a nice-to-have feature that I’ll hold onto in case the power cuts out this winter and I want to run other devices in the dark. With 1800 watts of output, the battery is strong enough to power everything from a microwave oven to an air fryer.
That’s just a small bonus to push the value of Backup by BioLite a bit further into sanity because at $1,999 for a single battery and $3,499 for the pair, the math isn’t easy to justify. Realistically, the real benefit to the system comes almost entirely from its use in case of emergency, protecting what could be hundreds of dollars of groceries from spoiling because of a random ice storm—and making it possible to cook them, too, even if the lights in the rest of the house are out.

Automotive enthusiast-centric interactive streaming platform Driven has unveiled its initial original programming slate beginning with “Art of Speed” starring renowned engine builder Tom Nelson.
First announced last December, Driven comes from car-enthusiast co-founders including longtime producer Michael George, “Top Gear USA” host Tanner Foust and “Gran Turismo” actor Emelia Hartford.
Additional original series include programs starring automotive talent like Hartford (“Gran Turismo”), Foust (“Top Gear USA”), Ben Collins (“Top Gear”), Ant Anstead (“Wheeler Dealers”), Jenson Button (Formula 1 World Champion), Tom Nelson (renowned car builder), Antron Brown (award-winning drag racer) and more.
Per Driven, this starting lineup will “anchor a library of content from established and emerging creators, and complement conversations in dedicated communities where enthusiasts can connect, discuss their interests, share projects, and exchange knowledge.”
Driven unveiled its original series lineup ahead of its upfront presentation to advertisers, which is scheduled for Nov. 3 at SEMA in Las Vegas. According to the company, the platform’s initial beta program has brought in more than 15,000 users over the last few months and “helped shape the platform’s technology, features and community experience, with members continuing to influence its development.”
The ad-supported, subscription-free platform is available on iOS, Android, web, Apple TV, Google TV, and Amazon Fire TV, with additional connected-TV platforms planned.
“We built Driven to bring premium storytelling and authentic car culture together,” Driven CEO Michael George said. “Enthusiasts want to go deeper into the people, the craft and what’s really at stake. These four originals deliver that – without fabricated timelines, fake ticking clocks, or manufactured drama. The ambition, setbacks, and breakthroughs are real. Driven is giving those stories a home, and look forward to sharing them with our audience.”
Additional series premiering exclusively on Driven in early 2027 will include “Pikes Peak” (starring Tanner Foust, Jenson Button and Ant Anstead), “Queen of the Mountain” (starring Emelia Hartford) and “Go or Go Home” (starring NHRA champion Antron Brown).
Descriptions for each series, provided by Driven, can be found below.
ART OF SPEED
Six 1-hour episodes. Starring Tom Nelson. Created and Directed by Michael George. Produced by Emelia Hartford. Executive Produced by Michael George, Matt Swanson and Tom Lofthouse.
The man behind the most powerful street cars on earth, and the over five years it took to build them.
Tom Nelson left street racing to build a company around what he understood better than anyone: horsepower. Nelson Racing Engines became the place you go when 1,000 horsepower is the starting point, and the cars that roll out of his Chatsworth shop have gone on to Hollywood, to magazine covers and to the kind of owners who want something nobody else has. Art of Speed was shot over five years inside that shop. Each episode follows one build from a bare block to the first time its owner turns the key, including Maximus, the twin-turbo Charger built for Furious 7, and F-Bomb, David Freiburger’s 1,500-horsepower Camaro. The engines are the easy part. The hard part is everything around them: the deadlines, the customers, the physics, and a builder who has never once accepted the number on the dyno as the final answer. It ends in Iceland, with a machine on roads it was never meant for.
PIKES PEAK
Three 1-hour episodes. Starring Tanner Foust, Ant Anstead and Jenson Button. Directed by Tom Lofthouse and Dan Hack. Produced by Jake Cardew and Ed Sanders. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse.
One hundred days to build a car. One mountain to prove it.
A customer handed Radford Motors a million dollars and told them to build whatever they wanted. Ant Anstead decided to race it up America’s deadliest road before delivering it. One hundred days on the clock, a company that had never raced anything, and a car nobody had driven in anger. Ant and Jenson Button put Radford’s name on it. Joe Scarbo and Martin Jung built it. Tanner Foust, who has raced almost everything with wheels, agreed to take it up 12.42 miles of mountain with no barriers where it matters, in a car that was still being finished the week it shipped. No insurance if it crashes. No second attempt if it fails. Pikes Peak: A Race to the Clouds follows the whole thing, from a bare chassis in a California shop to practice mornings above the treeline, through the breakages, the all-nighters and the clashes, to a result nobody saw coming: Radford’s first race ever, and a win.
QUEEN OF THE MOUNTAIN
One 90-minute documentary. Starring DRIVEN co-founder Emelia Hartford. Featuring Jeff Zwart, Tanner Foust, Betim Berisha, and Robin Shute. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse.
12.42 miles. 156 corners. One run. The mountain decides.
A year ago Pikes Peak sent DRIVEN co-founder Emelia Hartford home before the summit. So she built a car to go back: a brand new Corvette ZR1, 1,064 horsepower to the rear wheels, a cage she welded herself, and a crew she moved to Colorado for a month. Race week nearly broke the program. Her carbon wheels were banned mid-week, the car failed tech, and two days out she was tearing it apart to re-weld the cage while the coolant boiled over. Then the green flag. Ten minutes and eleven seconds later, she was the fastest woman ever up Pikes Peak, in the fastest rear-wheel-drive production car the mountain has seen, on her first run to the top in the race’s 104th year. Queen of the Mountain tells the story behind that time, featuring Jeff Zwart, the champion who coached her corner by corner, Tanner Foust, Betim Berisha, and Robin Shute, the veterans who know what fast really costs up there, and the question none of them can quite answer: why this road, at this price, every June. Emelia’s answer is already in. Just wait till next year.
GO OR GO HOME
Three 30-minute episodes. Starring Antron Brown. Directed by Ben Carter. Produced by Lisa Hughes Kennedy. Executive Produced by Michael George and Tom Lofthouse.
A season inside NHRA drag racing, where runs last under four seconds and every driver says goodbye to their family before strapping in.
Top Fuel dragsters are the fastest accelerating machines on earth. Go or Go Home spends a season with the people who drive them and the people who pay for them: four-time champion Steve Torrence, who nearly died twice before he ever sat in a race car. Antron Brown, racing toward the win most drivers want, at Indy. And the young drivers and family-run teams trying to stay on the track against billionaire budgets. Shot across Bristol, Sonoma, Charlotte and the U.S. Nationals at Indianapolis, with full access to the pits and the homes behind them. The results are in there. What stays with you is the rest of it: fathers and sons, the money it takes, the fear nobody talks about, and the hour between rounds when a crew tears an engine down to nothing and rebuilds it.

Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Monday accused Pakistan army of derailing Chinese investments under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (
CPEC
), alleging that the country's mineral wealth was being used to advance foreign interests and facilitate a shift towards United States.
In a social media post on X, Rehman claimed that Pakistan had disappointed Beijing by halting CPEC-linked investments midway and warned that the loss of Chinese confidence could deter other countries from investing in Pakistan.
"You have disappointed China, you have halted their investment midway, and when China is disappointed, the rest of the world will not come to invest in your country either," he said
He alleged that the US was stepping in to fill the space left by China, claiming that American officials had acknowledged this to him.
"And who is taking China's place? America is taking its place. This has been admitted by the Americans themselves in front of me," he said.
Rehman clarified that he was not opposed to foreign investment in Pakistan's mineral sector, saying the country urgently needed international capital, development projects and economic opportunities.
"We do not disagree with the principle of investment from around the world here. 
Multinational companies come, they invest; America is not immune to this, Russia is not immune, China is not immune, Britain and France are not immune," he said.
"And who is taking China's place? America is taking its place. This has been admitted by the Americans themselves in front of me, and our esteemed elders here have taken those beautiful, beautiful stones to their offices and presented them, and the ambassador they have here at the time has also said it in her interview," he added.
The JUI-F chief also alleged that politicians backed by the military establishment prioritised their personal interests and the demands of their patrons over Pakistan's economic well-being.
"These Pakistani politicians - whose priorities I know - in all such matters, they first determine their own share, and only then do they think about the country," he said.
Fazlur Rehman also questioned the imposition of governor's rule and the declaration of an emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, alleging that the measures were linked to concerns over the region's mineral reserves.
"On what grounds? Terrorism? The provincial government is aligned with the narrative of terrorism; it is the federation that is not providing support for that narrative," he said.
He further alleged that the focus on terrorism had subsequently disappeared from the debate, while discussions surrounding mineral reserves had also been dropped.
"As soon as governor's rule was imposed and as soon as the emergency was declared, the topic of terrorism simply vanished, and from their side, the discussion of mineral reserves was dropped," he said.
His remarks come amid Pakistan's efforts to attract foreign investment into its mineral sector, particularly in resource-rich regions such as Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
CPEC, a flagship component of China's Belt and Road Initiative, includes infrastructure, energy and industrial development projects. The initiative has faced challenges over the years, including security threats, delays and concerns over the safety of Chinese personnel and investments.

BMW says that it will expand its navigation-guided, partially automated driving capabilities into urban environments starting in 2027, launching first in Germany with other markets to follow.
BMW is taking on Tesla’s FSD with urban driver assist starting in 2027
BMW will bring navigation-guided city driving to select models via software updates in 2027, taking on Tesla’s FSD while facing growing scrutiny over Level 2 driver safety.
The new system can help steer, speed up, and slow down the vehicle on both highways and city streets using its built-in GPS navigation. While driving in town, it can assist with changing lanes, making turns, yielding to other cars, and driving through roundabouts. But as a Level 2 driver assist system, it still requires drivers to keep their eyes on the road and stay ready to take over at any moment. On the highway, BMW will allow drivers to remove their hands from the steering wheel — but on local roads, they’ll need to keep their hands on the wheel.
BMW is the latest automaker to commit to releasing a partially autonomous city driving feature to its customers, as the industry races to keep up with Tesla and its Full Self-Driving (FSD) system. BMW, in particular, recently introduced its next-generation Neue Klasse platform, which includes a driver assist system partly powered by Qualcomm’s technology. And with hands-free highway driving now widely available in many mass-market vehicles, the next frontier is a safe and capable city driving feature that rivals FSD.
BMW says its system works cooperatively with drivers rather than fighting their control, which means they can steer, brake, or speed up at any point to adjust their driving without shutting the system off. At the same time, the car shows what it sees and what the assistance system is doing right in your line of sight through the heads-up display and in a clear 3D map on the main dashboard screen.
The necessary cameras and sensors already come built into models like BMW’s 3 Series, 7 Series, X5, iX3, and iX4. BMW can activate the feature through an over-the-air software update. The system follows new European safety rules that let cars suggest and make automated driving moves on city streets for the first time. BMW says that outside experts have already road-tested the setup and confirmed it meets the technical standards, with final official government approval expected in early 2027.
With more cars equipped with partial automation hitting the road, safety researchers are growing increasingly worried about driver attention and the potential for these systems to cause crashes. There is compelling evidence that, regardless of the company, most driver-assist systems are less safe than normal human driving. Drivers tend to develop an overreliance on these systems to drive the car for them — even after a short period of use. And when it’s time to take back control of the vehicle, their reaction times are slower than what’s considered safe.
BMW is entering risky territory with the adoption of a Level 2 driving feature. Much like Tesla, the company is emphasizing that drivers remain responsible for the vehicle even while using the partially autonomous system in urban environments. Tesla does the same for its FSD feature, but some customers have successfully argued in court that the company bears some responsibility for crashes when they occur.

More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
- Published
More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.
Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.
The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.
In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.
Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.
The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.
Testing and treatment is under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.
The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain.
DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said.
The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.
The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate".
Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.
Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.
Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.
In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.
In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.
Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing.
Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.
The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

Sen. Chris Murphy, 53, suffers stroke during son's hockey game
Murphy has spent nearly two decades in Congress, winning a House seat in 2006 before moving up to the Senate in 2012

Connecticut senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke at his son’s hockey game.
His office disclosed the 53-year-old Democrat's condition in a statement on Sunday.
Murphy's chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said that the senator “started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game” on Saturday.
“He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke,” she said. "He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment.
“The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery.”
Murphy has spent nearly two decades in Congress, winning a House seat in 2006 before moving up to the Senate in 2012. He is not on the ballot in Tuesday's election.
Within the Senate, Murphy sits on the Appropriations Committee and has made his name on immigration and restrictions on guns. He is viewed as a possible candidate for more senior leadership positions in the chamber, and his name has also been raised as a potential 2028 presidential contender.
Murphy is the third Senate Democrat in recent years to have a stroke. Ben Ray Lujan of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland both had strokes in 2022 and have since recovered.
Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman had a stroke that same year while campaigning for his seat. He now uses adaptive technology in the Senate, including live captioning on a phone or tablet that transcribes words as people speak to him and helps him process the conversation.
Fetterman said on social media Sunday that his family “is rooting for Chris and his family for a full and speedy recovery.”
Prayers for Murphy were also offered by several Republican senators, including Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska.
