A video showing a man attacking a street vendor over allegations that he mixed contraceptive pills into sugarcane juice is going viral on social media. The incident is being shared with claims of ‘food jihad’ and as a warning to people to be cautious when buying food from street vendors. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows a customer attacking a Muslim street vendor for allegedly mixing contraceptive pills into sugarcane juice.
Fact: The viral video is scripted and was created by Mohammad Ruhul, a content creator from Bangladesh, for social awareness. It does not depict a real incident. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, a reverse image search of the viral footage led us to the original video (archive), which was uploaded on 24 September 2026 on a Bangladeshi Facebook page called ‘Ruhul Vlog’. The page is run by Mohammad Ruhul, who also has a YouTube channel where he regularly posts scripted videos for social awareness and entertainment.
In the viral video, Mohammad Ruhul is seen arguing with a street vendor and attacking him, alleging that he is making people sick by mixing an artificial sweetener called saccharin into sugarcane juice. However, towards the end of the video, Ruhul clarifies that the incident is scripted and was created solely to raise awareness. He also mentions that they will continue making similar videos on social issues. This confirms that the viral video does not depict a real incident but is a scripted video created for social awareness.
However, opinions differ regarding the safety of saccharin in food and beverages. Experts suggest that further research is needed to understand its potential health effects. The FSSAI permits its use only within prescribed limits. However, several media reports (here and here) have raised concerns about the use of saccharin in food and beverages in India and Bangladesh, including instances of its alleged use beyond permissible limits without adequate quality testing.
To sum up, this viral video being circulated with the ‘food jihad’ narrative is scripted.

What to do if your smart home devices keep disconnecting from Wi-Fi
It could be something very simple.
It's strange that Apple is only now beginning to take the smart home market seriously with the launch of the HomeView smart display and the rest of the Apple Home Collection. Affordable consumer gear has been around for years, and when it's well-made and well-configured, it can not only simplify your life but also save you money. Smart thermostats are more efficient, and smart lighting can be set to turn on only when and where you need it — although it's more fun to make your living room look like Los Angeles in Blade Runner 2049.
One hassle is that some accessories don't play well with Wi-Fi. They have a tendency to drop out of apps, assuming you can even set them up in the first place. And needless to say, a home fixture you can't count on is all but worthless. You wouldn't put up with a microwave that only cooked dinner on Tuesdays and Fridays.
Thankfully, there are a few tactics you can use to cope with these misbehaving devices. We're not going to lie, though — in some circumstances, a hardware upgrade is in order. You may want to minimize the number of Wi-Fi-based products in your home in general.
Why Wi-Fi accessories drop out, and how to fix it
If you're still using a Wi-Fi 5 router, stop everything and upgrade to Wi-Fi 6 or 7. The issue is connection limits. On Wi-Fi 5, the practical limit for simultaneous connections is around 10 to 25 devices, perhaps 30 if you're lucky. That's plenty in a home without smart home gear, but once accessories start filling up those connection slots, problems are inevitable. Your router is going to start kicking some devices to make room, and chances are your phone and laptop are going to win out over a lamp.
Another problem is that many cheaper accessories are limited to the 2.4GHz band. On a mesh Wi-Fi system, setting up these accessories can be difficult or impossible, since there's a unified SSID (network ID) with automatic band steering — your phone might end up on 5 or 6GHz, preventing some apps from detecting the new gear. If you're lucky enough to successfully configure a product, there might still be a possibility of later detection failures.
Speaking of which, let's talk about HomeKit. Apple's platform is prone to "No Response" errors in situations where Amazon Alexa and Google Home operate just fine. The company has tried to smooth this out in recent years with an overhauled framework, but if you want a bulletproof setup, you may need an equally bulletproof Wi-Fi network. That could include two or more Apple home hubs for the sake of control redundancy. You can use a mix of HomePods, HomeViews or Apple TV 4Ks.
There's also a more basic concern we haven't touched on yet, and that's range. If an accessory is sitting on the fringes, it's naturally going to drop out when conditions are less than ideal. If you can't reposition devices or your router, it may be time to upgrade to a mesh system, as long as that doesn't wreak havoc for specific accessories. Alternatively, if you have a standalone router, you might try enabling separate 2.4 and 5GHz SSIDs, and forcing all of your smart home accessories over to the longer-range 2.4GHz band.
The best Wi-Fi is the least Wi-Fi
Ultimately, the best approach is to transition as many accessories as possible over to alternate protocols, namely Thread, Zigbee or Z-Wave. These do require a Wi-Fi hub, or in the case of Thread, a Wi-Fi-enabled "border router" accessory. The benefit, however, is that they not only reduce the burden on your Wi-Fi network but they also tend to be faster and more reliable. They're mesh-based — extending their reach — and hub-based accessories (like Philips Hue Zigbee lights) can continue to run some automations when the internet is down.
Thread is probably your best bet, since some routers, speakers and displays have border router features built in, as do products like Nanoleaf light panels. There is an asterisk, though: bandwidth. Like Zigbee and Z-Wave, Thread is a low-power standard, so it simply can't carry enough data for functions like audio, video or even vacuuming. It's mostly limited to bulbs, locks, plugs and sensors.
Some degree of Wi-Fi reliance is unavoidable, then. But if you find the right mix and know how to troubleshoot recurring issues, it shouldn't be a big deal. Just have fallbacks ready for internet outages.

The reminders to vote in Tuesday’s midterms are ubiquitous. Some health scholars have another reminder: that elections, especially divisive ones, can stress the heart.
Studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.
“Your political party doesn’t matter to your heart; stress does,” Lindsey Rosman, assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University, told STAT on Thursday. “Your emotional health and your heart health are connected.”
Take the last two presidential elections. Compared to other timeframes, researchers noted distinct changes in early November that aligned with heightened anxiety. Even if transient, higher blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms can turn serious for people diagnosed with cardiovascular disease, or for those unaware of a condition that might make them more vulnerable.
What research on 2016 and 2020 found
To see how elections may stress the heart, Rosman studied people who already had a heart rhythm disorder, taking advantage of data provided by their implanted cardiac devices. Her team found a 77% higher rate of irregular heartbeats during the six weeks around the 2016 election, compared with a control period.
The arrhythmia pattern was similar across age, sex, race, and other health conditions; Democrats and Republicans had similar risk. The retrospective observational study was carried out in North Carolina, when Rosman was at the University of North Carolina. Because it was a swing state in 2016, residents saw an especially heavy volume of political ads and campaign events.
After the following presidential election, Matthew Mefford, a cardiovascular disease epidemiologist and research scientist at Kaiser Permanente Southern California, asked whether hospitalizations for acute cardiovascular disease went up immediately after Election Day, akin to admissions after natural disasters. The answer was yes, with the rate of heart attacks significantly higher compared with the same five-day period two weeks before. The retrospective cohort study looked at people with and without a history of heart disease.
“Stress comes in many forms, including both positive and negative, and the stress impact associated with elections is just one situation that can result in adverse heart outcomes,” Mefford told STAT Thursday. “Being aware of how stress, generally, can impact your body is important especially for those with pre-existing heart disease.”
While stress responses in the body follow the same mechanisms, they’re not the same in all cases. “Not everyone responds to stress in the same way or to the same magnitude that triggers a heart event,” he said.
Other caveats: The two studies can’t establish cause and effect, just an association between health events and exposure to political campaigns.
How does stress play out in the body?
Ten years after Rosman’s study, today’s exposure may be magnified beyond political ads, thanks to the saturation of social media. Whatever the source, the deluge of news can cause acute stress and anger, triggering a fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline rises, the sympathetic nervous system ramps up, and the calming influence of the vagus nerve drops.
These changes can alter the heart’s electrical activity, making abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them, Rosman said. Stress hormones like cortisol and inflammation may also play a role, as can stress-related behaviors, such as sleeping poorly, skipping medications, eating more foods high in fat or salt, or drinking more alcohol or caffeine.
Her findings apply most directly to people at higher cardiac risk, she said, but she pointed out that nearly half of U.S. adults have some type of cardiovascular disease, including high blood pressure.
“People with existing heart disease are more vulnerable to arrhythmias triggered by emotion, but these events can also happen in people without known heart disease,” she said, citing reports of more heart attacks and cardiac events after 9/11, earthquakes, and World Cup matches. “Chronic stress is also an established risk factor for heart disease over time.”
Next up for Rosman is using wearables to study acute stress events. She hopes a larger, nationwide follow-up study looking at the 2020 and 2024 elections will offer some answers before the next U.S. presidential election.
What’s a voter to do?
In general, acute stress raises heart rates and blood pressure readings in the short term. But for people with uncontrolled hypertension or coronary disease, spiking stress adds strain.
Rosman suggests setting limits on news and social media, especially before bedtime. Focus on sleep and physical activity. Take your medications. Both Rosman and Mefford recommend meditation or yoga, taking a walk, hiking in nature, or engaging in exercise.
“Listen to your body,” Mefford said.

The night before an important Under-13 club final, Nitin Gawande and the Citi Gymkhana Cricket Club had resigned themselves to being without their star batter, Danish Malewar. The then 12-year-old was away at a VCA U-14 tournament and would return to Nagpur only at 2 a.m..
Then came a phone call that surprised Gawande. Malewar wanted to play.
“He reached Nagpur at 2 a.m., got home at 3 a.m., then slept from 3 to 6. By 7 a.m. he was at the ground. We ended up batting first, so he said he would bat two-down, wore his pads and went back to sleep. We were two down within 10 overs, so I woke him up. He splashed some water on his face, went out to bat and scored 140 not out!” Gawande recalled.
Today, a board outside the Citi Gymkhana Cricket Club features two faces: Malewar in his Mumbai Indians jersey and Virat Kohli. For a boy who once put on his pads and went back to sleep while waiting for his turn to bat, it has been quite a journey.
The hunger to bat
Malewar’s appetite for batting has remained undiminished. Perhaps nowhere was it more evident than in the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy final against Kerala.
Walking in at 11 for two on the first morning, with Vidarbha soon slipping to 24 for three and MD Nidheesh finding his rhythm, Malewar spent 89 overs at the crease, scoring 153 off 215 balls to put his team on course for its third Ranji Trophy title.
“Scoring a century in a final is a special feeling,” Malewar reminisced to Sportstar. “To do it in front of such a big crowd, against such a strong team, is just special.”
The desire to bat for as long as possible was ingrained in him from a young age.
“When Danish came to me for the first time with his father, he was very young, around six years old. At that time we didn’t even take six-year-olds,” remembered Gawande. “I asked him how he would play because he was so small, but he said, ‘ nahi, mujhe cricket hi khelna hai’.”
Malewar’s placid temperament was one of his biggest strengths from a young age. “He has had a very calm attitude since he was child, always very focussed. He would go about his work and do whatever he was told properly, and if he made a mistake he would come and ask what to do. The qualities of a good batsman were inbuilt in him from the beginning,” he explained.
Perhaps the only trait that hasn’t stayed with Malewar since childhood is his leg-spin, much to his coach’s chagrin.
“He used to bowl excellent leg-spin. I don’t know why he stopped bowling, otherwise he could have been a proper all-rounder!,” he said with a rueful smile.
Time to get set
What immediately stands out about the 23-year-old is the range and elegance of his strokeplay. His straight drive, his self-professed favourite stroke, is particularly pleasing to watch against the quicks. He is equally adept at driving and flicking them with aplomb, while his sweeps and ability to use his feet stand out against spin.
“Initially, I’ll always try to take my time, but once I’m set I always try to keep the runs coming. I like to ensure the runs are coming after I’m set,” Malewar explained of his mindset.
Gawande sees this ability to build an innings as one of his biggest strengths. “He knows how to stay at the wicket and carry the game. Once he has played 20-25 balls, he plays long. If you want to get him out, you have to do it in the first 15-25 balls, after that he just doesn’t get out.”
A stellar debut season
Having been a prolific run-scorer in age-group cricket, Malewar was quickly in line for his First-Class debut at the start of the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season. The opportunity came three days after his 21st birthday, against Andhra in Nagpur.
“I was told the day before the match that I was playing, and for that day I was quite nervous about making my Ranji debut,” he remembered. “I had just come from the U-23 team, and even though I had played trial matches with the senior team before I was still pretty nervous.”
His first innings lasted just 21 balls and yielded eight runs. He found his rhythm in the second innings, however, notching his maiden half-century at the First-Class level.
“Once I had scored that fifty, I got a lot more confidence,” he said. “Whatever nerves I had in the first innings were all gone. After that second innings everything became normal.”
That maiden half-century proved to be a turning point. Back-to-back fifties followed in his next two games before he finally reached three figures against Gujarat. The shot that took him to the milestone, a loft over mid-on against left-arm spinner Vishal Jayswal, remains clear in his mind.
“I was on 99 (98) and they had brought up all the fielders because they knew I was close to the century. I knew that I was going to step out and hit over the top, and luckily the shot went over.”
“The first is always special. Even today when I think about it I feel good,” he mused. “Luckily it was in Jamtha (VCA Jamtha Stadium in Nagpur). Jamtha mein ek alag hi feeling aati hai.”
Malewar maintained his prolific run through the competition, producing some of his best performances when it mattered most. In the semifinal against Mumbai, he top-scored in the first innings to help Vidarbha post a sizeable total before scoring a century in the final against Kerala.
“I was out for 79 in the semifinal against Mumbai, if I had converted that to a hundred it would have been a really special innings for me. To score against a team like Mumbai on that stage, if you can convert it’s very special.
“Even in the final, I scored 153 in the first innings and then 73 in the second, so those knockouts were truly special for me. I really enjoyed scoring those runs in a big final.”
Soon after whipping Aditya Sarvate through midwicket to reach his century in the final, Malewar raised his hands towards his ears, as if to block out the noise. The gesture was a tribute to K.L. Rahul, one of his inspirations alongside Sachin Tendulkar, AB de Villiers and Virat Kohli.
“I like his style of batting, and even outside of cricket he is very humble,” Malewar said of Rahul’s influence. “Even the way he wears his clothes, I like a lot about what he does both on and off the field.”
Malewar finished the season with 774 runs at an average of 52.20. That average rose further after he scored his maiden double-century in the quarterfinals of the Duleep Trophy for West Zone against NorthEast Zone. He then added two more fifties in the semifinal and final on the way to winning the competition.
“During the season, I felt that I can compete at the India level. The Ranji Trophy is just a step away from India, so I got the belief that I can make that extra one or two steps. I also got a lot of understanding about preparation, and had the special memory of winning the final,” he reflected on that season.
IPL call-up
Unfortunately, Malewar managed only two appearances in the 2025-26 season, missing most of the campaign with a shoulder injury. However, the disappointment was tempered by the excitement of being picked by Mumbai Indians in the IPL 2026 player auction in November 2025.
Malewar had attended trials with the franchise, but his selection was still something of a surprise, considering he was yet to make a white-ball appearance for Vidarbha. When auction day arrived, he chose to follow the proceedings away from the rest of his family.
“I wasn’t at home. I had left intentionally, because I didn’t know if any team would pick me or not. So I took my iPad and watched it outside in the car. My name came only in the evening, but when MI picked me up everything changed.
“I was getting calls from everywhere, so I had to go back home. A lot of people had gathered there before I even left, so when I got back everyone was dancing and congratulating me. It was a special night.”
Alongside the Vidarbha Cricket Association, MI shared responsibility for Malewar’s recovery and rehabilitation during its camp. The tournament also gave him an opportunity to work alongside some of the biggest names in cricket, both among the players and the coaching staff. It was an experience that gave him plenty to take away.
“There are so many big names. [Kieron] Pollard sir, [Mahela] Jayawardene sir, Sachin sir, all of the coaches and staff groomed me so well. They helped me understand what is needed at this level, and I was able to learn so much by watching them.
What happens on a big platform, how to plan, how to prepare, all of these things were new for me. I learned a lot in those two months, now I have an idea about what happens on an international level,” he said.
It also gave him the opportunity to share a dressing room with his childhood idol, Tendulkar. “I met Sachin sir for the first time, I had never met him before that. I got to tell him that he was my idol, that I had been following him since childhood,” he remembered.
With MI’s batting order in a tricky situation, Malewar made two appearances for the side, opening the batting against Gujarat Titans and Chennai Super Kings. Although neither outing was particularly successful (he scored two and zero), both offered valuable learning opportunities.
“I was so nervous before the first match (against Gujarat Titans). It was my first time on such a big stage, in front of so many people. It was another level of experience, a learning process.
“In the first match, I couldn’t process everything on such a big platform against such big bowlers. By the second match I had become normal, but unfortunately I got out first ball,” he recalled.
Staying in the present
With his injury behind him and an IPL cap to his name, Malewar is now enjoying his first sustained run of red-ball cricket since recovering. After a couple of indifferent scores, he registered his first half-century against Goa. For now, however, his focus remains firmly on the present.
“The season has just started, but I’m trying to focus on each match, each innings. Whatever has happened in the past, where I’ve scored runs or not, whether I’ve got out or not, doesn’t matter. What matters is how I prepare for the upcoming matches.
“I’m trying to stay in the moment, but keep an eye on the future. I don’t want to have any regrets for the season. With a lot of matches coming up, I’m going to need to be prepared.”

French school protests resume on smaller scale as holidays end

French student protests resumed on Monday on a much smaller scale than in past weeks as pupils returned from a two-week break, with youngsters trying to blockade a few high schools in Paris, Marseille and Rennes, French media reported.
By 0830 GMT some 41 high schools – about 1 per cent of those nationwide – were blockaded, the Education Ministry said.
Hundreds of France’s more than 3,000 high schools were blockaded in the weeks before the break. How Antonelli 'blew everyone away' to make Formula 1 history
- Published
Just after Kimi Antonelli clinched his first title to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen were united in their assessment of his achievement.
"Incredible," they both said. Coming from the two most successful champions on the current grid, the men who are first and third in the all-time list of F1 record-holders, it meant something.
That Antonelli shared the Mexico City Grand Prix podium with these two titans meant something, too.
To Antonelli, firstly, who said: "I will definitely frame the picture and put it in my house because it's just an incredible moment. And as well to see so much respect from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is truly special and a moment that will live and will always be remembered."
So, too, though, for its symbolism. Antonelli seems destined to join them among the list of all-time greats of the sport, judging by the scale of his achievement this year.
"There are going to be others," said 1996 world champion Damon Hill, commentating for BBC Radio 5 live.
"I don't see anything else other than him getting better and better. He's going to have to go through hard times as well, but no one is going to doubt his incredible talent."
No one indeed. Not any more, anyway.
- Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who became world champion 
  - Published4 hours ago
- Antonelli heads list of F1's youngest champions 
  - Published4 hours ago

  - Published4 hours ago
Antonelli's first title comes at the end of only his second season in F1. When he was drafted into Mercedes last year - to replace Hamilton, no less - there were those who said he was too inexperienced.
For some of last year, he looked it. There were flashes of promise, but by and large it was a shaky debut season, one that did not live up to Antonelli's billing as potentially the next generational talent.
So when it became clear that Mercedes would start this season with the best car, it was his team-mate George Russell, who had comfortably beaten him in 2025, who was favourite for the championship.
But that was without reckoning on the remarkable step forward Antonelli made in his development over last winter.
He finished the first race on Russell's tail. He took his maiden victory in the second, the first of five consecutive wins with which he took control of the championship. Since then, he has never looked like losing it.
Even when Mercedes' early season advantage was wiped out by their rivals, Antonelli was always there, always a factor. Which is more than can be said for Russell.
In that sense, it is important to see his achievement in context. Had the comparative performance between Russell and Antonelli carried on as it did last year, this championship may well have had a different complexion.
It could have been a season during which Russell and Hamilton were neck and neck in the title fight for most of the year - indeed, Russell has now slipped behind both Verstappen and Hamilton in the points table.
Instead, it has been a story of one driver's domination. His performances have been so strong that he has removed pretty much all jeopardy from the title fight.
That has not made it the most exciting season to watch, but it speaks volumes for the level at which Antonelli has performed. All because of the progress he has made - and his remarkable consistency.
"At his age," said Verstappen, "to be so solid, not make big mistakes, and of course also beat your experienced team-mate, he's just driven incredible, and I'm very proud of him, how he has handled himself this whole season."
Lando Norris, the outgoing world champion, was also effusive in his praise.
"It couldn't have gone to a better person," he said. "He's a genuine guy, very, very kind, and he has driven unbelievably well this year, better that what everyone was expecting of him.
"He's certainly not had an easy season in terms of his competition being incredibly high. He has gone up against the best drivers in the world, all in very good cars, and he's blown everyone away.
"I hope everyone gives him enough credit for what he's achieved this year. He's made everyone else look silly. He's driven that well and he's been able to click with his car, he's worked hard to understand how to drive this car and he's exploited it better than anyone else.
"So he should be very proud. He has achieved history and I am very, very happy for him."
For Antonelli, the difficulties of last year were formative, and critical in what he has been able to achieve this.
"The fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to F1," he said, "or I wasn't ready for it - which at some point last year I probably looked like I wasn't - being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year.
"Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver, as a person.
"Still this year I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better, so it's just a constant learning process.
"Last year being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."
One of those moments was this weekend.
He admitted after qualifying that he had been "tight", not driving as well as he could have, a result of the pressure of the moment.
"Austin, I was much more aggressive, much more present in the moment," said Antonelli, "while in Mexico, yesterday in qualifying, I was a bit more tense in a way because I also wasn't as intense in the way I was driving.
"So definitely, it hasn't been easy on that side. But now finally, we clinched it and now we can just enjoy the rest of the season."
The potency of the moment was clear to see after the race.
Antonelli admitted he was so emotional on the last lap as he followed Verstappen and Hamilton home that he was struggling to see.
"I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying basically and I couldn't see clearly ahead," he said. "I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears.
"It was very special and a lot of memories went through my mind in that moment."
Then his father Marco and mother Veronica, who have been so important in his rise to F1, were there to greet him at the end.
Marco has been virtually ever-present this season, providing quiet support for his son whenever needed.
"To have my dad during the whole season was very important," said Antonelli, "because, first of all, he was the one keeping me grounded, especially after very high moments, but as well he was the one that was always there when I was facing a difficult situation or I wasn't feeling the best ahead of a session."
Then, in the champions' news conference, he became so emotional at one point as he remembered his late grandfather that he could not talk, and had to take a minute to compose himself.
"Oh my god," he said, after he had collected himself. "I cried way too much today. But it's good."

The revised Maximum Retail Price (MRP) list of anti-cancer medicines published by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) raises serious concerns about excessive pricing and the exploitation of patients, noted medical health activists on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
Editorial | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The NPPA, under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, has released a list of 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with their revised MRP that will be effective from November 9.
“The revised price list reflects the information submitted by companies up to October 27, 2026, and it will be updated as and when manufacturers submit their revised prices of non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs,” said a release issued by the Union government on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
On October 17, the NPPA had announced Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in public interest to address excessive trade margins, make cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines. Manufacturers were instructed to submit their revised list to NPPA.
The 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs include immunotherapy medicines used in the treatment of over 20 types of cancer, Denosumab used by breast and prostate cancer patients, Pegfilgrastim used to prevent neutropenia in cancer patients, and Bevacizumab, which is approved for the treatment of colon, ovarian and cervical cancers.
Curbing profiteering
Stating that cost-based price control can further reduce medicine prices and curb excessive profiteering, Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India), an organisation working for accessibility of medicines, said that controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.
In their statement, the group explained: “For example, the reported MRP of one brand of palbociclib fell from approximately ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 per pack, while thiotepa fell from approximately ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 per vial. Such drastic reductions raise serious questions about the pricing practices of pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian manufacturers of generic cancer medicines that have reportedly offered substantial trade margins while patients continued to face unaffordable prices.’’
It added that, several patented cancer medicines remain exorbitantly priced. The Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) policy has failed to ensure affordability, while excluding medicines supplied free under Patient Assistance Programmes from its calculations has further limited its potential impact on patients, said the group.
“The policy’s formula is also deeply flawed. Allowing a 42.8% markup over the Price to Stockist [PTS] legitimises excessive margins, particularly in a supply chain often involving only one or two intermediaries or direct sales to hospitals. A substantially lower markup, comparable to the 16% margin applicable to scheduled formulations under the DPCO framework, could have delivered greater benefits to patients. A one-time MRP reduction is not enough. Without permanent, enforceable margin caps, regular monitoring and verification by NPPA, excessive pricing can persist or re-emerge,” JSA stated in the release.
The NPPA must also strengthen its collection and maintenance of price data across supply chains and distribution channels, the group said, adding that companies should not be left to calculate and self-report revised MRPs without adequate independent verification.
Tanvi Singh, medical oncologist, MOC Cancer Care, said that cancer is an ailment whose treatment demands are extensive so when drug costs are high, patients may end up delaying treatment initiation, or skipping doses, or even discontinue therapy prematurely. All of these will in turn affect and compromise outcomes.
“Lowering drug costs is an imperative that can improve treatment continuity, reduce financial toxicity, and help patients complete the prescribed course of therapy. However, price caps are not enough on their own. Meaningful and sufficient improvement in affordability can be said to be achieved when price regulation is complemented by wider insurance coverage expansion of government reimbursement schemes, increased availability of quality generic and biosimilar medicines, robust Patient Assistance Programmes (PAPs), and greater access to comprehensive cancer care across the country,” said Dr. Singh.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru, said: “The price control introduced by the government is a positive move. But low cost life-saving drugs should remain viable to manufacture and seller.”

22 అక్టోబర్ 2026న, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ సరిహద్దు వెంబడి పలు ప్రదేశాలలో భారత సైనికులకు చైనా బలగాలతో ఘర్షణలు జరిగాయని ఇండో-టిబెటన్ బోర్డర్ పోలీస్ (ITBP) డైరెక్టర్ జనరల్ శత్రుజీత్ కపూర్ అంగీకరించారు. చైనా సైనికులు నిర్ధారిత గస్తీ పద్ధతులను పాటించనప్పుడు వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LAC) వెంబడి పరిస్థితి “అస్తవ్యస్తంగా” మారుతుందని విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ (MEA) ప్రతినిధి రణధీర్ జైస్వాల్ మరుసటిరోజు పేర్కొన్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో భారత్, చైనా సైనికుల మధ్య ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలంటూ కొన్ని వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అక్టోబర్ 2026లో అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ సరిహద్దు (LAC) వద్ద భారత, చైనా సైనికుల మధ్య జరిగిన ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలన్నీ పాతవి లేదా అక్టోబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధం లేనివి. ఇవి 2021, 2024, 2025 సంవత్సరాలకు చెందిన పాత ఘటనలు, జూలై 2026 నాటి అమర్నాథ్ యాత్రకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు. కావున, ఈ వీడియోలు తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉన్నాయి.
వీడియో 1
ఈ వీడియో కనీసం డిసెంబర్ 2022 నుండే ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అంటే, ఈ వీడియో అక్టోబర్ 2026లో రిపోర్ట్ చేయబడిన భారత్-చైనా సరిహద్దు ఉద్రిక్తతల కంటే ముందే ఉందని, తాజా పరిణామాలతో దీనికి సంబంధం లేదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది. డిసెంబర్ 2022లో ప్రచురితమైన ఒక CNN కథనంలో, ఇదే దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తూ, ఈ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2021లో చిత్రీకరించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ వీడియో వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ సమీపంలో అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లో చిత్రీకరించినట్లుగా భారతీయ సైనకాధికారి ధృవీకరించారని ఈ కథనం పేర్కొంది.
వీడియో 2
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలు రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో కనీసం నవంబర్ 2024 (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోకి చొరబడటానికి ప్రయత్నిస్తున్న చైనా సైనికులను భారత సైనికులు అడ్డుకుని దాడి చెయ్యడం ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని ఆ పోస్టులు పేర్కొన్నాయి. ఇండియన్ ఆర్మీ ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ విభాగం కూడా ఈ వీడియోను ఖండిస్తూ ‘X’లో చేసిన పోస్ట్ చేసింది.
వీడియో 3
ఈ వీడియోకి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు కనీసం జూలై 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, అమర్నాథ్ యాత్ర 2026 సందర్భంగా, జమ్మూ & కాశ్మీర్లోని బాల్తాల్ వద్ద ప్రవేశ ద్వారం దగ్గర యాత్రికులు నమోదు చేసుకోవడానికి, RFID కార్డులను పొందడానికి గుమిగూడిన దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుంది. ఇండియన్ ఆర్మీ ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ విభాగం కూడా ఈ వీడియోను ఖండిస్తూ ‘X’లో చేసిన పోస్ట్ చేసింది.
వీడియో 4
మా దర్యాప్తులో డిసెంబర్ 2025 నాటి అవే దృశ్యాలతో కూడిన అనేక సోషల్ మీడియా పోస్టులను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) గుర్తించాం. ఈ పోస్టుల ప్రకారం, ఆరోగ్య సమస్యలతో బాధపడుతున్న ఒక భారతీయ సైనికుడు వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LAC) సమీపంలో విధి నిర్వహణలో ఉండగా స్పృహ కోల్పోయాడు. మీడియా కథనాల ప్రకారం, చైనా పీపుల్స్ లిబరేషన్ ఆర్మీ (PLA) సిబ్బంది అతనికి ప్రథమ చికిత్స, వైద్య సహాయం అందించిన తర్వాత, అతని సొంత యూనిట్కు అప్పగించారు.
చివరిగా, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లో 2026 అక్టోబర్లో జరిగిన భారత-చైనా ఘర్షణల దృశ్యాలంటూ సంబంధంలేని పాత వీడియోలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

From Chelsea reject to Watkins 'upgrade' - Jackson makes fast Villa start

Nicolas Jackson's double to defeat Manchester City on Saturday capped an excellent start to the striker's spell at Aston Villa.
Signed from Chelsea as a direct replacement for Ollie Watkins - Villa's main source of goals for the previous six seasons - it was imperative the 25-year-old Senegal international hit the ground running in claret and blue.
Jackson has done just that, scoring seven goals in his first 11 appearances for Villa - six in the last six - and helping his new side to a 100% start in the Champions League and spearheading their recovery after a slow start to the Premier League campaign.
"The players, the manager, the team - everything is incredible," Jackson told BBC Match of the Day.
"I'm very happy that I'm here and hopefully we can do amazing things together."
Improved form at Villa Park
Jackson spent two full seasons at Chelsea after joining in 2023 and had a year on loan at German giants Bayern Munich before moving to Villa in the summer for a deal worth up to £65m.
There is a much smaller sample size from his time at Villa Park compared with his spell at Stamford Bridge, but on several metrics, he is showing signs of improvement.
Jackson scored 24 goals in 65 Premier League appearances for Chelsea, netting every 210 minutes on average, with a shot conversion rate of 15%.
That compares with four in seven games for Villa, averaging a goal every 138 minutes with a shot conversion rate of 21%.
One of the criticisms of Jackson at Chelsea was he had lots of chances and did not convert as many of them as he should.
In his early weeks at Villa, he is outperforming his expected goals tally by exactly two.
Both of their shots on target against City came from Jackson's right foot - and both ended up in the net.
'He looks like a really good piece of business' - Keown
England international Watkins scored 91 Premier League goals in 221 league appearances for Villa before moving to Saudi Arabia club Al-Hilal in August.
He was a consistent scorer, never failing to reach double figures for Premier League goals during each of his six seasons with the club.
The respective statistics of Jackson and Watkins from last season suggest Jackson is more involved in general play than the England forward, while also being involved in more chances.
If Jackson's current run of form continues, his fee may prove to be a bargain.
Former Villa and England defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport: "I've liked him all season. I think he's key to Villa's success.
"I think he's an upgrade on Ollie Watkins, I really do.
"Ollie was magnificent for them, but this guy is more of a predator [in and around the penalty area]. Pace will always trouble top defenders and he's got it in abundance.
"I think having worked with the manager before at Villarreal, he's sort of fast-tracking his quick development.
"He looks like a really good piece of business right now. The team suffered and you need a striker who can give you belief you can win games when suffering and this guy is a special talent.
"With a talent like that you can go a long way."
'So many players improve and thrive' under Emery
Saturday's win was achieved on the fourth anniversary of Emery's appointment as Villa boss.
Under the Spaniard, they have become fixtures in the upper echelons of the Premier League, regulars in European competition and ended a 30-year wait for a major trophy by winning the Europa League.
Results are one thing, but there are also numerous examples of players who have been rejuvenated or scaled new heights in their careers under Emery's management at Villa Park.
Former Scotland defender Rachel Corsie, who had a spell playing in the Women's Super League for Aston Villa late in her career, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Emery is quite unique. A lot of coaches will focus on the tactical detail, but he's so intense with it.
"I remember from when I was here that his car is always at the training ground. I know people will say that's a natural thing and the life of a manager, but I would say it's an incredible amount of time.
"He loves to get the detail right. He never gets tired of trying to better people individually and that takes an incredible amount of work. So many players come here, improve and thrive."
Jackson has prior experience of playing under Emery, having been coached by him at Villarreal, where he spent three years before Chelsea signed him for £35m.
Emery told BBC Match of the Day: "I knew him at Villarreal and he started playing the level he is now. I know his capacity to exploit his qualities and I know, as well, his humility.
"The mentality is coming through - how focused he is in life and professional career."
Speaking to TNT Sports, Jackson added: "It's not easy [to settle at a new club] but easier because of the coach and the players.
"It's an incredible dressing room with an incredible manager. I'm very happy to be here and hopefully I will score many goals."

Hans Christian Andersen once said, “To travel is to live,” and while that’s a romantic notion, he probably wasn’t careening through Gyeongju, South Korea, at midnight in the back of a taxi with a driver who didn’t speak a lick of English.
A lot has changed since the 1800s, to be fair. Today’s world traveler has it awfully easy when it comes to understanding the local lingo, as even a basic modern cell phone app can offer a pretty good translation of common phrases delivered in everything from Abkhaz to Zulu. Type or speak a sentence or two into the app, tap a button, and out it returns in the language of your choice. Tap another button, and your phone can even speak those sentences aloud. It takes a little doing to turn this into a credible two-way conversation—especially if the cab driver isn’t slowing down—but with some patience and good humor, two strangers can engage in a reasonable discussion this way.
Casual travelers merely in need of directions to the farmacia or who want to know exactly what they’re getting into with a plate of kycklingtallrik can get by with a phone and a translation app, and if you’re going to a place with a fairly common tongue, you may not even need an active internet connection if you download the relevant language file for offline use. Google Translate, Apple Translate, or DeepL Translate will all do the job for free, though Google’s product is widely considered the gold standard for cross-language chitchat.
But what if you want to push past translating menus and asking for extra towels and carry on a conversation with a new friend you met on a trip or the in-laws who are visiting from halfway across the world? That’s where a handheld translator device can prove invaluable. These pocket-sized digital interpreters can help you seem like a polyglot, even if you don't know simple phrases. I have been testing and reviewing handheld translators for WIRED for five years, and I've developed a keen sense of how a good product should work and which ones I'd recommend.
What Do Handheld Language Translators Do?
Handheld translators are exactly that—stand-alone devices that up the ante on language interpretation, and their real value is revealed when you use them for sustained, voice-based conversation. Alongside the spoken word, some have a screen that shows the translation in text, often displaying the other side of the conversation upside down, so you don’t have to constantly pass the device back and forth.
Having a translator in a separate piece of hardware has further advantages. Namely, you can use your phone for something else while you’re talking—like snapping pictures or taking notes, for example—instead of tethering it to a translation app. You may also feel more comfortable handing a less costly stand-alone device to someone you don’t know versus trusting them with your $1,000 smartphone.
Many handheld translators can operate independently, either via Wi-Fi or with preloaded data plans that generally work worldwide. That means you can take one on a global jaunt and have access to interpretation services without having to pony up for an international plan on your smartphone. Better yet, download all the language packs you want before your trip, and you can use a handheld translator in offline mode, even when you’re in the sticks.
Earbud-based translators are the next game changer. These are over-ear devices that come in a pair—one for you, one for your conversation partner. Each of you wears one earbud, and the software on your phone handles the translation, both ways, behind the scenes. The best earbud translators make for the most natural way to communicate with someone in a foreign language that I’ve found to date, though handhelds tend to have more capabilities. (Earbud-based designs seem to be the direction the industry is heading.)
When shopping for a handheld translator, watch out for expensive subscription plans. Many devices come with free service, but only for a time, and re-upping after the trial period ends can be pricey. Check the fine print before you buy. Also, make sure the translator you’re considering covers all the languages you need. Note that while some translators support hundreds of languages, they may be limited in the language pairs they can translate between.
Who Really Needs a Handheld Language Translator?
Again, if you only need casual translation for occasional or emergency use, you can definitely get by with a free translation app on your phone. Translation devices are best for frequent users who expect to carry on multiple sustained conversations with speakers of other languages over time.
Those scenarios could include attending a reunion with your Swedish wife’s extended family or a lengthy workshop series with colleagues from other parts of the world. These tools are also often marketed to first responders who need to quickly assess a situation when human translation services aren’t available.
In situations where you may need to communicate with several speakers, each speaking a different language, a portable translator can make even more sense. If you expect your journeys to take you to far-flung areas or off the grid entirely, where internet service may be poor or nonexistent, a translator can be a helpful tool in your travel bag, even if you only expect to use it for emergencies.
The Best Stand-Alone Translator
The Timekettle T1 is a reasonably affordable and very pocketable device that makes for an easy addition to your travel kit. Built for two users to communicate, each with access to half the screen, the T1 translates each side of a conversation—written or spoken—into that user’s own language. Using it can be a little tricky: A color-coded button on the side of the device or a virtual one on the 4-inch touchscreen must be held down to tell the T1 which language to listen for. But once you get the hang of it, the system works pretty well.
Accuracy is solid, and translations are fast, popping up in well under a second. One challenge I had with the device relates to its small screen. Like most translators, the T1 supports photo-based translations via its 8-megapixel camera, but the 540 x 1080-pixel screen is too small to display much text at once. Also, while the unit includes a global eSIM with two years of free service included ($50/year after that), I encountered plenty of signal gaps, even in my own home. The good news is that if Wi-Fi’s available, that works, too. The unit also supports 31 offline language pairs (10 in combination with English), so if you plan ahead, service woes may not be an issue at all.
Best Translator Earbuds
If you want to upgrade your translation experience and make it more immersive, you’ll want to invest in a pair of earbuds, which give you a more personal and natural way to communicate. As described above, the iconic way to use these is to pop one on yourself and give the other to your friend. An app on your phone handles two-way translation, back and forth.
These 12-gram on-ear earbuds are the best I’ve tested, primarily because once they’re configured, they work completely hands-free. No clicking buttons or tapping the side of your head every time you’re ready to speak: The earbuds understand who’s talking and when, and they work with remarkable speed, almost like a professional interpreter whispering in your ear.
You can also wear both earbuds and use them for one-way translations, including phone calls. The only trouble with the setup is that there’s no offline mode, so you’ll need internet access on your phone for them to do anything.
Another excellent choice is Timekettle’s W4 Plus AI Interpreter Earbuds. While these $379 earbuds are smaller at 6 grams each and work nearly identically to iFLYTEK’s (completely hands free), I found the form factor to be a little less stable and the bulky charging case much more awkward to tote around. The extra outlay does however get you a limited offline mode and some built-in AI tools, including a meeting summarizer.
Best AI Translator Companion Device
The InnAIO T10 is a hybrid device that serves as both an AI notetaker and a language translator. It has no screen and only one button, and a MagSafe ring allows it to clip to the back of your phone to ensure it’s always in reach.
Like other translators, the device is designed to record, transcribe, and summarize thoughts and meetings, but it can also translate them in real time. It’s better with written translations, but it also supports audio translations, though using this feature is slightly more difficult, requiring each party to hold down a button in the mobile app every time they speak.
The T10 has been upgraded since I wrote my review, adding an offline mode and enhancing a few other features, but note that you’ll still need a subscription ($179/year for unlimited service) to make the most of it, as the free tier only supplies 120 minutes of real-time translation per month.
Best Large Group Translation System
The X1 Meeting Interpreter Hub works a lot like other translation systems, except it’s designed for multiple participants. The brick-like device contains two earbuds for live audio, plus a screen that displays translated spoken dialogue in real-time. If everyone in a room is outfitted with a hub–up to 10, total–each user can understand what everyone else is saying, with a maximum of 5 languages supported simultaneously. This can be further extended to remote users accessing the meeting online by sharing the meeting via a QR code that’s generated for each new discussion. Online, 60 remote participants can get live access to both text and audio translations, and contribute their own thoughts via voice by holding down a button on the web-based interface whenever they wish to speak. (There’s no app involved with the X1, no matter how you use it.)
The X1 is versatile and can also be used for one-on-one conversations (wherein each user shares an earbud) or as a simple streaming media translation/captioning device. A total of 52 languages and 106 accents are supported, and you can even change the gender of translations to match that of your conversation partner. After a meeting, the device can optionally generate AI summaries of the discussion (in your own language, naturally); these are delivered via web browser and a QR code link and expire after seven days.
The X1 is not a simple device–everything is done by tapping on its 3.4-inch touchscreen–nor is it an inexpensive one at $849. And remember, a separate unit is required for each seat in the room. You can do the math on what ten of these will cost you (or your company’s) bank account.

The 57th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu explores how researchers are using advanced imaging and reconstruction techniques to create detailed, three-dimensional maps of the human brain.
Zubeda Hamid, senior assistant editor, The Hindu, speaks to Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam, Head of the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras, about the technology, how the maps are created and what they could reveal about the human brain.
The episode looks at C-STROKE, a recently released three-dimensional atlas of a stroke-affected brain. Unlike conventional MRI scans, which provide images of the brain at a particular resolution, the new approach allows researchers to examine brain structures in greater detail and build comprehensive 3D maps.
The discussion explains how researchers prepare brain tissue, use imaging techniques and reconstruct the data to create these maps. It also looks at the different scientific and technological disciplines involved in the process and how detailed mapping could help researchers study the brain’s structure and changes associated with neurological conditions.
Another focus is the Centre’s plan to map more than 100 human brains across different stages of life. The project aims to build a larger collection of brain maps that could help researchers understand variations in brain structure, study neurological conditions and expand the available resources for brain research.
The episode also examines the potential applications of these atlases in clinical research and healthcare, including how they could contribute to a better understanding of stroke and other brain conditions. It discusses the possibilities as well as the work needed before such maps can be translated into clinical applications.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

Antonelli heads list of F1's youngest champions
- Published
Kimi Antonelli has made history by becoming the youngest title winner in the 77th year of the Formula 1 World Championship.
The Italian, at 20 years and 68 days, has beaten the record of Sebastian Vettel, who was 23 years and 134 days old when he won the first of his four drivers' championships in 2010.
Antonelli, who was still a teenager until 25 August, has secured the title in his second season in the sport.
We take a look at F1's other young champions and how Antonelli's achievement compares with theirs.
Kimi Antonelli
First championship: 2026
Age: 20 years and 68 days
Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season
F1 debut: 2025 Australian Grand Prix (aged 18)
Antonelli has already broken a number of records on the way to becoming F1's youngest champion.
In his second season, he became the youngest driver to achieve a pole position in China and the youngest to lead the championship at the next race in Japan.
In Monaco, he became the youngest driver to complete a 'grand slam' of pole position, fastest lap, leading every lap and winning the race.
All this after a rookie season in 2025 in which there were occasional highs but plenty of errors, and his final total of 150 points was less than half of the 319 accumulated by Mercedes team-mate George Russell.
Sebastian Vettel
First championship: 2010
Age: 23 years and 134 days
Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Third full season
F1 debut: 2007 US Grand Prix (aged 19)
Vettel was one of four drivers who could win the title going into the season-ending 2010 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.
He was far from the best placed, though, trailing Ferrari's Fernando Alonso by 15 points before the race and his Red Bull team-mate Mark Webber by seven.
The German did what he had to do by winning the grand prix and Alonso could only finish seventh, having become stuck behind the Renault of Vitaly Petrov.
With Webber in eighth, Vettel won the championship by four points from Alonso.
It was yet another F1 record for Vettel. He had become the youngest F1 points scorer on his debut for BMW Sauber in Indianapolis in 2007, before becoming the then youngest pole sitter and race winner at the 2008 Italian Grand Prix for Toro Rosso.
Lewis Hamilton
First championship: 2008
Age: 23 years and 300 days
Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season
F1 debut: 2007 Australian Grand Prix (aged 22)
Lewis Hamilton's debut season in 2007 almost delivered a fairytale title but he faltered in the final two races of the year.
He failed to score in China and finished seventh in Brazil, which allowed Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen to pip both Hamilton and fellow McLaren driver Fernando Alonso by a single point.
Somehow the climax to the 2008 championship, also in Brazil, was even more dramatic.
Hamilton was battling for the title with Ferrari's home favourite Felipe Massa and the Briton's fourth place was going to be enough to secure the crown when a late rain shower changed everything.
Leader Massa and Hamilton were among those who changed to intermediate tyres but Toyota's Timo Glock stayed out, which lifted him up to fourth.
Hamilton, now in fifth, had Toro Rosso's Vettel right behind him and couldn't afford to lose another position. With just over two laps to go, he ran wide and Vettel was through.
Massa crossed the line to win the race with Hamilton still sixth. The Ferrari pit crew, Massa's family and the Brazilian fans celebrated but with the rain intensifying, Glock was slowing on his dry-weather tyres and Hamilton passed him into the final corner to take the title by a single point. It was heart-stopping stuff.
Fernando Alonso
First championship: 2005
Age: 24 years and 57 days
Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Fourth full season
F1 debut: 2001 Australian Grand Prix (aged 19)
Alonso established control of the 2005 championship early in the season by winning four of the first seven races and never relinquished it.
The Spaniard's speed and consistency ensured he prevailed over Raikkonen, whose McLaren-Mercedes was fast but fragile. A third place at the Brazilian Grand Prix was enough to give Alonso the title with two races to spare.
He won a second consecutive title in 2006, also for Renault, and the 45-year-old remains one of the great personalities and outstanding talents in F1.
He'll be back for another season with Aston Martin in 2027, 26 years after his debut for Minardi.
Max Verstappen
First championship: 2021
Age: 24 years and 73 days
Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Seventh full season
F1 debut: 2015 Australian Grand Prix (aged 17)
Hamilton won the title on the final lap of the 2008 season but he would lose it on the final lap in 2021 in circumstances that remain a source of huge controversy.
His rival in a thrilling and intense season-long duel was Red Bull's Max Verstappen. There were plenty of flashpoints along the way and it all came to a climax in Abu Dhabi.
Verstappen and Hamilton went into the final race of the season level on points. The Dutchman qualified on pole but Mercedes' Hamilton beat him off the line and largely controlled the race thereafter, until Williams' Nicholas Latifi crashed with five laps to go, bringing out a safety car.
Hamilton did not have enough of an advantage over second-placed Verstappen to pit for fresh tyres and maintain the lead, so stayed out. Verstappen, with nothing to lose, came in and fitted softs.
Race director Michael Masi allowed the lapped cars between Hamilton and Verstappen to go past, but not those behind the Red Bull. He allowed the race to restart for one final racing lap and Verstappen overtook Hamilton, who was a sitting duck on his old hard tyres.
Verstappen and Hamilton, in their own ways, were both stunned and Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff shouted over the radio to Masi: "No, Michael, no! That was so not right!"
As happened with Vettel from 2010-13, this was the first of four consecutive titles for a Red Bull driver with Verstappen dominating the 2022, 2023 and 2024 seasons.
Emerson Fittipaldi
First championship: 1972
Age: 25 years and 273 days
Stage of his F1 career when title was won: Second full season
F1 debut: 1970 British Grand Prix (aged 23)
Emerson Fittipaldi became the first Brazilian driver to win the F1 world title in 1972, with five wins from 12 races enough for the Lotus driver to get the better of Jackie Stewart.
Fittipaldi would secure another drivers' title for McLaren two years later but his race-winning days, in F1 at least, were over once he joined his brother's Fittipaldi team in 1976. He would have late-career success in IndyCars, winning the 1989 title and the Indy 500 twice, in 1989 and 1993.
He remained F1's youngest champion for 33 years until Alonso's first title ushered in an era where the record would change hands more regularly.

If you give an AI agent a robotic arm, an injector, and a live mouse, it might just perform brain surgery.
Biotech founder Gabriel Ocana Santero recently did that using an agent to successfully carry out a brain injection procedure on a living mouse. Though it required some extra steps, it offers a glimpse into how AI could eventually become an active participant in laboratory research.
Santero posted about the experiment on social media and tells WIRED he was interested in exploring what happens when AI agents are given direct access to lab equipment, rather than simply being asked to design experiments or analyze results.
“We’ve realized that we need to connect these agents to a lab to get the maximum value from them,” he says. Santero is the CEO and cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco–based startup using AI to analyze brain activity to develop drugs for epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases.
AI models are trained primarily on published scientific literature. That means they may miss important information about the research process, including failed experiments, unexpected observations, and decisions scientists make in real time. Integrating AI models with real-world experiments can make the models more reliable, Santero says.
It’s why his team decided to connect an AI agent to a custom-built surgical setup used for performing brain injections on mice. The rig included a motorized device used to immobilize a mouse and a camera that allowed the agent to observe the procedure, move an injection needle, and control the delivery of a compound. For the experiment, his team was testing a gene therapy to see whether it could reduce seizures in a mouse with epilepsy.
They asked the AI model to choose a treatment from 19 options in a spreadsheet. A veterinary surgeon first performed a craniotomy on the mouse while the AI agent observed. The agent selected the therapy, brain region, and injection coordinates, then controlled the robotic arms and injector needle, as well as all the parameters, such as volume and speed.
The team initially tested Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 model, but it refused to guide the needle into the mouse’s brain, suggesting it might stop midway through the surgery, which could endanger the animal.
“He did the experimental planning, but when it was time to inject, he said, ‘something on my output is telling me I shouldn't do this,’” Santero says, referring to the agent. “That was very interesting.”
The team switched to using Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Opus is a heavy-reasoning intelligence specialist best for complex multistep problem-solving, according to Anthropic, while Sonnet is better suited for everyday tasks, though it may be a stretch to call mouse brain surgery a common chore. (Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment.)
Frontier labs have been planning for more widespread physical manifestations of AI, and researchers have already begun enlisting agents to do other things in the physical world. In August, Anthropic put out a framework for how its models can interact with the real world. More recently, AI engineers put GPT, Claude, and Grok in charge of a car to pick up lunch at In-N-Out Burger. Only one of the models succeeded.
The brain injection procedure wasn’t without hiccups either. The researchers had established safeguards, including requiring the AI to propose an injection plan for human approval and installing an emergency button a human could hit that would disconnect the rig’s motors. They also restricted the agent's access to the underlying equipment code to prevent it from modifying its own operating rules.
However, a technical glitch disrupted the equipment's coordinate system. Although the agent correctly recognized that the calculated injection position was wrong, it refused to modify the code to correct the problem because its instructions explicitly prohibited doing so.
The team resolved the issue by using a separate AI agent on Opus 5 to make the necessary code changes, but they didn’t tell the agent that a live surgery was happening. The resulting back and forth delayed the procedure, Santero says: A typical brain injection surgery like this takes about 45 minutes, while this experiment lasted slightly longer than an hour. They’re now waiting for the therapy to take effect before assessing its impact on seizures.
Despite those glitches, Santero and his team were impressed by the agent’s performance. They’re testing Grok and other models next to figure out whether one model performs better. The company is also experimenting with agent-controlled craniotomies—a much more complicated task—but wants to be absolutely sure of their safety before moving to live surgeries.
“A mistake at that stage could seriously harm the mouse,” he says.
Santero thinks AI agents will increasingly work alongside human scientists, with direct access to lab equipment. For now, he says human oversight is key, particularly when experiments involve living animals. And it’s far too soon to unleash an AI agent on a human brain.
As for the mouse, Santero reports it’s recovering well.

How Dart revived career with help of Wimbledon champion
- Published
In the hour following her first WTA title win, Britain's Harriet Dart had little time to respond to the stream of congratulatory messages flashing up on her phone.
Most pressing was making a call to her proud parents, Nick and Susie, who had been watching the final with friends at their local tennis club in north London, and her sister Phoebe.
The next person she spoke to was 2013 Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli.
Dart has been coached by the French former world number seven since the start of the season on a part-time basis, and she credits Bartoli for helping her achieve what some thought was beyond her.
On Sunday, with Bartoli watching from home, the world number 115 won the Guangzhou Open in China by beating rising Austrian teenager Lilli Tagger.
"It's been quite incredible to work with Marion, and I was really fortunate she was open to working with me," Dart, 30, told BBC Sport in a video call from Guangzhou.
"I'm obviously at a very different stage of my career to someone who is, say, 20. But I still feel I have a lot to improve and there are gains to be made.
"She really believes in me - that means the world to me. Seeing a Grand Slam champion having that belief has made me believe a lot more in myself."
- Britain's Dart wins first WTA title in 'wild week' 
  - Published4 hours ago
When Dart started working with Bartoli, she was ranked outside the top 160. The pair live close to each other in Dubai and spend training blocks together there when Dart is not on the road.
Dart and Bartoli, who has a young family, are not travelling full-time together on tour, but there have been opportunities for them to work on the ground, particularly during this year's Grand Slam tournaments.
Dart says 42-year-old Bartoli still hitting the ball "really well" in practice is another benefit of the partnership.
In Guangzhou, Dart was accompanied by her fitness trainer Dario Gonfiantini and boyfriend Stephen Falck. Without her coach, Dart had to largely rely on figuring things out herself - with the help of Bartoli sending over observational notes.
Dart is projected to rise to 83rd on Monday after lifting the Guangzhou trophy to cap a stunning second half of the season.
Dart has won 19 of her 24 tour-level matches on the hard courts since Wimbledon, taking her overall record on the WTA Tour this season to 23 victories from 34 matches - the highest winning percentage of her career.
"More than anything, Marion is just a great person. She cares about me as a person first and foremost, as well as improving me as a tennis player, of course," Dart said.
"It's been invaluable and amazing for her to share her experiences to make me better.
"I've learned a lot from her and look forward to continuing to learn more. I hope we will be able to spend more weeks together next year."
Dart reached a career high of 70th in the world in 2024, having made the Wimbledon third round and US Open second round, but has languished outside the top 100 for most of the past two seasons.
During this period there have been clear vulnerabilities with her game, with opponents learning they could take advantage of a slow second serve that tended to produce double faults.
There have also been questions about her on-court mentality and whether she could handle the pressure moments.
In Guangzhou, she answered those doubts with a series of gutsy wins where she needed to fight back from behind.
"She's always had a fantastic work ethic and has always set the bar high with her professionalism," Anne Keothavong, Britain's women's team captain, told BBC Sport.
"But there is certainly more belief and confidence now. She's in a very good place.
"She's been grinding away on the tour for a long time and it's great to see someone who has put in a lot of time to succeed and win a big title."
Keothavong named Dart in her squad for September's Billie Jean King Cup Finals and although she did not select Dart to play in the tie, she was impressed by her ball-striking during practice.
Taking that level back on tour has helped Dart continue what has been an encouraging few weeks for British women in the Asian hard-court swing.
Sonay Kartal reached the final of a WTA 1000 event in Wuhan, Katie Boulter made the semi-finals at a WTA 250 in Osaka and now Dart has won her maiden title at WTA 250 level.
Last week, teenager Hannah Klugman won the biggest title of her career at the Wrexham Open - a W100 event on the second-tier Challenger tour.
"The way they're all performing towards the end of the season - at whatever level - has been impressive," added Keothavong.
"It's not easy at this time of the season because there has been a lot of tennis played, but they've all capitalised and risen to the occasion.
"It's great reward for all their hard work and is encouraging for British tennis."

Ryanair may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
- Published
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff to pay for a sharp rise in its fuel costs which have surged following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The carrier said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and said it expects European airfares to increase to help cover the cost.
But it said that was unlikely to be enough and, among a number of measures, it is looking into "temporary pay freezes". The BBC has contacted Unite, the union which represents Ryanair employees, for comment.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to higher fuel costs,
Ryanair said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder had doubled.
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the war in the Middle East, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair's chief executive, Michael O'Leary, said last month he expects the firm and other airlines to increase fares by 15% to 20% next year.
He said at the time: "You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months.
"The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don't think it will be."
