France seethes again as youth-led protests sweep Europe
PARIS — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.
France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.
At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.
The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
The marchers' grievances are diverse.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.
Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."
The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.
Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.
Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.
Police impose curfew and other measures
The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.
While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.
Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.
Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands
In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.
Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.
Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.
In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.

Though the news broadcast is fake, the clip within it showing Trump speaking is real, meaning it is not the product of an artificial intelligence tool. Though Trump did say the words that can be heard in that section of the footage, he was quoting someone else. He was not saying that he, himself, has a husband. The clip featuring the president has been cropped for satirical purposes to omit this crucial context.
In late October, a video spread purportedly featuring a news broadcast showing U.S. President Donald Trump telling his supporters that he has a husband.
Social media users shared the footage on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X, where one user said (archived), "Trump says he sat down with his husband, they started writing, but ran out of paper!"
At one point in the alleged 15-second news clip, Trump seemingly says, "We sat down and I sat down with my husband and I started writing and I went on and on and in a little I realized I ran out of paper."
Trump says he sat down with his husband, they started writing, but ran out of paper! I ask this often, but I'll ask it again, what is wrong with him? https://t.co/FAHGyIq1xd
— BlueDream (@58bugeye) October 28, 2026
The story spread as the president attended campaign rallies in support of Republican candidates across the country ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Some users seemed to interpret the rumor as true. Snopes readers also contacted us to check if Trump said he has a husband.
To investigate the claim's legitimacy, we first used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. If Trump had authentically said he has a husband, journalists at reputable news outlets, such as The Associated Press or Reuters, would have likely reported on it, and those search inquiries would have uncovered such evidence. That was not the case.
The origin of the claim is a set of social media pages called The BSN Network. Its Facebook bio notes that it posts, "News reimagined through satire," and, "Comedy built from 'real' headlines."
A manager of the network posted a video to Facebook and Instagram on Oct. 28 (archived, archived) seemingly showing Trump saying he has a husband as part of a news broadcast. From two seconds onward, the footage features text that says, "Commentary | Comedy | Cultural Absurdity."
The news broadcast itself is not authentic. It includes an anchor who appears to have been generated using an artificial intelligence tool. It is not clear whether the character is based on a real person.
The BSN Network's video does contain authentic footage of Trump, though. That genuine clip originates from a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, on Oct. 3, during which Trump did say, "We sat down and I sat down with my husband and I started writing and I went on and on and in a little I realized I ran out of paper."
However, that section has been taken out of context for comedic purposes in The BSN Network's posts. An original recording of Trump's speech shows he was quoting a woman who he said was defending his presidential record. From the 1:16:23 mark, he says (emphasis in bold ours):
You know, a woman was on the other day and she was defending me against false charges. Just false crap, you know, political stuff. And she said, "You know, last night I sat down in my kitchen and I started writing out all the things that President Trump has accomplished during the second," this is our second term, probably you could say third term. We just don't, we just don't want the results of the second.
But, "We sat down and sat down with my husband, and I started writing, and I would on and on. And in a little while I realized I ran out of paper. I didn't have that much paper. We went all over the house looking for paper." So many things, it's true.
Snopes contacted The BSN Network for its response to the video being stripped of its "comedy" label in other users' posts and some people mistaking the satirical story as real news. We will update this article if we receive a response.
For further reading, Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before. For example, we alerted readers to a satirical claim that Trump asked why "we are wasting time counting ballots" when everyone "already knows the Republicans won the 2026 midterms."
Since satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call whether you agree.

In late October, a video spread on social media with claims it showed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being attacked and seriously injured in Tel Aviv.
"Breaking 🚨 A very dangerous attack on Netanyahu in Tel Aviv it appears he has sustained severe injuries, and an aircraft is being dispatched to transport him to the United States. This is clearly evident from the footage," one X post (archived) captioned the footage.
Other X users also shared the video. Snopes readers searched our website for information about the alleged attack.
The video is authentic, meaning not generated with artificial intelligence or digitally edited. However, it does not show Netanyahu. It shows an attempted attack on Bulgarian politician Ahmed Dogan during a party conference in January 2013. We have therefore rated the claim miscaptioned.
We found no credible reports of such an attack on Netanyahu. He remained politically active following Israel's Oct. 27 election and delivered a speech in Jerusalem the following day.
What we know about the video
On Jan. 19, 2013, Dogan, then the leader of Bulgaria's Movement for Rights and Freedoms party, was giving a speech in Sofia when a man came onto the stage and pointed a gas pistol at his head. The gun did not fire, and Dogan was not injured. Security guards and other people at the conference then stopped the attacker, according to reporting by the BBC and bTV, a Bulgarian broadcaster. The Guardian also shared footage of the incident.
Although a thumbnail attached to the circulating video appeared to show Netanyahu (see screenshot below), the footage of the attack itself didn't.
(X user @AsifAli_Haider)
The video's low quality also made it difficult to identify the person in the footage, which may have made the claim more believable to social media users.
This was not the first time social media users falsely linked the video to Netanyahu. In 2024, Reuters, AFP and Soch Fact Check debunked posts claiming the footage showed Netanyahu being attacked by members of Israel's parliament. Similar claims were debunked again in April 2026. When the video resurfaced in October, fact-checking outlet Lead Stories also investigated it.

Indian cuisine is gaining popularity across the United States, with Yelp, a crowd-sourced local business review and social networking platform, releasing its first-ever list of the Top 100 Indian Restaurants in the US, just ahead of the festive fall season and Diwali celebrations.
The list, released in 2026, highlights restaurants that have been winning over diners in America with traditional Indian dishes, regional specialities and innovative fusion offerings.
California and Florida feature prominently among the restaurants recognised, with several establishments receiving praise for their curries, biryanis, momos, tandoori preparations and vegetarian options.
The rankings come amid growing interest in Indian food across the US. According to Yelp, searches for Indian food buffets near users surged 437% in 2026, while searches for Indian tiffin services increased 76%. Searches for butter chicken also reached an all-time high on the platform in February 2026.
Yelp's findings suggest that diners are exploring Indian food beyond familiar favourites such as butter chicken and chicken tikka masala.
Biryani, samosas, street-style chaat and different varieties of curries remain popular choices. Meanwhile, momos, the steamed or fried dumplings popular across Nepal and the Himalayan region, are emerging as another favourite, particularly among younger diners.
Regional Indian cuisines are also finding a wider audience. Restaurants featuring the coconut-rich flavours of Kerala, the tangy and spicy preparations of Goa and the smoky tandoori cooking associated with Punjab have found a place on the list.
The growing popularity of vegetarian food is another notable trend, with restaurants offering dishes such as saag paneer, aloo gobi, vegetable korma and other plant-based preparations.
Yelp said it identified businesses listed under the Indian restaurant category and ranked them using several factors, including the total volume of customer reviews and their ratings.
To ensure geographical diversity, the platform included a maximum of 10 businesses from each US state. It also said that, wherever available, the restaurants featured on the list had a passing health score as of August 11, 2026.
Here are the top 10 Indian restaurants in the US, according to Yelp:
1. LA Indian Cuisine, Castaic, California
Taking the top spot is LA Indian Cuisine in Castaic, California. The restaurant has received more than 500 five-star reviews, with diners praising its extensive menu, generous portions and friendly service.
Its popular dishes include butter chicken, chicken tikka masala, tofu coconut curry, aloo gobi and saag paneer. Complimentary chai is another attraction for customers.
2. Mumbai House, Park City, Utah
Mumbai House offers a fine-dining Indian experience in the mountain resort town of Park City. Its popular dishes include vegetable samosas, chicken tikka masala, saag paneer and chicken makhani, commonly known as butter chicken. Its garlic naan is also a customer favourite.
3. Zen Curry and Grill, Temecula, California
Known for its Nepalese momos, Zen Curry and Grill serves the dumplings with roasted sesame-tomato sauce or in a warm tomato-based soup. Its menu also features vegetable korma, lamb curry, biryani and several varieties of naan.
4. Spice Station, Kingsville, Texas
This casual restaurant has earned a following for its chicken 65, butter chicken and freshly baked garlic naan. Owner Zohair Charania is also appreciated for helping customers explore Indian cuisine and offering food samples.
5. Tikka Indian Cuisine, Venice, Florida
The restaurant showcases Goan flavours through coconut-based curries, vindaloo and other regional preparations. Its popular offerings include butter chicken, chicken 65, samosas and eggplant chana chaat.
6. Hot N Chili, San Clemente, California
Inspired by Punjab, Hot N Chili serves North Indian dishes, including chicken tikka masala, butter chicken, palak paneer, lamb saag and goat biryani. Its all-you-can-eat lunch buffet is a major attraction.
7. Mesa, Jacksonville, Florida
Mesa combines Kerala cuisine with American flavours. Its signature offerings include Kerala shrimp and grits, made with basmati rice grits and tamarind sauce, and chicken wings prepared with ginger and sweet-sour tamarind.
8. Himali Bistro, Burlingame, California
Himali Bistro offers Nepalese and Himalayan specialities, including momos, lamb shank, chicken tarkari curry, tandoori chicken and gobi manchurian.
9. Mirchi Indian Cuisine, Newbury Park, California
The restaurant is known for its chicken tikka masala, jalfrezi and coconut curry. Its extensive vegetarian menu and variety of freshly prepared naan breads are also popular.

Indian opposition parties stage new protest against the elections chief
India’s opposition parties have renewed calls for the resignation of the country’s elections chief, staging fresh protests in the latest display of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government
NEW DELHI -- India’s opposition parties on Sunday renewed calls for the resignation of the country’s election chief, staging fresh protests in the latest display of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.
The protest, called by opposition bloc INDIA, drew tens of thousands of demonstrators, some carrying musical instruments and waving various flags, as they chanted slogans against the policies of the central government. Several opposition parties of the alliance, formed in 2023 to unseat Modi, mobilized their cadres from different states for the protest, which comes weeks after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.
Led by Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, and backed by the youth “Cockroach” movement, the protesters called for the safeguarding of India’s democracy while demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a contentious voter roll revision.
The protesters gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling public square in New Delhi, after police last month withdrew Jantar Mantar from the list of officially designated venues for demonstrations. The historic observatory had long served as the capital’s main protest site.
Authorities deployed thousands of police and paramilitary soldiers and mounted extensive surveillance, with more than 200 CCTV cameras, drones and body-worn cameras at the venue and along the protest route, officials said.
The ongoing review of voter lists has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
The Election Commission and Modi’s administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
Human Rights Watch on Thursday said the accusations over the voter roll revision raise “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections.”
“The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services,” said Elaine Pearson, the group’s Asia director, in a statement.
The call for Kumar’s resignation has for weeks been a rallying cry for opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. Opposition parties, mainly the Congress, say the ruling BJP has undertaken systemic manipulation of the electoral process, accusing the party of “vote chori”, or vote theft.
Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchists” and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.
In July, protests led by the youth “cockroach” movement forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister, a rare setback for Modi, who has been in power for more than 12 years. The movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites.
Suresh Sharma, a protester from northern Haryana state, said the country’s system needed reform as democracy was being throttled.
The process of voter roll revision needs to be scrapped, Sharma said, adding: “We demand that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign and be arrested.”

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

The SP chief’s public show of support for the veteran leader comes amid questions over the Azam Khan family’s influence on the party’s prospects ahead of the 2027 elections.
NEW DELHI: "Azam the, Azam hain aur Azam rahenge" (Azam was, Azam is and Azam will remain).With that emphatic declaration, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav sought to end speculation about his equation with one of the party's tallest Muslim leaders. But the political reality surrounding Mohammad Azam Khan is far more complicated than the slogan suggests.Nine days after Akhilesh's October 22 visit to Azam at Rampur jail, the veteran leader walked out of prison with his son Abdullah Azam after the Allahabad high court granted them bail in the dual PAN card case. His freedom, however, lasted barely minutes. The Enforcement Directorate arrested him in a separate money-laundering case linked to Mohammad Ali Jauhar University, and a court subsequently remanded him to 14 days' judicial custody.The dramatic turn has put Akhilesh's declaration to the test. Once among the most powerful figures in the SP, Azam remains central to the party's political calculations in Rampur and its relationship with Muslim voters. But his legal battles, the erosion of his family's electoral stronghold and the growing challenge from Asaduddin Owaisi have turned his return into a complicated political proposition.As Uttar Pradesh heads towards the 2027 assembly election, Akhilesh faces a question that goes beyond personal loyalty: can he hold on to Azam's political legacy without becoming hostage to its baggage?
The brief freedom
Azam and Abdullah had been in custody since November 2025 following their conviction in the dual PAN card case.
The Allahabad high court's order suspended their 10-year sentences and granted them bail, paving the way for their release.However, the ED had a separate case waiting. The agency arrested Azam shortly after he walked out of Rampur jail, while Abdullah was allowed to go home.The money-laundering investigation relates to alleged financial irregularities in the construction of Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur. The ED has alleged that government funds were diverted for the university's construction. Azam is the founder of the university and heads the trust that runs it. These are allegations being investigated by the agency, not findings of guilt in the present case.Speaking to reporters after his release, Azam alleged that he was being punished for being a Muslim and for establishing a university and schools. "What is there left to say? What can I say? The law has ceased to exist. Is this the punishment for being a Muslim?" he said.The following day, a special PMLA court in Ghaziabad sent him to 14 days' judicial custody. The court proceedings ensured that the brief release did not translate into a return to political activity.
Akhilesh turns arrest into political battle
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav responded sharply to the ED action, accusing the BJP government of using cases to repeatedly send an elderly political leader to jail.In a post on X, the SP chief said: "Let today's rulers remember that thrones change when the time changes. The conspiracy being hatched against Mr Azam Khan through these cases is being watched not just by the entire country, but by the whole world."He added that repeatedly implicating an elderly man in cases and sending him to jail was "an utterly cowardly act", warning that injustice could eventually turn into a calamity for those responsible.
The response was significant because it came barely nine days after Akhilesh had visited Azam in jail. That meeting had already signalled that the SP chief was unwilling to distance himself from the veteran leader despite the legal controversies surrounding him.The ED arrest has now sharpened the political messaging. For Akhilesh, the issue is no longer simply Azam's return to the party's political fold. It is also about positioning the SP against what it describes as the misuse of investigative agencies to target opposition leaders.The BJP, on the other hand, has defended the ED action, maintaining that the law applies equally to everyone.
The Muslim vote and the Owaisi challenge
For the Samajwadi Party, the stakes in the Azam Khan question go well beyond the fortunes of one leader. They concern the party's hold over a crucial section of its traditional support base: Muslim voters. Muslims account for roughly 19% of Uttar Pradesh's population, making them one of the state's largest voting blocs. Their concentration in several constituencies gives them considerable electoral influence. In the 2022 assembly election, the community was a decisive factor in around 70 constituencies where Muslims formed at least 30% of the population.The 2022 results also showed how strongly the community rallied behind the SP. The party fielded 64 Muslim candidates, of whom 31 won, taking the total number of Muslim MLAs in the assembly to 36, up from 24 in 2017. The BSP fielded 88 Muslim candidates and the Congress 75, while AIMIM fielded more than 60. Yet neither the BSP nor Congress managed to elect a single Muslim MLA. The results suggested that the SP had emerged as the principal beneficiary of Muslim consolidation, even as smaller parties remained relevant in individual constituencies.
Muslims account for at least 30% of the population in around 70 constituencies.
Azam Khan was central to this political equation. His influence in Rampur and his standing among sections of the Muslim community gave the SP an important local and regional network. His electoral record, along with that of his wife Tazeen Fatima and son Abdullah Azam, made the family one of the most prominent Muslim political establishments in the state. His absence from active politics has therefore left a space that other political players may seek to occupy.It is this space that AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi is attempting to enter. His October 18 rally in Tanda was a reminder that the SP cannot take Muslim support for granted. Owaisi accused Akhilesh of treating Muslims as a vote bank while prioritising the Yadav community, and questioned why the SP leadership had not done more for Azam Khan. His pitch was for independent Muslim political representation, arguing that the community should produce its own MLAs and MPs rather than remain a support base for established political families.Owaisi's intervention is significant because the SP's electoral arithmetic depends not just on retaining Muslim support but also on preventing its fragmentation. The 2022 results showed the limits of smaller parties: although BSP and AIMIM fielded substantial numbers of Muslim candidates, neither managed to convert that presence into Muslim representation in the Assembly. However, even without winning seats, such parties can potentially affect the outcome in closely contested constituencies by splitting votes.Akhilesh's October 22 visit to Azam in Rampur jail was therefore also a political signal. His declaration, "Azam they, Azam hain aur Azam rahenge" (Azam was, is and will remain), aimed to reassure the veteran leader's followers that the SP had not abandoned him. The visit came amid growing questions over whether Owaisi could use sympathy for Azam to make inroads among Muslim voters.The challenge is compounded by the SP's wider social coalition strategy. Akhilesh has sought to move beyond the traditional Muslim-Yadav combination through his PDA (Pichhda, Dalit, Alpsankhyak) framework, bringing backward classes, Dalits and minorities under a broader political umbrella. But the party cannot afford to lose its Muslim support base while attempting to expand its reach among other communities.
Owaisi has attacked Akhilesh Yadav over the treatment of Azam Khan's family.
As the 2027 assembly election approaches, Akhilesh faces a delicate balancing act. He must reassure Azam's supporters that the SP continues to value the veteran leader and his political legacy, while ensuring that the party's Muslim support base does not become an opening for Owaisi or other rivals. The 2022 election demonstrated the electoral value of Muslim consolidation behind the SP. The question now is whether Akhilesh can hold that coalition together without relying too heavily on one leader or one political family.
From kingmaker to political liability?
To understand Akhilesh Yadav's dilemma, one must first understand the extent of Azam Khan's influence in Rampur. For decades, Khan was not just the Samajwadi Party's most powerful face in the district but the man who dominated its political landscape. He challenged the influence of Rampur's erstwhile Nawab family and gradually built a formidable political network, winning the Rampur Sadar assembly seat 10 times. His influence extended beyond his own electoral victories: his wife, Tazeen Fatima, succeeded him as MLA in a 2019 bypoll, while his son Abdullah Azam twice won the Suar assembly seat. The Azam family's political presence became so entrenched that Rampur's electoral fortunes were often seen through the prism of Khan's influence.That hold was not easily broken. In the 2022 assembly election, Azam Khan won Rampur Sadar for the 10th time despite campaigning from jail. The BJP's Akash Saxena, one of his most prominent political adversaries who had pursued several cases against Azam Khan and his family, lost that contest. But the equation changed after Khan was disqualified following his conviction in a hate speech case. In the December 2022 bypoll, Saxena defeated Azam Khan's close aide Asim Raza by around 34,000 votes, delivering the BJP its first victory in Rampur Sadar and making Saxena the first Hindu candidate to win the constituency. The result marked a significant breach in a political stronghold that Khan and his family had dominated for decades.The erosion of the Azam family's influence became more apparent in the 2024 Lok Sabha election. With Khan, his wife and son facing imprisonment, the SP fielded Maulana Mohibullah Nadvi from Rampur. The choice reportedly upset Khan's loyalists, many of whom stayed away from campaigning, exposing a growing rift between the local Azam camp and the party leadership. It was a reminder that Azam Khan's network could still matter to the SP even in his absence, but also that Akhilesh could no longer assume the family would automatically fall in line with the party's decisions.His treatment by the central agencies gives the party an opportunity to frame the issue as one of political targeting and due process. But the party will have to contend with the electoral consequences of being closely associated with a leader whose legal record has become a recurring political flashpoint.The challenge for Akhilesh is to retain the political value of the Azam network without allowing the controversies surrounding Khan and his family to define the SP's wider campaign. In Rampur, the question is no longer simply whether Azam Khan can return to politics. It is whether the political machinery he built can still deliver for the Samajwadi Party, and on whose terms.
BJP's counter: 'Mafia raj' and law and order
In 2022, UP CM Yogi Adityanath famously said: "Even Akhilesh doesn’t want Azam Khan to come out of jail because it will pose a threat to his position [chair]. The state government has nothing to do with these cases, whether they are related to Azam Khan or anyone else. It is the court that grants bail.""Under previous governments, mafias were running a parallel administration. When we took action against the land mafia who grabbed poor farmers' land for private universities and personal fiefdoms, the Samajwadi Party developed sympathy for criminals instead of the victims," he had said.The above remarks are at the core of the BJP's attack.The BJP has consistently used the Azam Khan issue to attack the Samajwadi Party's record on law and order. The party's broader political narrative has sought to associate the SP's previous tenure with alleged criminal influence and what it describes as 'mafia raj'.That gives the BJP an obvious line of attack if Akhilesh makes Azam's rehabilitation a central political theme. The ruling party can frame the SP's outreach as evidence that it has not moved away from its past.
UP accused Akhilesh of opposing Azam Khan’s release out of concern that the veteran leader could challenge his position in party.
The SP, meanwhile, has to navigate the distinction between allegations, court findings and the political narrative built around them. It can point to the legal process and the need for due process, but it cannot wish away the electoral impact of the cases and convictions.The BJP's attack also puts the SP's broader coalition strategy under pressure. Akhilesh has sought to expand the party's social base beyond its traditional support groups through the PDA framework. A campaign dominated by the Azam Khan controversy could complicate that effort.Akhilesh's jail visit, his response to the ED arrest and the party's continued engagement with Azam Khan send a message to the SP's traditional supporters: the party has not abandoned a leader who played a major role in building its political presence.But the message also carries risks. The SP has to decide how much political space to give the Azam family, how prominently to project its association with them and how to prevent the issue from becoming a defining feature of its 2027 campaign.
For Akhilesh, the Azam question will ultimately be about the political arithmetic as much as loyalty. He needs to reassure sections of the Muslim electorate that the SP remains attentive to their concerns, while keeping the PDA coalition broad enough to bring together backward classes, Dalits and minorities.As Uttar Pradesh moves towards 2027, Akhilesh's tightrope walk will be to retain the political value of an old ally without inheriting all the baggage that comes with him. Azam may be an asset the SP cannot easily discard, but he may also turn out to be a liability the party cannot afford to let define its next election.

Audacious Indian jailbreak saga ends with 17 prisoners recaptured
- Published
A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.
Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.
It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.
The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.
The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.
All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.
On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.
The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.
Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.
Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.
Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".
"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.
On Thursday, he was replaced as the head of state prisons and transferred to a different department.
At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.
The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.
"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.
Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.
A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.
Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.
News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.
Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.
The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.
While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.
Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.

UPI transaction volume rose 5.8% MoM to a record 25.47 Bn in October from 24.07 Bn in September, according to data released by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). The value of transactions processed through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) increased 7.4% MoM to a record ₹31.53 Lakh Cr from ₹29.37 Lakh Cr in the previous month. On a YoY basis, transaction volume grew 23%, while transaction value rose 16%. October marked the first month in which UPI processed more than 25 Bn transactions and payments worth over ₹30 Lakh Cr. Average daily transaction value also crossed ₹1 Lakh Cr for the first time. UPI processed an average of 822 Mn transactions a day in October, up from 802 Mn in September. Average daily transaction value increased to ₹1,01,707 Cr from ₹97,913 Cr. The daily averages provide a clearer comparison of payment activity because October had 31 days against September’s 30. Based on NPCI’s figures, average daily volume increased 2.5% MoM, while average daily value rose 3.9%. The increase coincided with the festive season. October’s growth followed a marginal decline in September, when transaction volume fell 1.8% MoM and transaction value dropped 1.5%. Merchant Charges On Horizon The latest figures come ahead of the proposed introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) charges on select UPI payments. The NPCI deferred the rollout, originally scheduled for October 15, until after Diwali, saying the new implementation date would be notified separately. MDR is the fee merchants pay banks and payment companies to process digital transactions. Under the revised framework, eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) payments above ₹2,000 will attract a 0.4% charge, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. Person-to-person (P2P) payments will remain free of MDR. The revised structure would create a revenue stream for banks and payment service providers processing eligible transactions, potentially improving monetisation across the UPI ecosystem. However, merchant bodies have raised concerns over the additional payment acceptance costs and sought relief ahead of the rollout.

Udhampur, Nov 1: Inspector General of Police (IGP) and Director Sher-i-Kashmir Police Academy (SKPA), Udhampur Dr Mohd Haseeb Mughal has stressed the need for police personnel to remain technologically informed, develop specialised skills and keep pace with advancements in drone technology to effectively address emerging security and investigative challenges.
He was addressing the gathering at SKPA, Udhampur during a presentation-cum-valedictory session marking the culmination of a five-day course on “Drone Technology, Interception and Drone Forensics” for the officers of J&K Police, aimed at enhancing the professional knowledge and operational capabilities of police personnel in the rapidly evolving field of unmanned aerial systems.
Dr Mohd Haseeb Mughal, while delivering a comprehensive power-point presentation, highlighted the growing significance of drone technology in contemporary policing and its emerging applications in law enforcement, surveillance, security and crime investigation.
During his presentation, the Director elaborated on the fundamentals of drone technology, different types of drones, their operational capabilities and the need for police personnel to develop a sound understanding of drone systems.
He also highlighted the importance of drone forensics, particularly in understanding digital evidence, identification and examination of drone-related data, preservation of electronic evidence and its relevance in criminal investigations.
The Director also drew attention to the emerging challenges associated with the misuse of drones, including security threats, unlawful surveillance, smuggling and other technology-driven criminal activities.
The presentation provided participants with valuable insights into the practical and investigative dimensions of drone technology and reinforced the importance of integrating technological understanding with professional policing.
The session was followed by the valedictory function, during which the course was formally concluded. The participating officers and officials were encouraged to utilise the knowledge and skills acquired during the course in their respective fields of assignment.
The programme concluded with an emphasis on continuous learning, technological up gradation and capacity building to make policing more effective, responsive and future-ready.

Travel distribution platform TBO Tek reported a 12.5% year-on-year (YoY) increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹76 Cr for the September quarter of FY27 (Q2 FY27) from ₹67.6 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue rose 52.6% YoY to ₹865.6 Cr. On a sequential basis, the company's performance was more muted. Its operating revenue fell 6.5% from ₹925.8 Cr recorded in the June quarter, while net profit fell 8.8% from ₹83.4 Cr. Including other income of ₹14.8 Cr, total income for the quarter stood at ₹880.4 Cr. On the other hand, total expenses jumped almost 54.8% to ₹780.7 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹504.5 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Service fees, the largest expense item, surged49.2% to ₹304.6 Cr, while employee benefits expenses increased 76.8% to ₹190.7 Cr. TBO Tek reported an exceptional expense of ₹8.14 Cr during the quarter, relating to suspected collusion involving current and former employees of its overseas subsidiary and the holding company. Based on a preliminary assessment, the company estimated a net financial loss of ₹8.14 Cr and said it had initiated legal action and the process for an insurance claim. The final loss may change after the detailed assessment. Further, tax expense for the quarter increased 46% YoY to ₹15.5 Cr. Consequently, profit before tax stood at ₹91.5 Cr, against ₹78.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. Profit before tax, after accounting for exceptional items, stood at ₹91.5 Cr, up 17% from ₹78.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. The Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, on Monday (November 2, 2026) challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to an open debate, alleging that it was with “foreign help” that Mr. Modi became Prime Minister and continues to occupy the position.
The Congress leader’s challenge came after the Prime Minister had accused the Opposition of taking foreign help to destabilise the country.
“Mr. Modi, stop lying to this nation. You became PM because of foreign help. You remain PM because of foreign help. Your financial system is fully controlled and supported by foreigners. Foreign social media fully backs you,” Mr. Gandhi alleged in a post on X.
“I challenge you to an open debate about this. Any stage, any time. Come if you have the guts. You won’t dare, because you are terrified of what I know about you,” he added.
He also shared a screenshot of a media report on the Prime Minister’s allegation that obstructionist forces were trying to divide the country and that social media was being used to spread rumours.
“When the country was seeking solutions to external challenges, some forces within the country were also creating instability by spreading lies and rumours. But the countrymen stood shoulder to shoulder with the nation,” Mr. Modi had said on Saturday (October 31) in Gujarat.
“It is our misfortune that at this time in the country, the Opposition has turned into an avrodh paksh (destructive force) rather than virodh paksh (opposing side). In their frustration, these people are standing as obstacles in the way of the country’s development. This is not opposition; this is obstruction,” the Prime Minister had said, adding that “these people were engaged in shredding the boundaries of the Constitution”.
Mr. Modi also took a dig at the Opposition leader’s trips abroad without directly naming him.
“Due to the frustration of more than a decade, these people have now come out in the open. Who is secretly meeting whom abroad? Whom are the anti-India forces supporting? Who is speaking the language of India’s enemies? We will have to recognise all these patterns,” the Prime Minister had said.

Rural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump

President Donald Trump's administration has pledged $15 billion to agricultural producers in the final weeks before the midterm elections.
The funding aims to help farmers offset elevated diesel and fertilizer costs stemming largely from tariffs and the war in Iran.
Whether this package will boost voter turnout in farming states where historically safe Republican seats are now competitive remains uncertain. It helps explain his heightened focus on rural communities, including visits to Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before the vote.
A look at the Republican administration's pledges to farmers:
Who these efforts will help
Besides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump's Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice.
Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines.
Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to “more than cover the increase in fuel costs,” and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices.
At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects.
On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs.
The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock.
Why farmers are struggling
It has been a frustrating year for farmers. Increased costs for fertilizer and fuel have made it difficult to turn a profit. Last year, tariffs drove up expenses for other equipment that farmers use, and the trade war with China resulted in a near boycott of U.S. agricultural goods.
On Friday, diesel was averaging $6.32 per gallon, down slightly from its peak in September but 70% higher than the price a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Filling up a 100-gallon tank now costs $260 more than it did one year ago.
“That input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about what’s going to happen in the world,” Ibendahl said.
He said he expects these ad hoc payments to be a big help for farmers who otherwise would not make a profit this year, but they do not address the broader issues driving up prices.
“It’s hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, ‘OK, well, we’re looking pretty good this year, but it’s all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?’” he said.
Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said she has heard mixed reactions from farmers, who are happy their business will survive this year but see these programs as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution.
What farmers may vote on
Rural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump.
Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said many rural voters like the president, but some of his policies have hurt the agriculture industry. Immigrant deportations have threatened the agricultural labor force, and cuts to foreign aid and SNAP food stamps hurt the market for agricultural products.
“Some people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man,” he said. “But it doesn’t mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isn’t on the ballot this year. His policies are.”
Cost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy.
Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates.
“Independent voters make or break elections," she said. "And so that’s really what it’s going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they’re breaking for.”

In a major blow to both the terminally online and the criminally horny, the fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) has temporarily shut down due to a “security incident,” according to an update posted on the site.
On October 29, an admin for AO3 posted that the website was “down for maintenance.” The statement said that it could take up to four weeks for service to be fully restored, though it was possible the site would be back up in a “degraded state” sooner, with some of its features disabled.
Though the original statement did not specify the reasons for the closure, subsequent updates said that a “security incident” had taken place, though “we are still in the early stages of response [and] determining its scope.” While the statement said that AO3 did not believe that its user database had been stolen, it urged users to exercise caution and change their passwords for the site.
Run by the Organization for Transformative Works, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving fandom communities on the internet, AO3 was founded in 2007 in part due to concerns about censorship and corporate interests overtaking fandom spaces. The website has 11 million users, according to a 2026 press release, and hosts more than 18 million original works. The explosive popularity of the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry TV series generated a surge of new interest last year, resulting in the publication of tens of thousands of stories featuring the show’s main characters, Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, on the platform.
Those reliant on AO3 for their daily dose of Destiel- or Dramione-inspired smut are not taking the news well. “No ao3 for possibly 4 weeks SOMEONE DO SOMETHING,” one Heated Rivalry fan account posted on X, tagging not just AO3 itself but also the official X accounts for the FBI, the CIA, and, for some reason, Uber Support. Other fans are compiling Google Docs of links to downloaded stories, touting them as “survival guides” for the “AO3 apocalypse” and organizing them by fictional character pairings, or ships. (Be warned, however: One such doc is difficult to load due to “heavy traffic” on the file.)
Others commented on the timing of the outage, pointing out that it coincides with “No Nut November,” the internet-based challenge that encourages people to abstain from masturbation throughout the month. “AO3 taking no nut november a little too seriously,” one person wrote.
A representative for the Organization for Transformative Works did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the chaos inspired by the site’s shutdown underscores the prominence of fan fiction in everyday lives, driving mainstream publishing trends and generating hundreds of millions of views. It also serves as the engine for the burgeoning vertical video industry, with streaming platforms constantly scouring fan fiction websites for works to adapt.
“All life forms dependent on AO3 are literally withering right now,” one fan wrote. “This is our 9/11.”

As AI tools and agents have continued their march across all aspects of digital life, many companies are trying to use LLMs to improve the experience of purchasing goods and services on the Internet. Thus far, though, a vanishingly small number of people seem to be taking advantage of those capabilities, at least when it comes to using the popular food delivery app DoorDash with an outside AI agent.
In a third-quarter earnings call Thursday, DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu responded to an analyst question by noting that “AI agents are generating several hundred orders [on DoorDash] across the time that they’ve been up and running.” In a marked understatement, Xu called this a “very low use case” for a company that handled just shy of 1 billion orders total in the third quarter of 2026 alone.
Speaking generally, Xu said he sees the potential for AI agents to be genuinely helpful for “long consideration purchases” and major decisions where agents would be “doing work on your behalf proactively in the background.” However, Xu added, “when it comes to a task that’s as simple as ordering food, we tend to see that come directly to DoorDash.”
Give it time?
To be fair to the AI boosters, DoorDash only rolled out its Model Context Protocol (MCP) connector less than a month ago. The connector provides a standardized, open-standard way for third-party AI tools to easily order through DoorDash’s platform. Without that kind of linkup—which is still only available to a small number of “early beta partners” and mainly used to streamline corporate lunch orders—AI agents have to go through a bit more effort to access DoorDash through a web interface, for instance.

New Delhi [India], November 2: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has reduced the cooling-off period for offer for sale (OFS) of units of illiquid private listed Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) to eight weeks, with the revised provision coming into immediate effect.
The move is aimed at facilitating ease of doing business and follows feedback received from market participants, according to a circular issued by the market regulator on Monday.
Revised Cooling-Off Period Takes Effect
Under the revised framework, the cooling-off period for private listed InvITs whose units are illiquid will be ±8 weeks. The change has been incorporated into the existing OFS framework governing the sale of units of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and InvITs through the stock exchange mechanism.
SEBI said the broader OFS framework applicable to equity shares of listed companies would also apply to the sale of REIT and InvIT units, subject to certain conditions.
Trading Lot And Retail Provisions
For InvITs, the trading lot will continue to be the same as the lot applicable in the secondary market under the SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014.
The regulator has also clarified that provisions relating to retail investors under the general OFS framework will not apply to OFS transactions involving private listed InvITs. Such offers will remain open for only one day, or the trading day on which the offer takes place.
Changes To Existing OFS Framework
The revised provision modifies paragraph 19.2 under Chapter 1 of SEBI's Master Circular dated December 30, 2024, which had laid down the comprehensive framework for OFS of shares, including units of REITs and InvITs.

Stock Exchanges Directed To Implement Changes
SEBI has advised recognised stock exchanges to put in place the necessary systems to implement the changes and make amendments to their relevant bye-laws, rules and regulations wherever required.
The exchanges have also been directed to inform market participants, including investors, about the revised provisions and disseminate the circular on their websites.

Dutch police offer record €2m reward in hunt for drug lord
- Published
Dutch authorities have offered a record award of €2m (£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.
The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.
Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".
Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.
He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.
In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.
Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.
West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.
In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling more than seven metric tons of cocaine.
Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.
Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch authorities estimate he has made tens of millions of euros from cocaine smuggling, and accuse him of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence.

Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.
Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – to declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.
“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.
Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.
But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.
Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.
“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.
Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.
The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.
Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.
“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.
The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.
The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.
José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”
Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.
Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.
Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.
The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.
Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.
Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.
Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.
Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
When New York became the first state in the country to enact a moratorium on data center development, Adrienne Yocina was excited. For the past two years, the mom of three has been organizing in western Genesee County to stop a 600-megawatt data center from coming to a site close to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation’s reservation and a federal wildlife refuge.
But almost four months after the one-year moratorium began, Yocina tells me that she’s “getting nervous.” She’s worried that Democratic governor Kathy Hochul won’t sign a stronger bill to impose a stricter moratorium, and is concerned that the state Department of Environmental Conservation is not adequately involved in the process of evaluating data centers in New York.
“I feel like she’s just trying to shut us up,” she says of Hochul.
Data centers are at the center of midterm races across the country, with politicians of both parties making promises to enact regulations or moratoriums on development. After next week comes the tough part: Newly elected officials must either break their word or follow through on those promises as they weigh large infrastructure projects coming to their states and residents who say they’ll reject data centers no matter what.
How will those compromises go—and will they appease voters? New York’s moratorium, and the continued opposition from some groups, may offer clues.
In July, just two months after dismissing the idea of a data center moratorium, Hochul signed the nation’s first executive order to put a pause on development. Her order was a compromise. Just weeks prior, the state legislature had passed an omnibus bill that would have implemented a one-year moratorium throughout New York. The bill contained several provisions that made it more aggressive than Hochul’s moratorium, including stricter limits on the size of data centers and a mandate that the Department of Environmental Conservation conduct a thorough environmental impact review of data center operations. Rather than sign the bill, Hochul issued her own order. (The governor has until the end of the year to sign that bill, and her office says they are still looking at it.)
One of the bill’s State Senate sponsors, Democrat Kristen Gonzalez, has been publicly supportive of Hochul’s moratorium. The governor’s office, Gonzalez says, proactively reached out to her after her bill passed to help design the moratorium for more immediate relief for New Yorkers.
Gonzalez went on a data center tour of New York at the end of the summer, talking to residents around the state about their concerns. She told me that the people she talked to overwhelmingly wanted Hochul to go further and implement more aggressive measures to protect communities from data centers.
“There are local communities statewide that are living near existing data centers, dealing with significant air pollution and noise pollution, who are struggling with rising utility bills and rising water bills,” she told me. “We see the moratorium as a first step, but it can’t be the last.”
Hochul has a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman ahead of Tuesday’s election—something that may have been helped by the moratorium’s passing. In a recent Quinnipiac poll of New York voters, 53 percent of respondents said they trusted Hochul to do a better job in handling AI and data centers, compared to just 31 percent trusting Blakeman. Blakeman, who has voiced support for data centers, called Hochul’s moratorium “crazy” when it was passed in July. His campaign didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Hochul has also touted her tough-on-data-center bona fides on the campaign trail. Early last month, she hosted a roundtable discussion on data centers with agricultural, environmental, and business leaders at a farm in the Hudson Valley. There, she told reporters that she wanted to work with the state legislature to implement more aggressive protections, including banning tax breaks for data centers. At the event, Hochul was flanked by Gonzalez and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of Washington’s most prominent data center critics.
I asked Hochul at the event how she anticipates handling continued opposition after her moratorium ends. How does New York balance economic development with community opposition if some people don’t want data centers in their backyards under any circumstances, even with the assurances from the state that Hochul’s office is working to create?
The purpose of her pause, she said, was that communities should be able to choose. “This is democracy in action,” she said. “If you want it, it should come with all kinds of guardrails and restraints, but if you don’t want it, it doesn’t come.”
More New Yorkers may end up choosing the latter option. A Siena poll from September found that 63 percent of New Yorkers would oppose data centers being built in their area even after Hochul’s moratorium expires. (It’s even higher for New York Democrats, with 75 percent saying they’d remain opposed to data center development post-moratorium.)
Many newly elected (or reelected) governors will face a similar dynamic: At least 20 gubernatorial candidates have promised a data center moratorium or pause, according to research compiled by government relations company MultiState. Even more have promised to regulate the industry more tightly. Formerly data-center-friendly incumbents like Texas’s Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro have also made pledges to be stricter on their development.
Come January, new governors will face highly engaged constituents who are finding a political home for the first time in the fight against data centers. That includes Yocina, who says she had never voted in a local election before.
She says she understands the need for industries and jobs in upstate New York: Her youngest son decided to join the Army after a fruitless job search and is about to be deployed. Now, her organizing group is moving from focusing on just stopping the data center to brainstorming new ideas for the site.
“We’re trying to figure out what we can say yes to that’s not a data center,” she says.
What We’re Writing
Buried in Anthropic’s IPO documents filed last week was a startling admission. The tech giant’s plan to develop its own data centers exposes it to financial risk, thanks to its projected reliance on natural gas. Of course, Anthropic isn’t alone in its reliance on gas, and the filing acknowledges that’s a real problem. The heavy demand could “drive up the price of natural gas” and make it harder to purchase. I took a look at Anthropic’s plans for data centers and the brewing competition between data centers over natural gas supply in the US.
What We’re Reading
- The Verge’s Gaby Del Valle takes readers out west for a deep dive on data centers’ water woes in Arizona—and why a massive and thirsty chip manufacturing plant seems to have escaped the public’s ire.
- New findings from Pew Research Center show that advertisers spent $12 million on political ads mentioning data centers in a 90-day period leading up to the midterms.
- Two professors who study real estate and urban economics write in The Conversation about their most recent research on data centers and job creation. Their findings: Data centers lead to modest job growth in certain sectors like transportation and warehousing, but not in local services like restaurants and retail.
