Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it’s unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.
A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name “chasm” was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name “tengu_heron_brook”—reads as follows:
Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.
XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the “tengu_heron_brook” rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.
Following chasm’s initial report, Anthropic software engineer Addy Osmani confirmed on social media that the company had “added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.”
He added that the new prompt was designed to still allow “original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets,” even as a handful of issue reports on Anthropic’s GitHub suggest the new prompt is getting in the way of some game development use cases.

The world is set to miss its 2030 conservation goals as finance and action have fallen short, leaders recognized at a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia’s capital, where they agreed to step up efforts after a final overnight session.
Representatives from almost 200 countries gathered in Yerevan over the past two weeks to review progress on a landmark agreement set four years ago to protect about a third of the world’s land and seas by 2030.
The COP17 talks on biodiversity concluded on Saturday with a recognition that conservation efforts were so far too slow to realistically achieve the goals of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
A plan was agreed to accelerate progress ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway. It would mean redoubling efforts to tackle subsidies and incentives that are harmful to nature, increasing financial, scientific, and technical support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Steven Guilbeault, former Canadian minister of environment and climate change, said that finance remained one of the biggest obstacles to achieving global biodiversity goals.
The fact that a fund agreed at the last meeting—for companies profiting from genetic materials to voluntarily contribute to—stood largely empty was “especially disappointing.”
“We need to mobilize substantially more public and private finance, reform subsidies that harm nature, and ensure that funding reaches the countries and communities on the front lines of the nature crisis,” he said.

On Sept. 23, I sat in a small glass reading room at Yale’s medical library, turning the rag-paper pages of the Medical Dissenter, a London journal from the 1830s. At the bottom of one page, under the headline, “Report from Mrs. Butt to Mr. Hudson,” I met Jane Butt. Her letter was dated Sept. 23, 1834. I was reading it 192 years later to the day.
Jane lived in the village of Broughton and explained that measles had spread through the children around her earlier that year. She described how one of her own children had caught it. She then reported 36 other cases in her community. Some, she noted, developed severe inflammation of the lungs, one of the complications that can make measles deadly. She believed a cold east wind aggravated their symptoms. Nevertheless, she reported, all of them recovered.
Jane attributed the recoveries to Morison’s pills. James Morison was a merchant with no medical training who believed that a purgative could expel “impure blood” from the body and restore its natural balance. She administered the pills to the sick — sometimes twice a day — and gave as many as six at once to a toddler not yet 2 years old. She also gave the pills to women and, later, to their newborns, she wrote.
Morison’s followers called themselves Hygeists and attacked physicians as a monopoly that bled and poisoned its patients, which was not inaccurate in the 1830s. Much of medicine before the advent of germ theory and bacteriology provided incorrect diagnoses and problematic treatments.
When Jane wrote her letter, women could not train as physicians and were being displaced as midwives by the growing professional authority of doctors. She lacked medical credentials or the authority that came with them, but the Hygeist movement gave her a platform and a space to speak. She said that because “so much [was] said and done to prejudice the public mind against Mr. Morison’s most invaluable medicine,” she was left with no choice.
The journal that printed Jane’s letter sold the cure she praised. The office of the Medical Dissenter on the Strand was one of Morison’s official London depots for the pills in 1837. The same periodical mocked Edward Jenner, who had effectively used cowpox as a vaccination for smallpox, and ridiculed “vaccinic mania.”
After reading Jane’s story, I pulled out my iPhone and took photos of it, which I turned into a PDF. As a historian of medicine, I have seen cases of measles often in historical sources from the Civil War to life among the poor in tenement houses, but when I read those cases measles had long been the province of the past.
As I read Jane’s letter measles was back and raging in my home state of Pennsylvania, where six measles-associated deaths have been reported and federal health officials have disputed how many of them to count. In 2026, the United States has already recorded more than 4,500 measles cases, the largest number since 1991. Last school year, a record 4.2% of kindergartners were exempted from at least one required vaccine, and coverage for the measles vaccine fell to 92.4%, below the level needed to keep outbreaks from spreading. In some communities, the percentages of children who are vaccinated are far lower.
The current explosion of measles in the present had changed how I see the past. I didn’t preserve Jane’s story to indict her or to provide an antecedent to the unfounded arguments against vaccination, which have directly harmed innocent children. I documented her story instead because I had just finished a book on the ways ordinary people changed health care in the United States, and yet their stories have often been neglected, marginalized, or perceived to interfere with the real work of physicians. I wrote the book to show that medical knowledge is not an unalloyed concept created by professionals, but that ordinary people have continually provided evidence, offered interpretations, or even, in the case of Jane, simply counted the number of people who were sick in their communities.
Today, health populism takes shape in the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is rooted in part in grievances over how medical authority has dismissed patients, especially women. According to Politico, MAHA is “made up largely of women who followed Robert F. Kennedy Jr. into the MAGA fold.” Many of these women are moms. MAHA has, in turn, capitalized on the chauvinism of medical authority that began nearly 200 years ago that dismissed women as caregivers and often neglected their insights, their concerns, and their fears about epidemics.
The very act of counting, which might seem obvious or like a natural response to an epidemic, was part of a broader movement that eventually provided a framework for public health. Long before epidemiology developed as a discipline, patients and practitioners observed contagion — that disease seemed to spread from person to person, through households and across villages and nations. Before there was an official public health authority to count, people counted. Counting was also a move toward empiricism. It offered a bird’s-eye view of an epidemic and could provide local physicians or municipal authorities with some sense of the extent of an outbreak.
Counting mattered more than it might seem. Jane lived between two ways of explaining illness. In 1832, when a cholera pandemic reached New York City, clergy called for a national day of fasting and prayer. President Andrew Jackson refused to proclaim one, citing the separation of church and state, so states and churches held their own. Meanwhile, the city published daily counts of the sick and the dead. As the historian Charles Rosenberg showed in “The Cholera Years,” Americans read the epidemic as a judgment on sin even as they tracked it case by case. Jane blamed the wind and thanked God for her family’s recoveries, and she counted, reflecting the beginning of the shift from supernatural explanations to an empirical rationale. Documenting which children grew sickest and following an illness from house to house was a method aimed at articulating an explainable pattern. That method was not dissimilar to what physicians, ship surgeons, and military officials did in the first half of the 19th century when an epidemic erupted.
Jane’s method of dosing pills suffered from one problem: She did not observe what happened if a child did not receive the pills. Most children who caught measles in 1834 survived it, with or without pills. Thirty-seven recoveries indicated to her that the pills worked. They could not tell her what the pills did, or whether children like that toddler recovered despite them. Around the same time, the Paris physician Pierre Louis was also counting patients, and his numbers challenged bloodletting, one of medicine’s most trusted treatments, as a treatment for pneumonia. Louis asked what happened to comparable patients treated differently.
The vaccine does what Jane believed her pills did, and it was tested in ways her pills never were. Parents who refuse it are making Jane’s mistake in reverse. She credited a cure that did nothing. They discount a protection that works, because measles has become a stranger.
Jane wrote her letter two years after the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, a precursor to the British Medical Association, was founded in 1832 and more than a decade before the American Medical Association was founded in 1847 — a period in which men on both sides of the Atlantic were defining themselves as the institutional medical authority.
Ordinary people have been actively involved in the conversation since the beginning, but the medical populism of MAHA is making it appear as a new, novel, and even groundbreaking rebellion. Jane’s document reveals that ordinary people’s ideas have often been part of medicine, but medical authority has grown in ways that make them appear as dissenting.
Jane could not be heard in traditional medical circles. Sexism landed her in a fringe periodical, and her endorsement of the quackery of purgatives gave her a headline.
If men had not systematically excluded women from medicine and had recognized that ordinary people’s ideas, insights, and concerns are part of it, Jane might not have reached for purgative pills, and women today might not be reaching for pyrotechnic platforms to be heard.
I have been trained not to write in the conditional tense but instead to explain what happened and how it all went down. I wasn’t looking for her. I found her by accident, but I am drawn to ordinary people’s stories. That’s why I found Jane’s letter so appealing. Before I contextualized it and realized it was part of a radical publication, I was amazed to see the name of a woman in a headline in boldface in a rare book.
Although Jane does not appear in my book, she embodies its thesis — even though her method was wrong. In fact, much of medical practice was wrong or ineffective before the late 19th century, and plenty remained so afterward. There were many ordinary people, like Jane, who witnessed outbreaks and illness in their communities and reported what they saw.
When I closed the volume containing Jane’s letter and walked out of the secure room, through the Victorian reading room, through the rotunda, and past the portraits of physicians whose names circle its walls, Jane’s name was not there, nor were those of any other women from 200 years ago.
It does not have to continue to be that way. Ordinary people’s voices matter and they often begin not in the throes of a national polemic or screamed through a speaker at a MAHA rally but begin, like Jane, with an observation of a child’s health.
Jim Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare” (W. W. Norton, October 2026). He is the Gilder Lehrman–NEH professor of history at Gettysburg College and a visiting faculty fellow at Brown University’s Center for the Study of Race and Ethnicity in America. He is a 2025–26 Guggenheim fellow.

What Vance's midterm push reveals about his potential 2028 bid
What Vance’s midterm push reveals about his potential 2028 bid
At a Thursday speech in Weatherford, Texas, Vice President JD Vance seemed to relish the opportunity to snipe at Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
"Now James Talarico has also said that he really has to grapple with his masculinity in addition to his whiteness," Vance said. "And you know, James, the good news is, there ain't a whole lot to grapple with," he finished to cheers from the crowd.
Vance gave the speech the same afternoon that President Trump spoke in Rock Hill, South Carolina, as part of his pre-midterm blitz of rallies. And while Vance's delivery was different from the president's – less borscht-belt comedian, more practiced politician – it contained plenty of MAGA DNA, from insulting a candidate's masculinity to promising a return of American greatness. It all gives a sense of what a Vance presidential pitch might look like once 2028 campaigns begin in earnest next year.
Vance paints a rosy picture of the America of his youth, in his speeches – in North Carolina this week, he invoked the "sense of pride and unity and fellowship" Americans had after September 11, 2001.
He added to that message in multiple speeches remembering his childhood football teams being sponsored by local small businesses.
"I distinctly remember looking in my old jerseys and seeing the names of the businesses that had sponsored those teams and realizing that most of the teams I played for, those businesses no longer existed," he said in Howell, Michigan. "They were casualties of politicians in a faraway place who didn't give a damn what happened to Michigan or Ohio, and it was us that paid the consequences."
Culture warrior
It's a story about a Norman Rockwell vision of America corrupted by Washington elites. The story Vance tells is that his brand of populist politics can bring that back.
But it's not just about economics; Vance leans hard into the culture wars fought during the Trump years. In his stories about peewee football, Vance talks about racial harmony well before the advent of Black Lives Matter: "the children of working-class Black families and the children of working-class white families would play football together, would cheer with one another, would never worry about the color of their skin or who had more privilege," he told the crowd in North Carolina.
It amounts to a more traditional, more eloquent packaging of Trump's anti-woke MAGA message. However, Vance also is experimenting with crassness in his remarks, dropping the occasional swear word or telling the Texas crowd he was "sweating my balls off" at the podium.
The challenge for Vance right now is in promoting GOP candidates while the Republican president he serves is unpopular.
That challenge is particularly acute where the president's policies have directly caused economic woes. Vance doesn't tend to bring up the Iran War up in his stump speeches – a war that sent gas and diesel prices spiraling upward – but he does cast the gas prices caused by the Iran war as an unfortunate, recurring result of geopolitics:
"Remember in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine and gas prices skyrocketed? They skyrocketed, by the way, far higher than they are today," he told a Montana crowd. "They skyrocketed in 1979. They skyrocketed in 2001. They skyrocketed in 2007. They skyrocket every time some tin pot dictator decides to throw a tantrum."
Likewise, Vance has acknowledged the high price of beef, casting it as a problem of consolidation among meatpackers, while sidestepping that Trump's own policies have angered beef producers.
Anti-fraud czar
Interspersed with his campaign speeches this year have been appearances as the head of President Trump's anti-fraud task force, which has a goal of rooting out malfeasance in social safety net programs.
The task force provides Vance with both resume material and an opportunity to talk about his personal story.
"I worked as a cashier at a grocery store for a couple of years, this was my very first job, Dillman Foods, probably 20 miles from where we're standing today," he told a crowd in Cincinnati last week. "I also had a lot of members of my family benefit from these food benefit programs provided by federal tax dollars."
Vance was first propelled onto the political scene as a result of his memoir about growing up in poor, rural southern Ohio.
His biography gives him some political tools that President Trump does not have, like the ability to talk personally about military service and economic difficulties.
However, crowds loved Trump not because of his biographical relatability but because of his bombast and unfiltered anger. The challenge for any would-be 2028 Republican candidate is figuring out how to follow Trump's singular, decade-plus-long performance, and what – if anything – can replace that in the hearts of GOP voters.
Correction Nov. 2, 2026
A previous version of this web story misquoted JD Vance as saying that his first job was at Dhillon Foods. He said Dillman Foods.

బంగాళాఖాతంలో ఏర్పడిన అర్నబ్ తుఫాను, 28 అక్టోబర్ 2026 ఉదయం ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ తీరంలోని నరసాపురం సమీపంలో తీరం దాటింది. ఈ తుఫాను గంటకు 125 నుండి 135 కిలోమీటర్ల వేగంతో, గరిష్టంగా 150 కిలోమీటర్ల వేగంతో వీచిన ఈదురుగాలులతో విరుచుకుపడింది. ముందస్తు భద్రతా చర్యల్లో భాగంగా ప్రభుత్వం తీర ప్రాంతాల నుండి ప్రజలను సురక్షిత ప్రాంతాలకు తరలించింది. దీని ప్రభావంతో ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్, ఒడిశాలోని అనేక ప్రాంతాల్లో భారీ వర్షాలు, వరదలు సంభవించి, చెట్లు కూలిపోవడం వల్ల విద్యుత్ సరఫరాకు తీవ్ర అంతరాయం ఏర్పడింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, అర్నబ్ తుఫాను ప్రభావంతో వీస్తున్న ఈదురుగాలులను చూపుతుందంటూ రెండు వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్లో అర్నబ్ తుఫాను సమయంలో వీచిన తీవ్రమైన ఈదురుగాలులను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోలు అర్నబ్ తుఫానుకు సంబంధించినవి కావు. మొదటి వీడియో 26 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న బీహార్లోని వైశాలి జిల్లా మహీసౌర్ గ్రామంలో సంభవించిన సుడిగాలికి సంబంధించినది. రెండవ వీడియో జూలై 2026లో అమెరికాలో సంభవించిన బావి తుఫానును చూపుతుంది. కావున, పోస్టులలో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, మొదటి వీడియోని వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 27 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియో బీహార్లోని వైశాలి జిల్లా మహీసౌర్ గ్రామంలో సంభవించిన సుడిగాలిని చూపుతుందని పేర్కొనబడింది.
స్థానిక వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 26 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న బీహార్లోని వైశాలి జిల్లా మహీసౌర్ గ్రామ ప్రాంతంలో బలమైన సుడిగాలి భీభత్సం సృష్టించింది. దీని ధాటికి చెట్లు, పంటలు, ఇళ్ల పైకప్పులు దెబ్బతిన్నాయి.
ఇక రెండవ వీడియో 06 జూలై 2026న అమెరికా ఆదీనంలో ఉన్న దీవుల్లో సంభవించిన బావి తుఫానును చూపుతుంది. ఈ దృశ్యాలను కలిగి ఉన్న జూలై 2026 నాటి మీడియా కథనాలకు ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, అర్నబ్ తుఫాను దృశ్యాలంటూ సంబంధంలేని పాత వీడియోలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

The U.S. health regulator has accepted Merck’s experimental targeted drug for a priority review based on data from a late-stage trial where it extended survival in women with an advanced form of endometrial cancer.
The drug, sacituzumab tirumotecan, also known as sac-TMT, delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein called TROP2, which is common in endometrial tumors.
The trial enrolled 776 patients whose cancer had returned or progressed after earlier treatment. Patients were randomly assigned to sac-TMT or to a chemotherapy their doctor chose, either doxorubicin or paclitaxel.
Results showed sac-TMT reduced the risk of death by 32%, with patients living a median of 19 months compared with 12.1 months on standard chemotherapy.
The treatment also reduced the risk of cancer progression or death by 41%, with patients remaining progression-free for a median of 7.2 months compared with 3.9 months on chemotherapy.
In addition, about 35% of sac-TMT patients saw their tumors shrink, compared with 17% on chemotherapy.
A regulatory decision is expected by June 2027, Merck said. The trial data was presented at the ESMO medical congress.
“Based on discussions with the FDA, the company is hopeful for an approval before the PDUFA date to bring sac-TMT to patients as quickly as possible,” said Dean Y. Li, president, Merck Research Laboratories.
Severe treatment-related side effects were more frequent with sac-TMT, affecting about 54% of patients compared with 41% on chemotherapy. About 3% of patients stopped treatment due to side effects.
About 68,000 cases of endometrial cancer are expected to be diagnosed in the United States in 2026, with over 14,000 deaths, according to the American Cancer Society.
Jefferies analysts project peak sales of roughly $900 million in endometrial cancer for the drug and $9 billion across all potential indications.
Merck is developing the drug with Chinese biotech firm Kelun-Biotech, which discovered the therapy.

The Trump administration truly cut down not one but four large, old cottonwood trees on the border in Lochiel, among the many efforts to clear land for border wall construction. Crews cut down three trees on July 27, followed by the fourth on Oct. 5. A widely shared video highlighted the moment crews felled the fourth tree. However …
… Reported estimates placed the collection of trees anywhere between 100 and 250 years old. A scientist examining a sample of the fourth tree estimated its age at a maximum of 146 years — still a very old tree, though at least a century short of some claims.
In October, people shared a story alleging U.S. President Donald Trump's administration cut down a 250-year-old "grandmother" tree located directly on the southern border in Lochiel, Arizona, to make way for border wall construction.
For example, on Oct. 7, a YouTube account posted a video (archived) captioned, "A giant cottonwood 'Grandmother Tree' was torn down in Lochiel, Arizona, to expand Trump's border wall. Despite activists trying to protect the 250-year-old tree for more than two months, DHS removed the tree as protesters screamed."
Other users shared the story about the purported 250-year-old "grandmother" tree on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and Reddit (archived). One popular political commentator, Brian Tyler Cohen, claimed (archived) the tree was not just 250 but rather 300 years old — dating back to the early 18th century.
Research of all available data concluded that the Trump administration truly cut down a large, old cottonwood tree — which some people referred to as a "grandmother" tree — directly on the border line. The Department of Homeland Security oversaw crews that reportedly cut down not one, but four old Fremont cottonwood trees on the border in Lochiel, among the many efforts to clear lands for the president's double border wall construction. The fourth tree appears in the above video.
However, a thorough reading of all the data found the collection of trees, while older than 100, to perhaps be well below 250 years old. A scientist examining a sample of the fourth tree estimated its age at a maximum of 146 years — still a very old tree.
Due to the apparent embellishment of the tree's age, we've rated this claim mostly true.
The Washington Post reported that the trees were located in a 60-foot-wide strip of federal land known as the Roosevelt Reservation. Former President Theodore Roosevelt established the swath of land in 1907 along the southern borders of California, Arizona and New Mexico to combat opium smuggling and enforce immigration policies.
Snopes contacted locals connected with this story to receive more insight. We also emailed Customs and Border Protection to ask questions. The White House declined comment and referred us to CBP.
Building the wall
During Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, he repeatedly touted strict immigration policies, perhaps most notably promising time and time again that Mexico would pay for a wall to help bring down the number of people crossing into the U.S. over the southern border.
Fast forwarding to Trump's second term, on July 27, crews reportedly associated with the Arizona-based Fisher Sand & Gravel Co. — receiving billions of dollars in U.S. government funds for border wall construction, including in Lochiel's Santa Cruz County — cut down three cottonwood trees, as shown in several different videos.
DHS official monitored the situation and reportedly handcuffed at least one person.
A group of activists with concerns about the trees and the local ecosystem then formed a "tree sit" together at the fourth and final tree.
After more than two months of banding together, on Oct. 5, Fisher crews reportedly cut down the fourth tree, once again with DHS officials, some wearing face masks, on guard and making at least a dozen arrests — if not more.
We contacted Fisher to confirm its crews were directly involved with chopping down the four trees, as well as to ask if the company wished to share a statement, and will add that information if it responds.
Estimating the trees' ages
Our research to find estimates of the trees' ages located news media outlets citing various figures. For example, a High Country News article identified the collection as "the 100-plus-year-old trees." An NPR headline, citing Phoenix's KJZZ, mentioned "250-year-old trees," while the story itself identified the trees as residing in "a 150- to 200-year-old grove."
Aside from those reported estimates, at least one scientist visited the site to collect tree samples for further study. Ceci Martinez, a graduate student at the University of Arizona's Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, obtained at least two tree samples, the Arizona Republic reported — including one sample from the fourth tree before crews cut it down. For that tree, she estimated the age as "a maximum of 146 years old."
Asked by the Republic about how important the actual age is when it comes to the threat of being cut down, Martinez applauded the activists who attempted to save the trees. She mentioned that while "tree people are obsessed with how old trees are," cottonwoods serve "a very different function":
They're intended to grow tall, big, provide shade and habitat. They get a lot of attention because, like the jaguar, they are these big important things.
But being old is not what I think of when I think of how important they are. The value for me in these trees isn't them being ancient or 200 years old. The value is the role they play in the ecosystem. And these cottonwoods do a lot.
Kate Scott, who who cofounded the local Madrean Archipelago Wildlife Center and was one of the activists present during the tree sit, reportedly referenced "the eastern-most cottonwood" — possibly the tree crews felled on Oct. 5 — as "grandmother." The "grandmother" term for the trees possibly originated from her or was at least popularized by her own conservationist efforts, if not also possibly by locals and indigenous people.
Russ McSpadden, working with the Center for Biological Diversity, credited Scott with "largely" establishing the "grandmother" term as one of "endearment and respect used for the trees." McSpadden sent a statement to us about the loss of the trees, saying in part, "Where those trees brought life together, the border wall now cuts it apart."
We also reached out to Scott to request comment and will update this article accordingly.
Agency response
In an email, a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told us the agency recognized the importance of protecting the environment, wildlife and cultural resources during border wall construction. The statement also highlighted the purported harms of unauthorized border crossings resulting in "substantial amounts of trash, pollution, and damage to natural resources, including sensitive habitats and agriculture."
That statement read, in part:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection identified four cottonwood trees on federal land in Lochiel, Arizona, that needed removal for planned border wall construction. Preconstruction surveys found no active migratory bird nests, and environmental monitors were present at the start of clearing activities to ensure work was limited to the identified trees. As of Oct. 5, 2026, all four trees have been removed.
In a news release, the Grand Canyon Chapter of the environmental conservation organization the Sierra Club featured alleged video proof from July 26 showing a kingbird actively nesting in one of the three trees that crews cut down the following day. The organization claimed that evidence showed CBP "lied" about being careful to not destroy trees with active nests.
Erick Meza, who works as a border program coordinator for the Sierra Club, told us he recorded the video. He said in the group's release, in part, "Without any justification, double walls are going up everywhere and they are being built without environmental impact studies, without community consultation, and without regard for the species that depend on these habitats." He also mentioned arrests of people protesting the border construction work.
For further reading, we previously reported about other claims of the Trump administration chopping down trees for projects happening in Washington, D.C.

The AI software-development platform Cursor, which is owned by SpaceX, had a malicious Anthropic Claude Code extension for Windows, macOS, and Linux live in its integrated development environment extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on Thursday. The company says the rogue extension was downloaded by “at most 5,000 users.” Cursor briefly shut down the extension marketplace while it investigated the situation, which the company says did not impact any other extensions.
The tainted extension was designed with a backdoor to give attackers access to victim devices—the type of implant that malicious hackers often use as a stepping stone to deeper control inside a target network. Cursor published remediation steps on Thursday for the roughly 5,000 affected targets. A saving grace of the situation, though, was a flaw in the malware's design that blocked it from fully establishing itself on the vast majority of targets.
“Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first researchers to spot the malicious extension after detecting it on a customer's Mac.
What is still unclear is how the malicious extension made its way into the Cursor marketplace at all. Some researchers initially speculated that it came from a compromised Anthropic system. But Cursor said in its Thursday security alert that “these malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.”
Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted on X on Friday: “We’re working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn’t build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected and this only impacts Cursor users.”
David Dworken, who works on security at Anthropic, posted on X shortly after, explaining that “this did not involve a compromise of any Anthropic systems … We were not involved with building, publishing, or hosting this.”
Cursor did not return WIRED's request for comment about how the malicious upload happened and whether it was the result of a breach at Cursor.

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Women recruited from economically weaker sections were being offered ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 for an egg donation cycle, while those operating the alleged racket made an average of about ₹3 lakh from each cycle.
Malkajgiri police widened their investigation into the exploitation of women, falsification of records and the role of IVF and fertility establishments.
The 43 women rescued during simultaneous raids in Hyderabad have undergone medical examinations, including blood-group and fitness tests. Police are now verifying their medical histories with IVF centres to establish their treatment records.
The investigation has raised concerns over how the women were recruited and whether they gave informed consent for the procedures. Police said women from economically weaker sections were targeted and that, in some cases, intermediaries allegedly even completed their signatures on documents. Investigators are examining possible falsification of records and whether the women fully understood the procedures they were being recruited for.
Police are tracing the payments and commissions involving organisers, recruiters and intermediaries who connected the women with fertility-related establishments.
The investigation is now expanding to medical establishments. Police are preparing to serve notices to the District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) and conduct searches at ART and fertility centres. Some hospitals have also approached police and informed them that employees found to have been involved had been removed.
Investigators are examining how women from West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and other states were recruited, transported and accommodated in Hyderabad before being referred for egg retrieval procedures. Their medical records, consent documents and the procedures they underwent are also being scrutinised.
All eight accused arrested in connection with the Hyderabad cases have been remanded to judicial custody. Further investigation is underway.

The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.
As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.
Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.
On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.
The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.
The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.
Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.
At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”
Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.
“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

Nagaland Tourism Minister Temjen Imna Along has drawn attention to the state's unique ‘Honesty Shops’, where customers can purchase goods without interacting with a shopkeeper or being monitored by CCTV cameras. Instead, these small roadside outlets operate on a simple belief that customers will pay the right amount for whatever they take.
Along, who also holds the Higher Education portfolio, shared a post on X highlighting the unusual business model and the trust that keeps these shops running.
“No shopkeeper. No CCTV. Just trust. Would this work where you live?” Along asked in his post, before explaining how the unattended shops function.
An image accompanying his post described the concept: “A shop that runs without a shopkeeper. No one standing at the counter. No one watching over customers. Just a roadside stall where people can stop, pick what they need, and pay on their own."
The shops operate without salespersons or anyone keeping an eye on customers. Visitors can select the products they want, check the prices displayed alongside them and deposit the payment in a designated cash box before leaving.
Some of these outlets have also adopted digital payment methods, displaying UPI QR codes for customers who prefer cashless transactions.
The concept is particularly dependent on mutual trust. Farmers leave their produce at these roadside stalls and attend to their agricultural work or other daily responsibilities, without having to remain present to oversee sales.
Such self-service shops are not limited to Nagaland but can also be found in other parts of India's Northeast.
According to a 2025 report by India Today, women farmers operate approximately 20 such outlets across Pfutsero in Nagaland.
The roadside shops offer a variety of locally produced goods, including seasonal fruits and vegetables, along with homemade pickles, jams and juices.
With no shopkeeper present, customers are expected to select their purchases, calculate the amount payable and leave the money in the collection box. The arrangement allows farmers to sell their produce while continuing with their everyday activities.
Along, a BJP leader, said the shops reflect the culture of trust prevalent in Nagaland. Their functioning demonstrates how customers are expected to pay for their purchases honestly, even when there is nobody around to monitor their actions.
Reflecting on the idea, the minister highlighted that businesses do not always need supervision or strict monitoring to function.
“Sometimes, trust is enough to keep businesses moving. Because a business is not always built on transactions alone. Sometimes, it also depends on the honesty people bring to the simplest everyday things,” he wrote.

Health tech startup Clinics On Cloud has raised ₹120 Cr (around $12.5 Mn) in its Series A funding round from Model42, the medtech-focused investment arm of UAE-based backer Enlightened Minds Investments. The Pune-based startup raised the fresh funds at a valuation of ₹600 Cr ($63.3 Mn) In a statement, the startup said that it plans to utilise the fresh capital to bolster its AI-led healthcare capabilities, expand research and development (R&D), and accelerate the growth of its micro-clinic ecosystem. A chunk of the funding will also be used to strengthen its manufacturing capacity, scale strategic partnerships with healthcare providers and expand global footprint. “For eight years, we have built Clinics On Cloud with a simple belief that quality healthcare should never depend on someone’s pincode. This investment gives us the opportunity to take that vision global…,” said Clinics On Cloud cofounder and CEO Abhay Agarwal. Founded in 2018 by Abhay and Manashrri Agarwal, Clinics On Cloud manufactures and deploys AI-powered “health ATMs”, portable box clinics and mobile medical units that deliver point-of-care preventive health checkups and telemedicine consultations. These solutions enable hospitals and government agencies to set up temporary micro-clinics. It claims to have so far seen more than 3,500 deployments across 200 cities in India and seven other countries. Having screened more than 1.2 Cr patients so far, the startup claims to cater to the Indian Army, Navy and the Border Security Force (BSF). The Pune-based startup now plans to position UAE as its global expansion hub, with an eye on exploring new markets across Africa, the US and Southeast Asia. The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in the healthtech sector, which is seeing renewed funding activity on the back of AI adoption. In September this year, smart ring maker Ultrahuman raised $70 Mn to fuel its integrated healthtech playbook. In July, another AI-powered healthtech startup CARPL.ai also bagged $10 Mn in its Series A funding round led by International Finance Corporation (IFC). In the same month, actor Kunal Kapoor banded together with crowdfunding platform Ketto’s cofounders Varun Sheth and Zaheer Adenwala to launch healthtech startup MetaGO. At the heart of all this is the homegrown healthtech market, which is projected to become a $37 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Shah Rukh Khan marked his 61st birthday on November 2 by greeting fans gathered outside his Mumbai residence, Mannat. The celebrations began at midnight with a special message from the superstar. Since Mannat is currently undergoing renovation and the family has temporarily moved out, Shah Rukh did not appear on the balcony as he usually does. Instead, a large projection outside the residence displayed a handwritten note from the actor, along with visuals from his upcoming film King.
The note read, “Thank you all for your wishes and love. Sending mine right back to you all. Lots of love and a big hug.”
The display also featured visuals and dialogues from King, including “King Akela Kaafi Hai” and “Darr Nahi, Dehshat Hoon”. The first song from the film, ‘Tu Mil Jaaye’, was also released at midnight, adding to the birthday celebrations.

Major fire breaks out at Hindustan Petroleum's refinery in Visakhapatnam; explosion suspected
According to an HPCL employee, the blaze is believed to have erupted within the refinery's premises. Firefighting operations are underway.
A major fire broke out at Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL)'s refinery in Gajuwaka industrial area in Andhra Pradesh’s Visakhapatnam late on Monday night, people familiar with the matter said.
According to an HPCL employee, the blaze is believed to have erupted within the refinery's premises. "We have heard sounds of an explosion in the area. Flames quickly spread to nearby areas, sending thick clouds of black smoke into the sky and engulfing the surrounding locality,” the employee said.
Alarmed by the massive flames and thick smoke, residents in nearby areas rushed out of their homes.
Soon after receiving information about the fire, the refinery's internal firefighting teams, along with fire engines from different parts of the city, rushed to the spot and launched firefighting operations.
As a precautionary measure, refinery officials suspended power supply to the affected area and evacuated personnel to safer locations.
Police personnel were deployed around the facility to prevent people from entering the affected premises.
Firefighters were continuing efforts to bring the blaze completely under control. There was no immediate information about casualties or the extent of damage caused by the fire.

Another major difference has to do with the breakout box, called the Samsung One Connect. With the S95H, it’s no longer required or included in the box, so you have to connect all of your devices like a video game console or a streaming device directly to the television. That means the S95H is thicker at 1.04 inches compared to just 0.4 inches for the S95F. However, I actually preferred not using the One Connect. It meant less hassle with another device to plug in and set up. You can always buy the One Connect box later if you decide you want less clutter by your TV stand or on the wall.
The S95H has four HDMI ports on the right side (including one for gaming at 165 Hz and one for eARC passthrough audio for surround sound), an Ethernet jack, optical audio out, two USB ports for playing files off a storage drive, and a headphone jack. It supports Wi-Fi 6E for faster speeds and compatibility than older standards (like the Wi-Fi 5 used on the S95F). Both TVs mount flush to the wall, although I used the included pedestal stand, which attached easily.
For the UI, Tizen OS is not terrible, but as we noted in our previous S95F review, it’s still a bit of a maze. The setup process including adding apps and tweaking picture settings is far easier on a Google TV model like the Sony Bravia 7 II. I’m used to Tizen OS, since I test TVs often, but I still don’t love it. (At least I didn’t need to use the Samsung SmartThings app for setup.)
I really like the Samsung remote—It doesn’t overwhelm you with buttons. Hisense remotes tend to have way too many buttons, in my experience. Most of us need channel, mute, and volume, plus maybe a few shortcuts to apps like Netflix.
Samsung doesn’t officially list the color gamut specs like DCI-P3 or BT.2020 for the S95H. Equally so, there is no official mention of brightness rating in nits or contrast ratio, but I’m okay with that as well. Those specs can be misleading and really depend on the picture quality settings, the brightness of the room, and (mostly) the content you watch. Instead, I subjected the S95H to rigorous real-world testing to see how it measures up to recent models.
Competitive Color Quality
The S95H measures up to the competition quite nicely when it comes to color quality. It excels in many areas but is not always the de facto winner for every movie, show or game. Once again, there is so much competition that buying a flagship OLED like this one is no longer the obvious choice.
I started with the movie Awake because several scenes in that movie (about people who can no longer sleep) are extremely dark. Time and again, even top-end televisions can’t seem to show key scenes with enough color or clarity. The S95H performed surprisingly well, but it took some tweaks. On Filmmaker, Dynamic, and even Standard and Eco modes, scenes with the main character biking at night looked too dark. Enabling AI Optimized picture mode helped a lot, beating out what was possible on the Samsung Micro RGB R95H in the same scenes.

Polls are looking pretty bleak for Republicans—and the Trump administration’s various attempts to interfere with the elections haven’t been too successful either.
In recent weeks, the Department of Justice, helmed by Attorney General Todd Blanche, a proponent of conspiracy theories about widespread noncitizen voting in the 2020 election, has pulled out all the stops to sow doubt in voters’ minds about the security and validity of the electoral process.
To do this, the DOJ has spent the last year demanding unredacted voter rolls, issuing executive orders to wrest control of elections from states, raiding election offices, proposing new laws to disenfranchise millions of citizens, and claiming that noncitizens were voting en masse across the country. (Incidents of verified noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare, as multiple bipartisan investigations have shown.)
There have also been escalating threats by the DOJ against election officials. On Thursday, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states warning them that they would pursue criminal action if they failed to preserve election records for 22 days. Earlier that week, a federal judge had admonished the Trump administration for making similar threats around criminal prosecution against election officials in a different case.
“They're trying to create chaos and distrust in the system,” says Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at UCLA Law’s Safeguarding Democracy Project. “They're trying to file these now knowing they have virtually no chance of winning and then after they can claim the election was fraudulent.”
“This Department is following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable,” a spokesperson for the DOJ tells WIRED, pointing out that the previous administration’s Justice department sued Alabama and Virginia ahead of the 2024 election, claiming the DOJ was at the time trying “to stop them from removing suspected noncitizens from their voter rolls.”
Experts say that while the DOJ’s current legal efforts, including escalating fights in Alaska and California over candidates and voter rolls, are faltering, they’re also designed to lay the groundwork to question the results of this week’s vote.
“We have to expect absolutely, if the election doesn't go the way the president wants, that we will see the administration’s attempt to sow doubts in the election and maybe even challenge those results, but I'm also not worried about it,” David Becker, a former DOJ lawyer and the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, tells WIRED.
“They have failed at everything they've tried to do. Our systems have held firm. Our institutions have held firm.”
34 federal district courts have ruled against Trump since he took office in 2025 blocking access to voter rolls and preventing executive orders being implemented, according to analysis from the Brennan Center.
Former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division Justin Levitt thinks that a lot of the actions taken by the Trump administration are about a show of force and optics more than anything else. “What you’re seeing now is a ton of marketing. They are trying to communicate that they're in charge, and I think it's not working,” says Levitt, now a law professor at Loyola Marymount University. “But it is really important to remember that the federal government isn't in charge of the election process. State and local officials are.”
WIRED has laid out the details of the DOJ’s legal efforts in California, Nevada, Washington, and Alaska below, which have all been met with disdain from local and state officials.
California
California is officially a hotbed of election controversy. In October, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking a court order against California to compel them to sequester mail-in ballots associated with approximately 20,000 voters, claiming that these voters were noncitizens. On Wednesday, a federal judge in a strong-worded order rejected the request.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” US District Judge David Carter wrote in his order filed late on Wednesday.
Almost immediately, the DOJ filed an appeal and a federal court quickly denied it.
The judge pointed out that similar claims from the administration about noncitizens on voter rolls hadn’t held up to scrutiny, and he had “further questions of credibility” about how they arrived at that number in the first place.
Last week, a federal judge also ruled that the DOJ had to turn over its list of around 20,000 names to the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, so that the group could analyze the dataset. On Saturday, the group submitted a legal filing stating that an analysis of the list found that over 40 percent of the names weren’t even in the state’s current voter files. In response, the DOJ has suggested that the publication of their analysis violated the terms of the lists released to them, and is urging a federal judge to consider whether contempt charges might be applicable here.
“The DOJ has clearly written rules that prevent it from engaging in any investigative activity close to an election—rules that private attorney Todd Blanche cited when representing his client, Donald Trump, in September 2024,” Becker says. “But the DOJ continues to violate its own policies.”
To cap it all off, the DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas to California’s local election officials last week, indicating that despite repeated court losses it has no intention of backing down.
Alaska
In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit designed to block certification of the election result in Alaska’s Senate race if Democrat candidate Mary Peltola wins.
The reason for the lawsuit is the presence of a spoiler candidate on the ballot with a similar name as the incumbent Republican candidate Daniel Sullivan. The DOJ’s lawsuit was filed despite the Alaska Supreme Court ruling in the summer that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr could remain on the ballot as no laws had been broken.
A New York Times investigation last week alleged that Democrat-aligned operatives were involved in getting a spoiler candidate on the ballot, though Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement in the effort to get Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the ballot. Asked about whether the common practice of putting spoiler candidates on the ballot was illegal, Todd Blanche said “it certainly should be.” On Truth Social, Trump said Peltola “should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.”
“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau last week. “I am not interested in tricking voters.”
On Thursday, Alaska Governor Michael Dunleavy ordered an investigation to determine whether state criminal or civil charges could be pursued against Peltola. In an interview with NewsNation, Dunleavy said that he could not commit to certifying victory for Peltola if that investigation was still ongoing.
“Dunleavy’s threat to overrule the will of Alaskan voters exemplifies what Alaskans hate about partisan politics and shows why he’s the least popular governor in the country,” a Peltola campaign spokeswoman tells WIRED. “Mary won’t be intimidated by Dunleavy, Sullivan, or any of their DC allies who are trying to steal this election from Alaskans before votes are counted—and she’s going to win this race by focusing on solutions to Sullivan’s price hiking policies and putting Alaska first.”
On Friday, the DOJ held a press conference in Anchorage and said that, in addition to their lawsuit seeking to block the certification of the election result if Peltola wins, they were also launching their own investigation to determine if federal civil or criminal charges could be applicable in this case. "We are aware of … the sprawling conspiracy to prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate,” said US Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman.
On Sunday, a federal judge threw out the DOJ’s lawsuit, ruling that their request likely violated Alaskans' right to a secret ballot. Hours later, the DOJ asked a federal appeals court to overturn the ruling.
Nevada
In July, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed that they had identified over 270,000 noncitizen voters in just four states: California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. But that bold assertion soon started to unravel.
DHS officials had also claimed that there were 15,903 noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls, but then later conceded in a meeting with Nevada officials that they didn’t have evidence. The number of suspected noncitizens on voter rolls then dropped down to 185, but there was no evidence to support that claim either.
“As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens,” Nevada’s Deputy Attorney General Greg Ott wrote in a letter to DHS. “You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise.”
“The Department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED about the situation. “It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”
Ott added in the letter that while Nevada takes allegations of noncitizen voting seriously, “it also has a strong interest in preventing the wrongful disenfranchisement of voters” and is “committed to preventing the chilling effect on the right to vote from taking actions based on unfounded and unverifiable allegations of noncitizen voting.”
Washington
Last week, the DOJ claimed that federal data appeared to show that 400 noncitizens were registered to vote in the state of Washington and demanded that officials isolate those ballots, describing them as “the tip of the iceberg.”
They received another withering letter in return: “The timing of your letter is profoundly disappointing,” wrote Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs. “If you had valid concerns about voter registrations, the time to raise them was a month ago.” Hobbs added that their decision to publicly raise their concerns so close to the election was “not a sign of good faith to ensure a free, fair, and accurate election.”
Hobbs added that the DOJ had failed to provide individualized proof that any of the people on the list were ineligible to vote, and didn’t offer any information about how they arrived at the lists of names or what sources were used. “Given the Department of Justice’s recent acts of election interference in California, Alaska, and now in Washington, it would be particularly inappropriate for Washington to simply assume the Department’s unsupported allegations here are credible.”
Texas
While not a filing by the Justice department, the Potter County Republican party has filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the state from certifying the vote unless all Texas ballots are counted by hand.
The GOP’s basis for demanding a manual audit include purported threats from artificial intelligence’s ability to supposedly hack into virtually any voting machine undetected, a claim presented without evidence, and the presence of voting machine parts manufactured in China. Levitt, the former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, described the lawsuit as “nuts.”
“That would be the technical term,” Levitt said. “I wish that they had filed the thing in Comic Sans on the back of a Burger King placemat, because I think that would help people evaluate how serious it is.”

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.

Whose sight matters? How gender shapes access to eye care in India
Across their lifespans, from childhood to old age, women face disadvantages in access to eye health and care. For many, treatment depends on how their health is prioritised by the men in their household. Late care, or lack of access can leave girls and women with preventable visual impairment and loss
From families questioning the value of sight-saving treatment for girls because of concerns about marriage and appearance, to older women who receive treatment later or have poorer access to effective care, gender shapes whose vision is prioritised. File photograph used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: The Hindu
“I remember a patient, a little girl with retinoblastoma,” says Rohit Khanna, a community ophthalmologist and network director from L.V. Prasad Eye Institute, Hyderabad. “We told the family that the child required surgery and that the eyeball would have to be removed for her to survive. We were immediately met with resistance. The father asked, what was the point of her living if she was going to be disfigured. They would not be able to get her married later.”
Retinoblastoma is a rare, fast-growing tumour of the eye and is often seen in early childhood. It is a type of cancer, and can lead to death if not treated.
