Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.
Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
Following GM’s $220 million settlement, Ford promises to never sell customer driving data to data brokers, attempting to set itself apart in an industry rife with tracking.
As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.
In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”
“We know that trust is earned.”
— Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer
The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information.
Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.
In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties.
Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. Forty-one percent said they were extremely or very concerned about data privacy in the auto industry, which was less than other groups like social media companies, the government, and financial institutions.
To be sure, Ford’s promise isn’t just words on a screen. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission stops companies from misleading the public through deceptive claims. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. The actual rules that apply to you are found in Ford’s official privacy policy and connected vehicle terms. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has de-notified and withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023) where medical colleges were liable to face penalty fines for violations of educational standards and infrastructure requirements at medical colleges.
Earlier reports in The Hindu stated NMC’s withdrawal of MSMER-2023 weakens accountability in medical education by removing provisions to fine individual faculty members and administrators up to ₹5 lakh for submitting false information. Although the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) can still penalise institutions up to ₹1 crore under separate regulations, institutional penalties may be less effective in deterring individual misconduct. Misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk.

It's true that on Oct. 27, Couric published an article under her own byline criticizing Trump. The veteran journalist didn't label it an "open letter" but it appeared to serve that purpose. She made the piece available as a paid, members-only story on her Substack blog. However …
… Some social media users shared the article with dozens of changes, including apparent omissions, that weren't reflected in Couric's published piece as of this writing. For example, Couric's article didn't call Trump's rhetoric "disgusting." The full article on her blog featured more paragraphs, sourcing with links and other details that were missing from the social media versions.
In late October, people shared a claim alleging journalist Katie Couric wrote an open letter to U.S. President Donald Trump in which she called his rhetoric "disgusting."
According to social media posts, Couric penned the piece to criticize Trump on a range of issues including immigration policy, "weaponization of the Justice Department," corruption and tariffs. She also purportedly wrote that Trump started the war in Iran contrary to his own campaign promise of no new wars and chided him over his "love affair" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
While it's true that Couric wrote and published a members-only piece excoriating Trump on her Substack blog ("How Do I Oppose Thee? Let Me Count the Ways"), it's false that a version of the letter rapidly spreading on the internet is identical to what Couric actually wrote. Therefore, we've rated this claim a mixture of true and false elements.
As the prime example, on Oct. 28, a Facebook user posted (archived) some text allegedly sourced from Couric's piece. The user wrote an introduction reading, "Most people outside of MAGA consider Katie Couric a thoughtful and fair journalist. Here's her letter to President Trump that lists the reasons she opposes him. Please share."
Snopes readers searched our website using various queries, for example "Katie Couric letter," "Katie Couric letter to Trump" and "Did Katie Couric write a letter to Trump." A search also located a similar X post (archived).
Couric truly published a paid, members-only article that appeared to double as an open letter to Trump, titled "How Do I Oppose Thee? Let Me Count the Ways," on her Substack blog. She labeled the article as "A few things to note before you vote (OK, maybe more than a few)."
However, the version of Couric's article circulating on social media contained dozens of changes, including apparent omissions, that distinguish it from the original. As one of many examples, Couric's piece did not call Trump's rhetoric "disgusting." The social media version also stripped out all evidential links sourcing Couric's many claims and omitted some of the paragraphs featured in her original text. Therefore, we rated the claim that Couric wrote the piece a mixture of true and false information.
The above-mentioned Facebook user published his post on Wednesday and only later updated it to add a link to Couric's Substack article.
About eight hours before that user shared the post, someone captured an archived version of the beginning of Couric's article. At that point in time, the word "disgusting" did not appear, indicating the Facebook user may have taken some liberties editing Couric's piece for social media.
The general drift of Couric's criticism remained mostly the same in the Facebook post. Even so, we make note of the fact the latter was worded differently and was inauthentic.
We contacted a representative for Couric to request comment and to ask if Couric changed her article after its initial publication. We haven't yet located evidence suggesting Couric updated her article without making note of the changes. We also sent a message to the Facebook user to ask if he changed words and omitted parts of Couric's text for his post, and will update this article if we receive any further information.
Regarding open letters to Trump, we previously investigated whether musician Tommy Lee wrote an open letter to Trump calling him a "f***ing lunatic."

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

A federal judge dismissed criminal charges against two former FBI officials who were accused of lying about their involvement in the investigation into Hunter Biden, the son of former president Joe Biden, on Monday.
Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said prosecutors failed to show probable cause that the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, had knowingly made false statements.
Faruqui also suggested prosecutors purposefully brought the charges at a sensitive time, just 10 days before the midterm elections.
“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization,” Faruqui said during the court hearing. “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar.”
The judge criticized federal prosecutors for rushing the prosecution and making “critical mistakes”. Faruqui said that some of the former officials’ statements were not actually false and others could be attributed to “honest mistakes of memory”.
Federal prosecutors in Washington DC charged Floris and Benavides last month with making false statements to members of Congress in 2023 while testifying to the House judiciary committee.
The two former officials were testifying about the bureau’s role in investigating the contents of a laptop that belonged to Hunter Biden.
Floris and Benavides served on an FBI taskforce that examined potential foreign influence in American politics. The taskforce was initially formed after the 2016 presidential election when officials raised concerns that Russia attempted to interfere with the election.
The FBI taskforce had raised concerns in the lead-up to the 2020 presidential election that Russia could have engaged in another disinformation operation to assist Donald Trump’s campaign by bolstering claims about Hunter Biden’s laptop.
Last week, an FBI agent testified last week that the probe into Floris and Benavides began with the president’s primetime address in July on election security, during which he announced the FBI would investigate whether US intelligence agencies had suppressed information about Chinese meddling in the 2020 election.
The next day, the FBI director, Kash Patel, tasked the bureau’s Kansas City field office with scrutinizing Floris, who had cast doubt on an FBI intelligence report claiming that China sought to interfere in the 2020 election to boost Joe Biden over Trump.
Trump has publicly criticized individuals that he believes undermined his efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential results.
But since returning to office in January 2025, the justice department has targeted people that Trump views as enemies through indictments and complaints. However, some high-profile attempts have failed to bear fruit.
While the justice department’s complaint against Floris and Benavides has been dismissed, prosecutors could try to charge them again by asking a grand jury to review evidence and approve charges.

Srinagar, Nov 2: Russia’s increased targeted attacks on Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure risks creating a new humanitarian catastrophe for civilians ahead of winter, Amnesty International warned today.
It said the civilian death toll during Russia’s full-scale ‘illegal’ invasion has increased significantly in recent months, with October 2026 expected to be one of the deadliest periods for civilians in years.
Based on prior Russian military attacks in the approach to previous winters, there is overwhelming evidence that the deliberate targeting of energy and heating infrastructure intended to cause civilian suffering will result in immense harm. The International Criminal Court (ICC) has indicted Russia’s Lieutenant General Sergei Ivanovich Kobylash and Admiral Viktor Nikolayevich Sokolov on charges of war crimes for allegedly directing attacks on Ukrainian electrical infrastructure.
“The Russian Federation is once again implementing a large-scale campaign against Ukrainian energy and heating infrastructure ahead of a freezing winter, including attacks far from the front lines of conflict,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.
“These attacks on essential infrastructure are creating a deadly situation for civilians, who directly suffer the consequences. This is an illegal campaign, carried out with flagrant disregard for the rules of war, and appears to be designed to create unliveable conditions for Ukrainian civilians.
“Whatever the motives behind the Kremlin’s plan to make life unbearable for civilians, it is criminal and cannot be tolerated. World leaders seeking to end this conflict must immediately use their leverage to minimize any potential harm to civilians, before another intentional humanitarian catastrophe begins with the arrival of winter.”
On 26 October, the International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine reported that Russia had committed war crimes and crimes against humanity in Ukraine by intentionally attacking energy infrastructure, leaving millions of people without electricity and heat in freezing temperatures.
Amnesty International has previously documented how Russia’s widespread attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure may constitute war crimes and highlighted their life-threatening consequences for the civilian population.
Civilian casualties and widespread power cuts
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine found that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September 2026 as a result of Russian attacks, an 85% increase over September 2025. Casualties were recorded in 22 of 24 regions in Ukraine. The Mission also described the first half of October 2026 as one of the deadliest periods for civilians in years.
On 13 and 14 October, strikes reportedly hit multiple energy installations, including Kyiv’s three principal power stations, temporarily leaving approximately 600,000 people without electricity. On 17 October, further Russian attacks reportedly killed at least eight people, injured 60 and interrupted electricity supplies to more than one million people across nine regions.
Both the Russian Ministry of Defence and President Vladimir Putin have made public statements announcing intentional attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Prior attacks on energy and heating infrastructure in Ukraine caused widespread and widely reported civilian suffering that is known to Russian military and strategic planners.
During the winter of 2025–2026, the Russian Armed Forces carried out at least 423 attacks on electricity infrastructure and 74 strikes on heating facilities, according to UN monitoring. These attacks caused rolling outages affecting millions of people and interrupted heating for hundreds of thousands as temperatures fell below -20°C. The resulting loss of electricity, water and heating disrupted healthcare and education, and also disproportionately harmed older people, persons with disabilities, women and families with children.
Under international humanitarian law, electricity and heating installations are civilian objects unless and for such time as they meet the strict definition of a military objective. Even where an installation constitutes a military objective, attacking forces must comply with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution. Intentionally directing attacks against civilian objects, launching indiscriminate attacks, or carrying out attacks expected to cause excessive civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated can constitute war crimes.
Ensuring accountability for such crimes requires strong and independent international justice mechanisms capable of investigating and prosecuting those responsible, including the most senior officials.
Meanwhile, the US administration is currently engaged in a campaign to dismantle the work of the ICC. Amnesty International has called for all relevant states to take appropriate measures to resist this attack and actively protect the Court and the broader international justice system. President Vladimir Putin is wanted on charges of war crimes by the ICC, and Amnesty International has called for President Putin to be arrested and surrendered to the ICC by any parties in a position to do so.
Calls to Russian authorities
Amnesty International called on Russian forces to end their systematic attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The Russian authorities must also immediately end other violations of international humanitarian law, including attacks on other civilian infrastructure in Ukraine, such as residential buildings, hospitals, and schools, and end its campaign of targeting non-combatants.
All parties to the conflict must respect the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution and protect civilians and civilian objects. States supporting accountability mechanisms must provide the expertise and resources needed to effectively investigate allegations of violations, secure evidence, and identify suspected perpetrators, including commanders and senior officials who may bear responsibility. All states must urgently act to protect the functioning of the ICC and should execute arrest warrants when and where they can.

Meesho has spent much of its journey building scale in India’s value commerce market. Its low-cost marketplace model has helped it expand its reach beyond large cities, bring more sellers online and attract consumers looking for affordable products. But as the company moves towards its next phase of growth, the goalpost is shifting from acquiring users and expanding transactions to extracting more value from the ecosystem it has built. Advertising is emerging as one of the key opportunities. With 284 Mn annual transacting users (ATUs) and 1.13 Mn annual transacting sellers as of Q2 FY27, Meesho has a large marketplace that it can potentially monetise through sponsored listings and other advertising products. The company expects advertising to become a more meaningful contributor to its revenue mix from FY28. At the same time, Meesho is exploring newer business lines, including lending products for consumers and sellers, while expanding branded commerce through Meesho Mall and discovery-led shopping through content commerce. These initiatives could open up additional revenue streams, although their contribution to the company's financials remains at an early stage. The opportunity comes as Meesho makes progress on its marketplace economics. Its Q2 FY27 performance shows that the core marketplace is growing and its operating economics are improving. Revenue from operations increased 34% year-on-year to ₹4,119.9 Cr, while net merchandise value (NMV) grew 23% to ₹12,911 Cr. In the reported quarter, its contribution margin improved to 6% of net merchandise value (NMV), compared with 4.6% in the previous quarter and 3.3% a year earlier. Its marketplace adjusted EBITDA loss also narrowed to ₹130.5 Cr from ₹371 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, management cautioned that the 6% contribution margin recorded in Q2 FY27 should not be viewed as the new normal, as some of the logistics efficiency gains may be passed on to consumers and sellers to support growth. The question, therefore, is whether Meesho can turn its growing consumer and seller base into higher-value revenue streams without compromising the affordability that underpins its marketplace. Advertising: Can Meesho Monetise Its Scale? Advertising offers Meesho a way to generate more revenue from the traffic and transactions already flowing through its platform. As its user base and seller ecosystem expand, the company has an opportunity to charge sellers for better visibility and access to consumers who are actively browsing products. For sellers, sponsored placements can help products stand out in a crowded marketplace. For Meesho, they can create an additional revenue stream without requiring it to take ownership of inventory or significantly change its core marketplace model. This is particularly relevant in a business where affordability and low prices remain central to customer acquisition. The scale of the opportunity is supported by Meesho's operating metrics. Its ATUs grew 21% year-on-year to 284 Mn in Q2 FY27, while annual transacting sellers increased 60% to 1.13 Mn. Placed orders rose 17% to 819 Mn during the quarter, and NMV grew 23% to ₹12,911 Cr. “A larger marketplace gives Meesho more opportunities to connect seller advertising with consumer discovery. However, the size of its user base alone does not determine how much it can earn from ads. The company will need to demonstrate that sellers are willing to spend consistently on advertising and that paid placements generate measurable returns through product views and orders,” an ecommerce analyst said. Advertising monetisation is still at a relatively early stage. On the Q2 FY27 earnings call, it said the sequential improvement in contribution margin was primarily driven by logistics efficiencies, rather than a significant increase in advertising monetisation. It also expects advertising to become a more meaningful contributor as a percentage of NMV in FY28. Motilal Oswal expects higher advertising monetisation to support contribution margin expansion from FY28, citing seller demand for advertising and the potential to improve the platform's monetisation. However, Meesho will have to balance monetisation with the shopping experience. Its value-commerce positioning depends on offering consumers affordable products and a wide selection. If sponsored placements make discovery less relevant or push sellers towards higher advertising expenditure that is eventually reflected in product prices, the company could risk weakening some of the advantages of its model. The other consideration is the distribution of advertising benefits across sellers. Larger and more established sellers may have greater capacity to spend on visibility, while smaller sellers could find it harder to compete for prominent placements. Meesho will need to build an advertising ecosystem that delivers returns for sellers across different sizes and categories, the analyst added.. The key monitorable, therefore, is not simply the growth in advertising revenue, but how much of that revenue Meesho can retain as incremental contribution after accounting for the cost of serving the marketplace. If advertising can scale without materially increasing operating costs or affecting affordability, it could become a more durable margin lever. New Initiatives: Lending, Mall And Content Commerce Beyond advertising, Meesho is looking to deepen its engagement with consumers and sellers through a wider set of services. These initiatives could increase the number of ways in which the company earns from its ecosystem, although they are at different stages of development. One area is lending. During the earnings call, management confirmed that Meesho is working on both consumer-side and seller-side lending products. The company is expanding its network of non-banking financial company (NBFC) partners and is also looking to work with banks. For consumers, access to credit could potentially support purchases on the platform, while seller financing could help merchants manage working capital and grow their businesses. If structured effectively, these offerings could strengthen Meesho's relationship with both sides of the marketplace. However, the company has not disclosed lending-related assets under management, revenue targets or the expected financial contribution of these products. It is also not clear how much of the lending opportunity Meesho intends to capture directly versus through its lending partners. For now, it is better viewed as an emerging business opportunity than an established monetisation engine. Meesho Mall and content commerce represent another route to deepen marketplace engagement. Meesho Mall, which had around 1,800 brands in Q2 FY27, recorded 81% YoY growth in NMV. NMV from Tier 3 and smaller markets grew 89%, while around half of Mall customers during the quarter were first-time buyers on the branded-commerce offering. The growth indicates that Meesho is making progress in bringing branded products to a consumer base that has traditionally been associated with unbranded and lower-priced merchandise. A broader product mix could help the platform attract new customer segments and increase the range of purchases made by existing users. Content commerce is also expanding. Its NMV grew 160% YoY in Q2 FY27, while the number of content pieces generating orders increased 144% to 2.2 Mn. The ecosystem had more than 4 lakh sellers participating in content-led commerce. The proposition is to use videos and other content formats to help consumers discover products, rather than relying entirely on search-led shopping. This could create more product discovery opportunities and potentially improve engagement. Meesho has also said that the share of orders coming from discovery-led recommendations has increased, alongside time spent on the platform. However, rapid growth from these offerings does not automatically translate into a meaningful revenue contribution. Meesho has not disclosed the share of total NMV generated by Mall or Content Commerce, nor has it provided specific monetisation targets for either. Their longer-term value will depend on whether they can increase purchase frequency, attract higher-value transactions and create additional opportunities for advertising. AI is another part of this effort. Meesho is using AI across product discovery, ranking, fraud prevention and logistics, while also deploying AI agents in engineering and other internal functions. The company said 65% of its engineering pods were operating with one engineer directing AI agents. It reported a 41% reduction in code-review approval time and a reduction in data-science model deployment time from 17 days to three days. These productivity gains could help the company develop products and improve operations faster. But AI also brings infrastructure costs. Meesho's GPU footprint increased 150%, while server costs rose to 2.3% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 1.9% in the previous quarter. Management expects these costs to normalise towards the previous baseline as a percentage of NMV by Q4 FY27, but that remains an expectation to be tested. The newer initiatives are also still investment-heavy. Management has indicated that it is keeping investments in these businesses within a cap of around ₹200 Cr, while emphasising that product-market fit and unit economics will be important before scaling further. This suggests that Meesho is not yet positioning these offerings as immediate contributors to profitability. The Profitability Test The monetisation opportunity has to be seen alongside Meesho's broader effort to improve its marketplace economics. The company reported a contribution margin of ₹775 Cr in Q2 FY27, up from ₹531 Cr in Q1 FY27. As a percentage of NMV, the margin improved to 6% from 4.6% sequentially. The improvement was largely driven by lower logistics costs, supported by better order density, network redesign, improved route utilisation and efforts to reduce return-to-origin (RTO) orders. Management also indicated that it intends to recover some of the logistics-related margin spread lost in FY26 towards FY25 levels during FY27. However, it has cautioned against extrapolating the Q2 contribution margin as the new normal. Some of the savings could be passed on to sellers and consumers through lower prices, while a part may be retained to improve profitability. The timing and extent of this balance will matter as Meesho enters the festive period and continues to invest in growth. There are also costs that could absorb some of the gains. Meesho's advertising and sales promotion expenses increased ahead of the festive season, taking growth spending to 2.9% of NMV in Q2 FY27 from 2.1% in Q1. Server costs also rose, reflecting the higher computing requirements of the platform. The company reported a consolidated adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹172.1 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its consolidated net loss narrowed to ₹132.4 Cr from ₹411.4 Cr a year earlier. Although the marketplace business is moving towards better unit economics, its newer initiatives continue to add to the overall loss. Cash flow also needs to be viewed over a longer period. Meesho reported positive consolidated free cash flow of ₹345 Cr in Q2 FY27, compared with an outflow of ₹226 Cr in Q1. But its last-twelve-month consolidated free cash flow remained negative at ₹565 Cr. The quarterly improvement was partly supported by seasonal working-capital movements, as collections from consumers ahead of the festive sale preceded settlements with sellers. This makes the quality and durability of cash generation an important measure of progress. Advertising could help improve margins because it allows Meesho to monetise marketplace activity without taking on inventory. Lending and other initiatives may create additional revenue opportunities, but their economics will depend on partner arrangements, customer adoption and the cost of scaling. Brokerage views reflect both the opportunity and the execution risks. Motilal Oswal sees advertising as a medium-term margin lever and expects contribution margins to remain well above FY26 levels. Nomura, however, has flagged the possibility of some margin improvement reversing in Q3 FY27 as the company reinvests gains into growth and category expansion during the festive season. Ultimately, Meesho's next phase will depend on how effectively it monetises the scale it has already built and whether new businesses can add revenue and improve customer and seller engagement without pushing up costs or weakening Meesho's low-price proposition. For a platform that has built its position on affordability and scale, monetisation will have to deepen the business without changing what makes it attractive to consumers and sellers. Editor's note: After the publication of this story, news broke on Oct. 29 that, following an order from a Texas district judge, legal filings identified those responsible for the "Texas Transgender Student Union" mailers as the Republican Women's Caucus Fund and a person named John Braun. The Republican Women's Caucus Fund has denied involvement and said the group was "wrongfully named" in the lawsuit. As of this writing, it is not clear who Braun is.
- There is no evidence that a legitimate trans rights advocacy group sent mailers to Texas homes, purportedly sharing resources for transgender and LGBTQ+ minors with unsupportive families.
- Credible reports indicate that pamphlets with resources for trans minors were sent en masse to Texas families. However, public business records indicate the return sender listed on the envelopes these flyers came in — the "Texas Transgender Student Union" — is based at an address in Wyoming, not Texas. That address is known for its ties to scam operations and shell companies.
- The main organization promoted within the pamphlets, the Transgender Education Network of Texas, is a legitimate advocacy group that has denied all involvement with the mailers and said the messaging within them does "not represent the official position or communications of the organization."
- Wyoming allows business creators to be anonymous, so the name of the person who is actually behind these flyers is not known, as of this writing. Snopes has reached out to the registered agent tied to the so-called Texas Transgender Student Union for more information. We await a response.
In October, photos spread purportedly showing mailers sent to Texas homes, apparently sharing resources for transgender and LGBTQ+ minors with unsupportive families.
Pictures of the pamphlets, titled, "Texas Trans & LGBTQ+ Student Resource Guide," were shared on X, Facebook and Reddit.
They include directions to advocacy organizations that could supposedly help minors navigate emancipation, or the legal process that allows minors to become legal adults before they turn 18.
The flyers also share resources to allegedly receive gender-affirming care outside of Texas, where prescribing hormone medication for gender dysphoria is prohibited for youth under the age of 18. However, the "guide" does not appear to actually contain any detailed step-by-step instructions for anything.
This was sent to my home. Addressed to the "students" of our family from the "Texas Transgender Student Union." It coaches minors on what to do if their parents are not supportive of their "trans" identity and walks them through getting emancipated. THIS IS EVIL!!!!! https://t.co/lTTy7cz18N
— Sara Gonzales (@SaraGonzalesTX) October 19, 2026
Photographs of the envelopes the flyers came in show the sender was the "Texas Transgender Student Union."
Snopes readers who found the mailers suspicious contacted us to ask about whether they originated from a legitimate organization.
Skepticism is, in fact, warranted. As of this writing, there is no organization based in Texas named "Texas Transgender Student Union." Public business records indicate a Wyoming-based LLC registered under that name on Sept. 2. The LLC uses an address that multiple reporters have previously linked to scams and shell operations. 
We have not rated this claim as information continues to emerge about this incident. Here's what we know:
No evidence of 'Texas Transgender Student Union' in Texas
A search (screenshot) of Texas' business records found no evidence of any organization named "Texas Transgender Student Union." The return address attached to the envelopes is also not a valid mailing address, according to a USPS search (screenshot). A nearly identical address, 11611 W. Airport Blvd., leads to a nearby mailbox at a UPS store. Therefore, it is possible the address on the envelopes includes a typo.
There is no online presence for any group called Texas Transgender Student Union aside from a Wyoming business license (more on that below), per searches on Google and social media platforms, including X, Facebook, Bluesky and Instagram.
It is unclear how widespread the mailing list is for whichever organization sent the pamphlets. On Oct. 20, Houston Chronicle reported that the so-called resource guide "appears to have been sent in recent days to many past GOP voters, including a handful of prominent right-wing influencers who posted images of them on Monday."
Wyoming address tied to campaign
Reporters on X were quick to connect the Texas Transgender Student Union to a Wyoming-based LLC called Northwest Registered Agent, which is listed in Wyoming business records as the agent for the so-called Texas Transgender Student Union.
Northwest Registered Agent is one of the largest registered-agent companies in the United States and offers LLC formation for as little as $39 (excluding state fees). Snopes contacted the Northwest Registered Agent organizer listed on the business license — Taylor Newman — to see whether they had any additional information about the Texas Transgender Student Union.
While Newman did not immediately respond, following the publication of this report, Northwest Registered Agent reached out via email.
"We are immediately beginning the process with the Wyoming Secretary of State's Office to officially resign as the registered agent for the Texas Transgender Student Union," the email said. "Because of our privacy commitment to our customers, we can't confirm any additional details."
The company also said our references to it were "highly misleading" because we did not describe, in detail, how forming a business works. (Businesses are legally required to name a registered agent, and Northwest Registered Agent provides those services.)
"We have no way of knowing someone's intent when they're forming a new company, and Northwest Registered Agent has no knowledge of, or involvement in, any of our clients' business operations," the company added. "We follow all state and federal laws."
Records also list 30 N. Gould St. in Sheridan, Wyoming, as the Texas Transgender Student Union's principal office and mailing address. There are thousands of companies represented by registered agents at that address, according to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and The Sheridan Press, the community's daily newspaper. Wyoming's business laws are permissive, allowing people to anonymously set up shop without actually living in the state. (In fact, Northwest Registered Agent advertises its services as involving "privacy by default.") 
The businesses connected to that address "include a mix of reputable companies and those that have a history of scamming customers out of money and hiding behind a Sheridan address to do it," a Sheridan Press reporter wrote in 2024.
According to the Sheridan Press, the Sheridan County Chamber of Commerce "receives about five calls a week from customers desperate to get ahold of a 30 N. Gould company to get their money back," and the paper itself "receives dozens of correspondence regarding the issue weekly."
No evidence legitimate groups are involved
The main organization listed as a resource in the mailer — the Transgender Education Network of Texas — has denied any involvement with the document.
TENT, which has a legitimate business registration in Texas, released the below statement on its website, updated as of Oct. 17:
We are aware of text messages and now physical mailers that have been circulated concerning TENT that appear to have been issued by or on behalf of the organization.
These text messages and mailers were not authored, authorized, approved, or distributed by TENT and are not affiliated with our organization. The texts do not represent the official position or communications of the organization.
We will continue to monitor the situation and remain committed to our organizational values of unequivocal support for trans Texans, their families, and their loved ones. Trans Texans belong here. This is our home and we're not going anywhere.
Underneath the statement, TENT included a GIF of singer Mariah Carey with the caption "Why you so obsessed with me?"
Reporters have also pointed out that TENT likely lacks the resources to launch a widespread mailing campaign. The organization lost its nonprofit tax-exempt status in 2021 after failing to file tax forms for three consecutive years, but its most recent filing in 2017 states it made only $13,300 in revenue that year. USPS' bulk mail cost calculator suggests sending even 10,001 to 50,000 mailers would cost more than $44,000, depending on how big the pamphlets are. 
The documents spread as Texas news outlets reported that TENT sent cease-and-desist notices to two digital messaging companies over a series of texts that linked to TENT resource guides.
Are conservatives behind the pamphlet?
Following the texts, Texas state Rep. Jeff Leach, a Republican, asked state Attorney General Ken Paxton to investigate organizations like TENT for supposedly "violating" state Senate Bill 12, an act that prohibits diversity, equity, and inclusion policies and programs and instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in K–12 public schools.
Leach has since sent a follow-up letter demanding an investigation amid "the possibility that the communications … may not originate from the group whose name it was sent under."
Paxton, the Republican nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, has a well-documented record of opposing transgender rights. Some people, including at least one Snopes reader, have speculated that he was somehow involved with the mailers in question.
As of this writing, there is no evidence Paxton had anything to do with the flyers; he reportedly denied involvement in the mailers to Dallas-area news station KTVT. We also reached out to the Texas attorney general to ask whether he had any involvement and await a response.
The cryptic campaign has caused some online infighting among Republicans, some of whom also seem to believe that conservatives sent the pamphlets as a political tactic ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
The Texas Tribune reported that its reporters tracked a mailer ID attached to two pamphlets sent to Tribune employees to a Maryland-based mail tracking company called SnailWorks, which the National Republican Congressional Committee has a record of using. However, NRCC has denied involvement with the pamphlet.

China made Mbappé apologise - but many people don't know exactly what he said
- Published
On Monday night, as Kylian Mbappé was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media.
Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country.
China's sophisticated censorship system, which cuts 1.4 billion people off from the global internet, meant many didn't know exactly what had happened.
The accusation of "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" alone seemed enough to trigger a tsunami of anger, amplified by social media algorithms and a heavily controlled internet, where people are wary of disagreeing with the majority view.
It wasn't long before Mbappé, one of the biggest football stars in the world, said he was "sincerely sorry" for his "ill-judged" comment. His club, Real Madrid, and the Spanish league La Liga, also issued apologies. China is a huge market for the world's most popular sport.
Beijing later confirmed it was taking the footballer's apology "seriously". China Media Group has yet to say whether broadcasts will resume.
But the anger online lingered.
"An apology is the least he should do, but I don't forgive him. I support a ban on him," read a top comment on Weibo.
Mbappé did not mention Mao by name in the interview, but many felt any joke that involved the founder of Communist China crossed a line.
"Do you know who you hurt? He is the spiritual pillar of the Chinese people," read one Weibo comment liked by more than 700 users.
"He's the most important figure in our history. Do you think a simple apology can make everything okay?" another wrote.
Ironically, despite the heavy backlash, many on Chinese social media are still asking what exactly the French forward said. They tried AI chatbots, which are just as censored as the Chinese internet and couldn't provide any answers. Others attempted to explain, but skirted around any mention of Mao.
References were made to "the person on the 100 yuan note" and "the teacher", a title Mao once used for himself. Screenshots of the meme and interview were shared, with both the word "dictator" and Mbappé's face blurred out.
Neither the Chinese foreign ministry statement nor the apologies issued by Mbappé, Real Madrid and La Liga mentioned Mao directly.
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.
Despite the turmoil of his rule, including the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society, he remains a revered figure in China.
A portrait of Mao overlooks Beijing's Tiananmen Square, a symbol of how central he is in the modern Chinese imagination. Unlike other former Chinese leaders, his embalmed body is placed on public display there, drawing tens of thousands of visitors every day. In recent years, there has been a revival of interest in him among young people, who read his works and watch clips of him on social media.
Chinese history books downplay the devastation during Mao's rule. The Chinese Communist Party's verdict on Mao is that his achievements outweigh his mistakes. In their eyes, he is "a great revolutionary and a great Marxist".
But outside China, history sees Mao as both a revolutionary and a dictator. And so reactions among the diaspora - dissidents as well as people whose families fled China decades ago, in the wake of Mao's rule - was very different.
"You don't need to apologise, you are not wrong," a highly liked comment written in Chinese under the football star's X statement read.
"The ones who should apologise are the CCP; they kidnapped the Chinese people and brainwashed them," another Chinese user wrote.
On X and Threads, neither of which are accessible in China, the controversy spawned even more memes. Some feature Mbappé's face on other images of Mao, while others go further, placing him on the body of current Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
And then there was the rest of the internet which was simply puzzled.
"It's honestly hard to understand... It seems like people aren't allowed to speak out against their leaders. And they expect the whole world to think the same way they do? That's ridiculous," read a top comment under Real Madrid's apology on Instagram.
"How dare you call a dictator a dictator? Terrible," another user on X wrote.

6 things to watch for on election night
It can be hard to know what to focus on in midterm elections. There are so many races, from elections for governor and senator to the House and state legislatures. For a better idea of how the night might go to see which party might control Congress, here are six things to watch:
1. The early bellwethers for Republican turnout and the Latino vote
There are two states, Indiana and Kentucky, that will see results in the 6 p.m. ET hour. And then there's Florida, which is split between the Eastern and Central time zones. But most of the state is on Eastern time. So lots of House race results will be coming in during the 7 p.m. ET hour, even if statewide contests like the Senate and governors races won't be called at the earliest until 8 p.m. ET.
Some races to watch for early indicators of what might come later in the evening — Indiana's 5th Congressional District, Kentucky's 6th and Florida's 22nd and 27th. Indiana's 5th and Kentucky's 6th are seats held by Republicans that are more competitive now than at the beginning of the cycle. If these are close or tipping to Democrats, it could be a sign of low Republican turnout and a bigger Democratic wave.
Florida's 22nd is held by a Democrat but redrawn to tip in Republicans' favor. Trump won Florida's 27th by double-digits so this heavily Latino district could be an indicator of how this key subgroup votes.
2. Do Republicans get 46% with independents?
Independents are a key swing group, but they are also a lower-propensity voting group in midterms.
It used to be that Republicans had to win a bigger share of independents before the Trump era. Mitt Romney, for example, won 55% of independents in 2012 but lost the presidential election. But there's been a political realignment in this country with blue-collar white voters trending toward Trump, fewer people identifying as Democrats and better-educated white voters shifting toward Democrats.
So in the decade since Trump has been on the political scene, Republicans have done well when they win at least 46% of independents. When they haven't, they've lost.
3. Black voter turnout in key states
The Michigan Senate race is important for control of the Senate. If Republicans flip it, the magic number for Democrats goes from four to five, meaning Democrats would have to win five seats held by Republicans to win control of the Senate.
For Abdul El-Sayed (D) to win in Michigan, a key is going to be Black voters in Wayne County. If he runs up the score in and around Detroit, he has a path to victory, but if he doesn't, it becomes that much harder — and it's been an area of vulnerability for him.
During the Trump era, Democrats have needed 68% or more in Wayne County to win Michigan unless, like Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024, they can overperform in the suburbs.

4. The margin with young voters
Voters 18 to 29 see a drastic drop off in turnout between presidential and midterm elections. During presidential races since 1992, 43% of registered young voters cast ballots. But in midterms, that falls to 21%, just 1 in 5 who show up at the polls.
But they are crucial to Democratic success. In the last 20 years, when Democrats won this group by more than 20 points, they have done well, winning presidencies or making gains in midterms. The only exception was 2022, but arguably, the strong margin Democrats won with young voters that year, helped them stem what could have been a much larger Republican tide. That year, Democrats lost nine House seats, but gained a Senate seat.

5. In Texas, the keys will be the difference between Gov. Greg Abbott (R) and Ken Paxton's (R) vote totals – and the Latino vote in South Texas
Given past polling errors in Texas that underestimated the Republican vote, there's a healthy skepticism that Democrat James Talarico's margin of error lead in polling averages is enough to win.
There was lots of enthusiasm in 2018 for Beto O'Rourke's (D) 2018 bid against an unpopular Republican senator in Ted Cruz, but Cruz still won, although by less than 3 percentage points. No Democrat has won statewide in Texas since 1994, and no Democrat has been elected to the Senate from Texas in 38 years.
For it to actually happen in this state Trump won by 14 points in 2024, two groups are key – Republicans and Latinos. Ken Paxton (R) is unpopular. Republican Gov. Greg Abbot is also facing a tight race, but he's thought to be in better shape than Paxton. In 2018, Cruz won about 400,000 fewer votes than Abbott, but Cruz still won by more than 200,000 votes. So watch if the difference between Abbott and Paxton is more than 400,000 for Talarico.
The second part of Talarico's path to victory runs through South Texas. Statewide, O'Rourke won 64% of Latinos in 2018, and they were 26% of the electorate, according to exit polls. If Talarico is north of both of those, that's how he wins the seat. Talarico would need to improve on O'Rourke's totals in these Latino-heavy counties: Cameron 63%, Hidalgo 69%, Webb 71%, Nueces 51%. As a bonus, watch the fast-growing and heavily populated Dallas suburbs – Collin 47%, Denton 46%, Tarrant 51%.
6. Party identification
Because of the political realignment that's taken place in the Trump era, watch how people identify in exit polls.
The percentage of those saying they were Democrats hit a low in 2024 at 31%. That trend is happening as the base of the Democratic Party has become more liberal and more disaffected with their own leadership. This year, though, Democrats were among the highest in enthusiasm levels, according to the latest NPR poll, but they are likely going to have to be far higher than 31% as a share of the electorate to do well.

That's quite possible given the opposition to Trump in this election is sky high – 53% of likely voters in the latest NPR poll said they strongly disapproved of the job he's doing. That is very likely to be a unifying force for the left in this election. As the saying goes, the enemy of my enemy is my friend.
Along these lines, it's going to be important to watch races like the Michigan Senate race and the contest for Michigan's 7th Congressional District, both of which have very progressive Democratic candidates trying to win in purple places. Democratic unity – and the party's ideological future – is going to be a key storyline of the 2028 presidential primary and could define the American left for years to come.

Serbia marks the second anniversary of a train station tragedy that fueled student protests
Thousands of students and supporters in Serbia have marked two years since a deadly train station disaster
NOVI SAD, Serbia -- A week after a student movement toppled Serbia's strongman Aleksandar Vucic in an election, thousands of students and their supporters on Sunday marked two years since a deadly train station disaster that gave birth to their anti-corruption campaign.
The demand for accountability over the Nov. 1, 2024 collapse of a concrete canopy at the station in the northern city of Novi Sad that killed 16 people launched two years of student-led protests that eventually brought about the stunning defeat of Vucic’s right-wing government at last week's parliamentary elections.
In steady rain and silence, thousands marched in Novi Sad on Sunday in a gesture of respect for the victims. Unlike a year ago, when huge crowds gathered for the first anniversary of the tragedy, participants this year said they now have hope that those responsible for the disaster will be punished.
The students brought 16 wreaths and 16 red hearts — one for each victim — outside the station building. The inscribed names of the victims included children. People cried as they laid down flowers and lit candles. A moment of silence was held.
Many in Serbia believe that the concrete canopy crashed because of flawed renovation work caused by corruption and negligence that prevailed in major state infrastructure projects championed by Vucic's government.
The station renovation was part of a bigger railway reconstruction project with China and neighboring Hungary. Vucic and his ally, former right-wing Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban together toured the renewed Novi Sad station back in 2022.
“It was a murder and a murder demands accountability and justice,” a student said in a speech Sunday, promising that Serbia’s young people will build a more just society in the future. “We will not forget them (victims).”
Since the election in which the Students’ List defeated Vucic’s long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, last Sunday, the students have demanded a review of high-profile investigations, including the probe into the canopy collapse. Previously, 13 people had been charged, including a government minister, but no trial was held as the probe stalled.
The head of the European Union mission in Serbia, Andreas von Beckerath, wrote on X that the canopy collapse “shook Serbia to its core and moved citizens across the country to demand transparency and accountability.”
“May their memory keep inspiring a Serbia built on solidarity, public trust and rule of law," he added.
Also Sunday, prosecutors ordered a 48-hour detention of Marko Kricak, Vucic's chief of criminal police. Another senior officer was detained along with Kricak, both on suspicion of abuse of office in connection with a murder investigation.
Kricak was accused of orchestrating violence during the student protests, and of personally threatening a female student with rape, allegations that he has denied.
After it took office 14 years ago, Vucic's SNS party gradually took control of all state institutions. The students' movement has promised to restore the rule of law and democracy, and root out rampant graft that they say flourished under Vucic.
On Nov. 1, 2024, the huge concrete construction at the outer front wall of the Novi Sad station crashed without warning at 11:52 a.m., crushing people underneath as they were waiting for trains on a sunny autumn day.
Fourteen people died at the scene, and two died later. A young woman survived with life-changing injuries.
Authorities first said that the canopy had not been renovated at all, and promised an investigation. But protests started almost immediately with people blocking traffic every day across the country at the exact time of the collapse and demanding justice.
Some of the student-led rallies held in the last two years were among the biggest anti-government protests in Serbia's history.
And unlike last year when Vucic was in power, Sunday's anniversary memorial was broadcast by state RTS television, following resignations among officials at the TV station in the post-election week.
Commemoration ceremonies were also held in other cities and towns throughout Serbia.
An independent investigation by a group of experts into the canopy collapse found the renovation work had been rushed under political orders. The experts' report alleged a “systematic degradation of construction standards” and said that the "state of Serbia violated its citizens' right to life.”

The Best Alexa Speakers I’ve Tried
Featured in this article
Amazon started the smart speaker game, but finding the best Alexa speaker has only gotten harder as the company launches more and more devices. Amazon has the largest range of smart speakers and displays by a long shot, which can be overwhelming to dive into. The most recent were launched late last year: the Echo Dot Max, the Echo Studio (2nd Gen), the Echo Show 11, and the Echo Show 8 (4th Gen). But Amazon has plenty of older, cheaper models available, too.
If you're looking for something small and simple to control your home, either an Echo Dot ($80) or the Echo Dot Max ($120) is your best bet. The Dot Max has really impressive sound for its compact size and is my overall favorite Alexa speaker, but if you're only going to use it for voice commands rather than jam sessions, you can get away with the older, cheaper model, especially if you want to buy a few to place around your home. For anyone looking for a smart display, the Echo Show 11 ($250) is the best of Amazon's newest smart displays that come designed for the updated assistant, Alexa+. The older third-generation Echo Show 8 ($150) is still a great value if you want something cheaper.
Read on to see every Alexa speaker I've tried (hint: it's all of them) and what I think after testing each one. You can also learn more about Alexa+, and we've got guides on setting up your Echo speaker, creating Alexa routines, and the best tricks an Echo Show can do.
Updated September 2026: I've updated this guide with Amazon's increased pricing that affected several models, and details about the price hike.
Comparing the Best Alexa Speakers
| Model | Speaker Array | Screen Specs | Camera Specs | Other Features | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon Echo Dot Max | One 2.5-inch woofer; one 1-inch tweeter | None | None | Tap controls; smart home hub | 
| Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) | One 1.73-inch speaker | None | None | None | 
| Amazon Echo Show 11 | One 2.8-inch woofer; two full-range drivers | 11-inch display with 1920 x 1200 resolution | 13-MP camera with auto-framing | Zigbee smart home hub that supports Matter and Thread; spatial audio; Dolby Atmos | 
| Amazon Echo Show 8 (3rd Gen) | Two 2-inch speakers | 8-inch display with 1280 x 800 resolution | 13-MP camera with auto-framing | Zigbee smart home hub; spatial audio | 
Honorable Mentions
While I wouldn't call these smart speakers my absolute favorites from Amazon, they have some excellent qualities that make them stand out among the vast lineup of Echo models.
The Echo Studio (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for sound quality. This is the second version of the Echo Studio to be our audiophile pick. The current version is a similar size to the old Echo (4th gen), but the musical power on this speaker is almost ridiculous. It filled my entire second floor's long great room with music, and I didn't even need to reach the highest level of volume to pull it off. Honestly, I'm almost afraid to use it at full blast. Not only was it loud, but clear and delivered a nice amount of bass, beautifully playing soft tones of Tracy Chapman's “Fast Car” and the piano riffs of “Dark Blue” by Jack's Mannequin with its three 1.5-inch drivers, plus a 3.75-inch woofer. The harmonizing of “What Is This Feeling?” by Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo sounded beautiful, too. If you're looking for big sound in an Alexa box, this is it. It's a similar size to the Apple HomePod, but I like the sound much better and it's cheaper, too. You'll also get a built-in smart home hub, spatial audio and Dolby Atmos, tap controls like the Echo Dot Max, and early access to Alexa+ right away.
The Echo Spot (2nd Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for bedside tables. The Echo Spot returned in 2024 after a few years of discontinuation, and it's a great little bedside companion thanks to its half-circle screen that displays the time, plus any alarms you have set are also visible under the main time. You can customize the clock with a couple of different color and face options, and the screen dims nicely when the lights are out to a gentle red that's easy to read without lighting up the room. I like asking for alarms set to my latest playlist or some lo-fi jams, and it's easy to set that up with a voice request. Unlike the Echo Shows, it doesn't have a distracting, constantly moving slideshow that would be annoying for the bedroom, nor does it display ads or have a built-in camera. (Nobody wants a rogue camera in their bedroom.) It does not have fantastic sound, but it's plenty loud for an alarm or casual listening while you get dressed in the morning.
The Echo Dot Kids (5th Gen) is the best Alexa speaker for kids. Do your kids really need their own Alexa speaker? That's up to you. This special edition of the Echo Dot is nearly identical to the fifth-gen Dot above, but it has easy-to-use parental controls that allow you to set time limits, filter explicit content, and review activity. The owl- or dragon-themed sphere comes with a year of Amazon Kids+, which includes thousands of Audible books and other special games and features. After that, you'll be charged $3 per month. Alexa can help your kids spell, play their favorite music, or—via another speaker in your house—remind them of dinner time.
More Alexa (and Alexa-Compatible) Speakers
There are a lot of Echo devices out there, and some third-party speakers that are Amazon Alexa–compatible. Here's every Alexa smart speaker we've tried and what we thought of it. Some of these speakers didn't raise in price like the models above, which might make them more appealing than before if you're looking to spend less.
Amazon Echo Dot (5th Gen) With Clock for $60: I like this version of the older Echo Dot that adds an LED clock to the front of the speaker, and was thrilled to see it in stock again last year. The LED clock can also display information like the weather when you ask Alexa questions. It's once again temporarily out of stock as of this writing, and has had spotty availability (it's out of stock right now, but Amazon says it's temporary). Still, it's a good find when it's available.
Amazon Echo Hub for $180: The Amazon Echo Hub is similar to an Echo Show, but without the speaker. Instead it's a thin device that feels a bit like a tablet, designed to be mounted on the wall (or placed on a separately purchased stand, which is how I used it) and used to control your smart home devices. It's a great choice for anyone who wants something focused on smart home control only. You can still ask Alexa questions and even play music, but the thin speakers aren't worth playing music from. But you can tell your Echo Hub to play music on a different set of speakers, and even set up default speakers to work with it. It's a great companion device if you already have a smart home setup.
Amazon Echo Pop for $40: The Echo Pop is a perfectly fine little speaker, and the cutest one in Amazon's lineup. Does it have great sound? No. It's fine enough for background tunes or if you're limited to a dorm room, but you'll get much better sound for a similar size from the Echo Dot (but you'll pay a little more, and you won't get as cute of colors)!
Amazon Echo Show 5 (3rd Gen) for $100: This smart display is another just-fine option, but it's too small to be a great display, and the included camera makes it a no for a bedside table; better to go with the above Echo Spot or an Echo Dot. This model did raise in price by $10.
Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $200: I usually love an Echo Show 8, but this model didn't have the same sound quality as the older model. If you're going to get one of Amazon's new displays, you're better off getting the Echo Show 11 ($220) for the same experience with a slightly larger screen (while it's a 3-inch difference, it doesn't feel that big) and better sound. This smart display raised in price by $20.
Amazon Echo Show 15 (2nd Gen) for $350: This smart display is a good display, but it clearly wants to double as a TV and isn't very good at it yet. I'm hoping we see better TV-related performance in the future to make it worth adding to a kitchen or office. It does a great job with widgets, though, thanks to the massive 15.6-inch screen. There's also the larger Echo Show 21 ($500), which is essentially the same thing but larger. Both of these large displays rose in price—the Show 15 went up $50, while the Show 21 went up $100.
JBL Authentics 200 for $380: This JBL smart speaker supports both Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa, letting you switch between them for different tasks without changing your preference in the app. That makes this speaker particularly appealing for folks with a sprawling collection of smart products from both.
Sonos Era 100 for $219: If you're looking for a speaker that can talk to Alexa but isn't necessarily made by Amazon, the Sonos Era 100 is a great option. We just wish we liked the Sonos app better. You can catch our entire guide to the Sonos ecosystem here.
Why Did Amazon's Prices Increase?
Amazon increased many of its prices last month for its products, affecting the Amazon Echo line as well as Kindles, Fire TV streaming sticks, and Eero routers. It's not a huge surprise after other companies have done the same this summer, claiming rising costs and chip shortages. Amazon made a similar claim, with a spokesperson blaming increased storage and memory costs. Still, it's disappointing to see and will lead to a fall sale season with prices that won't be as impressive as earlier this summer.
Amazon's Echo devices saw increases from anywhere between $20 and $100, with the larger price increases being for the Echo Shows. The following Echo speakers all faced a price increase:
- Echo Dot (5th Gen): $80 (up $30)
- Echo Spot (2nd Gen): $110 (up $30)
- Echo Dot Max: $120 (up $20)
- Echo Show 8 (4th Gen): $200 (up $20)
- Echo Show 11: $250 (up $30)
- Echo Show 15: $350 (up $50)
- Echo Show 21: $500 (up $100)
What’s Alexa+?
Amazon has rolled out the new-and-improved Amazon Alexa, named Alexa+, which is built on generative AI and promises a more powerful assistant that can handle more conversational topics and requests. It's available for a free 30-day trial; after that, you either pay a $20 monthly fee or become a Prime member. Being a Prime member is the better deal, likely by design. Neither my colleagues nor I have been impressed enough by Alexa+ to say it's worth paying for on its own. I do like the updated, more conversational voice, and Alexa+ did a good job answering all kinds of questions quickly and thoughtfully. Check out our early access hands-on for everything I thought while testing.
Alexa+ has brought some changes, even for those not using it. It now requires that all voice recordings be sent to Amazon for processing, which wasn't required before. Amazon has changed its features to support this, and now all recordings with regular Alexa go to Amazon, too. There used to be a “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” privacy feature you could select to have voice requests processed locally, but it was discontinued on March 28, 2025, per an email Amazon sent to current users.
FAQs
What’s the Difference Between an Echo and an Echo Show?
A regular Echo is a smart speaker, or a speaker with microphones in it so it can hear you speak to it and respond. An Echo Show is a smart display, which has a screen and a camera to let you make video calls, stream content, and see your questions answered on a screen. Both have similar capabilities when it comes to smart home control, answering questions, and playing music, but Echo Shows have extra abilities thanks to the screen. All Echo Shows have a camera and come with a physical camera cover for privacy.
When’s the Best Time to Buy an Echo?
The best time to buy any Amazon speaker is during a major sale event like Black Friday or Amazon Prime Day, when there are often steep discounts. You'll often see the cheaper speakers for around 50 percent off, and the larger speakers see some nice sale prices too.
How and Where Should You Set Up Your Alexa?
Alexa speakers get the best use in spaces you're in often. I like setting mine up in my kitchen and living room—usually a display in the kitchen, so I can pull up a recipe or the weather while I make my morning cup of tea, and a speaker in the living room so I can play music and command the lights without a screen to distract from the TV or playing with my son. You can also set one up in the bedroom to use as an alarm clock, but make sure it's a model without a camera for the best privacy.
Ultimately, what's most important is that the speaker is somewhere it can hear your commands. Where that will be will vary based on your home, but think about where you'll be when you ask for the weather or to dim the lights, and place your speaker accordingly.
You'll set up Alexa speakers using the Alexa app, which allows you to manage multiple Alexa speakers if you own more than one through your Amazon account. Third-party speaker setup methods may vary.
Is Alexa Always Listening?
Alexa is always listening, to a certain extent. It's designed to only listen for its wake word and shouldn't be recording or processing any audio unless it hears that word. But Alexa can sometimes mishear a word and think it's the wake word, or it might hear a word similar enough to activate the speaker. If you've owned an Alexa, there have likely been times when the assistant suddenly responds when you weren't speaking to it. Once it hears the wake word (or what it believes to be the wake word), it will start listening to everything in an attempt to hear what you need and respond.
Alexa+, the latest version of Alexa, will also remain on for a little bit after you ask a question to listen for follow-up questions, no wake word required. Both Alexa and Alexa+ light up in some fashion (regular speakers will turn the light ring blue, while the displays will have a blue bar appear on the screen) to let you know the assistant is listening. Most Echo devices also have a physical mute button and will display a red light or red bar to let you know when the mute is activated.
How Do You Remove Ads and Spam From an Echo Show?
If you're using an Echo Show device, you've likely noticed there is a ton of default content the device will show you. Sports scores! Local news! A recipe you might be interested in! It makes the device exhausting and annoying to be near.
Here's how you can control what you see:
- Swipe down from the top of your Echo Show to pull up the menu, and select Settings.
- In the Settings menu, choose Home Content.
- There are more than 40 options you can toggle on and off on this menu, and you should remove as many as you can that you don't use. I usually remove all but weather forecasts and recently played audio.
While you're able to turn off interest-based ads from third-party skills (this is under Alexa Privacy in the Settings menu), it won't stop all ads. The only setting that is ad-free is choosing Photo Display mode, which can use either Amazon's included library of photos or your own. The downside is that it turns it into a digital photo frame, so you won't even see a clock or features like widgets.
Can I Have My Alexa Requests Locally Processed, or Do They Have to Go to the Cloud?
There used to be a privacy feature called Do Not Send Voice Recordings that let you have all your voice requests processed locally on your Alexa device instead of being sent to Amazon's cloud storage. That feature was killed in March 2025 to support Alexa+, and even if you continue to use the old Alexa, you don't have access to that feature any longer.
How Does WIRED Select Smart Speakers to Test? How Are These Speakers Tested?
For this guide, we specifically test speakers that are compatible with Amazon Alexa. It's a big limitation and narrows down the options significantly, especially compared to speaker options you'll see in our other guides like the Best Bluetooth Speakers. That's mainly Amazon's own ecosystem of speakers, and while there are third-party options, the best options tend to be of Amazon's own design to work with its own voice assistant.
Each speaker gets installed in a tester's home for day-to-day use, to see how the microphone performs, how the speaker sounds with different types of music, how well the smart home control features work with compatible devices such as smart lights and video doorbells, and to test other features as necessary (e.g., streaming features on smart displays).
How Does WIRED Get Models? What Does WIRED Do After Testing Them?
We acquire review units usually as a press sample, though we will also independently purchase samples if need be. All review units in this guide were provided as press samples with no obligation to cover or promises for what that coverage would be.
After testing, we keep most of our picks either installed for long-term testing in our homes or in storage to compare against updated models and new speakers that come out. If the sample becomes irrelevant or unnecessary to keep, we donate it locally.
