With polls indicating that the Democrats are poised to win big in the midterm elections, the Trump administration is already attempting to mount legal challenges in certain races and cast doubt on the results.
A post published last month by the Center for Renewing America, an influential right-wing think tank, suggests a more radical strategy, asserting that a number of Democrats could be prevented from holding office even if they win their elections.
The post, titled, “Can Congress Seat a Member-Elect Who Vows to Destroy our Constitution?” argues even winning candidates from what it believes to be a purported “Red-Green Alliance” between “neo-Marxist progressives and anti-Western Muslims,” can and should be kept from being seated in Congress. The post, in effect, claims that Muslim and progressive candidates don’t have to be legally accepted into their elected positions.
“This is another attempt to contort and twist basic norms that have never been used this way for their own partisan purposes,” says Richard Pildes, a professor at New York University’s School of Law.
The CRA was founded by Russell Vought, one of the main architects of Project 2025 and now the director of the Office of Management and Budget. Vought faced criticism for his anti-Muslim comments—he once said that Muslims had a “deficient theology” and “do not know God”—when was nominated for OMB director during the first Trump administration.
The Center for Renewing America (CRA) did not respond to a request for comment.
Though Vought has described himself and allies, including members of the CRA, as “radical constitutionalists,” he has taken several steps that have infringed on the powers of other branches of government to expand the power of the executive branch. Most notably, although Congress is tasked with allocating and approving funds for the operation of the federal government, Vought has impounded, refused, or delayed the disbursement of funds, including billions of dollars that Congress has approved. Last year, Vought put a freeze on $5 billion in foreign aid funding, which was followed up by clawing back more than $800 million this year, a move that may violate the Impoundment Control Act, Maine senator Susan Collins said in late September.
The recent CRA piece—authored by Benjamin Osborne, a Georgetown Law School graduate who is serving as the organization’s legal fellow—argues that the beliefs the organization has imputed to so-called Red-Green politicians are against the US Constitution. Osborne writes that “when someone elected to Congress has personally embraced the destruction of the constitutional order espoused by these groups, he or she cannot truthfully swear to support that order as a condition of taking office.”
According to another CRA publication from earlier this year written by the organization’s executive director, Wade Miller, the so-called Red-Green Alliance includes the “Squad,” the nickname for the group of four progressive women of color who all won seats in Congress in 2018: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, Ayanna Pressley, and Ilhan Omar. It also includes politicians like New York mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. These politicians, the publication claims, are purveyors of “ideology dedicated to destroying capitalism, Christianity, and the Western political tradition.” None of the politicians named in the piece have self-identified as Marxists, though some, including Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani, are Democratic Socialists.
Corey Brettschneider, a professor of politics and constitutional law at Brown University and host of the The Oath and the Office podcast, says that both posts are “engaged in an attack on the Constitution and then trying to use the law of that as an attack on opponents,” something he believes a court would quickly be able to identify and quash.
Trying to use a Muslim politician’s religion as a reason for them to be disqualified from holding office, says Brettschneider, would likely be even more difficult than taking aim at a certain political group. “The protections I'd say are even stronger against that maneuver because the Constitution is explicit in saying you can't have a religious test for office,” he says.
El-Sayed’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment about whether they were aware of the Renewing America piece, or what, if any, steps the campaign is taking to prepare for challenges to a possible win.
While any successful legal case based on the logic outlined by the CRA would be unlikely to hold up in court, says Brettschneider, “clearly what they're doing is floating it to see if it will stick.”
Christian Grose, a professor of political science at the University of Southern California, says that the effectiveness of a strategy like the one outlined by the CRA would likely vary widely depending on the margins of a possible Democratic victory. If the Democrats win one or two seats in the Senate, he says, Republicans could try to dispute results in order to maintain control of the Senate. “But if Democrats win the Senate by something like four seats, I think we will be less likely to see those kinds of things,” he says. “The bigger the margin is on either side, the less likely this will be a viable strategy, and it becomes more preposterous the larger number of winning candidates that someone would try not to seat.”
For members of the House, the outcome could depend on whether Democrats can snag a majority. If Republicans maintain the majority, they could vote to refuse to seat incoming Democrats. In 1967, the House refused to seat Adam Clayton Powell, Jr, a Democrat representative from Harlem and the first Black person from the state of New York to be elected to Congress, due to allegations that he was misappropriating funds.
Grose says that any legal case would risk going unresolved beyond the start of the new Congress in 2027, meaning that whether or not a senator whose win was challenged could be seated would likely be determined by a judge issuing an injunction. “It could become a Congress versus courts showdown,” he says.
Pildes is more direct: “This isn't going to happen.”
But just because the legal strategy may not work, it doesn’t mean the administration or Republicans wouldn’t make the attempt. Brettschneider noted the administration’s multiple attempts to charge former FBI director James Comey with various crimes, even if prosecutors are unlikely to secure a conviction. “We absolutely need to take it seriously because Trump has been dismantling the guardrails and the norms that are supposed to protect against this, or trying to influence the courts through appointments,” he says. “Even if they don't get away with it directly, threatening and shutting down opponents creates fear, and makes people worry ‘They might come after me next.’”

Man dies after ambulance hits scooter, runs over him in Lucknow
A speeding private hospital ambulance hit a scooter and allegedly ran over Ashish Kumar Srivastava in Lucknow. CCTV footage is being examined as police seek the fleeing driver.
A man was killed and his colleague seriously injured after a private hospital ambulance rammed into their scooter from behind in Uttar Pradesh's Lucknow on Monday morning. The ambulance driver allegedly ran over one of the men as he lay on the road after the collision and fled without stopping. The entire incident was captured on a CCTV camera near the accident site.
The accident took place near Parking Number 9 in the Transport Nagar area under the Sarojini Nagar police station limits. The two men, who worked together at a private pharmaceutical company in Transport Nagar, were on their way to office when the ambulance hit their scooter.
The deceased has been identified as 40-year-old Ashish Kumar Srivastava, a resident of Wazirganj. His colleague, Vedant, who was riding pillion, sustained serious injuries.
According to the police, the two men had left for work on Vedant's scooter on Monday morning, with Ashish riding the vehicle and Vedant seated behind him.
When they reached near Parking Number 9 in Transport Nagar, a motorcyclist allegedly approached them from the wrong side. Ashish applied the brakes after spotting the motorcycle coming towards them. At that moment, a speeding ambulance belonging to a private hospital rammed into their scooter from behind after its driver allegedly lost control.
The impact threw both men off the scooter and onto the road. The ambulance driver allegedly failed to stop and ran over Ashish before fleeing the spot.
Passers-by and police personnel rushed the injured men to Lok Bandhu Hospital, where doctors declared Ashish dead. Vedant, who was seriously injured, was admitted to the hospital and is undergoing treatment.
Ashish's death left his family devastated. He is survived by his wife, Richa, and their eight-year-old son.
Sarojini Nagar police took custody of the body and sent it for a post-mortem examination. The accident was captured on CCTV footage from a camera installed near the spot.
Police are examining the footage to identify the ambulance and trace its driver, who fled after the crash.

Climate change must be declared a "global health emergency" to shape governments' policies after heat caused three million deaths between 2016 and 2023, a report in The Lancet said Wednesday.
Published by the British medical journal ahead of the COP 31 climate summit in November, the 10th edition of the report brought together 146 researchers from 30 countries to assess the impact of climate change on the health of the world's population.
It said there were a record 710,000 heat-related deaths in 2023 with more than 70% of that toll linked to human-caused climate change.
Marina Romanello, the executive director of the health and climate research project Lancet Countdown, said there were "three million heat-related deaths globally in an eight-year span since the Paris Agreement" of 2015.
"That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat," she told a news conference.
And "68% of those deaths are directly attributable to climate change."
The legally binding international climate treaty adopted in the French capital aimed to limit global warming to well below 2C and pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5C compared to pre-industrial levels.
Climate change impact
Romanello said the global health emergency due to climate change should have "an integrated approach so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency".
Instead she called for "a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities, and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies moving forward".
To determine the share of deaths attributable to warming caused by human activity, the researchers compiled the number of heat-related deaths recorded by states, then subtracted those that would have occurred in the absence of climate change, said Professor Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney.
Jay said the intensity and frequency of periods of intense heat were amplified by climate change, pointing out that last year an extreme drought affected more than half of the world's land surface for at least one month.
Economic cost
By reducing worker productivity, warming has cost the global economy more than one trillion dollars per year over the past three years, the researchers said.
Southeast Asia and Africa, the hardest-hit regions, are estimated to have lost the equivalent of 3.9 percent and 3.2 percent of their GDP, compared with 0.2 percent for Europe and 1.5 percent for the Americas.
However there has been concrete progress in some areas.
Since 2016, 56 of the WHO's 194 member states have adapted their health and early-warning systems to anticipate extreme events.
Investment in clean energy reached $2.1 trillion in 2025 -- double that of the amount invested in fossil fuels, which cause climate change.
However fossil fuels still account for 80 percent of global energy, causing air pollution that results in 2.73 million deaths per year, the study said.
Meanwhile, roughly 323,000 deaths have been avoided in "at least" 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016, according to the report.
Although funding for climate-related medical research has increased sevenfold to reach $316 million in 2024, 84% of these funds go to researchers in wealthy countries, even though the least developed nations are the most affected by the growing climate-related health threats.
Romanello said this year for the first time the researchers' work was complicated by the disappearance of certain data sources, particularly from the United States, such as fossil fuel subsidies, which have not been made public by the US authorities.
And for the past two years, global geopolitical instability has pushed global warming and its health impact into the background, she said, stressing that inaction was exacerbating the situation.

Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
- Published
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.
The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, including a request for election officials to separate ballots that rank retired teacher Dan J Sullivan.
Senator Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.
"I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."
Alaska's Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered an official inquiry earlier this week into the alleged scheme.
Heyman did not immediately provide details of specific crimes his office would investigate.
Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times, external reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.
The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to her campaign.
But those denials have not stopped the justice department (DOJ) and Republicans from attacking Peltola.
The DOJ has begun issuing subpoenas targeting Democratic officials allegedly connected to the recruitment effort, according to CBS News, the BBC's US news partner.
No charges had been filed as of Friday evening.
"There is both a civil investigation and a criminal investigation that are ongoing," Michael Heyman, the US attorney for the district of Alaska, said at a Friday afternoon press conference.
Later that day, lawyers for the Trump administration asked a federal judge to issue an order before Monday that would direct state election officials "to preserve and segregate" all ballots that rank Dan J Sullivan.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward argued in court documents that the move would be to investigate whether such ranking "was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary".
"These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration," he said.
But the state's Republican attorney general - the top prosecutor in the state - asked the court to toss the lawsuit and said the request from the Trump administration was "inappropriate and not even possible given Alaskan voters' vital right to ballot secrecy".
The filing said there was "no reason for this Court to entertain this meritless lawsuit any longer".
What legal experts say about 'spoiler candidates'
Scott Kendall, an attorney who worked with Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski in her 2010 and 2016 campaigns, told the BBC he was sceptical the actions described in the New York Times story broke the law.
Alaska law does not have specific good-faith requirements for candidates, Kendall explained - noting that spoiler candidates sometimes emerged in their contests.
"I freely admit there could be more facts, but I'm not going to speculate they exist," he said.
The spectre of a federal crimes could come into play if there was potential evidence of campaign finance violations, Kendall, as well as other legal experts, told the BBC. But such evidence has not yet emerged.
Kendall believed the primary risk to Peltola from the allegations is "absolute reputational harm".
The Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing the presence of both of them on the ballot could confuse voters.
On Wednesday, the justice department amended its lawsuit to include the reporting by the Times, citing significant sections of the story as well as Governor Mike Dunleavy's announcement of an investigation.
A federal judge has expedited consideration and will weigh motions to dismiss brought by Alaska election officials and backed by the Peltola campaign and voting rights groups.
The legal action comes days before voters across the US head to the polls. This race in Alaska is among the closest-watched in the country, as it could be the deciding factor in who controls the Senate.
The non-partisan Cook Political Report currently classifies the race as a toss-up.
As the final weekend of campaigning approaches, President Donald Trump will appear at back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday.
The in-person appearances were previously cancelled, but a source familiar with planning told the BBC that they were rescheduled to accommodate remote appearances by Trump at tele-rallies.

Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display. The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.
However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table?

Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
- Published
Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.
In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a child.
In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.
The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.
The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53. The ministry called the attack a "horrific massacre" by Israeli forces.
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.
Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.
Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.
People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroaches have shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.
This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.
The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.
So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.
The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.
The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.
Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.
One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.
Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Neha was released from detention the following morning, and Abhijeet could walk free on conditional bail.
For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.
The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.
For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.
On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.
Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.
Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.
- Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
- Published
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.
In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.
The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."
Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.
There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.
As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

‘Don’t travel by air': SC refuses urgent listing of plea alleging 700% hike in airfares
The Supreme Court refused the urgent listing of a plea alleging nearly 700 per cent increase in airfares.
Don't travel by air, the Supreme Court told a petitioner on Monday while refusing urgent listing of a plea alleging nearly 700 per cent increase in airfares. An advocate mentioned the matter for urgent listing before a bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh.
"The aviation fare has increased by 700 per cent," the advocate said. "Don't travel by air," the bench observed.
The advocate then said air travel is an essential service. “It's a violation of Article 14.” Article 14 of the Constitution deals with equality before law.
The apex court is already hearing a separate petition filed by social activist S Laxminarayanan, who has sought a robust and independent regulator that ensures transparency and passenger protection across the civil aviation sector and regulatory guidelines to control "unpredictable fluctuations" in airfare and ancillary charges imposed by private airlines in India.
During a hearing on that plea on October 16, the Centre informed the top court that administrative approval has been granted to rules under a 2024 legislation aimed at regulating India's aviation sector, and is likely to be published in two weeks.
The apex court had asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to place the published rules under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, 2024, before the court on the next date of hearing -- November 16.
On August 17, the Centre told the top court that it had fast-tracked the framing of rules under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, aimed at modernising India's aviation sector.
In November last year, the top court sought responses from the Centre and others on Laxminarayanan's plea.
While hearing the matter in January, the top court had said it would interfere with the "unpredictable fluctuations" in airfares and flagged the exorbitant rise during festivals.
It had termed the exorbitant hike of fares by airlines "exploitation" and asked the Centre and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation to file their replies on the plea.

The State government on Friday (October 30) told the Karnataka High Court that it would not insist, for now, on the implementation of the circular which mandates that all hospital pharmacies disclose the landing base/purchase price and maximum retail price (MRP) of medicines, medical devices and consumables on bills.
An undertaking in this regard was given to the court on behalf of the State’s Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) during the hearing of a petition filed by Private Hospitals and Nursing Homes Association, Bengaluru, and a private hospital. The petitioners have challenged the legality of the October 1 circular.
Justice C.M. Pooncha, before whom the petition came up for hearing, has adjourned further hearing on the petition till November 12 after recording the undertaking given by an Additional Advocate General on instruction from the officials of the FSDA.
Having a re-look
The government also informed the court that “the officials concerned are in the process of having a re-look at the circular dated October 1, 2026, and will not enforce the mandate of the circular till November 12, the next date of hearing on the petition”.
The undertaking was given while requesting the court not to stay the circular to allow the government to re-examine the issues raised by the petitioners.
It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the FSDAhad no statutory power to impose such conditions for disclosure of purchase price, which is a commercial agreement between the sellers and buyers that vary depending on suppliers, purchase quantity, discounts, credit arrangements and other factors.
Sans consultation
Mandating disclosure of purchase price would result in exposing confidential commercial arrangements between the suppliers and health establishments, it has been contented in the petition, while pointing out that the circular was issued sans adequate consultations with the stakeholders, even though the circular has direct implications on their finance.

Early in my career as a maternal fetal medicine specialist, I met two pregnant women who had ovarian cancer. One of them was expecting twins. They were introduced to be each other’s support network during and after the pregnancy, often meeting for coffee with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss from the chemotherapy they received.
The mother of twins is still alive today. The other didn’t survive beyond her child’s second birthday. When I spoke with the one who is still alive, she was distraught that her new friend died of her disease. “Why did she die and I am still alive?” she asked.
I didn’t know how to answer her out loud, but in my head, I thought: “Your doctor went to the library and researched managing ovarian cancer during pregnancy, and her doctor didn’t.”
The woman who lived was treated as if she were not pregnant. Without delay, she underwent a CT scan and workup of her ovarian cyst, and even received chemotherapy while pregnant. Her twins are now 28 years old, and all are thriving.
For the woman who died, treatment was electively delayed until her third trimester.
I do not know if removing her mass or giving chemotherapy earlier in pregnancy would have made a difference in her case, but I can’t help wondering.
Patients diagnosed with cancer are often advised to terminate their pregnancies without discussing the very real option of treating cancer during pregnancy. Other women diagnosed in their second or early third trimesters, after the fetal organs have developed, are advised to have an elective preterm birth.
But much of the time, chemotherapy can be safely administered during pregnancy and the infant delivered at term.
Compounding the problem, cancer is diagnosed significantly later in pregnant women. This is partly due to common symptoms between certain types of cancer and pregnancy, but also because physicians (and patients) are reluctant to perform imaging during pregnancy, which delays biopsies and management.
Why are doctors not offering cancer treatment to their pregnant patients? Is it fear of litigation, as obstetrics is one of the most litigated of all medical specialties? Lack of medical investigation? Or just paternalistic advice?
I recall a patient diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma in pregnancy. When I discussed starting chemotherapy in the second trimester, another physician told me: “She already had two kids. She should terminate.”
People often assume that ending a pregnancy, whether through termination or early delivery, improves the mother’s outcome. But that is not the case. When compared with non-pregnant women with the same cancer, pregnant women have similar survival rates. No study has shown an improvement in a woman’s survival if she terminates her pregnancy compared to if she continues.
When I observed during my fellowship that oncologists and obstetricians very infrequently faced a pregnant woman with cancer, I realized the medical community needed a way to pool all of the scattered cases into a central database to track these pregnancies and follow the outcomes for women and their babies. Six hundred and fifty cases later, I am still asking the same questions I asked when I encountered that very first pregnant cancer patient:
- How would the cancer be treated if the patient were not pregnant?
- How long can we safely delay this treatment without compromising her prognosis?
- Has this treatment been tried during other pregnancies? If so, what were the outcomes for mother and child?
Understandably, giving chemotherapy to a woman during pregnancy sounds dangerous, but the longitudinal research closely examining children exposed to chemotherapy backs up this approach. Children exposed to chemotherapy perform as well on standardized tests for development as unexposed children. This has been repeated at ages 18 months to 3 years, 6 years, 9 years, and 12-15 years of age. We did find that children exposed to chemotherapy are three times more likely to need eyeglasses.
And guess which children didn’t do as well? The ones electively delivered preterm to avoid maternal cancer treatment.
No options in such cases are without risk: an elective preterm birth to avoid cancer treatment, delaying cancer treatment until after delivery, or starting chemotherapy during pregnancy so the fetus can develop longer in utero and reach term. As any treatment in medicine, it is a balance between risks and benefits.
I understand many physicians are afraid to do something wrong when it comes to a pregnant woman. But denying cancer therapy by withholding or underdosing chemotherapy doesn’t serve her well, either. You can do everything to protect the fetus during the remainder of the pregnancy and forget that if their mother dies too young, due to delayed diagnosis or treatment, the child will still be affected. What is best for the mother/baby unit as a whole is a healthy mother.
I’ve worked with the Society of Maternal Fetal Medicine and the American Society of Clinical Oncology to publish guidelines to help other physicians handle this medical dilemma.
These guidelines address avoiding delays in pregnant women and discuss the safety to perform MRIs without contrast and CT scans with contrast. They also discuss performing necessary surgeries at any gestational age in pregnancy when this would be the clinical solution if the patient were not pregnant.
And they lay out how to give chemotherapy during the second and third trimesters and time treatment for safe delivery for mother and child.
I am honored to have participated in the development of these guidelines to increase the chances that when cancer and pregnancy collide, saving both lives will be considered.
Elyce Cardonick is a maternal fetal medicine physician and founder of the Cancer and Pregnancy Registry. She has spent nearly three decades caring for women diagnosed with cancer during pregnancy and advocating for mothers and their babies.

In 2011, Redditch Borough Council in England tried something that hardly anyone in the UK had heard of before. Staff announced they were going to warm the local swimming pool with heat from a nearby crematorium.
A public firestorm ensued. The plans were met with international headlines, and a labor union official branded them “sick and an insult to residents.” (A spokesman for the union, Unison, says this was not—and is not currently—the organization’s official position.)
“All you’re doing is basically heating a radiator and sending the heat down a tube,” says Guy Revans, of Redditch and Bromsgrove Councils, just south of Birmingham. “But death is always an emotive subject, isn’t it?”
Eventually, the relentless press coverage faded away. The project won a green award, and the crematorium has warmed Redditch’s swimming pool since 2013.
Although extremely rare in North America, European countries have been harvesting warmth from crematoria for years. The total volume of heat available from crematoria is modest, but as people search for ways of reducing the environmental impact of funeral rites, utilizing crematoria waste heat provides a way to lower their carbon intensity.
Roughly 1,200 cremations are carried out every year in Redditch. A heat exchanger captures heat from flue gases emitted by the facility’s two gas-fired ovens as part of a process to remove vaporized mercury from dental fillings, before venting the remaining gas into the atmosphere.
That’s a common process at many crematoria. In other words, excess heat is often captured by default, meaning the next question is, does it make sense to waste the heat—or use it? In Redditch, the heat exchanger connects to a water loop that travels 200 meters underground, eventually reaching another heat exchanger supplying the swimming pool.
Helpfully, such a sizable body of water “acts as a heat sink”, adds Revans. “You put heat into it during the day, it retains that heat for a considerable length of time.” The recreation center also has gas-fired boilers that can provide more heat when necessary. Overall, the system has saved the council tens of thousands of pounds per year in fuel costs.
Similar projects have emerged elsewhere recently. A school currently under construction in Aberdeen, Scotland, will receive excess heat from the city’s crematorium. The crematorium already relies on waste heat to warm its own premises.
“They were only utilizing a tiny amount of the heat available; the rest was going to the atmosphere,” says Ian Davidson, chief executive of Aberdeen Heat & Power, who says that the system now has full planning permission. The crematorium will provide just under 1 gigawatt-hour of heat annually, roughly half the school’s total requirement. A heat pump will cover the rest of the facility’s needs, and the entire system should be fully operational by February 2027.
Some crematoria are going even further in their pursuit of green credentials. The crematorium that will open in Kangasala, Finland, in 2028 will be connected to the town’s district heat network, a system of pipes that supplies more than 6,500 homes with hot water for heating. The crematorium will be fully electric, powered partly by solar panels on its roof.
“It’s a special thing,” says Timo Heikkilä, an energy and building systems consultant at Thenco Oy, who is working on the project. “I’m really glad I get to be a part of this.”
Winter temperatures in Kangasala can remain below 0 degrees Celsius for weeks on end. In Finland, there is a push to use less natural gas for heating, says Heikkilä. Although once cheaply available from neighbouring Russia, that country’s invasion of Ukraine and concerns over climate change have prompted Finland to seek alternatives. In some locations, this means utilizing waste heat from unusual sources, including crematoria.
“Finns,” says Heikkilä, “are quite practical.”
Ian Rudkin, who has managed multiple crematoria in the UK and is currently a board member of the Cremation Society of Great Britain, says many crematoria are becoming more eco-conscious. Today, software can schedule the firing of gas ovens to align with funeral services, ensuring they don’t waste energy and are only turned on when needed, for example. And some crematoria hold coffins for up to 72 hours, so that several may be cremated in a sequence, which is more efficient.
“When we first brought that in, [families] seemed a little bit shocked,” says Rudkin. Soon, however, people became more accepting. “They’d make comments like, ‘Dad always used to turn the light off at home to save energy.’”
But implementing heat recovery tech at crematoria in the US is more difficult, says Paul Seyler, director of strategy at Matthews Environmental Solutions. There, district heat networks are rare, and crematoria tend to be privately owned. That means the investment needed for heat exchangers and pipework necessary to link buildings together is higher.
“We’re studying this and watching it closely because, when the economics align, we’d like to be in a position to offer a solution,” says Seyler. Wasted heat is, after all, just a waste of resources, he adds. Besides a few small-scale experiments, Seyler says he isn’t aware of any fully operational systems in the US that utilize heat from crematoria.
The closest example is in Canada at a funeral complex in Sainte-Thérèse, Quebec. This 3,255-square-meter building houses family rooms, a large chapel, a crematorium, and a kitchen, among other facilities. Heat exchangers installed just over a decade ago soak up heat from cremation flue gases and distribute it around the complex, including the sidewalks to melt snow in the winter.
“The owner was not immediately on board as he thought it may have posed an ethical dilemma,” recall design engineers Martin Roy and Lianne Cockerton in an article about the project, published in the ASHRAE Journal.
Now, visitors pass an LED screen in the reception area that displays the energy performance of the building, based partly on the heat exchanger’s operation. While gas is still used for some of the building’s heating needs, as well as for cremations, the new system saves an estimated 29 metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually.
Recovering heat from cremations is one way of attempting to counter the “devastating impact” that humans have had on the environment, says Hannah Rumble, an associate at the University of Bath’s Centre for Death and Society. “I can see that would be a reason why people might choose to be cremated at a particular crematorium.”
Most crematoria contacted by WIRED say they do not emphasize the presence of heat recovery technology to families or mourners, though a spokeswoman for Aberdeen City Council adds that the council there will “undertake some public awareness-raising on the new system before it is operational to ensure transparency.”
Gaynor Doherty, an independent humanist funeral and wedding celebrant in the UK, says using waste heat from crematoria is “sensible,” though she suggests a natural burial, where bodies are simply shrouded or placed in biodegradable coffins and allowed to decompose in the environment, might be preferable to many eco-minded people. The carbon intensity of cremation varies from facility to facility, but could be around 250 kilograms of carbon per gas-fired cremation. Recovering heat from the process offsets some of those emissions (one company claims savings of 100 kilograms) but not all.
A study published in 2024 estimated that, if all crematoria in the UK were tapped for waste heat, they might only meet 1 percent of the county’s total heating needs. This sounds small, but decarbonizing heat is notoriously difficult, so any interventions to achieve that can be valuable. Plus, some people may feel that sharing the heat from their cremation could carry a lot of meaning.
In Finland, the all-electric crematorium in Kangasala will not produce as much heat as a gas-fired equivalent, though it will run 24/7 because it’s more efficient to operate by using electricity to gently top up heat retained in ceramic materials within the ovens. The connection to the district heat network means that, when mourners return home from funeral services at the new crematorium, it is conceivable that at least a small portion of that warmth they feel after stepping through their front doors will come from the cremation of the person they loved.
Heikkilä says working on the project has prompted some big questions for him. “I have thought about it, and once my time is up, I would like to be cremated, and I would like my waste heat to be recycled,” he says. “It’s the sensible thing. The last favor you can do for the world.”

A record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup, with more than two-thirds surveyed saying they have low or zero interest in the annual horse race.
Support for the Melbourne Cup has been sliding consistently for a number of years, but the Guardian Essential poll found just 9% of Australians said they had high interest in the race now – nearly half the proportion in 2025.
“The race that once stopped the nation is now just white noise for many,” Peter Lewis, chair of Essential Media, said.
The Guardian Essential poll of 1,003 Australians in late October highlights the latest erosion in popularity of the event amid growing ambivalence to the event.
Just 9% of people said they had high interest in the Cup, down 7 percentage points from 2025, with another 23% professing moderate interest, also down 3 points. About 29% of voters said they had low interest (up 5 points from last year), while another 39% said no interest at all (up 8 points).
The combined high and moderate interest came to only 32%, the lowest on record since Essential began asking this question in annual polling in November 2022. The combined low and no interest vote was 68%, jumping 12 points from last year to its highest on record.
In November 2022, the low and no interest vote came to a combined 52%; it was 62% in 2023, 52% in 2024, and 56% in 2025.
The “nup to the Cup” movement, backed by some high-profile politicians and celebrities, has contributed to declining support for the race.
But 62% of Australians nonetheless agreed the Melbourne Cup was a unique part of Australia’s national identity. That number remains a strong majority view, despite falling from 78% agreement when Essential asked this question in 2019.
Half of Australians (50%) believe the Cup promotes unhealthy gambling behaviour, up 3% since 2025, while 36% say they feel the Cup normalises animal cruelty, down 3 points from 2025.
Another 48% said they were less interested in the Cup than they used to be.
“The key driver appears to be a growing disdain for gambling, although concern for animal cruelty comes a close second,” Lewis said.
 
“More broadly this reflects the decline in unifying atonal moments in a world where more and more people have their experiences mediated by targeted advertising algorithms.”
Just 12% of voters in October’s poll said they regularly wagered on horse races and would bet on Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup, down 5 points from 2025. In contrast, 46% of people said they were not interested in the Cup and would not place a bet, up 6 points from last year.
Another 25% said they rarely bet on horses but would watch the race and place a bet, while 17% said they would watch but not bet.

Exit polls suggest Bulgarians elected first female president
Surveys by several polling organizations give Yotova about 52% of the vote.
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- Exit polls in Bulgaria suggest that incumbent President Iliana Yotova is the apparent winner in the country’s presidential runoff. Partial official results are expected later Sunday.
Surveys by several polling organizations give Yotova about 52% of the vote. If confirmed by official results, she would become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state.
Former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, backed by reformist pro-Western opposition parties, is said to be trailing with around 44%.
The vote was the first major test for Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party, which has endorsed Yotova. In April’s parliamentary vote, the party won 131 of the 240 seats in Parliament, securing an outright majority.
Observers say that a victory for Yotova will keep the presidency in the hands of the governing majority. Such a concentration of power could prevent the effective maintenance of checks and balances on policy decisions by institutions, they say.
Yotova, 62, took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and was seeking her own elected mandate. She's expected to continue Radev’s policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions.
After casting her vote on Sunday, Yotova said that she voted for a Bulgaria that makes its own decisions and maintains a strong voice on the international stage.
“I voted for national consensus through dialogue, for institutions that work for citizens, for a strong state with its own foreign policy in a strong Europe,” she told reporters.
The Balkan country joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country’s pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russia sentiments based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia have divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine but remain evasive about possible Russian involvement in drone attacks in the Black Sea region.
During a television debate between the two presidential contenders, Yotova advocated for a settlement involving both Ukraine and Russia, saying that “peace could come only through negotiations.” She also proposed a security meeting involving all six Black Sea countries to sign a moratorium on hostilities.
Bulgaria’s presidency is primarily ceremonial. Although the head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.
Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms.

The Best Star Wars Gifts
Featured in this article
I have received many, many Star Wars gifts over the years. I spent the first Christmas Day that I can remember flying Luke and his X-wing around the house. I met Darth Vader (David Prowse) when I was 6. I can still feel the shiver of fear as he strode through the double doors, reaching over the crowd to shake hands with me as my dad held me up. I never questioned why the Dark Lord of the Sith was in Woolworth’s.
When I became a dad, I had a fresh excuse to visit that galaxy far, far away and buy new toys. (I still regret selling my own in a garage sale to raise funds for our first home.) My wife and I love the original movies, and our kids prefer the prequel trilogy, but we all enjoyed watching the latest shows together. And because just about everyone knows I’m a fan, and I have received (and given) countless Star Wars gifts over the years. These are some of my favorites.
For more recommendations, check out my picks for The Best Gifts for Lego Fans, Best STEM Gifts for Kids, and Best Gifts Under $25.
Updated November 2026: I added a marble run, a jigsaw puzzle, and an advent calendar. I also updated prices throughout.
- A Helmet Hasbro Star Wars The Black Series Boba Fett Helmet Hasbro’s Black Series of Star Wars helmets strikes the right balance between quality and price. They look good enough to satisfy collectors but come cheaper than high-end movie replicas. My favorite is the sadly discontinued original battered Boba Fett helmet. You can still find it or the newer re-armored version if you're prepared to pay an inflated bounty. Many other Black Series helmets, including Vader and various Troopers, are also excellent and still available.
- A Lego Set Lego Star Wars Smart Play Throne Room Duel and A-Wing I have spent many hours building Star Wars Lego sets with my kids, and nothing compares to the Death Star (if you’re looking to push the boat out), but you may also want to check out one of the new Smart Brick sets. While it’s not perfect and lacks authentic Star Wars sound effects, I did have fun with the Star Wars Smart Play Throne Room Duel and A-Wing set. Recreating the iconic final light saber battle in Star Wars: Return of the Jedi, as Emperor Palpatine sits on his throne, watching Darth Vader and Luke Skywalker fight, with light saber swooshes as a synth version of “The Imperial March” plays, will put a smile on any fan’s face.
- Darth Darts Target Darts Darth Vader Darts Set If the Star Wars fan in your life also enjoys darts, you’ve just hit the mother lode. Target Darts has a Star Wars-themed line, and my top pick is this stylish set of Darth Vader darts. These tungsten steel-tipped beauties come in three weights with molded grippy barrels and black imperial flights. The zippy Darth case contains a spare set of red flights and tools. You can also get Darth Maul, Stormtrooper, and R2-D2-themed cases and flights, and Target Darts just released new themed sets of Mandalorian ($380) and AT-AT ($170) darts, and Grogu ($55) and Mandalorian ($55) cases. And don’t forget the Star Wars Millennium Falcon Surround and Dartboard ($200), which I tested with Target's Omni Auto Scoring System.
- A Metallic Print Displate Revenge Of The Sith 20th Anniversary If you’re unfamiliar, Displates are metallic artworks with a clever magnetic mount system that makes it quick and easy to switch your prints when you want a change. The artwork is layered and textured with gloss varnish on the details, and this one, released for the 20th anniversary of Revenge of the Sith, depicts Darth, flanked by Clone Troopers, with Anakin and Obi-Wan duelling on Mustafar in the foreground. If you don’t like this particular print, Displate has an enormous Star Wars section to browse.
- A Lightsaber Padawan Outpost Combat Saber Model Vader E6 Any aspiring Jedi or Sith needs a lightsaber. If you want a high-quality replica that’s right for you, be prepared to research. I tried a Combat Saber from Padawan Outpost, Model Vader E6 (Xenopixel), inspired by Darth’s lightsaber from Episode VI: Return of the Jedi. There is a learning curve, but this lightsaber really looks and feels the part. You can change the color, trigger countless sound effects, and even play music. There’s also an app, so you can connect to the saber from your phone and tweak the settings. No worries if you’re not a fan of Vader, because the Outpost offers a wide range of realistic lightsabers (check here if you’re in the UK) based on those wielded in the movies and shows by everyone from Obi-Wan to Count Dooku. WIRED readers can get a 5 percent discount with the code WIRED5.
- A Marble Run Ravensburger GraviTrax Star Wars Action-Set Death Star Marble runs are universally popular with kids (mine loved them when they were younger), and this Star Wars-themed one is part of the GraviTrax series. Kids can get creative when they construct it, building different types of runs with X-Wings, Tie Fighters, a Star Destroyer, and the Millennium Falcon—all on a Death Star board. They can also potentially connect it to other GraviTrax sets.
- An Arcade Machine Basic Fun Arcade Classics Atari Star Wars Ultra Series I spent an entire summer as a kid in an Atari Star Wars cockpit cabin at my local arcade, reliving the climax of the movie in wire-frame form as I blasted TIE Fighters, sped through the Death Star trench, and timed proton torpedoes to blow it up. That 1983 release is bundled with The Empire Strikes Back (1985) and Return of the Jedi (1984) games in this ROTJ-styled arcade cabinet. It takes some building and feels a little cheap, but it does include the original yoke flight controls, and it’s still very fun to play. Just make sure your giftee has room for it, as it’s 61.5 inches tall, 19 inches wide, and 24 inches deep.
- A Phone Case Casetify Star Wars Phone Cases A Darth Vader phone case will go down well with most Star Wars-loving dads, and this range from Casetify features some excellent Galactic Empire designs. My wife and kids have been using Casetify cases with a mix of iPhones and Pixels for over a year, and we find them durable and protective, if a little chunky. Unfortunately, it’s not just the Star Wars designs that are on the dark side; these cases are also pricey.
- A Book Basic Books How Star Wars Conquered the Universe Of the many excellent books about Star Wars, this might be my favorite. It charts the rise of the franchise, offers countless nuggets of trivia, and acknowledges the role fans have played in making Star Wars so special. It's an entertaining peek behind the scenes that is affectionate but also dares to be critical. Perhaps mercifully, it ends with the new trilogy still on the horizon.
- An Apron Hedley & Bennett Star Wars Aprons It’s way too easy to get messy when cooking, which is why aprons exist. Respected apron purveyor Hedley & Bennett makes some top-quality aprons, and it has a Star Wars line. I tried the Darth Vader Essential Apron (a great gift for dads), and my wife tried the Ahsoka Tano Crossback Apron. We love them. The thoughtful designs include lots of wee Star Wars character references (there are eight options). Mine has an adjustable neck strap, while the Crossback goes over your shoulders. Both are comfy, with lengthy straps to tie and three pockets. Made from protective cotton canvas, these aprons can be machine-washed cold.
- A Board Game Ravensburger Star Wars Villainous This beautifully themed spin-off of the Villainous series challenges players to take on the role of a Star Wars baddie. You can play as Darth Vader, Kylo Ren, General Grievous, Asajj Ventress, or Moff Gideon. Each has unique abilities and a specific set of victory conditions, and there are chances to meddle with your foes as the game unfolds. One of the best family board games, it works best with four players aged 10 years and up.
- Action Figures Hasbro Star Wars Action Figures Kenner sold over 300 million Star Wars action figures in the late ’70s and early ’80s. I spent every penny of my pocket money on them for years, and there’s a roaring trade in secondhand figures. When Hasbro realized its potential, it started making new figures under the Kenner brand, and there are three main lines today. The Retro Collection is all 3.75-inch figures like the originals Kenner sold, with a peg hole in the bottom of their feet and legs that don’t bend. The Vintage Collection figures are the same size but with more detail and bendable limbs. The Black Series figures are larger, at around 6 inches tall, and tend to be much more detailed.
- An Ornament Nemesis Now Three Wise Stormtroopers Based on the three wise monkeys and the Confucian maxim “See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil,” this trio of ornamental stormtroopers is a great gift for Star Wars fans. One of mine took a tumble and broke both his legs, but after a quick superglue treatment, he made a full recovery. I advise putting them out of reach of young kids and cats.
- A Jigsaw Puzzle Ravensburger Star Wars Universe 2000 Piece Jigsaw Puzzle This challenging 2,000-piece puzzle packs in more than 60 characters from the Star Wars universe (some appear twice), with a starship-filled space battle backdrop. It’s a fun activity for fans of any age, but expect to take a few days assembling it. The finished jigsaw is huge, measuring 39 x 30 inches, so make sure you've got a proper table for the job.

The National Disaster Management Agency should play a key role in building institutional expertise and developing specialized personnel for disaster preparedness and responses, former Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba has said.
The country needs to make the agency “capable of accumulating and passing on knowledge and experience” of disaster management, Ishiba, who advocated its creation, said in a recent interview with Jiji Press.
The Cabinet Office’s disaster management section, the predecessor of the new agency, was staffed by officials seconded from multiple agencies who typically rotate every two years. This system did not allow officials to accumulate or pass on knowledge or experience, Ishiba said.
He called for enhanced training for local government leaders and officials to strengthen disaster preparedness and emergency response efforts at a planned disaster management academy.
“Local leaders with knowledge can issue appropriate instructions and provide accurate information even when false information spreads on social media,” he said.
Ishiba criticized Japan’s disaster response system. “It has changed little since the Great Kanto Earthquake,” he said, referring to the 7.9-magnitude temblor that left about 105,000 people dead or missing in Tokyo and nearby areas in 1923.
“I’ve never seen evacuees sleeping side by side on gymnasium floors in a decent country,” he said.
To improve conditions at evacuation centers, Ishiba called for systematic stockpiling of emergency toilets, cooking facilities and beds as well as better organization of volunteer activities.

A major fire broke out at the Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) Visakh Refinery late on Monday evening. The fire reportedly originated in the Pitch Tower of the newly integrated Residue Upgradation Facility (RUF). The sudden explosion and intense flames caused brief panic among residents in neighbouring localities, according to the officials.
Reassuring the public, Malkapuram Inspector of Police E. Narasimha Rao issued a voice message that the situation was under control. He said that HPCL’s internal Fire and Safety Department responded immediately with their own fire tenders to suppress the blaze, eliminating the need for external fire engines. He confirmed that there were no fatalities or injuries reported.
The RUF unit processes heavy vacuum residue oil into high-value clean fuels like diesel and petrol. High operating temperatures and dense petroleum pitch generated thick black smoke during the fire outbreak. Automated safety protocols allowed on-duty personnel to be evacuated safely while firefighting teams isolated the unit, preventing the flames from spreading to the adjacent facilities. Although no casualties were reported, structural damage within the pitch unit is expected to be significant.
When contacted, HPCL officials confirmed the incident, and said that a technical committee would investigate the exact cause of the fire. They added that the primary processing units remain operational and fuel supply chains will not be affected.

Dia Mirza has responded after the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring her from its pollution-awareness campaign ahead of Diwali. The video was taken down after Mumbai BJP chief Ameet Satam objected to her participation in the campaign. The development has since triggered a political controversy, with Dia maintaining that her message was recorded at the civic body's request and was aimed at raising awareness about air pollution.
BMC removes Dia Mirza’s anti-cracker Diwali video after BJP’s objection
The BMC had launched a campaign encouraging Mumbaikars to celebrate an environment-friendly Diwali and avoid activities that contribute to air and noise pollution. The campaign featured several public figures, including Dia Mirza, Madhuri Dixit, Nishigandha Wad and cricketer Ajinkya Rahane.
Why was Dia Mirza’s BMC video removed?
Dia's video urged citizens to avoid bursting firecrackers and highlighted restrictions on bursting crackers on public roads, lanes and footpaths in accordance with Bombay High Court directions. While the videos featuring other celebrities continued to remain available on BMC's social media accounts, Dia's clip was removed.
The development came after Ameet Satam objected to Dia's inclusion in the campaign in a post on X. He wrote, “We don’t need lessons on how to celebrate #Diwali from @deespeak. Our traditions are deeply rooted in our culture.”
The BMC removed Dia's video within hours of Satam's post. The civic body did not initially provide an official explanation for why her video alone was taken down.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump brushed aside the high price of gasoline during a speech, instead boasting about how much money the country is making from oil, circulated in October.
People on social media, including someone who shared video clips, claimed Trump said, "We're making money like we've never made before," and "I don't give a damn, I'm going to say it. We're making a freaking fortune."
The rumor spread as the midterm elections approached in the United States. Some readers also reached out to Snopes to verify the quote's authenticity.
The quote was correctly attributed to Trump.
Trump made the statement during a speech on Oct. 24 in Perry, Georgia, where he appeared at a rally in support of Georgia Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. Georgia Public Broadcasting reported from the rally that "Trump announced that German automaker Audi will invest $4 billion in a new plant in Peach County," of which Perry is a part.
Trump's full speech can be viewed on Fox 5 New York's YouTube, where the statement in question begins around the 1:30:45 mark.
Trump appeared to be making an overall point that the U.S. economy is growing — with the Audi deal as one example — despite the current high price of gasoline, which he claimed would eventually "come down."
The president said (emphasis ours):
Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happening in the Middle East. They're coming to Texas, they're coming to Oklahoma, and they're coming to Louisiana, and they're taking that oil. They're making hundreds of billions, our country is, on oil. And then on top of it we have Venezuela, and we have Greenland. 'Cause Greenland has a lot of oil. So, we're making hundreds and hundreds of billions — trillions — of dollars. My people said, "Please don't mention that, sir. Because people are paying a little higher."
That number's going to come way down, but what we've done for this country, we're making money like this country has never made before. So I said, "Let me say it very gingerly, very softly..."
Because somebody will say, the fake news, "He's bragging about making money while people are suffering!" You know, you're still paying lower than Biden and Obama, and they [referring to Iran] don't have nuclear weapons. But they're going to be coming. I can just see the fake headlines.
"President Trump is talking about all the money they're making while people are suffering at the pump." That'll be the headline. But I said, "I don't give a damn, I'm going to say it." We're making a freaking fortune. Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time. And those pump prices are going to come down.
Some media outlets delivered on Trump's predicted mainstream headlines, with Newsweek running a piece titled "Trump Says He Doesn't 'Give A Damn' About Gas Prices As US Making 'Fortune'."
According to AAA's gas prices tracker, the average cost of regular unleaded gasoline across the U.S. was approximately $4.23 per gallon as of this writing.
AAA reported the highest national average for regular unleaded gasoline as $5.02 on June 22, 2022, during Joe Biden's presidency. The highest national average for diesel was $6.53 on Sept. 22, under the current Trump administration.
