At first glance, the Department of Education’s October 27 X post seems like generic Harry Potter-esque slop.
It shows a trio of students walking toward a sprawling Hogwarts-like castle while a young girl with long, flowing white-blonde hair watches them from the foreground, accompanied with the text “There’s Magic in Learning!” and “Make Education Great Again.”
But for a hyper-online, highly radicalized subset of the internet, the state was not just communicating a vague policy stance—it appeared to be adopting the deeply-coded visual language of the “Malfoid.”
The reaction online was immediate. On X, Bulwark reporter Will Sommer quickly diagnosed the situation, posting that the Department of Education was “embracing the ‘malfoid’ meme, a right-wing fan fiction idea about a female Draco Malfoy who Harry Potter could fall in love with.” Others responded with Malfoid art and AI-generated clips, including some featuring President Donald Trump.
The Malfoid concept did not come from conservative think tanks but began in creatively chaotic fan fiction websites like Archive of Our Own (AO3). Gender-bending characters—taking a canonically male character and rewriting them as female or vice versa—is a time-honored tradition in fandoms. However, in these specific stories, the gender-flipped female Malfoy character is not just a narrative experiment for someone’s crackship. She is a potent avatar for toxic elitism, with a ruthless obsession with “blood purity.”
The term Malfoid is a portmanteau combining “Malfoy”—the last name of Harry Potter’s school nemesis Draco—with “foid,” which is short for “femoid” or “female humanoid”—a highly offensive incel term used to describe women.
In the original books, Malfoy is prejudiced against wizards whose heritage is mixed with muggles (non-wizards), but it’s framed as a moral failing to be overcome or punished. In Malfoid fan fiction, however, the character's bigotry is romanticized, transforming her into a right-wing aesthetic vehicle actively propagated by far-right meme channels and Telegram groups. Potter is no longer a traditional hero, but a stand-in for disaffected young men who fantasize about a relationship with a beautiful, cruel silvery-blonde girl.
A quick search of platforms like Reddit and Tumblr for the term brings up a wide range of art, AI-generated and drawn in heavily stylized anime aesthetics, featuring a busty wide-eyed blonde demeaning a blushing and devoted Potter.
The character is also depicted as explicitly anti-queer and anti-trans, as the word “foid” becomes a way for the far right to claim that this gender swapping is correcting an error.
For young, radicalized internet users, the Malfoid provides a ready-made, pop-culture-literate mascot for ethno-nationalism. She is the ultimate “guy’s girl” updated for the digital age, injected with a dark, pop culture edge that makes her more appealing to a terminally online demographic than traditional political propaganda. It’s an effective way to package white supremacy and conservative purity ideals into a highly shareable, visually appealing internet aesthetic.
Prominent right-wingers using fantasy and fiction to promote their ideals is not a new phenomenon. For years, J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings has been relentlessly co-opted by several prominent figures on the political right, including Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Similarly, the Trump administration has normalized communicating to the public via memes. Trump’s own feed on Truth Social is a constant stream of AI-generated meme imagery, and various government departments, such as DHS, have previously utilized memes and Tolkien's work to make light of deeply serious issues like ICE raids. Since dropping the Malfoid meme, the Department of Education has continued its “There is Magic in Learning” X posts with images referencing The Lord of the Rings and Avatar: The Last Airbender.
Leslie Hahner, a communications professor at Baylor University, says the “collapse of boundaries between internet subcultures and mainstream institutions” is a defining feature of modern politics. “Symbols that once circulated in niche online communities now regularly appear in political campaigns, government communications, and major media coverage,” she says, noting that while memes might have a bigger reach, this strategy becomes dangerous when adopting toxic internet culture.
She says the use of “incel imagery” raises uncomfortable questions. “Is the agency unaware of the symbol’s cultural baggage, or does it believe these associations are useful for attracting engagement from relevant audiences? Either possibility is significant,” Hahner tells WIRED. “If officials are unaware of the connotation, it suggests a lack of cultural literacy or an inability to safeguard learners from toxic symbols. If they are aware, it raises questions about why a federal institution would choose to amplify imagery tied to dehumanizing online discourse.”
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, the Department of Education quoted Albus Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: “Of course it’s happening inside your head, Harry. Why should that mean it’s not real?”
By utilizing the visual markers of the Malfoid, the institution signals continuing cultural alignment to a radicalized, terminally online base without ever triggering the alarm bells of traditional media oversight. It is an algorithmic wink, assuring the most extreme corners of their constituency that the institution shares their foundational worldview.
We are witnessing the end of traditional political persuasion. Policy papers, detailed legislative agendas, and traditional campaign speeches simply do not enthuse the youth anymore; aesthetic identity does. Modern political operatives understand that young voters have been trained on platforms like TikTok and Wattpad to consume information through hyper-specific tropes rather than cohesive, logical ideologies.
The internet is no longer a reflection of our political reality. Our political reality is simply executing the tropes of the internet, and the state is perfectly happy to play along.

Hard to believe, but smart bird feeders have been around for six years.
The idea started with Birdbuddy (then styled Bird Buddy), which launched a Kickstarter campaign in November 2020 for the world’s first app-connected, AI-powered smart bird feeder. Birdfy followed in 2021 with its first camera-equipped feeder, and today the two companies remain the most popular brands in the smart bird-feeder space, with a sizable catalog of offerings, including smart bird baths and smart nesting boxes.
Thanks to two new releases from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, you can now get a premium smart bird feeder experience for under $100—something that just a year or two ago would have cost $200 or more.
I tested both Birdfy’s Rookie and Birdbuddy’s Nook in my backyard for four weeks each, noting annoyances, especially helpful features, and which features were available without a subscription.
While both have a significant number of pluses and minuses, Birdbuddy’s Nook, despite costing $20 more and failing to capture every visit, came out just slightly ahead due to its more premium hardware experience.
Birdfy Rookie
Released in October of last year, Birdfy’s Rookie was positioned as a smart feeder for beginners, with USB-C charging only, no solar (though you can buy a more expensive model that has it), and no complicated assembly process. It functions basically as a lightweight gravity pet feeder with a 1.3-liter seed capacity and a camera on the side—just snap the three main pieces together, charge the camera, and you’re good to go. It can only be pole- or wall-mounted, not hung.
While I loved the simplicity of the Rookie and appreciated that it uses the same excellent app as the pricier Birdfy feeders, the 1080p camera’s picture quality was noticeably lower than the Nook’s, and while it did capture every bird that visited, there were also plenty of false-alarm motion detections.
I also found some significant drawbacks to the design over my four-week test. First, though the feeder itself is IP66 rated for water resistance, there’s no overhang on the roof, which means water is going to get into the seed if it rains (as it did off and on throughout my testing period).
Second, the lid just sits loosely on the top, so it kept blowing off whenever there was a big gust of wind. And third, perhaps most frustratingly, because the camera is on the side, it didn’t do the greatest job capturing larger birds, though the camera lens stayed relatively clean, being farther away from the action, and small-bird shots were well framed. Birdfy advertises the battery charge as lasting seven weeks, but my test unit lasted less than two.
One big advantage the Rookie has, however, is its seed capacity. At 1.3 liters, it’s only slightly less voluminous than Birdfy’s popular original feeder, which packs 1.5 liters. (Though note that this still pales in comparison to Birdfy’s Bamboo feeder, a top pick in our guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, which holds 3.5 liters.)
Feeder capacity aside, Birdfy’s app is well designed and simple, and it makes it easy to see which birds visited that day. You can even watch your feeder on TV if you have Roku—the Birdfy app is available on devices running Roku OS 15.1 or higher. Best of all, as of November 1, Birdfy offers unlimited automatic AI-based identification without a subscription, which is a rarity among smart bird feeders. Birdfy’s ID is pretty decent, with nearly no mistakes during my test.
If you want to spring for more storage or longer video recording (free tier is limited to 5 GB and 20 seconds), you can opt for Birdfy Plus for $80/year or Birdfy Pro for $150/year.
Birdbuddy Nook
Birdbuddy’s Nook launched in late October this year and is also aimed at beginners and budget-conscious shoppers. It looks a lot like Birdbuddy’s flagship Home (previously the 2 Pro), just smaller and squatter. It has the same thick plastic construction with a roof to keep out rain, but the Nook’s hinged lid makes filling a breeze. (Note that the $99 version does not come with the extended perch or solar roof, as pictured.)
Like the Home, the camera is a half-sphere about the size of a ping-pong ball that pops in and out with a magnet; you can position it vertically or horizontally depending on which style of photos you prefer. My test unit came with the solar panel, so I was not able to test the battery life of the camera, but know that the Nook’s battery only delivers 3,900 mAh compared to the Rookie’s 5,200 mAh.
The Nook shoots in 2K HDR, resulting in noticeably crisper imagery and sound. Unlike the Rookie’s side camera, the Nook’s is centered on the feeder—which makes for better full-bird shots, but its close proximity means it tends to get dirtier and smudged more easily than the Rookie’s side camera. I was also surprised by how fast the seed disappeared—within a day in some cases. Birdbuddy states that its seed hopper holds 0.9 liters, or 3.8 cups, which is only slightly less than the Rookie, but the difference in empty rates was noticeable.
My test unit also came with the optional Extended Perch for bigger birds like Steller’s jays and crows, though the big birds in my yard have always managed to find a way to visit the Birdbuddy Home, which has Birdbuddy’s usual tiny perch, so I’m not entirely convinced this is worth the extra $40. However, I do like that I can hang the IP67-rated Nook, especially since its pole-mount option doesn’t have a fastener. This means it tends to swing around when it’s mounted on a 1-inch-diameter pole, especially when larger birds land and take off.
Birdbuddy’s strength has always been its app, which remains easy to use and presents a library of shareable photos from each bird visit, though its interface is quickly being bested by newer brands like Kiwibit and even Birdfy, which just began offering AI ID for free with all its feeders. (Birdbuddy’s app also offers free AI ID, which is excellent, but you have to manually engage it for each photo, making it harder to see at a glance which species visited that day.)
Birdbuddy cameras have also historically struggled to capture all bird visits, and while the Nook was advertised to have a faster wake time, it still missed many bird visits I saw, though I did notice more captures than previous models, with no false alarms.
One new feature of the Birdbuddy app—and one I have not seen before—is the ability to ID other birds from sounds in the background, à la Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s Merlin ID app. It currently states it’s a “free preview,” though, so I suspect it will ultimately be locked behind a subscription tier. Still, I found it to be a neat complement to the Nook’s superior onboard microphone. Other features requiring a subscription (Birdbuddy Premium for $70/year or Birdbuddy Family for $99/year) include Ultra resolution, guest access to the livestream, and the ability to name individual birds.
Rookie vs. Nook
| Specs | Birdbuddy Nook | Birdfy Rookie | 
|---|---|---|
| Base-model price | $99 | $80 | 
| Camera | 2K HDR | 1080p | 
| Orientation | Horizontal or vertical | Vertical | 
| Battery | 3,900 mAh rechargeable | 5,200 mAh rechargeable | 
| Camera location | Front | Side | 
| Standard solar charging? | No (available for extra) | No (available for extra) | 
| Seed capacity | 0.9 liters | 1.3 liters | 
| Subscription cost | $70–$99/year | $80–$150/year | 
| AI ID without subscription? | Yes, manual | Yes | 
| Mounting options | Hang, wall, pole | Wall, pole | 
| Supported Wi-Fi networks | 2.4 GHz | 2.4 GHz | 
| Color options | Blue | Tan, blue | 
The Winner: Birdbuddy Nook
If you’re looking to spend under $100, the Rookie is a perfectly respectable smart bird feeder, with excellent free AI ID. However, if you want the whole package, I have to give the edge to the Nook. It won’t show you every bird that visits, which is disappointing, but you’ll get great shots of the ones that do, and its sturdy housing and versatile camera make it a great value that will hold up well in inclement weather.

TD tried to make grieving mom pay $38K in student debt after daughter died of cancer
After Go Public investigated, TD backed down in case of Quebec mother
Joyel Singfield struggles to hold back tears as she recounts losing her 30-year-old daughter Maari to breast cancer last year— and the bitter dispute with TD Bank that followed.
In 2020, Singfield co-signed a $40,000 TD student loan for Maari which included life insurance. She only learned after Maari's death that the insurance had expired, making her responsible for the $37,806 outstanding debt.
"It was honestly shocking," said Singfield, who lives in Gatineau, Que. "We committed to that loan in 2020 with insurance."
An internal TD investigation determined Singfield was on the hook for the full amount, plus growing interest. She fought back, battling the bank for more than a year-and-a-half. Following a Go Public investigation, TD backed down and wiped out the entire debt.
"I'm very relieved. I'm very grateful. I'm also a little bit disheartened at how this had to get to this point," Singfield said.
"Nothing can prepare you for the loss of a child. … That's what our family should have been focusing on."
Account handled properly, TD says
Singfield is one of tens of thousands of Canadians who launch complaints against their banks every year, often with large amounts of money at stake.
According to the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada, financial institutions reported handling 236,324 customer complaints in the 2025–2026 fiscal year, with about 31 per cent not resolved to the consumer's satisfaction.
Unhappy customers can escalate complaints to the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI), an independent resolution service funded by financial institutions. But a 2025 internal feedback survey of 1,598 Canadians who used OBSI found that only 20 per cent were satisfied with the outcome.
Maari Singfield passed away from cancer in January 2025 at the age of 30. (Submitted by Joyel Singfield)
Following TD's investigation, Singfield appealed to OBSI, which sided with the bank that she was liable for the debt. However, both agreed that TD should cover Singfield's $1,577 in unpaid interest and pay her $500 for distress.
"It's an insult," said Singfield, who rejected the offer. "Two thousand dollars doesn't even cover any of the pain and suffering that this has caused."
After Go Public got involved, TD cleared Singfield of all liability. Spokesperson Ashleigh Murphy said in an email that the bank handled the account appropriately, but decided to help Singfield due to her "difficult circumstances."
- Got a story you want investigated? Contact Sophia and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca
OBSI spokesperson John Bowes declined to comment citing "confidentiality obligations."
Go Public investigates
In 2020, Maari got a student line of credit to pursue a graduate degree in counselling psychology. In remission from breast cancer at the time, she secured life insurance as added protection for her mother as co-signer.
Maari graduated in 2023, and she died in 2025, at which point the bank went after Singfield for loan payments. She pushed back, convinced the loan was insured.
It took the bank seven months to officially clarify that the original insurance policy was automatically cancelled when Maari's student line of credit converted to a personal loan upon graduation.
Singfield insists the bank failed to notify her or Maari about the expired insurance, depriving them of the chance to renew the policy.
"We would have taken action for sure," she said.
TD shared with Joyel Singfield this letter it says it sent her daughter in 2023, which included details about the need to renew her life insurance. Go Public discovered the letter is undated, and TD could only provide an estimated mailing date of 'November 2023.' (TD Bank)
TD shared with Singfield a letter it claimed to have sent Maari in 2023 outlining the loan changes and insurance renewal requirement. But Go Public discovered the letter is undated, and TD could only provide an estimated mailing date of "November 2023."
"Undated letters are always viewed with suspicion by the courts," said Duff Conacher, co-founder of the citizen advocacy group Democracy Watch.
"You have to actually prove things, not just claim you did something."
Meanwhile, Go Public confirmed TD never sent the letter to Singfield — even though Canada's Bank Act requires banks to send co-signers separate loan notifications.
The bank said this is because Singfield opted out of receiving notifications. But Go Public challenged this after discovering the bank had sent her several notices regarding Maari's personal loan — just not the critical one with details about the need to renew the insurance.
"That's pretty damning," said Erik Knutsen, a law professor at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont. "I think as a bank, you cannot dig your way out of that one."
Shortly after Go Public presented its findings, TD cleared the entire debt — which had grown to $41,188.
Knutsen says it's disheartening that her dispute required media intervention, "which is essentially relying on public shame."
Do customers need help to pursue complaints?
Conacher says Singfield's case highlights the power imbalance when average customers battle big banks.
"You're up against the bank with a team of lawyers and unlimited resources to drag it out and argue their case," he said. "On the other side is the lowly consumer on their own."
OBSI spokesperson Bowes said that people who turn to OBSI don't require legal representation or specialized knowledge "to be assured of a fair outcome."
Conacher disagrees and offers as a solution Democracy Watch's long-standing proposal for Canada to establish a Financial Consumer Organization. It would advocate on behalf of customers involved in banking disputes, giving them "lawyer help, expert help," he said.
Help earlier would have been good, Singfield says.
"Too many people don't have the energy to fight something like this," she said. "I think that's really unfair."

A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don’t need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time.
In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both.
But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn’t be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That’s despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat.
Further, while the data suggests many patients were being dishonest, clinicians responded with what could be considered their own form of dishonesty; in most cases, the dubious fibs led to antibiotic prescriptions. Specifically, 77 percent of adult patients and 87 percent of caregivers said their lies worked, leading them to get the antibiotic prescriptions they wanted.
“These findings signal a significant issue for health professionals making antibiotic prescribing decisions and for the fields of antimicrobial stewardship and public health,” Thorpe and colleagues concluded.
Detailed deception
For the study, the researchers reviewed survey responses from 1,371 online respondents and found 959 responses that were valid and complete. Of those, 268 (28 percent) respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms to get antibiotics. Of those, 108 reported exaggerating symptoms, 19 reported fabricating symptoms, and 141 reported doing both. In a separate analysis of 263 respondents who identified as caregivers, 63 (27 percent) reported misrepresenting symptoms of a child to get antibiotics.

For the first time in a dozen years, a leading OB-GYN group has updated its guidance on managing hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and other disruptive symptoms that often come with menopause.
Doctors stressed the importance of hormone therapies, which many women are considering again after the removal of federal safety warnings. On Friday, federal officials said the Food and Drug Administration has been taking steps to ensure there's an adequate supply.
Doctors also described various nonhormonal options in the new advice released this month by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, or ACOG.
“We would love our patients to go to their OB-GYNs regarding questions about menopause and really advocate for getting the treatment that they need,” said Camille Clare, the group’s president.
Menopause occurs when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. In the U.S., it usually happens around age 50. The time leading up to it is called perimenopause, during which the body’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone declines sharply.
Problems commonly arise. More than half of women in menopause report having “vasomotor” issues such as hot flashes and night sweats, said ACOG. As many as two-thirds report menopause-related sleep disruption. And more than a third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women worldwide report depressive symptoms.
In the past, doctors said, many women quietly suffered.
There's growing consensus that "these symptoms should be treated,” said JoAnn Manson, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. “This should help to empower women to discuss their symptoms with their healthcare provider.”
Manson said ACOG’s new guidelines are similar to those put out by other medical organizations.
"Moderate to severe or bothersome menopausal symptoms should be treated with hormone therapy as the first line of treatment,” she said. While it's not appropriate for all women, she added, it’s a good option for many.
But some have been wary.
In 2002, a landmark study in women taking a pill-based combination of estrogen and progestin was stopped early because of links to breast cancer, blood clots and other serious issues. Concerns lingered even though later studies showed the benefits of today’s hormone therapies outweigh the risks for many women. For more than 22 years, all hormone-based menopause treatments carried a government warning, which Manson said discouraged patients and doctors from using them.
But last year, the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warning from more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing the hormones estrogen and progestin. On Friday, the FDA approved updated labeling for three additional estrogen-based patches.
Removing the boxed warning has helped revive interest in and demand for the treatments.
Since the FDA labeling change, some women have reported difficulty obtaining estrogen patches in certain doses and formulations.
FDA officials said Friday that despite such reports, they are unaware of “an imminent risk of a nationwide shortage.” Officials also noted that drug manufacturers have doubled their output of the products over the last year by adding extra manufacturing shifts and production capacity.
Stephanie Faubion, medical director at The Menopause Society, said she’s glad to see ACOG’s guidelines stress the importance of these treatments. “It’s undisputed that hormone therapy is the first line and most effective therapy for hot flashes,” she said.
ACOG reviews the latest evidence on hormone therapy and includes detailed information about the various types. Whole-body therapies, which come in pills, patches, sprays, gels and a vaginal ring, deliver doses of hormones into the bloodstream at levels high enough to have significant effects on symptoms like hot flashes. Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is applied directly with very little circulating in the blood. It’s often prescribed to women whose biggest complaint is vaginal dryness.
ACOG recommends that decisions about hormone therapy should be made jointly by doctors and patients, and take into account the benefits and risks given a patient's age and medical history. If it’s appropriate, the group advises starting it before age 60, or within 10 years of menopause.
Some patients choose not to take full-body hormonal medications or are advised by their doctors to avoid them because of their medical histories or conditions.
For them, doctors pointed to different medicines. One is fezolinetant, which works in the area of the brain that controls body temperature and blocks a source of hot flashes and night sweats. Another is elinzanetant, which works similarly.
Doctors also said certain antidepressants can help manage symptoms like hot flashes and depression in patients with either or both of these problems.
There’s also evidence supporting some non-drug treatments for hot flashes, night sweats and sleep or mood problems, ACOG said. These include cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, exercise, clinical hypnosis and acupuncture. Such approaches can be used alone or alongside medications.
Clare said women may see misinformation and disinformation about menopause treatments online, and urged patients to come to their doctors with any questions. ACOG offers advice on sorting out truth from false claims as well as overall information on menopause.
“Women have options. They have lots of options, hormonal and nonhormonal,” Faubion said. “They shouldn’t be told that nothing can be done about their symptoms. Because again, we have evidence for many different things that can help.”

A brief ceasefire opens a perilous escape window from Kherson’s riverside kill zone
Nataliia Diadiuk uses a white towel to signal Russian drones that she is a civilian in Ukraine’s Kherson region
KOZATSKE, Ukraine -- A white towel on her gate and a white rag in her hand were Ukrainian Nataliia Diadiuk’s only ways to tell Russian drone operators she is a civilian. When a brief ceasefire kicked in on Oct. 27, she had a moment of respite.
The 53-year-old is one of a handful of residents left in Kozatske, a riverside village located in the kill zone of Ukraine’s Kherson region less than 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from a Russian-controlled area.
“I really want silence,” Diadiuk said, fighting back tears as she stood on an empty street lined with abandoned houses. “And I want to see the people who left, all of them. People left for both sides."
Diadiuk’s life has been reduced to basic survival: rainwater to drink, firewood gathered around town for heat, a radio she tries to tune in to for news, and the remnants of humanitarian aid that had not reached her in two years until the brief ceasefire that ended Sunday night just days after it began. Going out means dodging every kind of weapon, including mines scattered everywhere. The neighbors she mentions are more often the dead than the few still living nearby.
A team from The Associated Press gained rare access to a so-called red zone to see firsthand what life in the kill zone looks like, a visit made possible only because of a brief, localized ceasefire tied to the humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Oleshky has drawn the world’s attention, but civilians are trapped in many more places on both sides of the front line. During the mission, Ukrainian regional officials, police, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and volunteers, with the facilitation of civil-military cooperation specialists, used the rare window of time to reach people on their side of the river, some of them cut off for nearly two years.
In all, 180 people were evacuated from riverside communities and the city of Kherson, including 23 children, the regional administration said. About 140,000 people remain in the Ukrainian-held part of the Kherson region.
Before the war, the whole region, now nearly 70% under Russian control, had about 1 million residents. The riverside is designated a red zone, the highest level of military danger. With the ceasefire over, residents will again face drones, artillery, glide bombs and airdropped mines. Still, many refuse to leave. Some cannot afford to start over, and others will not abandon the places where they grew up.
On the road to Diadiuk’s village, burned-out cars sit abandoned where they were hit, alongside wrecked ground robots that Ukrainians try sending down roads too dangerous for people. A relic of peacetime still stands on that road: “Thank you for keeping the roadside clean.”
In the village, many houses are reduced to burned walls. Glide bombs have left craters, and the tail fins of shells stick out of the asphalt like flowers. Mines dropped from drones lie everywhere, some petal-shaped, others improvised and wrapped in foil or plastic, so every step must be taken with care. Thick vegetation swallows the ruins of empty houses.
What Diadiuk finds hardest to bear is the howling of the dogs left behind in the houses, surviving much as she is. “Even for the sake of these, I can’t leave them,” she says, pointing to two thin dogs that never stray far from her. But she shares what little food she has with other dogs as well.
Isolated and forced to fight for survival every day, she has lost track of time. “I turn on my phone only to see what day it is,” she says. She charges it with solar panels.
Diadiuk collects rainwater, strains it through gauze, treats it with chlorine and boils it. “The water here is more or less all right,” she says. “There are a lot of dead lying in the houses, so it’s good water only in a manner of speaking.”
The village’s ordeal began in the first days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, when it was occupied. After Ukrainian forces liberated it, Kozatske gradually came under siege by drones as the war turned increasingly technological.
“Before, I’d just open the door and walk out,” said Oleksii Shavokin, 54, who lives a little farther down the street. “Now I open it a crack, stick my ear out and listen to the sky."
His house burned down in early 2023 after a mortar attack, he said, but he patched it up and stays on there. He lives off old humanitarian aid and eggs from the hens he still keeps. “I ration my food so it lasts. I’m used to it,” he said. “Now I eat once a day, in the evening, and that’s quite enough.” He has lost 30 kilograms (66 pounds) from a weight of close to 100 kilograms (220 pounds).
Many of the people he knew were killed by strikes, and others left. He decided to stay.
“I value life, but where’s the guarantee a car won’t hit me somewhere else?” Shavokin said. “Wherever it’s written for you, that’s where you’ll lose your life, or go on living. And still, I hope this all ends soon.”
Many residents who stay do not know where they would go and fear they would be left to fend for themselves, said Oleh Tarabaka, head of the Nova Kakhovka city military administration. He was part of the team that tried to persuade Diadiuk and Shavokin to leave.
But it is difficult, he said. Many have lived there their whole lives and fear that once they leave, they will have nothing to live on. Not everyone has someone to go to. Some have no relatives.
“If there hadn’t been a period of quiet, we simply wouldn’t have gotten people out,” Tarabaka said. “We wouldn’t have been able to drive in here.”
What residents are living through goes beyond survival, Tarabaka said, adding that perhaps no word has yet been invented to describe it.
Some, however, can be persuaded to leave. That was the case for Yevhen and his mother, Antonina, who declined to give their last names for security reasons.
One of the military officials turned to Yevhen. “Just make the right decision, the decision of a man and a son,” a Ukrainian soldier from the 42nd brigade who was part of the evacuation group told him.
Eventually, they agreed.
All the way through her bombed-out town, Antonina wailed and wept, not wanting to leave. Her cries echoed through the empty streets.
The temporary truce allowed the Red Cross to evacuate far more people than usual from Kherson city. Normally, every route and every stage must be planned around the constant threat of drones and other weapons.
“Right now, some streets and places in Kherson are a kill zone too. It’s simply impossible to slip through there. The risk is very, very high,” said Mykola Taranenko, commander of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society’s rapid response team in the Kherson region.
His team usually evacuates about 10 people a week, but during the ceasefire week, it took out at least 40.
Among those evacuated were Volodymyr and Kateryna Yakuba, both 77, who divorced more than 20 years ago but left the city together. Their daughter arranged the evacuation, and they are going to stay with her in Odesa.
“We need to get out before the cold sets in,” she said, adding about the ceasefire: “I don’t know how we would have gotten out otherwise.”
“It’s scary to leave home,” her voice trembled. "You don’t know if you’ll come back, or if there will be anything to come back to.”

Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson prepare for the return of war as localized ceasefire ends
Civilians in Ukraine's Kherson region prepare for the end of a localized ceasefire
KHERSON, Ukraine -- Civilians in Ukraine’s southeastern Kherson region prepared Sunday for the end of a localized ceasefire that has marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine 4½ years ago.
The White House said U.S. first lady Melania Trump helped to broker the limited truce, which began early Tuesday and is expected to end Sunday evening. The pause in hostilities allowed besieged residents in the front-line city of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday.
An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of evacuating to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. For the safety of those who have stayed, exact numbers were not released after the evacuation.
At the Ukrainian border Saturday, family members waited for a glimpse of their loved ones, while the residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and flashlights to greet the humanitarian convoy.
But Moscow and Kyiv have continued aerial strikes elsewhere, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Sunday that Russia continues to target Ukraine’s energy systems ahead of winter.
In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said that hundreds of thousands of families had been left without power overnight as Moscow sought to exploit Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses.
“The intensity of the strikes is extremely high, and the Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors,” he said in a post on X.
Residents in the Ukrainian city of Kherson remained calm Sunday, despite knowing that the quiet of the localized ceasefire would soon end.
“Don’t be afraid, keep holding on,” Oleksandr Knyha, head of the Mykola Kulish Kherson Regional Academic Music and Drama Theater, told the audience as he opened a concert.
The theater performs every Saturday and Sunday. This weekend’s shows fell during the ceasefire, but the company plans to perform next weekend as usual, even as local officials warn that Russian forces have brought in more weapons and personnel and some residents expect shelling to intensify.
“Of course, we want peace to finally come,” Knyha said. But “we’ve been working on the front line for four years,” he added, referring to Kherson itself, and the theater has never canceled a performance.
“Whatever happens, the show is not canceled,” he said.
The company now performs in a basement and is equipping an additional bomb shelter. About 100 of the theater’s 120 staff members work in Kherson, and none has evacuated.
Costume maker Alla Vasylenko, 58, said the silence of the brief truce still frightens her. “Nothing will change. Everything will go back to how it was before the ceasefire, because believing the Russians means not believing yourself,” she said.
She has no plans to leave. “I have 10 dogs, so I can’t leave,” she said. “They urge us to leave, but you need somewhere to go and the means to get there.”
The trip alone would cost 30,000 to 50,000 hryvnias, a significant sum for her, she said. “Until we liberate the left bank, we have no certainty this will end,” she said, referring to the Russian-occupied part of the region.
For many in Kherson, a city that itself lived through Russian occupation, that belief is the reason they stay.
Knyha is from Oleshky, on the occupied left bank, and used to commute from there to work in Kherson. He hasn’t given up hope of returning home. “That’s also what keeps me here,” he said.
On the last day of the ceasefire, the theater staged a concert built around a “musical map of Ukraine,” with songs from the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Russia annexed in 2014, to the Carpathian mountains in Ukraine's southwest. “This is also our job — to unite people and give them hope,” Knyha said.
Russian drone attacks continued to target Ukraine’s Kyiv region for a second consecutive day, wounding a woman and damaging homes, energy infrastructure and a retail establishment, regional authorities said.
In its daily report Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said Moscow's forces attacked Ukraine with 433 drones overnight, of which 371 were destroyed or suppressed.
Elsewhere, more than 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the skies of Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region east of Moscow, local Gov. Gleb Nikitin said Sunday.
Nikitin said an industrial building in the town of Kstovo had sustained “significant damage” but did not give further details. Russian media outlets later reported that the attack sparked a blaze at the Kstovo oil refinery, sharing images of black plumes of smoke over the horizon.
Zelenskyy said Sunday that Kyiv had also struck a factory used to make missile components and air defense facilities inside Russia’s southern Rostov region.
"We are justly defending ourselves against Russian aggression and doing everything to reduce Russia’s capability to continue it,” Zelenskyy wrote.

The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.
A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he?
I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.
That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”
Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.
The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.
Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. Srouri says that their relationship will be even closer, as Apple has merged its hardware engineering and technology organizations with Srouji at the top, reporting to Ternus. “John is going to be a great CEO,” he said. “He's a product guy at heart, but Apple's secret weapon is the DNA, the culture, which is not going to change. Remember, John has been here for 25 years. It’s not like he's going to come and everything's going to be different.”
Being Apple’s CEO encompasses much more than products—there’s a $100 billion business in services, a huge infrastructure, and the general mishegoss of running a giant corporation. I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I'm super passionate about it.”
Like it or not, the CEO of a $4 trillion company has to be involved in policy and politics. It has been widely reported that as executive chair, Cook will still conduct some of Apple’s high-level policy duties, including the equivalent of stuffing gold-plated binkies in the presidential mouth. Ternus implies that the reality is more nuanced. “Tim is available to help wherever I ask him, and it's great to have him in that role,” he said. “He obviously has a ton of relationships he's developed over the years, and of course, I'm building new relationships in this role as well.” One relationship he has yet to build: the president. Ternus has yet to meet Donald Trump.
Then there’s the one thing that could possibly disrupt the way Apple has run its business for the past 50 years. Ternus is taking over the company during what may be the biggest technological shift ever. I suggested to Ternus that history may judge him on how he handles AI. I spelled out for him a couple of narratives people spin about Apple. One is that Apple has been hobbled by a failure to develop its AI product Siri, and even after an update it’s still in catch-up mode. The other is that Apple is smart to avoid the high cost of developing a frontier model and that the strategy of organically putting AI into its products, with a focus on privacy, will pay off in the long run.
“Everyone has an opinion—I really like where we’re at,” he said. “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that. We don't want to ship AI for AI's sake. When we're doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”
That assumes that AI, as powerful as it is, will wind up as a “normal” technology, organically integrated into our current gadget-sphere. Another school of thought is that AI is an apocalyptic disruptor that will shred the current ecosystem. In that vision, all those cool apps Apple supports will be subsumed by AI-concocted agents generated from prompts, or even autonomously. Ternus doesn’t buy that scenario. “That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do,” he said.
When I asked whether he’s in favor of AI regulation, he replied, “We all read the stories and think about it from a cybersecurity standpoint—clearly these models are very capable of doing things. Our focus is on making sure that our products are secure and safe, and protecting the users' information.”
His non-answer shows that he might well be on the way to mastering political communication. But policy will never be the focus of John Ternus. He is, and probably always will be, the product-guy CEO. Before we ended our conversation, Ternus had one question for me: “What did you think of the logo?”

When Sarojini Nadimpally was diagnosed with HER2-positive breast cancer in June 2025, the Delhi-based public health researcher was staring at a hidden reality as daunting as the tumour. One dose of the targeted combination drug she had been prescribed would cost around ₹2.7 lakh — and she needed 18 doses.
As someone who works on access to medicines, she closely followed the government’s recent decision to cap trade margins on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs at 30%, extending a 2019 cap that covered 42. The government claims that the cap, which takes effect on November 9, can save patients about ₹2,500 crore a year.
“Any intervention to lower the prices of cancer drugs is a welcome step,” says Ms. Nadimpally. “But it remains to be seen how this cap will actually reduce what patients pay.”
Survival versus solvency
Cancer is said to be India’s leading cause of catastrophic health spending. India’s out-of-pocket share for cancer care — estimated by various studies to be 50%-80% of direct treatment costs — is far higher than in most high-income systems, where insurance or tax-funded care generally absorbs the bulk of these expenses.
Experts say that drugs make up around over half the costs of cancer care. “High costs of treatments such as targeted therapies and immunotherapy can lead many patients to defer treatment, opt for cheaper but less effective alternatives or give up altogether,” says Vedant Kabra, principal director, surgical oncology, Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Gurugram.
When pills threaten to outrun savings, the standard of care is down to a cruel trade-off between effectiveness and affordability. For example, at about ₹1.25 lakh a month, a lifetime course of osimertinib, the drug of choice in fighting EGFR-mutated lung cancer while reducing the risk of brain metastases, is beyond the reach of many. “These patients switch to gefitinib, which costs only about ₹2,500 a month, but return with brain secondaries and disease progression,” says Narayanankutty Warrier, senior consultant oncologist, MVR Cancer Centre and Research Institute, Kozhikode. “About 30% new-generation drugs are really good,” he says. “The rest are mostly claims. But even a slight improvement in survival means they become monopoly drugs.”
The pricing conundrum
With its latest order, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) is setting a common trade-margin ceiling on a broad range of cancer medicines, including patented, chemotherapy, targeted, immunotherapy, hormonal and blood cancer drugs. Manufacturers are required to report formulation-level information, including brand name, composition, pack size, PTS (price to stockist) and revised MRP.
The order spells out that a drug with a PTS of ₹70 and an MRP of ₹300 can have an MRP of no more than ₹100, excluding GST. Experts argue that the permitted margin — which amounts to 42.8% of the PTS — is a sizeable mark-up, especially for expensive drugs.
In effect, the government is putting a ceiling on the profit, not the underlying price. For example, the actual prices at which hospitals buy drugs, often after steep discounts negotiated for bulk purchases, are hidden from sight. “A cap on trade margins means little to patients if hospitals and dealers do not pass those savings on, and there is no way of knowing whether they do,” says Ms. Nadimpally.
On October 28, the NPPA published a revised price list for the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs based on data submitted by companies. The MRPs of 37 drugs remain unchanged, offering an early indication of what the final list may look like. The list also reveals margins that manufacturers, including some Indian generic makers, have had. For instance, palbociclib’s MRP for one brand is down from about ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 a pack, and thiotepa’s from about ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 a vial — drops of more than 90%.
The latest order also counts the cap from the PTS, not from the ex-factory price or the landed cost (price paid after discounts and freight), leaving out upstream additions. The mark-up for cancer medicines is unjustified, says Malini Aisola, co-convener, All India Drug Action Network. “With few middlemen involved in the distribution of these high-value, low-volume products, a hospital or distributor gets to keep nearly all the margin. That legitimises profiteering.”
When it comes to patented, mostly imported medicines, we are price-takers, insists Ms. Aisola. “The government is averse to using its legal powers under the Indian Patent Act and TRIPS (Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) — such as government use and compulsory licensing — to increase competition.”
The government, she adds, monitors and controls medicine prices based on a proprietary dataset owned by pharmaceutical companies. “This data,” she argues, “underrepresents or completely excludes institutional sales of cancer medicines because of the way the data are gathered and modelled.”
Besides, freebies under patient assistance programmes (PAPs) are now excluded from the calculation. “Including all PAP volumes would expose the true trade mark-ups to hospitals and force a bigger MRP cut,” says Ms. Aisola.
Beyond medicines
Medicines are only a part of the bill. Cut the margin, and the cost could mimic the cancer in finding another site. Other expensive components of treatment —diagnostic tests, surgery, radiotherapy, hospital accommodation, consumables, consultations, drug administration and associated clinical services — also need to be addressed. “Hospitals have several avenues to recoup the shortfall,” says a healthcare activist.
Running a hospital today is highly capital- and cost-intensive. Industry estimates suggest that each bed can cost ₹30 lakh to ₹1.5 crore, and a hospital needs around two-thirds of its beds occupied just to break even. The bills keep coming even when patients are not, says the COO of a Mumbai hospital. . “Hospitals have long relied on margins because they are legally allowed to,” notes Dr. Warrier.
Optimisation, Dr. Kabra avers, needs to go beyond drugs. “Hospitals and doctors get paid progressively less for the same procedure or disease depending on whether a self-paying patient, an insurer or a government health scheme is footing the bill. This squeeze can make care financially unviable, especially in complex interventions,” he points out. He also asks why caps have not yet been applied to manufacturers. “It seems unfair that manufacturers profit several times their production costs while everyone else is held to 30%,” he says. “Yes, manufacturers take greater risks and often only one of the dozens of drugs they research makes it to the market. But the profits they earn cannot be disproportionate forever.”
The price of exclusivity
Drug patents are another issue, point out experts. While many cancer therapies in India now have multiple generic manufacturers despite patents, generics in India are required to demonstrate bioequivalence — the degree to which they match the reference drug — before they can be marketed, says S. Srinivasan, co-founder of LOCOST, a not-for-profit maker of affordable generic medicines. “Affordability of cancer medicines depends not only on patent expiry, but also on whether generic firms can bear the exorbitant costs of bioequivalence testing,” he says.
Hospitals can add to their troubles. For instance, multinational brands of a targeted cancer medication like palbociclib can cost many times more than their generic equivalents, says a healthcare activist, giving hospitals a significantly bigger margin and thereby, an incentive to push the pricier option. “This only undermines affordable generics and entrenches multinationals,” he rues.
Limits of control
Murali Neelakantan, principal lawyer at advisory firm, amicus, calls price controls a “terrible” solution to a demand-supply mismatch. “It has second order, unintended consequences that are difficult to fix,” he says. “Price control can only be an emergency short-term measure to deal with market failure and catastrophic events that cannot be easily mitigated by market interventions.”
Mr. Neelakantan suggests treating drugs like food grains — not subject to price controls — and releasing government-procured drug stocks to stabilise prices whenever supplies fall short. The government, he says, can intervene by building more government hospitals and by procuring goods and services from private healthcare providers in an efficient manner rather than through fragmented schemes. The scale of procurement gives the government immense economic power to influence demand and facilitate price discovery and stabilisation, he points out. “Coercive regulation of prices will further distort the market and incentivise unethical practices, including evasive tactics by market participants,” he warns.
Trade margin caps are, at best, tokenistic, says Mr. Srinivasan. MRPs of anti-cancer drugs are high even after trade margins. “A better approach,” he suggests, “could be to base the MRP on API (active pharmaceutical ingredient) cost plus manufacturing and marketing expenses, with a 100–200% mark-up to recoup post-manufacturing expenses and trade margins.
The best solution for poor or middle-class cancer patients in India, however, would be free medicines provided by the government.” For now, though, a ‘cheaper’ cancer drug is no cure for exorbitant treatment.
(Harsh Kabra is an independent journalist and commentator. harshkabra@gmail.com)

Pandemic preparedness, support for Ukraine, and the fight against superbugs topped the agenda Tuesday as WHO and UK health leaders met in London to discuss their shared global health priorities.
In their first one-on-one meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and UK Secretary of State for Health and Social Care Steve Barclay MP spoke at length about their shared commitment to delivering a pandemic instrument – a new international agreement being negotiated by WHO Member States – to strengthen global collaboration to help protect the world from another pandemic.
Mr Barclay outlined the UK government’s priorities for a pandemic instrument, which include faster and more efficient data sharing between WHO Member States; quicker, more equitable access to affordable vaccines, tests and treatments; and stronger collaboration on scientific research and development.
“The World Health Organization has reached a significant milestone this year in the marking of its 75th anniversary, and I’m proud of the UK’s longstanding relationship with WHO to improve public health,” Mr Barclay said. “The UK is playing a leading role in tackling some of the world’s greatest health threats, including antimicrobial resistance for which we recently announced £39 million for research into new drugs to combat infections.”
In 2022 and in the previous biennium, the UK was the largest contributor to WHO’s Core Voluntary Contributions Account. The account provides flexible funds that WHO can use and allocate as needed within its approved programme budgets. 
Earlier in the day, Dr Tedros joined International Development Minister Andrew Mitchell and Health Minister Will Quince for the annual UK-WHO Strategic Dialogue to discuss how to tackle global health challenges together and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. 
They spoke about effectively responding to health emergencies, preventing the next pandemic and confronting threats to health posed by climate change.
Ministers Mitchell and Quince emphasized the importance of building strong health systems in countries and protecting the health and rights of women and girls. Ministers also cited the importance of reform to strengthen WHO as an organization, expressing support for WHO’s extensive efforts to prevent and respond to sexual misconduct.  
“WHO highly values its strong and impactful collaboration with the UK Government to promote and protect the health of people worldwide,” Dr Tedros said as the meetings concluded. “Today’s strategic dialogue with Ministers Mitchell and Quince, and my productive discussions with Secretary of State Barclay, demonstrated the UK’s commitment to global public health, its support of the World Health Organization, and the great potential and impact of our partnership. I look forward to continuing our joint work to make the world healthier and safer on many fronts, from combatting antimicrobial resistance to supporting the UK and countries around the world to develop a generational accord to prevent and respond to future pandemics.”
Read more about the UK and WHO’s partnership in global health.

‘Flight was unsafe’: DMK MP P Wilson alleges engine failure, seeks DGCA review
P Wilson urged the DGCA to conduct an impartial review of airworthiness certificates of all aircraft operating across the country.
Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) MP P Wilson on Monday raised concerns over aviation safety after an IndiGo flight from Kolkata to Shillong was cancelled following an engine failure while taxiing, alleging that the aircraft was "unsafe" and questioning how it was granted an airworthiness certificate.
Seeking the intervention of Union Civil Aviation Minister Kinjarapu Ram Mohan Naidu, Wilson urged the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to conduct an impartial review of airworthiness certificates of all aircraft operating across the country and undertake surprise inspections to ensure passenger safety.
In a post on X, Wilson said he was travelling on IndiGo flight 6E 7423 from Kolkata to Shillong along with three other MPs and 67 passengers to attend a Joint Parliamentary Committee public hearing when the aircraft suddenly stopped while taxiing towards the runway.
"Today, when I, along with three other MPs and 67 passengers, boarded IndiGo flight 6E 7423 @IndiGo6E from Kolkata Airport to Shillong to attend a Joint Parliamentary Committee public hearing, the flight suddenly stopped while taxiing from the parking bay towards the runway. Before take-off, an engine failed and was shut down. Passengers were stranded on board for about two hours. Afterwards, the pilot announced a technical glitch and cancelled the flight," he said.
Wilson alleged the incident raised serious concerns about the regulatory checks carried out before aircraft are permitted to operate.
"The truth is that the flight was unsafe, and it is unclear how the DGCA (@DGCAIndia) granted this aircraft an airworthiness certificate--a serious violation," he said.
He urged the Civil Aviation Minister to direct the DGCA to review all airworthiness certificates and establish whether aircraft operating across the country were genuinely fit to fly. He also called for surprise inspections by vigilance units wherever required.
"If they are not, the DGCA should cancel their certificates, ground the aircraft and prohibit them from flying," Wilson said.
The DMK MP further alleged an "unholy nexus" between certain airlines and DGCA officials, claiming that it allows unsafe aircraft, sometimes without certificates, to continue operating.
"The unholy nexus between some airlines and some DGCA officials that allows them to operate unsafe aircraft, sometimes without certificates, often leads to flight crashes (e.g. AI 171)," he alleged.
Highlighting the risks faced by passengers, Wilson questioned the consequences of technical failures occurring during a flight and said people travel by air trusting that the aircraft are safe.
"The innocent public trusts that flights are safe and undertakes journeys. What happens if a flight develops technical snags in mid-air?" he said.
Emphasising the importance of airworthiness certification, he said it was the most fundamental assurance that an aircraft was technically safe to fly.
"Airworthiness certification is the most fundamental assurance that an aircraft is technically safe to fly. An airworthiness certificate cannot be allowed to remain valid for an aircraft that is truly unworthy to fly," Wilson said.
He added that any compromise in the certification process directly affects passenger safety, operational integrity and global regulatory norms.
Calling for accountability, Wilson demanded punishment for those responsible for allowing unsafe aircraft to operate and sought strict action against officials found guilty of wrongdoing.
"The offenders should be punished, and erring officials should be sacked," he said.

Many forms of ear infections strike children and adults alike, but among the most common is acute otitis externa, also known as swimmer’s ear.
About 10% of Americans will experience swimmer’s ear during their lifetimes. Adults are affected more commonly, and children only rarely, generally ages 5 to 12.
But you don’t have to be swimming to get swimmer’s ear. Go out jogging or walking, or do yardwork on a hot day, and moisture from perspiration can drip in your ear. However, the occurrence increases fivefold in swimmers – thus the reason the condition came to be called “swimmer’s ear.” It also occurs more frequently in tropical climates because of humidity and higher temperatures.
As doctors who specialise in ear problems, we are actively involved in research and clinical treatment for children and adults struggling with ear, nose and throat problems. Practicing in the state of Florida, we’ve certainly seen our share of patients with swimmer’s ear.
Causes and symptoms of swimmer’s ear
Swimmer’s ear is an infection in the external ear canal, the tube leading from the ear opening to the eardrum. Typically, swimmer’s ear occurs only in one ear, and sometimes the eardrum itself is affected. Moisture trapped in the canal leads to a break in the skin barrier and creates an opening for certain bacteria types to enter or existing ones to overgrow.
One of these culprits is the bacterium Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is present in soil and water throughout the world. These bacteria favor moist areas, such as sinks, toilets, inadequately chlorinated swimming pools and hot tubs, as well as outdated or inactivated antiseptic solutions.
If you have the infection, you’ll know it. Symptoms generally appear a few days after infection. The main symptom of swimmer’s ear is severe pain and discomfort. It’s particularly noticeable when the outer ear is tugged, or by touching the tragus – that’s the small bump at the front of your ear. Other symptoms include itchiness inside the ear, redness, swelling and drainage. A feeling of fullness, or the perception of a plugged ear, may also occur, along with disturbed balance and temporary hearing loss.
Predisposition to swimmer’s ear
Numerous factors can predispose someone to swimmer’s ear. They include a narrow ear canal, and skin diseases such as eczema or psoriasis. In addition, individuals wearing ear plugs, ear buds or hearing aids may be at an increased risk. Diabetics may also be more prone to the infection.
Swimmer’s ear can also come from something getting stuck inside the ear, excessive ear cleaning or contact with chemicals in hair dye or hairspray.
Diagnosis and treatment
Swimmer’s ear is diagnosed after a health care provider has gathered a thorough history and examined the inside of the ear. The ear canal will typically look red, swollen and moist. There is also a possibility of fluid drainage or the appearance of scaly, shedding skin. Depending on the degree of swelling, the eardrum may be hard to see. A sample of fluid may be removed from the ear and sent to a lab to look for bacteria or fungus.
Eardrops are commonly used to treat swimmer’s ear. These drops often contain antibiotics to kill the infection and steroids to stop the swelling.
One such eardrop is Ciprodex. It contains ciprofloxacin, an antibiotic, and dexamethasone, a powerful steroid. Patients will need to place about four to five drops in the infected ear canal twice a day for seven to 10 days.
Another commonly prescribed drop is Floxin, which contains an antibiotic but not a steroid. It is commonly prescribed in less swollen but still infected ears.
Other drop preparations include Cortisporin, which contains a commonly used combination of neomycin and polymyxin B, as well as hydrocortisone. However, neomycin is also damaging to the inner ear, so doctors nowadays often turn to Ciprodex or Floxin.
In some cases, the ear canal is too swollen for drops to reach the infected area, so the physician may place a wick or stent in the ear canal to keep it open. This will usually be left in place for three to five days until removed by the doctor, although occasionally the wick falls out once the swelling subsides. Usually, after 10 days the infection is resolved and the ear canal skin returns to normal.
Managing a persistent infection
Sometimes swimmer’s ear may not resolve after seven to 10 days of treatment with eardrops. Oral antibiotics are typically recommended if the infection has spread beyond the ear canal or in patients with poorly controlled diabetes. Hospitalization for swimmer’s ear is rarely necessary; however, complications that can occasionally lead to hospitalization include fever, worsening discharge, extensive narrowing of the ear canal or failure of previous treatments.
Among the precautions you can take to prevent swimmer’s ear: Keep the ear canal dry. Tip your head to one side to help the water drain. Use a soft towel or cloth, or gently use a hair dryer near it. If the self-cleansing mechanism of the ear canal is impaired, then the ear canal should be cleansed by a physician.
Since most bacteria prefer a pH-neutral environment, reducing the pH in the ear canal can prevent bacterial overgrowth. A homemade liquid tincture can be mixed from a solution of half rubbing alcohol and half distilled white vinegar. The alcohol combines with the water in the ear and then evaporates. This removes the water while the acidity of the vinegar keeps bacteria from growing.
Two to three drops are usually sufficient and can be applied as a preventive measure soon after the ear has been exposed to moisture. This liquid solution is not a replacement for medical treatment of an actual ear infection and is meant to be used only in people who are prone to such infections because of prolonged or frequent exposure to moisture.
Also, it is important to differentiate swimmer’s ear from a middle ear infection, the most frequent reason for the use of antibiotics in children under age 5. Middle ear infections are usually associated with a viral upper respiratory infection, and they are more often seen during fall and winter, when influenza and cold viruses are more prevalent.
(Thomas Schrepfer, Assistant Professor of Pediatric Otolaryngology, University of Florida; Rex Haberman Associate Clinical Professor of Otology and Neurotology, University of Florida)
