Representatives from various student organisations submitted a memorandum to the vice-chancellor, demanding that necessary facilities, space, and support must be provided to students for their democratic right of free expression and protest. Within the next few days, six more students, Rehan Khan, Rehan Haider, Faizan Ali Khan, Rida Nausheen Khan, Ritik, Altaf, and Abuzar, joined the hunger strike and several students joined the sit-in demonstration around the Mirza Ghalib statue on campus. What followed is severe police crackdown, administrative retaliation, and a state-sanctioned attempt to curb what students described as a peaceful protest for their rights.
‘Students Beaten, Dragged & Detained’
Five days into the protest, around 5:30 am on October 17, Delhi Police personnel arrived in large numbers outside the university gate, and allegedly detained at least 10 students with the aid of the campus security guards. Students alleged that authorities turned off the lights, beat and dragged the protesters out of the campus in the break of dawn in the presence of the chief proctor of the university.
CPI(ML) Liberation alleged that Jamia Millia Islamia administration forcibly removed students on hunger strike from the campus around 5:30 am on Saturday while they were demanding the restoration of the students’ union. In a post on X, the party alleged that campus lights were switched off and students were beaten, manhandled and harassed before being handed over to Delhi Police. It said all detained students had since been released. The students are demanding the restoration of Jamia’s students’ union and the holding of union elections. CPI(ML) Liberation condemned the alleged action and urged the administration to stop what it called repression and restore the union.
— The Observer Post (@TheObserverPost) October 17, 2026
Footage surfacing on social media showed clashes between authorities and the students protesters on the morning of October 17, with videos showing police dragging and pulling students away from the campus.
View this post on Instagram
A video also showed Ebin Basil, writhing in pain, alleging that he had been brutally assaulted by the security guards.
Subsequently, as scenes of utter chaos kept emerging through the day, a large group of students were seen breaking the gate and storming inside the campus even as the police reportedly denied detaining anyone and only removing those attempting to break the gate.
View this post on Instagram
Admin Condemns Slogans, Shifts Classes Online
On October 18, a high-level committee comprising seven university professors was formed to mediate between protesting students, and to convince them to call the demonstration off. During this meeting certain slogans that were painted on walls by students also came under the administration’s scrutiny. These slogans included ‘Restore JMISU’, ‘Reclaim Jamia’, ‘Inquilab Ayega’, ‘Free Palestine’, ‘Free Sharjeel Imam’, and ‘RSS Se Azaadi’ among others.
In a press release published by the official handle of the university on X, the slogans were labelled “highly condemnable and detrimental to the nation’s integrity, security and sovereignty.” The release further stated that the administration has adopted two resolutions. First, to urge the protesters to vacate the protest site and call off their agitation, particularly at the Ghalib statue lawns, which they claimed had been “illegally occupied by the protesting students despite Gate No. 18 being the designated protest site at JMI”. Second, “to repaint the defaced walls and cover the slogans”.
The press release added that the administration had been compelled to issue a notification to shift all classes online allegedly due to the protesters’ resistance to call off the demonstration. “After two hours of efforts to persuade the students to call off the protest…the students continued chanting slogans, shouting that the faculty should “go back” and suddenly began pushing security guards, staff and teachers…even after their demands had been met earlier this week,” the release stated.
Further, the university administration took disciplinary action against Ebin and Jasim. Ebin was rusticated for one academic year and barred from campus while Jasim Khan was barred from campus for six months.
Following the administrative action, students held a press conference on October 18 and expanded their demands beyond the restoration of the JMI-SU — they demanded the withdrawal of disciplinary proceedings against protesting students and an end to further punitive measures. They also demanded the resignation of the chief proctor and security advisor.
Students Vow to Continue Strike, Clampdown Increases
Even as certain hunger strikers gave up due to declining health, the remaining students vowed to continue their hunger strike and sit-in protests. Solidarity for the protesting students poured in from within and beyond the campus, however, the police deployment outside the campus and administrative clampdown also intensified.
“The irony lies in the fact that the same administration that condemned unauthorised police clampdown on students during the CAA-NRC protests in 2019 is deploying that very body against its students in 2026 to suppress the constitutionally safeguarded right of free and independent expression,” Ateerah, a post-graduate student, told Alt News.
On October 23, Congress MP Imran Masood was detained by Delhi Police after he arrived at the university to express solidarity with protesting students.
Water, Electricity, Basic Amenities Cut Off
On October 24 — the 13th day of the hunger strike — through another notice the administration shifted all classes to online mode, shut its gates, suspended canteen services, and restricted access to the Central Library. In what students viewed as an attempt to discourage the protest, electricity and water supply were also cut off in the campus space, students told Alt News. “They have essentially converted our dissent into a question of law and order, to justify police action on a peaceful protest,” said Abdul, another student.
On the same day, a large number of Delhi Police personnel and paramilitary forces were stationed outside the university premises. The protesting students told Alt News that in the afternoon, the proctor’s team, along with university professors and non-teaching staff, had rounded up students who had gathered for a sit-in demonstration within Gate No. 7 of the university premises, at the Ghalib Lawn.
Students alleged use of force on both male and female protestors by the security guards. The protest site was allegedly dismantled, which compelled the protesting students to take shelter within the Political Science building and continue their hunger strike, they added.
View this post on Instagram
Mantasha, a post-graduate student, told Alt News, “The whole affair was an unpleasant reminder of what had transpired within the university premises in 2019. This time, our own professors joined in with the security guards. Some just watched, while others proceeded to manhandle us. Until our 13th day of protest, a solitary female washroom was kept open at night. However, after the protest site was dismantled in the afternoon of October 24, we found that it had been sealed off, leaving us no option but to share the male washroom.”
Students Reject Admin’s Notification
The next day, on October 25, the administration released a notification that said that a student election would be held after 15 days from the date of approval of the constitution of the JMI-SU.
It stated that show cause notices and suspension orders against students during the period of protest would be revoked, and a committee would be constituted to enquire into the actions of the security staff. It also added that students should issue a public apology for any defamatory statement, action, or posts made during the protest against the administration.
However, students expressed their apprehension regarding the notification, pointing out that the date of constitution of the union was unspecified. Those on hunger strike continued their fast, deeming the notification an incomplete victory as all of their demands had not yet been addressed.
They demanded an assurance on the resignation of the chief proctor and the security advisor, and the revocation of all disciplinary actions on protesting students, besides declining to issue a public apology. “The Constitution of the union is to be drafted by December 20, after which it is subject to approval from the V-C. This allows a lot of scope for administrative inaction and complacency, since the approval itself can be indefinitely stalled by the administration,” alleged Abdul.
On October 26, two gates — one in front of the Ibn-e-Sina reading library, and another which serves as a key access point to the campus for residents of the Boys Hostel — were sealed off by the administration, with the suspension of offline classes still effective.
A student protestor, speaking on terms of anonymity, told Alt News, “The gate provides access to facilities serving not only students and hostel residents but also members of the general public, including an Indian Post Office, a public sector bank, an Aadhaar centre, a university health centre and a dental hospital. Restricting access to such essential public services, including medical care for patients with scheduled appointments, warrants immediate reconsideration.”
Less than 24 hours after the administration released the notice, Delhi Police however went on to detain several students for merely attempting to enter the premises of their own university, students told Alt News. Video footage showed police personnel pushing students onto a detention bus.
Speaking to Alt News from the protest site, students alleged that they are not being able to leave the campus given the heavy police and paramilitary deployment in front of the gates. Food and water deliveries are allegedly being intercepted by security guards at the gates, cutting off the basic means of survival for students who have remained within the campus.
“We had earlier put out a message asking for people in solidarity to send in drinking water, but the guards would not let it through. Is this how a university treats its students?” a student, requesting anonymity, asked.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Quick Answer
The best free alternatives to popular Microsoft apps include LibreOffice for Microsoft 365, ShareX for Snipping Tool, Files for File Explorer, Everything for Windows Search, System Informer for Task Manager, and ImageGlass for Microsoft Photos. These offer more features, better speed, and greater control.
Microsoft bundles plenty of apps with Windows, and you probably use a bunch of them on your PC — some out of personal preference, others because there aren’t enough good alternatives.
Now, there’s nothing wrong with using these apps if they serve you well. But if you find their functionality limited or want a free version, you don’t have to settle. Here are some of the best free alternatives to popular Windows apps that are worth checking out.
Table of Contents
LibreOffice for Microsoft 365
Microsoft 365 is a subscription service that gives you access to Office, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and Teams, alongside 1 TB of OneDrive storage. You can get Microsoft 365 for free, but you need a paid subscription for unrestricted access. However, if you don’t wish to go that route and want unrestricted access to the office suite, LibreOffice is a solid Microsoft 365 alternative worth checking out.
LibreOffice doesn’t require an account or subscription; you can download the app and get started right away. The suite includes three tools — Writer, Calc, and Impress, which are free equivalents to Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, respectively. You also get a vector graphics editor (Draw), a database management system (Base), and a mathematical formulas and equations editor (Math). The app works completely offline and stores all your data locally on the device. It doesn’t have any AI features either, so you have full control over what you do.
ShareX for Snipping Tool
Windows has a built-in screenshot tool called Snipping Tool to help you take screenshots and record the screen. Although Microsoft has updated it over the years to include OCR/text extraction and screen recording capabilities, its functionality is still largely limited compared to many third-party screenshot apps. ShareX is one such app, which is quite popular among power users.
ShareX offers plenty of screenshot modes, including scrolling capture, active monitor, custom, and auto-capture, as well as those you get with the Snipping Tool. Scrolling capture and auto-capture are two standout modes here. The former comes in handy when you want to capture content that extends beyond what’s visible on the screen. On the other hand, the latter lets you automatically take screenshots of a specified area at set intervals, which may be useful when you want to document the steps or monitor some process.
However, that’s not all; ShareX is better than Windows Snipping Tool at a bunch of other things. For example, it supports batch operations and automation capabilities. This allows you to apply edits to a bunch of screenshots at once. Then there are a few extra tools like Imagine Combiner to stitch multiple images, Ruler to measure dimensions, Color to extract color values from elements in your screenshots, and more.
Files for File Explorer
File Explorer is Microsoft’s own file manager for Windows. Although it has largely remained unchanged from Windows 10 to Windows 11, it did receive some noteworthy changes in appearance and functionality. Still, some of its elements, like the dialog box, look archaic. Not to mention, it lacks customizability and many features you otherwise find on its alternatives. This is where Files comes in.
Files is a popular File Explorer alternative that gives you everything you get with File Explorer, along with plenty of other useful features, while blending well with Windows 11 aesthetics. For starters, it supports Miller columns, which makes navigating nested folders easier. Likewise, it has a dual-pane mode for side-by-side file and folder comparisons.
Among other things, Files lets you add color-coded tags to files, view folder sizes at a glance, and preview a bunch of different file types like Markdown and SVG natively. It also offers Git integration for developers and a built-in FTP/SFTP client to manage files on remote servers. Last but not least, Files has a Command Palette, which is essentially a search box pop-up where you can search for files, change settings, and perform a bunch of other actions without digging through different menus.
Everything for Windows Search
Windows Search — the built-in search tool on your Windows PC, which lets you find apps, files, settings, and more- has come a long way over the years. It feels more integrated into the system and gives you options to control the kind of results that appear. Still, Search can feel quite slow, especially on relatively older hardware. It actively scans folders in the background, which increases resource usage. For this reason, it’s best to switch to Everything.
Everything is one of the popular file search tools for Windows. Its biggest highlights are speed and low resource usage. This is partly because of the way Everything indexes files and folders. Instead of crawling folders, it reads the NTFS Master File Table (MFT) — a type of database Windows uses to track files on the drive. This also enables Everything to instantly reflect any changes you make to files on your PC.
Among other things, Everything supports Regex and offers granular search options to help you find exactly what you’re looking for. It also has a handy batch renaming tool built in that lets you rename multiple files at once. Everything also has excellent keyboard-based navigation support, if you prefer that. You can even customize your most-used actions to your preferred keyboard shortcuts.
System Informer for Windows Task Manager
im is a powerful Windows app for monitoring and managing apps and background processes running on your computer. It comes in handy when you want to know what (and how much) resources an app or process is using, manage startup apps, and close frozen apps and system processes. However, it doesn’t support advanced task-management operations and isn’t quite effective at many supported tasks. Switching to System Informer thus makes sense.
System Informer provides low-level control over apps and processes, allowing you to manage them more effectively. It uses interactive graphs to show you all the processes hogging system resources. You can click on any data point for more information. This way, you can see all the past and dead processes to find the culprit. Similarly, the app makes it easier to view, start, and stop low-level system drivers, which is useful when you want to fix system crashes.
For times when you see an unknown background process eating up resources, System Informer lets you learn more about it without leaving the app. Last but not least, System Informer lets you find all processes using a particular file and kill them easily. This can be useful when you’re unable to edit or delete a file because some process is using it.
ImageGlass for Microsoft Photos
Microsoft Photos is the app that your PC launches whenever yoscru open a peenso in File Explorer. It lets you view photos and do basic edits (crop, repair, stylize, and enhance). There’s also cloud integration support to help you view and manage photos from your OneDrive or iCloud account right in the app, along with a bunch of AI features. Honestly, though, all of this feels like overkill for an app meant just to view photos. Not only does it make the interface look cluttered, but it also slows the app down significantly. Hence, the need for alternatives like ImageGlass.
ImageGlass is one of the popular Microsoft Photos alternatives after IrfanView. Although IrfanView is packed with advanced features, it feels dated in today’s time. Add to that the fact that Microsoft Photos is primarily a photo viewer, and ImageGlass starts looking like the better option. It’s fast, thanks to its use of hardware caching, which preloads adjacent images so they load instantly when you use the left or right arrow keys. And unlike Photos, it supports over 90 image formats, including WebP, JXL, and multiple RAW formats, natively. As such, you don’t need to download external plugins or extensions to open images.
Another reason to choose ImageGlass is the clean experience. It’s an entirely local-first image viewer that doesn’t integrate cloud services, nor does it push AI or other unrelated features. The app just lets you open images to view them. That said, you do get basic editing options (rotate, flip, crop, resize, etc.), along with a few other useful tools like a color picker and an EXIF metadata viewer. The app’s UI is customizable too, and you get plenty of themes, layouts, and other options to play with.
Those are some Microsoft apps I’ve replaced on my Windows PC with better alternatives. All of them are free to download and use, though some, such as Files and ImageGlass, offer a paid version that unlocks access to a few additional features. You can visit their website to learn more about these features, and if your workflow demands them, upgrade to their paid versions anytime.

Key takeaways from this week's political meeting in Beijing
BEIJING— China's ruling Communist Party concluded its most important meeting of the year, confirming the expulsion of 33 senior party members, as leader Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign continues to widen.
The political meeting, known as the fifth plenum, began on Monday and wrapped up on Thursday.
Of the 376 full and alternate central committee members originally named in 2022, only 279 attended – more than a quarter absent. Many of them are believed to be under investigation.
The focus of the meeting was on anti-corruption and discipline, but Joseph Torigian, a professor of Chinese studies at American University in Washington D.C., says the meeting sends another signal amid wide speculation that he will seek a fourth term in office next year.
"This is Xi Jinping setting up for the next party congress next year by ensuring that everybody is on the same page as him," he says.
The meeting reveals how much work Xi thinks his party still has to do to become a more effective, loyal governing institution, according to Neil Thomas, senior fellow on Chinese politics at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
That is something he said Americans should also pay attention to, because it impacts the U.S. calculus on how willing China would be to use force over Taiwan, the South China Sea and disputes with the U.S.
"The focus of this fifth plenum suggests to me that Xi is unlikely to take that risk until he feels more comfortable with the party that he leads," Thomas says.
Here are other major takeaways from the meeting:
Who's in and who's out
Among the 33 expelled party members are Zhang Youxia, formerly China's most senior military general and Liu Jianchao, a senior Chinese diplomat previously tipped to be the next foreign minister.
China's military leadership ranks has "almost completely been purged in the last three or four years," according to Thomas.
However, one man not only survived the purges, but has been elevated – general Zhang Shengmin. He has been a key player in Xi's anti-corruption campaign. At the meeting he was promoted to the Politburo, which consists of more than 20 of the party's top officials. His promotion, according to Thomas, reinforces the importance of anti-corruption work in the military.
"There's a lot of churn going on," Torigian says. "That raises questions about just who [Xi's] going to look to to fill in the ranks when there's a big succession coming up at the next Party congress next year."
Instilling party discipline
One of the key themes out of the meeting was strengthening party governance.
Xi is looking to maintain the party's conviction from one generation to the next by convincing people to "put the Chinese Communist Party at the center of their lives and not their own selfish interests," according to Torigian.
He adds that this is a topic close to Xi's heart on how a communist regime can "maintain its purity and not degrade and collapse" like many other communist parties have in other countries.
Tackling corruption to "pointless formalities"
Xi's anti-corruption campaign started when he came into power in late 2012.
Since then, 7.9 million individuals have been punished, including over 960 senior officials, Zhang Fuhai, Deputy Secretary of the Communist party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, told reporters on Friday.
"The fight against corruption remains serious, complicated, and eradicating the breeding ground for corruption remains a formidable task," he said.
Xi has also complained about excessive formalities and bureaucracy, which according to Torigian is party language for going through the motions, having lots of meetings "but never actually achieving anything."
At the same time, there will be more regular reporting from discipline inspectors to central authorities to add scrutiny on local officials.
But to avoid attracting the attention of the discipline system, local officials may play things really safe, leading to more inertia, less experimentation, and "may end up having the opposite effect to what Xi intended," Thomas said.
No insight gleaned at the plenum on Xi's successor
Few political watchers believe Xi will pick a successor at the next party congress, and nobody knows exactly what he will do when he is ready to step down, according to Torigian.
Full decisions from the meeting, and perhaps deliverables, are expected to be published in the coming days.
Additional research by Jasmine Ling in Beijing.

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed to this report

On September 29, 2015, a memo went out from Swasthya Bhawan, the West Bengal Health Department’s headquarters in Salt Lake, to every medical college principal and every district’s chief medical officer of health. Its subject was a concern the Union Health Ministry had raised about rising Caesarean sections rates, especially where the operation was not medically needed.
The memo enclosed a statement the World Health Organization (WHO) had issued that April. It suggested that chief medical officers, who license private clinics, carry out periodic “prescription audits” of Caesareans in private and government facilities.
At the time, the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-4, 2015-16) had found that about one in four births were Caesareans in West Bengal (23.8%). The latest sixth round (NFHS-6, 2023-24) puts the figure at 44.5%, close to double that level, against 27.2% for India. In Kolkata and North 24 Parganas it was found to be 67.5%, meaning about two of every three babies were born via a C-section.
Why the concern
A Caesarean section saves mothers and babies when labour goes wrong. It is also, however, major abdominal surgery, with slower recovery rates and higher risks of infection and bleeding, and it leaves a scar that can complicate later pregnancies.
The WHO statement said that across a population, Caesarean rates above 10% are not associated with fewer deaths of mothers or newborns. While the WHO does not recommend a specific rate, the increasing numbers of Caesarean births in West Bengal, and more widely in India, deserve attention.
The opening of the gap
The NFHS’s first three rounds, from 1992-93 to 2005-06, found West Bengal close to the national average when it came to C-sections, at 10.2% against 8.5% by the third NFHS round.
The State then pulled away. Its rate reached 32.6% in NFHS-5, for which West Bengal was surveyed in 2019-21, and by NFHS-6 (2023-24) the gap with India had widened from 1.7 percentage points in 2005-06 to 17.3.
The climb has also grown steeper. The rise of 13.6 points between 2005-06 and 2015-16 took a decade, while the latest 11.9 points came in four to five years.
The data cannot reveal how many of West Bengal’s operations were necessary, though it does show when and where the rise happened.
Prevalence of C-section delivery, West Bengal

| NFHS-1 (1992–93) | 3.3 | 2.5 | +0.8 | — | — | 
| NFHS-2 (1998–99) | 10.3 | 7.1 | +3.2 | +7.0 | +4.6 | 
| NFHS-3 (2005–06) | 10.2 | 8.5 | +1.7 | −0.1 | +1.4 | 
| NFHS-4 (2015–16) | 23.8 | 17.2 | +6.6 | +13.6 | +8.7 | 
| NFHS-5 (2019–21) | 32.6 | 21.5 | +11.1 | +8.8 | +4.3 | 
| NFHS-6 (2023–24) | 44.5 | 27.2 | +17.3 | +11.9 | +5.7 | 
Source: NFHS reports
Private vs. government
Of every 10 women who give birth in a private facility in West Bengal, 9 nine now have a C-section (87.7%). In 2015-16, the year of the memo, the figure was 70.9%. West Bengal’s numbers are also significantly higher than current the national private-sector rate, 54.1%.
While numbers in the government sector are lower, they are also on the rise: government facilities performed C-sections in 28.8% of the births they handled, up from 18.8% in 2015-16 and 1.7 times the national public-sector figure of 16.9%. In Kolkata, the share of births in government facilities delivered by C-section rose from 32.4% in NFHS-5 to 59.1% in NFHS-6.
The move to private care
Births are also increasingly moving to private facilities. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6 their share of the total rose from about 19% to about 29%, even as the public share fell from 72.4% to 65.8%.
These private facilities now perform almost 6 in 10 of the State’s Caesareans (57%). Had births stayed where they were at NFHS-5, the same arithmetic would give a rate of about 38%. The move into private care accounts for more than half of the 11.9-point rise, about 6.6 points, and higher rates in government facilities for most of the rest, about 4.1 points.
The pattern holds outside cities as well. In rural West Bengal, 88.1% of births in private facilities are Caesareans, slightly more than the urban figure of 86.8%.
A belt around Kolkata
On a district map, the highest rates form one contiguous belt in the south of the State. Kolkata and North 24 Parganas are at 67.5% each, Hooghly at 66.6%, Nadia at 62.9%, Purba Medinipur at 59.1% and Howrah at 58.5%.
Urbanisation alone does not account for the belt. Purba Medinipur, a coastal district where 11.6% of people lived in towns at the 2011 Census, has a higher rate than industrial Paschim Bardhaman (48.1%), where 81.6% did.
Purulia, on the Chota Nagpur plateau in the West, has the State’s lowest rate at 21.6%, followed by Jhargram (27.4%), South 24 Parganas (28.5%), Maldah (29.9%) and Bankura (30.1%). Every district except Purulia is above the national average of 27.2%.
A low district average, however, can also obfuscate women in remote blocks who need an emergency Caesarean and cannot get one. Almost every birth in the two districts with the lowest C-section rates now takes place in a health facility (95.7% in Purulia and 97.7% in Jhargram, against 94.9% for the State), so what matters here, is whether those facilities can perform a Caesarean when one is needed. Block-level hospital records would show how often they do.
Behind the rise
Explanations for the rise need records the survey does not hold. The first concerns money.
Swasthya Sathi, the State’s health insurance scheme, was launched in 2016 and opened to every resident on December 1, 2020. It covers up to ₹5 lakh per family a year in government and empanelled private hospitals. Between NFHS-5 and NFHS-6, the share of households with at least one member covered by a health insurance or financing scheme rose from 33.7% to 88.2%.
The timing matches the shift to private care. West Bengal was surveyed for NFHS-5 before the scheme became universal, and the births counted in NFHS-6 straddle the change. A scheme that pays for care in private hospitals would be expected to move births into them. The same years brought the COVID-19 pandemic. By May 2020 the State had set aside 69 hospitals for COVID-19 patients, 16 government-run and 53 privates. The disruption fell on both sectors, and the survey cannot separate its effect from the scheme’s.
Whether the scheme’s payments also tilt private hospitals towards surgery is a question its claims records could settle. They would show what share of delivery claims are Caesareans and how package rates for normal and Caesarean births compare.
Another explanation feeds on itself. A woman with a previous Caesarean can safely try labour only where an emergency operation can follow at once, which most district hospitals in India cannot promise. Each first operation therefore tends to bring a second, and the rate keeps rising over years.
Additionally, more women of childbearing age today are overweight or obese (34.6%, up from 22.7%), and more have 10 or more years of schooling (40%, up from 32.9%). An analysis of NFHS-5 data links both to higher odds of a Caesarean.
What the memo asked for
The 2015 memo already proposed periodic audits by the officials who license private clinics. The WHO statement it enclosed put forward a common method for such audits, the Robson classification. It sorts women into 10 groups by details such as how labour began and the baby’s position, so that hospitals can be compared fairly.
Published for each hospital, including every private hospital empanelled under Swasthya Sathi, the results would show where Caesareans are common among low-risk women, the group most likely to have unnecessary operations.
Fewer unneeded operations also require labour wards that can manage a normal birth safely at any hour, and protocols that let suitable women attempt a vaginal birth after a Caesarean. In Purulia and Jhargram the task would have to run the other way, to keep emergency surgery within reach.
What is needed now
The first step is for the State to say whether the audits suggested in 2015 were ever carried out, and what they found. Caesarean audits must then become routine in government and private hospitals alike, under the health department’s supervision. Swasthya Sathi can check each Caesarean claim against the medical reason recorded for it and devise methods to ensure hospitals are given no reason to prefer surgery.
Every woman who needs a Caesarean should get one without delay, and no woman should have one when there is no compelling medical reason behind it.
(Dr. Margubur Rahaman is a public health researcher with the MAMTA Health Institute for Mother and Child, New Delhi. margubur48@gmail.com Ankit Mishra is an ICSSR Doctoral Fellow at the Govind Ballabh Pant Social Science Institute, Prayagraj. ankitmishrakoraon@gmail.com)

There’s an apocryphal quote attributed to the late, great George Carlin: “It’s the duty of the comedian to find out where the line is drawn and cross it deliberately.”
If that’s true, few have crossed it more frequently—or more fearlessly—than Sacha Baron Cohen. Very few, also, have had the global impact in feature comedy that he has had.
Over the last three decades, Cohen has permeated global pop culture with a range of original characters. In particular, Ali G, his faux-streetwise cultural appropriator from Staines-upon-Thames, and Borat, his blundering Kazakh journalist, have helped drive cultural conversation, even as the work has provoked backlash in equal measure to laughter.
Inclined until recently to let his characters speak for themselves, Cohen has generally taken the public’s response in stride, committed to the goal of helping to “make a slightly more tolerant society” through satire. A master of disguise, whose disruptive influence on comedy dates back to ’90s London, his M.O. has been to send meticulously crafted, memorably buffoonish characters careening through the real world. The goal? To expose the assumptions, prejudices and absurdities of those interacting with them in the real world — whether on the right or left, in a position of tremendous power or someone off the street.
Watch on Deadline
The work that goes into these films, and the stakes behind them are immense; repeatedly, across projects, Cohen has put his life on the line for the sake of a joke. Naturally, then, he’s spoken on more than one occasion about retiring from his work in undercover comedy. He makes the claim, once again, while discussing his latest feature, Ali G: Who Iz I? — his first film centered on the character in more than 20 years, and his first as director.
If this is indeed Cohen’s last outing with his experimental form of filmmaking, he’s gone out with a bang. He calls Who Iz I? his “most extreme and ambitious” movie to date — his version of The Avengers, as a film in which he inhabit multiple of his characters. Not just his breakout character, Ali G, but also two of his creations for Showtime series Who Is America?: the obnoxious ultra-liberal Dr. Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, who becomes the Dr. Evil to Ali G’s Austin Powers, as well as the Israeli anti-terrorism expert Erran Morad. (Notably, Cohen even consulted with Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, the screenwriters behind Avengers: Endgame and myriad other MCU projects, in constructing his narrative.)
Released last month, Who Iz I? finds Ali G resurfacing decades after the cancellation of Da Ali G Show when he learns that his girlfriend Julie (Morgana Robinson) is pregnant and he must find a way to support his family. When Nira Cain-N’Degeocello learns of the return of the “white culture appropriator,” he makes it his mission to get him canceled.
The film culminates in a sequence shot continuously over eight hours and 12 locations, involving nearly 200 crew members and hundreds of carefully choreographed beats. To achieve it, Cohen brought in specialists in prosthetics, animatronics and explosives, alongside magicians and world-famous psychologists.
“The end scene is, according to [VFX supervisor] Rob Legato, the most difficult scene ever shot,” Cohen tells me on today’s episode of Comedy Means Business, “and he worked on Titanic.”
On this week’s podcast, Cohen shares the backstory behind his decision to bring Ali G back, before getting into the extreme prep that’s made his films possible. We also discuss his career beginnings, and how his early academic work and lifelong interest in identity have fueled his films from Ali G Indahouse on — works whose intentions can be easily misinterpreted, which have more on their mind than some give them credit for.
Explaining how each of his character comedies has been approached with a different genre in mind — Who Iz I? is a fugitive thriller — Cohen talks pressing through fear on set, navigating the online discourse around his work, and the unsettling recent “move towards the acceptance of political violence” that inspired his latest film. Also: his studies under iconic French clowning guru Philippe Gaulier, who passed away this year; his concerns surrounding AI; mastering sword fighting for his new play The Popinjay Cavalier, marking a long-in-the-works collaboration with Quentin Tarantino; and more.

Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
- Published
Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.
In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".
In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.
The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.
"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.
Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.
In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".
He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.
He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.
Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.
However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.
"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.
She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which lead to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.
Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.
"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatised… the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.
Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.
Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.
The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.
Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.
Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

He accused the Congress of spreading negativity, obstructing Parliament and challenging election results selectively, and predicted further electoral losses.
Union home minister Amit Shah on Sunday launched a sharp attack on Rahul Gandhi over the INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi, saying the Congress leader had chosen November 1, a date associated with the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, to hold a ‘jalsa’, and that if he wanted to become prime minister, he should stay in a “mock parliament” his entire life.
“If you desire to hold a ‘jalsa’ for the Congress party on such a dark day of genocide, then Rahul ji, no one will be able to take anything except hatred from your ‘mohabbat ki dukaan’,” Shah said at an event in Chandigarh.
Shah said the Congress had been losing elections for 15 years and that Sonia Gandhi’s “dream of seeing her son become prime minister” remained unfulfilled. “For fifteen years — effectively spanning three elections — he has been losing. Sonia-ji’s dream of seeing her son become Prime Minister remains unfulfilled. She has come up with a new approach: holding a ‘mock parliament.’ I would like to tell Rahul-ji: if you want to be Prime Minister, then just stay in a ‘mock parliament’ for the rest of your life — because your turn is never going to come,” he said.

The Kerala government has issued orders for procuring 2,159 bottles of Risdiplam, the first at-home, oral treatment for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), to ensure continued availability of the medicine, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan has said.
Replying to a submission by P.K. Firos, MLA, in the Assembly on Thursday, the Minister said the government was taking several steps through the KARE (Kerala United Against Rare Diseases) scheme to provide timely treatment and life-saving medicines to children affected by SMA, a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function.
Medicines and related treatment were made available through the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, he said.
Keralam used to obtain Risdiplam, under its trade name, at a negotiated price of ₹5.5 lakh per bottle. Since October 19, it had been providing a less expensive generic version of the drug manufactured in the country by Natco Pharma. The drug Natsmart cost only around ₹11,000, significantly bringing down treatment costs and making the medicine available to more children.
Besides medicines, the government also provided physiotherapy, respiratory therapy, respiratory devices, rehabilitation, and surgery, the Minister said.
Keralam has been providing Risdiplam free of cost to children under 12 since 2022 through KARE. Steps have been taken to provide all eligible persons the medicine lifelong, he said.
Referring to two children of a couple who had registered with the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital on October 6 and had Type 2 SMA, the Minister said they were eligible for free Risdiplam. Urgent steps were being taken to provide them with treatment the approval of a technical experts committee. Natsmart was being provided to them. Medicines and treatment would be provided to the couple’s third child through KARE on completion of check-up, he added.
The government would also consider devising more comprehensive programmes in association with the Kerala Social Security Mission to provide treatment and financial and psychological support to the affected children and their families. The government, the Minister said, was committed to ensuring that treatment was not disrupted, medicines were available continuously, and the financial burden on families was reduced.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago, to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

In Summary
- Earclip-style earbuds are getting very popular these days, with the likes of Sennheiser and Samsung also launching buds in this style.
- While they are more stable than conventional earbuds and are designed to let ambient sound in, earclip-style buds have their own pros and cons.
- If you are thinking of grabbing a pair of earclip-style buds for yourself, here are some important points to keep in mind about these buds, which make them very different from traditional, ‘normal’ earbuds.
Sony has released its first. Sennheiser has released its first one too. And so has Samsung. And many others – including Apple and Google – are believed to be readying theirs. We are talking about the clip-style or clip-on earbuds that are now becoming increasingly popular in the personal audio market. As their name indicates, these earbuds are shaped like clips and are attached to your outer ear, rather than inserted into your ear canal. They generally comprise two tiny cylinders, one of which is a speaker and the other of which is a battery, connected with a band, and they are designed to clip onto your ear.
Although they were first seen on the market a couple of years ago, most notably from Huawei and Bose, and were released by many budget-friendly brands, clip-style earbuds are now taking their place in the audio tech spotlight. But what makes these relatively new totally wireless earbuds different from other TWS earbuds, and should you be thinking of getting one for yourself?
Well, here are thirteen points we think you need to know about clip-style earbuds before you clip a pair to your own ears:
Table of Contents
They are on-ear and “open” and generally more comfortable
Clip-style earbuds are on-ear buds, and clip on to the outer ear like an ear cuff. This means that they lie on top of or near the ear canal, and do not go inside it, like many other earbuds. This makes them more comfortable to wear for most users – you do not feel something is inside your ear or just dangling near your earlobe.
They are light
In terms of weight, clip-style earbuds are about the same weight as general buds – about 5-7 grams, based on the design and materials used. For instance, the Sony LinkBuds Clip are about 6.4 grams each, while the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless 5 are 7 grams each, and the AirPods are about 5 grams.
They are incredibly stable and almost NEVER fall off
Clip-style earbuds are among the most stable wireless earbuds. This is because they actually “clip” on to the user’s ear, gently pressing it between a speaker and battery cylinder or sphere. As a result, they are actually attached to your ear on both ends. You can shake your head violently, and they still won’t fall off. In our book, they are as stable as earbuds with hooks that go around your ears.
No ear tip options – one size fits all
As clip-style earbuds do not go into the ear canal, there are almost always no earbud options to let you adjust for a better fit. It is pretty much a one-size-for-everyone rule out there. This can cause a few problems, as the next point will show.
The size of your ear could affect your experience
The fact that there are no size adjustment options available at all in most clip-style earbuds and that they are basically clipped onto your ear means that your experience of them could depend on the size of your ear. Those with relatively large ears might find the speaker end of the buds lying farther away from their ear canal, while those with small ears might find the speaker end coming right on top of their ear canal. There is unfortunately no cure for this, other than making the connecting band on these earbuds adjustable or flexible, which no brand is doing so far.
They come with bigger drivers…
Most clip-style earbuds come with slightly larger drivers than those seen on most TWS. While most TWS have drivers of the size of 5 mm to 8 mm, most clip-style earbuds have drivers that are 10 mm or larger. For instance, the Sennheiser Momentum True Wireless have 7 mm drivers, and the AirPods are believed to have 7.5 mm drivers, while the Sony LinkBuds Clip have 10 mm drivers, and the Moto Buds Loop have 12 mm drivers.
…but are not the loudest
The interesting part, however, is that even though they have larger drivers, most clip-style earbuds are not as loud as other TWS. This is because the larger drivers push sound towards the ear, often going past pockets of air that lie between the buds and the ear canal. Some of the sound inevitably gets lost in this, resulting in lower volume levels.
Love bass? These are not great options
We are going to be up front about it – clip-style earbuds, and in fact most ‘open’ earbuds are not for those who love audio with plenty of bass. The open fit of these buds is not ideal for bass, which sounds best in a packed setup, allowing for reverberations and rumble. Many brands attempt to tune their buds to accent the bass and even use larger drivers, but the result is seldom close to what we get from in-ear earbuds.
External noise comes in…too much external noise sometimes
One of the biggest attractions of clip-style earbuds is that they allow external or ambient sounds to come in too, and do not seal you away from the outside world. However, this is a bit of a mixed blessing, as too much external noise, combined with the lower volumes of these ear clips, can drown out audio. We would not recommend using them in very noisy conditions like traffic jams, or even in gyms with loud noises – those sounds will come right in.
And there is no ANC either, but ENC exists
As they are “open” in design terms, and are actually made in a manner to allow external sounds to come in, clip-style earbuds do not have any active noise cancellation. The microphones on them – for phone calls – do come with some environmental noise cancellation, so call quality on many of these buds can actually be quite good.
Controls can be…challenging
Thanks to their design, which makes them very small, clip-style earbuds almost always have touch controls – there is hardly any room for buttons on them. And as the buds themselves tend to be small, these can be difficult to use and get used to. One inevitably figures out a way to get them working, but they are never quite as comfortable as those on other TWS and earbuds, especially those with stems. These are best controlled from the connected device.
Perfect for those times when you need to listen to your surroundings too (offices, large families, outdoor runs, etc.)
The fact that they are light, stay securely attached to your ear, and allow some ambient noise to come in makes the clip-style earbuds perfect for those places where you need to be aware of sounds around you. They are great for offices in which you need to keep your ears open for queries and remarks from colleagues or even for ringing phones, and even for those who stay in large families and need to keep their ears open, even while listening to music. And of course, we think they are perfect for those who love to go on outdoor runs and rides, as they stay in place and give one access to one’s phone and audio (when allowed) and also keep one aware of traffic and people around one.
Not for audiophiles, gamers, or for intense listening sessions
No matter what the brands tell you, clip-style earbuds are not for those who are very serious about their audio. They seldom deliver the kind of detail and audio quality that one gets from other TWS at their price points. At the most, one can hope for a reasonable level of clarity and a relatively balanced audio signature. While equalizers can make a difference to different frequencies, clip-on style earbuds are not really for audio purists or for those who like to listen very intensely to their music. Their relative lack of volume and limited bass also mean they are not the best option for gaming or even watching films, even though some of them do come with spatial audio. They are, however, excellent for podcasts and live streaming audio, absolutely super for audiobooks, and more than adequate for casual listening.
And one more thing…
They have a special ring carrying mode
One of the biggest problems with most TWS is putting them back in their cases. You need to find the case, open it, take them out of your ears, put them back in the case, and snap it shut. All of which can take some time, especially when you are in a hurry (say, when you want to talk to someone, or get on or off the Metro). Well, that can be avoided with clip-style earbuds. Thanks to their shape, you can simply wrap a clip-style earbud around one of your fingers. Just like a ring. Don’t worry, it won’t fall off easily. No need to fiddle around trying to find their case immediately.

Back to the cyber warfare we saw last night in the app hacking in Ukraine, and then Russia.
As I noted earlier, this was direct attack on a core channel of communications between Ukrainian authorities and citizens; this app is embedded in everyday life in a war zone.
And while the full impact of the hack is still unclear – how many Ukrainians were deceived and believed the warnings?- residents nonetheless have described how alarming it was getting a message on their phone warning of potential nuclear warfare.
Cyber-warfare expert Don Smith, from Sophos’ counter threat unit, says these sorts of attacks are aimed at grounding down people’s mental toughness.
Disinformation is as much a part of war as bombs and bullets. Targeted information attacks could aim to impact the mental resilience of the people of Ukraine.
Their resilience is a key part of their ability to defend against the Russian military.
However he noted the ameaturish nature of this attack. One of the message sent out, in Russian, was almost jokey and casual in tone, reading: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying”, a reference to Russia’s hypersonic missiles which can pretzel and outpace most interceptors.
Usually the best information warfare is not obvious or explicit, where this very clearly is. It could indicate desperation from Russia.
Belgian PM meeting with King to tender resignation
Belgium’s prime minister Bart De Wever is handing in his resignation this morning following failed attempts to pass a budget, local media are reporting.
De Wever has been trying to get budget cuts through, and failed in late-night coalition talks yesterday to secure a compromise.
He arrived at the Royal Palace in Brussels this morning to meet with King Philippe, Belgian media say.
However they report he may be instructed to try and secure a deal again, by a certain deadline.
In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.
Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.
But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.
One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.
The messages sent out were:
22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”
22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]
22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
23:53: An all clear is sent out
Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.
The air raid alert channel said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with the system, which had been temporarily taken off line. It urged users to not click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.
Ukraine and Russia have reported corresponding cyber-hacks on their app warning systems overnight.
These are the mobile apps which send alerts and air-raid warnings, alerting citizens to when missiles and drones are incoming (and thus advising residents to seek shelter or go down to a bunker).
This appears to be the first breach of the app, on such a scale, during the war so far; directly immobilising one of the most important channels of communication authorities have to help advise citizens.
In the Ukraine hack, the app started spewing out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night – warning residents of a nuclear radiation threat in the capital Kyiv, a chemical attack, street fighting and also incoming Oreshnik hypersonic missiles, which Ukraine lacks interceptors for.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued clarification within the hour on Telegram, urging people to remain calm and disregard the messages, one of which was written in Russian.
Some hours later, Russian authorities said its warning app had been hacked and had to be taken offline. A Ukrainian hacker group has claimed to have sent fake alerts warning of nuclear warheads to users inside Russia.
Amid the cyber warfare overnight, both sides also carried out strikes, targeting energy sites like oil refineries. Strikes have been reported in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.

A New South Wales local council has refused to show a world-renowned artwork about children killed in Gaza after asking organisers to investigate hiring “armed guards” to counter the risk of “community conflict” over the mural.
The group, Shoalhaven Friends of Palestine, was aiming to show the Wall of Tears installation by American artist Phil Buehler at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra on Tuesday, following the work being exhibited around Australia, including on the front lawns of Parliament House in Canberra in September.
The massive artwork pays homage to the 18,457 children killed in Gaza between 7 October 2023 and 19 July 2025 and was first shown in New York on 29 January to coincide with the second anniversary of the death of Hind Rajab, a five-year-old left to bleed out among the bodies of six family members after their car was targeted by an Israeli tank.
Shoalhaven city council asked the group to “investigate” the use of “armed guards” in a risk assessment seen by Guardian Australia. The perceived risks included “protest, counter-protest, community conflict,” and “verbal abuse, intimidation or disruption arising from politically sensitive subject matter”.
The group was also asked to reduce the exhibition window from eight days to three days and restrict attendance to RSVPs only in the gallery, which would have “locked doors”.
Organisers were also requested to no longer advertise the event due to potential “reputational risk” for the gallery or council due to their decision to host the exhibition.
“We were like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me,’ but we still wrote back to them and said we would meet all the requirements you want,” said Annette Pham, a member of the group.
 
“We didn’t even know where we could get armed guards, or if you could get them.”
Despite this, email correspondence shows Andrew Constance – the chief executive of the council and former Liberal MP – decided against hosting the event, citing staff safety concerns.
Pham wrote to the council stating she was “deeply disappointed” by the decision and said the “very suggestion that armed guards might be necessary for an exhibition commemorating dead children is deeply disturbing”.
“We are organising a memorial art exhibition, not an event for which Council has disclosed any specific credible threat of violence requiring consideration of armed protection and metal screening,” Pham wrote in her email.
A council spokesperson said in a statement that they had considered the request, but “the installation was deemed to present an unacceptable level of risk to gallery staff, visitors and tenants of the building”.
The council did not respond directly to a question from Guardian Australia about what had triggered the safety concerns.
Pham has now arranged for the work to be installed at Berry Uniting Church on Thursday.
‘They’re children’
Buehler said he was shocked his artwork, which has been shown in cities around the world, could be perceived as posing a safety risk.
“They’re children. They’re like your children, my children,” he said, adding it refers to death toll figures accepted by Israel. The artwork draws from Guardian reporting.
“If you look at the pictures on that mural … There’s kids in their little graduation outfits holding diplomas, they’re holding soccer balls. They’re there with their siblings, or on their father’s shoulder. It was the hardest artwork I’ve ever made, to just live with [what happened to these children], for the time it took to make it.”
“If people would just look at that, how can that be dangerous? The danger is put on by other people who are trying to turn it into something it’s not.”
The artwork has been touring around Australia, including in Adelaide where it was first shown, and Perth where it was shown at the Western Australian state parliament.
Dr Mairead Heaney is part of Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine which helped arrange the exhibition at the WA parliament and the federal Parliament House in Canberra.
She said a number of Labor, Greens and independent MPs visited the artwork when it was displayed in Canberra, including Labor MP Tony Zappia, who made a statement to parliament about it.
Zappia said in his speech: “The banner is a sad reminder of the level of Palestinian human losses, suffering, and daily violations they endure, while much of the world looks away.”

Cyclone Arnab made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts on 28 October 2026, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. Authorities evacuated more than 1.8 lakh people from vulnerable areas in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of the cyclone. As of 29 October 2026, the storm had weakened into a deep depression, but heavy rainfall and flash-flood risks persisted across parts of eastern India. In Andhra Pradesh, seven people were reported killed in cyclone-related incidents, while flooding, uprooted trees, and infrastructure damage disrupted power supplies and transport. The India Meteorological Department has forecast further heavy rainfall in several states over the coming days.
Amid this incident, several visuals are being shared on social media (here, here, here, here, and here) with the claim that they show Cyclone Arnab and the conditions during its landfall. Times Now (archived) and BBC News Telugu (archived) also shared some of these videos in their Instagram posts about Cyclone Arnab. Let’s verify the truth behind these videos in this article.
Claim: The videos show visuals of Cyclone Arnab and the conditions during its landfall.
Fact: None of the videos show Cyclone Arnab or the conditions during its landfall in October 2026. The first video shows a tornado in Bihar’s Vaishali district on 26 September 2026, the second shows a tornado in the US Virgin Islands on 6 July 2026, the third shows a severe storm in Antalya, Turkey, reported on 27 October 2026, and the fourth shows a tornado in Odisha on 15 March 2026. The origin of the fifth video could not be independently verified; however, it has been available online since at least 29 May 2026, predating Cyclone Arnab’s landfall on 28 October 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
Video 1
In our investigation, we found that the same video has been available on the internet since at least 27 September 2026, confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it. The video is reported to show a tornado in Mahisaur village in Bihar’s Vaishali district.
We also found that the same footage was published on TheWeather.net under the headline “A tornado wreaks havoc in the village of Mahisaur, India.” According to the description, the weather phenomenon caught residents off guard, with strong winds lifting objects, damaging structures, and causing destruction. The video was also shared in a Facebook reel by Digital Bihar Live on 27 September 2026, with the caption stating that it was from Mahisaur in Jandaha block of Vaishali district, Bihar.
According to local news reports (here, here), a strong tornado struck the Mahisaur village area in Bihar’s Vaishali district on 26 September 2026, damaging trees, crops, and the roofs of houses.
Video 2
In our investigation, we found that the video shows a tornado that struck the US Virgin Islands on 06 July 2026. The same footage was featured in media reports published in July 2026 (here, here), confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it.
Video 3
In our investigation, we found that the video shows (here, here) a severe storm that struck a construction site in the Kepez district of Antalya, Turkey. The same footage was featured in several media reports (here, here) published on 27 October 2026, reporting that a devastating storm had overturned workers’ accommodation containers and caused a crane to topple. According to local authorities and media reports, four construction workers died, and several others were injured in the incident.
Video 4
In our investigation, we found that the same video has been available on the internet since at least 16 March 2026, confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it. The video reportedly shows a tornado with wind speeds of 170 km/h that struck Odisha.
According to reports (here, here), a tornado triggered by a nor’wester struck four villages in the Karanjia block of Mayurbhanj district, Odisha, on 15 March 2026, killing two people, injuring 29 others, and damaging more than 100 houses.
Video 5
In our investigation, we found that the same video has been available on the internet since at least 29 May 2026, confirming that it predates Cyclone Arnab and is unrelated to it. However, we could not independently verify where the video was filmed or the context in which it was recorded. The available evidence confirms that the video is unrelated to Cyclone Arnab in October 2026.
To sum up, these viral videos are unrelated to Cyclone Arnab’s landfall.

Residents of Ukraine and Russia received fake emergency warnings through government-run mobile apps after the systems were hacked, authorities in both countries said. In Ukraine, some messages falsely warned of an imminent nuclear threat, while others claimed there were high radiation levels, a chemical danger and public disturbances in Kyiv.
The attacks took place late Sunday in Ukraine and early Monday in Russia. It was not immediately clear whether they were connected. Ukraine temporarily suspended its app, which residents use to receive warnings about Russian missile and drone strikes, but said it was back online. Russia’s emergency situations ministry said efforts to restore its app were continuing.
In Ukraine, the fake alerts appeared in English, Russian and Ukrainian, with spelling and grammatical errors in the English-language messages. One Russian-language notification warned: “There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming,” referring to a Russian ballistic missile.
A Russian Telegram channel linked to the country’s security services said hacking group Hitcore had claimed responsibility for the breach of Ukraine’s system. Though the claim has not been independently verified.
There was little indication that the messages caused widespread panic in Ukraine. 
Social media users instead responded with humour, sharing images of pets and AI-generated apocalypse scenes. Ukraine’s air raid alert channel said “unauthorized parties” had interfered with the app and urged users not to click links in suspicious notifications. The country’s Center for Countering Disinformation advised residents to follow other emergency channels while the breach was being addressed.
Ukrainian air force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said in a television interview that the attack had not affected the country’s security or defence operations.
In Russia, the Emergency Situations Ministry said a false alert was sent through its app at around 2.45am Moscow time across 33 of the country’s 89 regions. The ministry said it had identified the digital vulnerability exploited by the hackers and was taking steps to prevent another breach. It added that the wider public warning system remained operational through text messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian government agencies faced a constant threat of cyberattacks, including attacks increasingly involving artificial intelligence. “All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources,” he said.
The cyberattacks came as a limited ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region expired on Monday. The arrangement, which began on October 27, had allowed humanitarian aid and evacuation missions into front-line areas, including the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
