A video claiming to show a woman police officer mistreating a Muslim man is being shared on social media (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows a woman police officer mistreating a Muslim man.
Fact: The video is scripted content on the channel named‘Amit Dixit Social Message’. The video carries a disclaimer that the video is fictitious. The channel features several videos with the same characters seen in the viral video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the footage uploaded to a Facebook page named ‘Amit Dixit Social Message ‘. The video carries a disclaimer that the video is fictitious.
The same video from a different angle is uploaded to a YouTube channel with the same name on 19 September 2025, with the title in Hindi: ‘Salim misbehaved at the police station; The police put him inside.’
We found several other videos (here, here, here) on the same YouTube channel, featuring the same woman dressed as a police officer. We also found videos, including a video similar to the viral video on the channel, carrying a disclaimer clarifying that the content is scripted and does not depict real incidents (here, here, here).
To sum up, the video showing a woman police officer mistreating a Muslim man is scripted.

TRAI mandates AI-led complaint centres, 16-hour human support
TRAI mandates 24/7 AI-enabled complaint centres, human support for 16 hours daily, faster appeals and penalties up to ₹20 lakh for mishandled cases.
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has directed telecom operators and internet service providers (ISPs) to run round-the-clock complaint centres that can be handled by AI agents, while mandating human assistance for at least 16 hours a day. It has also introduced penalties of up to ₹20 lakh per quarter per service area for improper disposal or handling of consumer disputes, under amended telecom consumer complaint redressal rules released on Monday.
TRAI said the rules would be published in the gazette.
For the first time, the telecom regulator has included AI-based customer care services in a binding rule under the Telecom Consumer Complaint Redressal (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026. The rules, amended after more than a decade, were last revised on July 1, 2014.
The amended regulation 3(3) requires AI systems to “operate with appropriate human oversight” and consumers to receive “a notification” that they are speaking to an AI agent.
Under the amended rules, service providers will be charged ₹1,000 for every complaint and ₹5,000 for every appeal found to have been wrongly disposed of, with penalties capped at ₹20 lakh per quarter per service area.
TRAI also directed operators to submit quarterly performance reports, including number of complaints and appeals received, disposed of and pending, time taken for disposal and feedback survey results, in a format specified by the regulator.
Late submission of quarterly reports will attract penalties of up to ₹5,000 a day for 15 days and ₹20,000 a day thereafter, capped at ₹10 lakh per licensed service area.
The draft regulations were released on May 7, with stakeholder comments invited until June 12 and countercomments until June 19. TRAI received 32 comments and 24 countercomments, which it uploaded to its website. An open house discussion was held on July 17.
Operators opposed the 24x7 complaint-centre requirement on cost grounds. In its explanatory memorandum, TRAI said some stakeholders objected to round-the-clock operations, “citing disproportionate costs and limited benefit”.
The regulator responded that the requirement “does not necessarily imply deployment of the same level of resources 24x7”.
TRAI received 73,081 complaints in 2025-26, up from 44,733 in 2023-24, pointing to dissatisfaction with operators’ grievance redressal systems.
Some stakeholders have also questioned whether TRAI can impose penalties through regulations. The penalties under the current rule are new, however the regulator has been imposing financial disincentives under the Standards of Quality of Service of Access (Wireline and Wireless) and Broadband (Wireline and Wireless) Service Regulations, 2024. This was also a concern for some stakeholders who said this may result in double penalties on telecom service providers. But TRAI said the two serve “distinct regulatory objectives”.
The telecom regulator has also scrapped the advisory committees and replaced them with oversight committees in every service provider to oversee and periodically review the functioning of its grievance redressal mechanism. Consumer groups, who sent 22 of the 32 comments on the draft, opposed the move, with one saying it makes the system “operator reviewing operator”.
TRAI said the committees caused delays, making the appellate process inadequate. Appeal timelines have also been halved, with consumers getting 15 days instead of 30 to appeal and the appellate authority is required to decide within 15 days.
Other key changes
Helplines must use a standard IVRS menu with separate options for complaints, appeals and queries, along with a human option and a call-back facility. Complaints can be registered through apps and websites, with status updates by SMS and email, and service must be offered in a state official language besides Hindi and English.
After every closed complaint, consumers will be asked to rate the resolution from 1 to 5, and the results will be published quarterly. Disputes must be resolved through a non-chargeable numbers instead of a dedicated toll-free system, providers must set up dedicated desks and accessible apps for persons with disabilities, and records must be kept for six months, up from three.
ISPs with 10,000 or fewer subscribers are exempt from the rules, which consumer groups said leaves small-town and rural users without a remedy. Satellite service providers are also covered under the rules, while OTT services are outside TRAI’s jurisdiction.
The rules take effect 30 days after Gazette publication. The oversight committee, survey and reporting rules apply after 60 days, and the 24x7 centres, IVRS and app rules after 90 days.

An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers’ machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.
The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.
In search of cloud credentials
“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here.
Anthropic has yet to issue public notice of the incident to customers.
Cursor said that the malicious extension attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor using an added attacker-controlled SSH key, enabling the local SSH service, and opening a reverse SSH tunnel. The code was written to work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Because Cursor extensions run with the permissions of the tool’s Integrated Development Environment, the backdoored version likely would gain access to local files, source code, and developer tooling once it was installed.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

Pronto founder Anjali Sardana’s physical AI venture Provision Labs has acquired Mumbai-based hardware startup Basilisk Industries for an undisclosed sum. Basilisk founder Shourya Watwani will lead Provision’s hardware efforts and work on its in-house post-processing models, Sardana said in a LinkedIn post announcing the acquisition. Founded by Watwani in 2023, Basilisk focused on perception technologies, which help machines interpret their surroundings. According to Sardana, Watwani and his team have already developed a 3D hand-tracking model, redesigned Provision’s perception hardware, and built the first version of a lightweight tactile glove to capture touch-related data. Provision is also expanding its engineering and research teams across San Francisco, Toronto, and Bengaluru. It is hiring for work in computer vision, perception and tactile data, environment reconstruction, and hardware. Building Physical AI Infrastructure Sardana recently launched San Francisco-based Provision Labs to collect data for training and testing physical AI systems — AI designed to perform real-world tasks through robots and other machines. The startup plans to source training data from professionals across sectors globally to help developers deploy their physical AI models. Sardana serves as CEO of both Provision and Pronto. Provision’s launch followed scrutiny of Pronto’s household recording pilot, which involved service professionals wearing cameras while performing tasks such as cleaning, washing dishes, and folding laundry. The use of footage captured inside customers’ homes to generate training data for physical AI and robotics systems raised questions about privacy, consent, and data storage. Pronto maintained that customers had to opt in while booking and that the pilot covered less than 0.01% of its users. It also said the pilot complied with India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and that the footage would not be shared with third-party AI labs. Among its competitors, Snabbit said it had conducted a one-time simulation test at a training centre with data collection startup Human Archive. Urban Company said it had never recorded inside customers’ homes and had no plans to do so.

President Donald Trump is approaching the halfway point of his second term, raising the question of what — and who — comes next. And, more existentially: Can the MAGA movement survive without him?
The right is rehabbing…Richard Nixon?
You do not, under any circumstances, have to hand it to the 37th president.
To answer that question, some younger conservatives on the “New Right” are looking to a past US president for inspiration: Richard Milhous Nixon.
In June, Vice President JD Vance spoke at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum in California, downplaying the scandal that ended Nixon’s presidency. If Watergate happened today, Vance said, it would be “like a 12-hour news story. Like, the idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy.”
Watergate, of course, is the most famous scandal in presidential history and the reason so many of our contemporary imbroglios get tagged with the -gate suffix. It began with a 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee’s headquarters in Washington’s Watergate complex by operatives linked to Nixon’s reelection campaign. Investigations — and a huge volume of Oval Office tapes recorded by Nixon — exposed Nixon’s involvement in the cover-up, and he resigned in 1974 facing the prospect of impeachment and removal from office.
Nevertheless, some conservatives are now embracing a rehabilitation of Nixon’s image dubbed “Nixonmaxxing.” They portray him as a president brought down by the “deep state” — an entrenched network of unelected government officials that they believe also tried to undermine Trump during his first term (and is still trying today).
Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with political historian Michael Koncewicz, the associate director of New York University’s Institute for Public Knowledge, about what actually brought Nixon down, why Watergate was, in fact, a big deal, and why some conservatives are undeterred and looking to the 37th president for inspiration today.
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Because we live in a fallen world, we are here today to talk about something they’re calling Nixonmaxxing. Why are young conservatives interested in former President Richard Milhous Nixon?
Nixon’s ultimately known for Watergate, and Watergate for decades was the ultimate scandal in American politics. And younger conservatives are starting to revisit this history and they’ve started to compare the Watergate scandal to numerous attempts to bring down the Trump presidency.
Nixon is a martyr for the cause. Nixon is the guy who was successfully brought down by the liberal establishment. And so if younger conservatives can rescue Nixon from liberal historians and liberal journalists, they think that they can protect the current president for decades to come.
In the last decade or so, more and more media figures — and this has seeped down into conservative activists — have questioned a story that most Americans accept, which is that Watergate was a moment where the system worked. It’s a moment where Congress, the media, and the American public helped bring down a corrupt president.
Conservative activists want you to believe that that’s not true. And the main reason is that if they can make you believe that that’s a lie, then they can make you question any future scandal that could affect any one of their guys.
What was the Watergate scandal? What did Richard Nixon actually do?
Watergate can best be understood as a story that begins, at least, in the summer of 1971. After the release of the Pentagon Papers, which was a secret history of the Vietnam War compiled by figures in the Johnson administration, Richard Nixon is enraged.
In the summer of 1971, the reason that this matters and why it’s linked to Watergate is that in the wake of the Pentagon Papers coming out, Nixon authorizes the creation of the “Plumbers” unit: a group of shady guys with CIA and FBI on their resume, people who have experience doing black bag jobs.
“It remains to be seen how influential Nixonmaxxing is as a political phenomenon. Richard Nixon is still seen as one of the worst, most corrupt presidents in American history.”
The first operation that they pull off is breaking into Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist’s office — he’s the man who leaked the Pentagon Papers. It’s referred to by Nixon historians as Watergate West. But when they pull this off, they are not caught and it’s dismissed as just a weird moment. No one knows that at the time these are guys being paid by the White House to break into buildings and spy on political opponents.
There’s a lot of other activities that happened between summer of ’71 and June of ’72, but the Watergate burglars, the Plumbers, are caught at the Watergate Hotel. And what is at the Watergate Hotel? It is the offices of the Democratic National Committee.
They’re caught in June of ’72, and even then it’s dismissed as a so-called third-rate burglary because this just seems like some overeager campaign staff members who have nothing to do with the Nixon White House.
But on the tapes, we know that Richard Nixon, even if he didn’t have any link to the Watergate break-in, knows that he created this team. He knows that his advisers are aware of different parts of their activities over the previous year. That was not uncovered until 1973, which is when most of the American people and most people in Congress started to take this scandal seriously. Watergate ends Nixon’s presidency when it becomes clear to the American people that he has something to hide.
The famous phrase attached to Watergate is that it was not the crime, it’s the coverup. That’s true to an extent, in terms of what was on the tapes that made it very clear that Nixon was obstructing justice. But he was covering up pretty serious crimes. He was covering up a lot of improper uses of presidential power.
And so in the summer and fall of 1973, that is when Richard Nixon’s approval rating started to decline — a 25 percent approval rating. And when people ask why Richard Nixon stepped down, that’s the No. 1 reason. When his approval rating is that low, members of Congress feel the pressure to take on an unprecedented action, which is impeachment. The House was going to impeach Richard Nixon and the Senate was going to convict Richard Nixon.
And so in subsequent years and decades, there’s this understanding that Watergate was a bad thing. Watergate was a serious constitutional crisis and that it was good that Richard Nixon stepped down, that our democracy was strengthened as a result of Watergate. And today’s conservatives are increasingly questioning that narrative.
Richard Nixon wouldn’t be in the position he is in currently if he hadn’t done some things that a certain type of conservative today thinks is noble or laudable or important.
What was he doing at the time that makes a guy like Chris Rufo or the vice president say, “Hey, you know what? We need to reconsider Nixon”?
Figures like Christopher Rufo are drawn to Richard Nixon because the historical record shows that behind the scenes, he was a fierce culture warrior.
Other presidents in the post-World War II era were certainly guilty of improper uses of presidential power. Nixon’s key difference was he wanted to bring that into the White House and micromanage the hell out of it. And Christopher Rufo loves that about Richard Nixon. He believes that presidents should use their powers to go after groups that he thinks are hurting the country.
We now know that Nixon was a far more aggressive culture warrior behind the scenes.
He was someone who wanted to create a new establishment, one that would weaken liberals in the media. Richard Nixon said on the Nixon tapes in a meeting with his closest advisers, [“The professors are the enemy. Professors are the enemy. Write that on the blackboard 100 times and never forget it.”]
Both Christopher Rufo and our current vice president, JD Vance, love the quote. JD Vance, when he was running as a Senate candidate in late 2021, gave a speech at the National Conservatism Conference and he used that quote.
This was just five years ago, and it would’ve been unthinkable for any conservative politician to favorably quote Richard Nixon, especially if they had aspirations to be president of the United States someday. But our current vice president, JD Vance, someone who will likely run for president in 2028, has publicly embraced Richard Nixon’s legacy.
President Trump is apparently in decline and his hold on the Republican Party over the next couple years will weaken, right? With so many of these stories, you wonder whether it’s like a handful of coconuts being nutty or whether this kind of effort means something for the future of the Republican Party.
Do you think that this is notable, important, or significant?
It remains to be seen how influential Nixonmaxxing is as a political phenomenon. Richard Nixon is still seen as one of the worst, most corrupt presidents in American history.
I used to lead school tours at the Richard Nixon Library 10, 15 years ago, and I would regularly talk to high school students, sometimes even middle school students, and they came in with a little bit of knowledge about Richard Nixon, and that knowledge was usually centered around the fact that Nixon got in trouble and Nixon was bad.
I am slightly encouraged by that fact because it shows you that Watergate is still viewed as an exceptional period of time.
However, as I told people during Trump’s first administration, Watergate should be seen as a product of a very different political culture. It wasn’t just that the system worked — it did — but it worked because our democratic culture was far stronger than it is today. Our civic institutions were far stronger than they are today. You had a broader culture of dissent and a broader culture of questioning our president that contributed to Nixon’s downfall.
Unfortunately, our political culture today is far more divided and far less willing to rally around a single narrative that would lead to another Watergate resignation happening in the same way [as] what we saw in the summer of 1974.

TIRUPATI: The accused in the Raptadu classroom chainsaw attack, Hemanth, may have to undergo amputation of his right leg after sustaining severe gunshot injuries during a police encounter in the Atmakur forest area on Sunday evening.
Hospital superintendent Dr D Malleswari said Hemanth was stable but faced a serious risk of losing part of his right leg. Medical assessments found that severe damage to the limb had affected blood circulation, causing the tissue to deteriorate rapidly.
Doctors said amputation, potentially up to the knee, might be necessary to prevent further complications.
Preliminary X-rays of both legs did not show any lodged bullets. However, further tests, including additional X-rays and specialised scans, are being conducted. An anaesthetist is also monitoring his condition to assess his fitness for surgery.
A team of orthopaedic specialists and general surgeons will examine the extent of vascular damage in the operation theatre before deciding whether to proceed with the amputation.
Hemanth was allegedly involved in a chainsaw attack on two minor Class 10 students at a Zilla Parishad government school in Raptadu on Saturday morning.
One of the girls, who sustained severe injuries, was shifted to Manipal Hospital in Bengaluru, where a multidisciplinary team of doctors performed complex orthopaedic and plastic surgeries. She is now in the recovery phase.
Hemanth fled after the attack. Special police teams tracking him located him near the Atmakur forest area on Sunday evening. Police said the teams opened six rounds of fire after he allegedly tried to attack inspector Venkateswarulu during a confrontation.
The police took the severely injured accused into custody and admitted him to the Government General Hospital in Anantapur.

India’s clean energy transition is attracting significant capital, but much of it is flowing into utility-scale projects. Smaller installations across factories, commercial buildings and industrial facilities continue to face a financing gap, even when the technology is commercially viable and can help businesses lower operating costs. Two Point O Capital wants to channel capital into this underserved segment by bringing financing, technology and project execution under one platform. To fuel its ambition, the startup has now raised $10 Mn (nearly ₹95 Cr) in its Series A round led by Transition Venture Capital (TVC). The round also saw participation from existing backer Omnivore and angel investors Chiranjeev Singh Saluja and Sudhir M Reddy. The startup plans to utilise a major chunk of the fresh proceeds towards financing the deployment of clean energy assets for its commercial and industrial (C&I) customers. The capital will also be utilised to strengthen the startup's tech stack and ramp up hiring. The latest round comes two years after Two Point O raised over $6 Mn, via a mix of equity and debt, in 2024 . “There was a lot of capital that was getting pumped into utility-scale, grid-scale projects. But there wasn’t enough capital inflows into the distributed or decentralised energy projects, to put it simply, for industries and buildings,” cofounder and CEO Karan Bhutani told Inc42. Founded in 2024 by Bhutani, Archit Mehrotra, Manya Ranjan and Shashidhar Reddy, Two Point O provides financing, turnkey solutions and equipment leasing across areas such as rooftop solar, battery energy storage systems (BESS) and wastewater treatment. Unlike traditional banks and NBFCs, the startup claims to be focused on smaller-scale projects. Building A Full-Stack Clean Energy Platform Two Point O positions itself as a full-stack clean energy enablement platform for commercial and industrial (C&I) customers. Its offerings span four asset classes: Rooftop Solar: Distributed solar installations for commercial and industrial facilities BESS: Solutions to optimise energy consumption and manage peak demand Energy Efficiency: Upgrades across heating, cooling and air compressors Wastewater treatment: Projects to improve water treatment and resource utilisation The startup offers multiple financing structures. It operates a wholly-owned NBFC subsidiary, which handles loan disbursals, while a separate operating entity caters to lease and service-based requirements. Bhutani also claims that the startup has built a proprietary underwriting engine that uses technology to assess a project’s technical specifications, performance and credit profiles. This allows Two Point O to dish out a techno-commercial proposal for a client within 24 to 48 hours, he added. Two Point O also monitors assets after deployment. Bhutani said that all deployed assets are IoT-enabled, with real-time data used for preventive maintenance, performance optimisation and verification. Notably, the startup does not directly undertake installation and maintenance. Instead, it relies on original equipment manufacturers as well as engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) partners for execution, and oversees them through technology and contracts. Bhutani said that this “light-touch” model gives the startup the ability to scale its operations. Inside Two Point O’s Cross-Selling Model India’s clean tech market, as per IMARC Group, could become a $95 Bn opportunity by 2034. Two Point O is eyeing a much smaller piece of this market as it operates at the intersection of lending tech and B2B clean energy enablement segments. To carve a niche in the space, Two Point O has so far focused on roping in big-ticket clients and cross-selling additional solutions to these customers. This approach, as per Bhutani, allows the startup to keep customer acquisition costs low and get more out of its users. So far, the startup claims to have already onboarded around 25-30 large customers, including Premier Energies, Godrej, JK Tyre, Morepen Pharma, Wipro and Phoenix Mills. Bhutani estimates that its existing customer base could generate ₹400-500 Cr in transactions over the next two to three years. The startup also noted that its assets under management (AUM) grew 1.5X sequentially in each of the last three quarters. Not stopping there, the startup has much more in store going forward: Enter the SME segment and expand across India Build an AUM of $75 Mn to $100 Mn over the next couple of years Expand into new sectors like data centres, automotives, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and healthcare Inc42 Take: Can Two Point O Scale Its Multi-Asset Model? Two Point O is addressing a financing gap in distributed clean energy by combining capital, technology and project execution. What works for the startup is its multi-asset model, which could help deepen relationships with existing customers and generate repeat business. However, scaling across asset classes will require strong underwriting, consistent asset performance and effective oversight of operating partners. The planned SME expansion also brings additional challenges around technology risks, regulations and credit assessment. The startup's ability to turn its customer base and growing AUM into sustained revenue and profitability remains to be seen, particularly as it expands its portfolio and deployment commitments.

Britain’s medicines regulator on Friday approved Johnson & Johnson’s daily pill for adults and teenagers with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, a skin condition causing red, scaly and often itchy or painful patches.
The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved the oral drug Icotyde for people aged 12 and older who weigh at least 40 kg. The approval was based on four late-stage trials in 2,500 people with the disease, including 72 teenagers aged 12 to under 18. In all four studies, patients who took the drug saw better results after 16 weeks than those given a placebo, the regulator said.
Icotyde was approved in the U.S. earlier this year for the same condition — its first approved indication. The drug is made in collaboration with Protagonist Therapeutics. J&J is also studying the drug, chemically known as icotrokinra, for ulcerative colitis, psoriatic arthritis and Crohn’s disease.
The company expects the treatment to bring in $5 billion in peak sales across multiple indications. The drug competes with established psoriasis treatments such as Bristol Myers Squibb’s Sotyktu and AbbVie’s blockbuster Skyrizi.

What a new global study on pain reveals about women’s experiences
The study’s findings about women having a higher prevalence of pain across anatomical sites, resonate with observations from India, say experts, noting that even so, women’s pain has historically been under-recognised, misunderstood, or inadequately treated
pain killers and a woman in pain, expression of suffering.
| Photo Credit: blueclue
Women are more likely than men to report pain across every one of the 11 anatomical sites examined in a global study involving more than 6.1 million people across 118 countries. The study found that differences were particularly pronounced for facial pain, headaches and abdominal pain.
Published in Nature Medicine, the study found that women had 83% higher relative prevalence of facial pain, 74% higher prevalence of headaches and 60% higher prevalence of stomach or abdominal pain than men. Women were also more likely to report high-intensity and widespread pain, highlighting a disparity that extends beyond the occurrence of pain to its severity and distribution.

Sandy Frank, the veteran TV distributor and producer, has died at the age of 97.
Frank is best known for producing and distributing game shows such as Name That Tune and The Dating Game as well as bringing Japanese monster movies to the United States.
Starting out as a sales executive for Paramount Pictures in the late 1940s, Frank went on to work at NBC before becoming President of Worldwide Sales at Wrather Corporation, which produced and distributed Lassie and Lone Ranger.
He subsequently launched Sandy Frank Program Sales, where he sold series including You Asked For It before also moving into production with Sandy Frank Entertainment (SFE).
Series he worked on included Name That Tune, Face The Music, The Parent Game and The Dating Game.
Watch on Deadline
Sandy Frank Entertainment also produced Battle of the Planets, a U.S. adaptation of the Japanese anime series Science Ninja Team Gatchaman, after discovering the series at Mip TV in Cannes. The series was an after-school hit throughout the 1970s.
He was also well known for bringing other Japanese content to the U.S. including the Gamera films with a number of them including Fugitive Alien and Time of the Apes appearing on Mystery Science Theater 3000.
Well known as a syndicator and distributor, Frank also funded a children’s orphanage in Cannes and would regularly arrange for Mip attendees, including buyers, to attend the orphanage during the market.
“For over 50 years, SFE was synonymous with a take no prisoners style of television sales. Mr. Frank was a bigger-than-life TV executive. To say he was unrelenting and tenacious would be an understatement. The lengths Mr. Frank would go to make a sale were legendary [even] if it meant forcing a plane to land to get to a meeting or being relentlessly persistent until the TV station program buyer finally surrendered and made a deal,” said Frank’s longtime collaborator Bob Cohen. “Sandy Frank was the opposite character of the schlepper salesman Billy Loman in Death of a Salesman. Mr. Frank cut a glamorous style of a TV executive jet-setting around the globe, usually with the arm of a beautiful lady companion. Handsome, lean, fashionable, Mr. Frank left an indelible mark on modern TV production and distribution.”
Frank’s proudest moment was acquiring the rights to Anwar Sadat’s autobiography with Sadat, the miniseries, produced in 1983 by Columbia Pictures with Frank becoming the first Jew to address the Egyptian Parliament.
The executive also championed the cause of independent TV production by fighting the repeal of the Prime-Time Access Rule (PTAR). The PTAR limited the hours the networks could program, benefiting independent producers.
“For those of us who loved him, he was caustic, manic, tough, generous, smart, fearless, sensitive, and a genius. He truly was one-of-a-kind, and his gravestone will read America’s Best TV Syndicator,” added Cohen.

How do the world's largest economies stack up when it comes to educating the next generation? According to the OECD’s PISA 2025 results, released in September 2026, educational outcomes worldwide show a stark regional divide.
Measuring the proficiency of 15-year-old students in mathematics, science, and reading across 91 participating education systems, the assessment serves as a critical barometer for future workforce readiness.
While East Asian nations continue to set the benchmark, other major powers are navigating systemic shifts and pandemic-era learning losses.
Check where major world powers—including the US, China, India, the UK, and Russia—rank, based on Visual Capitalist's top-40 rankings:
East Asia is home to the world’s highest-scoring students, with the region occupying all six of the top spots globally. China’s participating regions—specifically Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang—lead the world in both mathematics and science.
Researchers attribute this regional success to academic discipline, rigorous curricula, strong teacher development, and cultural attitudes toward effort and achievement.
However, it is important to note that these Chinese results represent four relatively prosperous regions and do not reflect the country’s national student population as a whole.
Singapore, another Asian powerhouse, ranks first globally in reading.
The United States has been placed 16th overall with an average score of 485, according to the list.
A breakdown of the subjects shows a significant disparity: while American students scored 502 in science and 490 in reading, they struggled in mathematics with a score of just 463.
According to a Brookings analysis, American test scores have been declining since the 2010s, a trend severely accelerated by pandemic disruptions. Beyond learning loss, North American schools are facing heavy pressure from widening socioeconomic disparities, chronic absenteeism, and severe teacher shortages.
While the global rankings evaluate 91 education systems in total, specific placement data and scores for India, the United Kingdom, and Russia are currently missing from this draft.
No African nations appeared in the top 40 due to limited PISA participation and infrastructural challenges cited by UNESCO.

Kolkata witnessed an unusual procession on Saturday, October 31, as thousands of book lovers took to the streets carrying books instead of political flags. Called “Let’s Walk for Books”, the march was organised in protest against the alleged vandalism of Left-affiliated bookstalls by BJP workers and police during Durga Puja festivities across West Bengal.
The procession began at College Square, the hub of Kolkata’s literary and academic life as well as the publishing industry, following an appeal circulated on social media over several days. Among those who urged people to join were prominent academics, writers and public figures, including Pabitra Sarkar, Shamik Bandyopadhyay, Jawhar Sircar, Kumar Rana, Malini Bhattacharya, Ziad Ali, Paranjoy Guha Thakurta and Shobhanlal Dasgupta.
The appeal, which urged participants to carry a book each, said books were facing a ‘barbaric’ attack across the state.
Bookstalls have long been part of Durga Puja festivities in Bengal, along side fairs, music, theatre and poetry events.
This year, however, several bookstalls were allegedly vandalised, their organisers assaulted, and books thrown onto the streets and trampled underfoot, the appeal noted. In Jadavpur, an attempt was allegedly made to demolish bookstalls with the help of central forces. A Kolkata Municipal Corporation garbage truck was also brought in to remove newly printed books.
The appeal described the incidents as an assault on Bengal’s cultural traditions and warned that continued attacks on books could damage the state’s reputation and values. It called on writers, artists, students, teachers, publishers, booksellers and others to assemble in front of the Vidyasagar statue at College Square, carrying a book of their choice as a symbol of resistance.
The Rally
Responding to the appeal, people began gathering around College Street from 3 pm. Students from colleges and universities joined participants across generations, from middle-aged people to the elderly. Almost everyone carried a book.
The collection reflected a wide range of political, literary and religious traditions. Participants carried works by Rabindranath Tagore, Karl Marx, Bhagat Singh, Sukanta Bhattacharya and Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, alongside books by contemporary writers such as Arundhati Roy. Some carried works by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, while others held copies of the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and books on Swami Vivekananda.
Scheduled to begin at 3.30 pm, the march started around 3.45 pm, with several thousand people taking part. In a city accustomed to processions marked by political flags, banners and party slogans, this one stood out. Participants carried books and sang songs.
They sang the Bengali translation of Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet’s song “They Don’t Let Us Sing”, as well as Rabindranath Tagore’s “Bnadh Bhenga Dao”. International protest songs, including “We Shall Overcome” and its Bengali version, “Amra Korbo Joy”, also featured in the procession.
Large banners, or tifos, carried messages such as “Don’t Burn Books, Read Them” and “Books versus Bulldozer”.
The procession also offered glimpses of solidarity among participants. An elderly newspaper vendor distributed candies to those taking part. In a video shared on social media, he said he had joined the march because of his love for books. Although financial difficulties had prevented him from completing his education, he said, he had always loved reading and ensured that his daughter completed her education.
Starting in front of College Square and Calcutta University, the march passed the National Book Agency and the iconic sweet shops, Putiram and Mouchaak, on Surya Sen Street, before entering Bankim Chatterjee Street. It then proceeded past the College Street Coffee House and Presidency University before returning to College Square.
Several videos shared on social media showed people standing on balconies and outside shops, recording the procession on their smartphones. Marchers waved at onlookers along the route.
Left leaders Mohammed Salim, Sujan Chakraborty and Biman Basu also joined the procession, walking at the back.
After the march, the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA) organised a brief cultural programme in front of the College Square gate. Activists performed songs including “Tu Zinda Hai”, Paul Robeson’s “Ol’ Man River” and Bhupen Hazarika’s Bengali adaptation, “O Ganga Boichho Keno”.
Addressing the gathering, senior Left leader Biman Basu said people who believed in reading books had come together for the march. He added that efforts to promote reading must continue whenever books come under attack.
Participants said the protest was not about defending any particular political ideology. A book, they said, was neither Left-wing nor Right-wing; it was simply a book. Some described the attacks during Durga Puja as an assault on education, free thought and rationalism, and said they had joined the march to collectively resist such incidents in the future.
SFI central executive committee member Shuvajit Sarkar (in blue shirt in photo below), who participated in the march, said, “Fascists and communal forces oppose books because books promote rationality and reject blind subordination. We will defend books and continue the struggle against the divisive politics of the RSS and BJP until we defeat it.”

Prices on gaming laptops are out of control. The ongoing memory shortage has made laptops more expensive across the board, but it's hit gaming laptops especially hard. Some manufacturers have even resorted to launching “new" gaming laptops in 2026 with the RTX 4050 as the starting configuration—and that graphics card is more than three years old.
Given this landscape, there's really only one gaming laptop under $1,500 that I feel comfortable recommending. That's the Lenovo LOQ 15. It's not the thinnest or most powerful gaming laptop in the world, but for this price, there's nothing else like it.
It's not that the price of the LOQ 15 hasn't gone up over the past year alongside its gaming-laptop brethren. (It certainly has.) For the first few months of 2026—the good old days—it was selling for less than $1,000. But even then, it was technologically ahead of its rivals in a number of ways, offering strong performance paired with a high-quality IPS display. So many cheap gaming laptops come with pitifully desaturated screens that put a damper on the gaming experience. That's really what sets the LOQ 15 apart from the competition.
Also significant is the fact that, right now, you can buy the LOQ 15 with an RTX 5060 for just $1,300. That's not any cheaper than it normally has been (at least not for the past few months). However, the RTX 5060 is a big upgrade over the RTX 5050, especially with the 100 watts of power that the system can throw at it. Every game I tested could play at well over 60 frames per second at the medium preset, including heavier games like Black Myth: Wukong and Monster Hunter Wilds. You can always push frame rates higher by adjusting settings further or by adding a dash of upscaling.
Amazon has the RTX 5060 configuration, which also comes with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, for $1,300, but Lenovo also has a killer deal on the RTX 5050 configuration that's about as cheap as it gets: $999 for an RTX 5050 (and otherwise identical specs). I've tested a number of other gaming laptops that sell for around this price, such as the MSI Cyborg A16 and the Acer Nitro V 16, and none can compete with the LOQ 15. I've also tested the Alienware 15 and Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 recently, and both suffer from the same problem.
As much as I wish I could recommend a budget gaming laptop that's newer, none I've tried have successfully dethroned the Lenovo LOQ 15. While you could wait until Black Friday to see if prices dip further, note that I haven't seen much fluctuation over the past few months. For example, it wasn't on a deeper sale during the October Amazon Prime Day—and yet, it was still the best gaming laptop deal you could get.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, seventeen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty five startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO and Razorpay alone could raise nearly ₹20,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 AceVector Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands. The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025. Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price. On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025.
