Australia’s world-leading under-16s social media ban will face its first major legal challenge on Tuesday, as Reddit and an advocacy group headed by a libertarian politician seek to overturn the law in the high court.
Nearly 11 months ago, 10 platforms – Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Kick, X, Twitch and Threads – were required to deactivate or suspend the accounts of users they determined to be aged under 16 years.
Since then, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has said more than 5m accounts across the 10 services have been suspended as part of the ban.
Whether the ban will stay will be the subject of the high court hearings on Tuesday and Wednesday this week as Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project – led by New South Wales state Libertarian MP John Ruddick – seek to overturn the ban.
Australia does not have a guaranteed right to freedom of speech, and the case largely focuses on whether preventing under-16s from holding a social media account impermissibly burdens the implied freedom of political communication in Australian law.
Reddit has argued in its submission to the court that online platforms are a “common source of news and political information” in Australia. The company pointed to its “Ask Me Anything” sessions on the site where users have historically asked questions of politicians of candidates.
Teens, Reddit said, would not be able to make posts on politics, comment or react to political content, or engage with the social media accounts of the youth wings of the major political parties.
The Australian government has argued in its defence that the law serves the legitimate purposes of seeking to reduce the risk of harm for under-16s from social media platforms for the “harmful features” including algorithms, infinite scroll, persistent notifications and likes.
While the Digital Freedom Project adopted many of the same arguments on political communications burden as Reddit in its submission, the group is likely to face an additional hurdle with the government challenging the standing of the group to bring the case to the court.
Digital Freedom Group had initially had two teens – Noah Jones and Macey Nyland – as the original lead plaintiffs for the case as teens affected by the ban. However in July both were withdrawn from the case, leaving it to the advocacy group.
It is understood there was concerns that the teens would face potential legal costs against them in the event of a loss.
Digital Freedom Project has argued in its submission that some of its members are between the ages of 13 and 15, and the teens are likely to be presented as examples in the case, but the federal government has argued that as the plaintiff, Digital Freedom Project does not have standing to bring the case.
The federal government’s submission argues the group has not identified any activity of the group that is impeded by the ban.
Legal experts have been divided on the prospect of success. The constitutional law expert Prof Anne Twomey wrote last year that Reddit could be successful in highlighting the mismatch between the intended purpose of the law and the practical effect – if the restriction is not preventing children from the harms while also restricting their freedom of political communication.
Luke Beck, professor of constitutional law at Monash University, wrote in the Guardian last year the cases were likely to fail, as the social media account ban only slightly reduces the overall volume of political communication in Australia, and 13-, 14- and 15-year-olds were not engaging in much political communication before the ban.
Beck said last week the extra hurdle for Digital Freedom Project to prove standing would also be difficult.
“The government is arguing that DFP is not impacted by the law so therefore can’t challenge it,” he said. “We’ll see what the high court says about advocacy groups having standing to challenge laws: traditionally the courts aren’t too keen.”
Many other countries are considering following Australia’s lead, but there have been concerns teens have been able to easily circumvent the ban. The federal opposition has also raised concerns that the number of accounts suspended may be inflated, while the government has refused to release numbers broken down by platform.
As the legal challengers get their day in court, the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, is also using new powers passed by parliament this year to investigate whether TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook are in compliance with the law, given the number of teens still holding accounts.
The companies could be facing the prospect of fines of up to nearly $100m a breach, if the regulator decides to take the case to the federal court.
The federal parliament is also debating the digital duty of care legislation mandating platforms take actions to prevent users experiencing harm on their platforms. Beck has said the passage of this legislation could present a pyrrhic victory for Reddit if it successfully overturns the ban.
The Australian government has made this argument in its submission in the case, stating the obligations of the digital duty of care bill would “require the same action” as the social media ban legislation.
“Namely, preventing children having accounts or providing children with accounts that do not have any of the [restricted] features.”

Mumbai: Maharashtra Congress president Harshwardhan Sapkal on Monday launched a scathing attack on the BJP and Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, accusing the ruling party and the RSS of being the real opponents of the Constitution and democracy. He described the BJP's 'Save Democracy, Save Constitution' rallies as an example of "the thief crying foul" and alleged that the party was attempting to divert attention from questions surrounding electoral irregularities.
Sapkal Claims INDIA Bloc's Delhi Rally Prompted BJP's Nationwide Campaign
In a statement issued on November 2, Sapkal claimed that the INDIA bloc's massive 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' rally at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi had rattled the Modi government, prompting the BJP to organise similar rallies across the country. He said it was ironic that the BJP was now claiming to protect the Constitution when its ideological parent, the RSS, had never accepted Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar's Constitution.
"The BJP has the Constitution on its lips but Manusmriti in its mind. Its claims of protecting democracy and the Constitution are nothing but the thief crying foul," Sapkal said.
Congress Questions BJP's Record After 13 Years In Power
Reacting to Fadnavis's allegations against Congress and Rahul Gandhi, the state Congress chief said the BJP had remained in power for 13 years but continued to blame Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi instead of highlighting its own achievements.
Alleging electoral manipulation in the 2024 elections, Sapkal claimed that the BJP-led governments at the Centre and in Maharashtra had come to power through 'vote chori'. He alleged that the exposure of electoral irregularities had unsettled Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Fadnavis, who feared action after losing power.
Congress Chief Raises Concerns Over Voting Rights Of Nearly 13 Crore Citizens
Sapkal also accused the government, with the support of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, of attempting to deprive nearly 13 crore citizens of their voting rights. Challenging Fadnavis, he demanded that the Chief Minister disclose figures of infiltrators allegedly identified in the country and cautioned against using the issue to take away the voting rights of legitimate citizens.
Questioning the BJP's criticism of the Opposition's demand for 'regime change', Sapkal said political parties existed to bring about a change of government through elections. He asked why Modi, Shah and Fadnavis were apprehensive about such a democratic process.
Congress Alleges Growing Political Influence Over Constitutional Institutions
The Congress leader further alleged that constitutional institutions, including universities, the Election Commission and the judiciary, were increasingly coming under the influence of the ruling establishment. He claimed that individuals associated with the BJP and RSS were being appointed to key positions in educational institutions, while the Election Commission was failing to act against the ruling party. He also referred to allegations of government interference in the judiciary, claiming that retired judges had publicly raised concerns.
Sapkal recalled that several BJP leaders had spoken about changing the Constitution during the 2024 Lok Sabha election campaign while seeking more than 400 seats. He accused Fadnavis of conveniently overlooking those statements.
Taking particular exception to the BJP's criticism of the red-covered Constitution carried by Rahul Gandhi, Sapkal asked why the ruling party was so uncomfortable with its colour. He said Gandhi was displaying the Constitution authored under the guidance of Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar.
"Earlier, the BJP asked who Rahul Gandhi was. Today, the Prime Minister and the Home Minister appear to be preoccupied with him. They see Rahul Gandhi even in their sleep because he has begun challenging their political authority," Sapkal said, adding that those responsible for electoral wrongdoing would eventually face consequences.

Despite an overall decline in tobacco consumption, disadvantaged and rural populations in India and the U.S. continue to be disproportionately affected, according to a comparative analysis presented at a national pulmonary diseases conference here.
The analysis highlighted that smokeless tobacco and bidis remain major concerns in India, while cigarettes and e-cigarettes remain public health challenges in the US.
The paper, titled "Two Countries, Two Tobacco Epidemics, One Hidden Inequality", was presented on October 25 by Akanksha Anand, assistant professor at Morgan State University's School of Community Health and Policy in the US, during the 28th National Conference on Pulmonary Diseases (NAPCON) concluded on Sunday.
The study examined tobacco-use patterns and disparities using national survey data from both countries, highlighting the role of gender, income, education and geographical location in tobacco exposure.
According to the Global Adult Tobacco Survey (GATS), tobacco use among adults aged 15 and above in India declined from 34.6 % in 2009-10 to 28.6% in 2016-17.
However, smokeless tobacco remained a major concern, with a prevalence of 21.4 % in 2016-17, nearly twice the 10.7 per cent prevalence of smoked tobacco.
The National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-21) showed that 38%of men and 8.9 % of women used tobacco.
The rural-urban divide was particularly significant, with 42.7 %of rural men reporting tobacco use, compared with 28.8 % of urban men.
Among women, tobacco use stood at 10.5 % in rural areas against 5.5 % in urban areas.
The presentation noted that focusing only on cigarette smoking could overlook substantial tobacco exposure through bidis, smokeless tobacco and other products.
It also highlighted the risks associated with secondhand smoke.
In the US, data from the 2024 National Health Interview Survey showed that 9.9 %of adults smoked cigarettes, while 7 % reported using e-cigarettes.
Cigarette use was considerably higher in non-metropolitan areas at 15.4 %, compared with 8 % in central metropolitan counties.
Similarly, e-cigarette use stood at 9.2 % in non-metropolitan areas against 6.1 % in central metropolitan counties.
The analysis found that while tobacco products differed between the two countries, social and geographical inequalities remained common challenges.
Gender, wealth, education and geographical location were important factors influencing tobacco use in India, while rural residence, education and age played significant roles in the U.S.
The presentation highlighted the need for targeted public health interventions to address tobacco use among vulnerable populations and reduce associated respiratory health risks.
It also cautioned that the figures were drawn from surveys conducted in different years using different methodologies and should not be treated as directly comparable.
The analysis was based on published national estimates rather than an original combined analysis of individual-level survey data.

MUMBAI: Bombay high court on Monday continued its interim relief against Centre’s Leave India Notice to actor Imran Khan Pal, 44, a US citizen and an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI), after he furnished a prepared undertaking and added an unconditional apology which the court sought. The central government’s Foreigner Registration Regional Officer (FRRO) had given him 2 weeks to leave India, four days after registering an FIR against Khan for unlawful assembly in Mumbai during an October 10 protest against the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls and the CEC.
Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said, “OCI card holders are not Indian citizens." They were hearing a petition Khan filed to challenge the Leave India notice as arbitrary and in violation of his right to life.
“You cannot behave like an Indian citizen. You are not even remotely associated with the SIR process,’’ said the CJ orally to Khan, via his senior counsel VR Dhond, who said he was ready with the undertaking.
“Right to protest is not even available to you as an OCI…” added Justice Sethna. Dhond said they are not getting into the legality of the Constitutional rights but under Article 21—right to life and liberty which is available to non-citizens, principles of natural justice do accrue.
The CJ asked what was Khan doing at the protest site and how was he connected? “What for were you there? There is a complete difference between rights of an OCI card holder and a citizen of India. You will have to categorially make a statement that you have no association with the protest…”
Dhond referring to pleadings in the petition said, “glad you asked. He (Khan) has no association or affiliation with those who organised the protest the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)."
Additional Solicitor General Anil Singh for the FRRO tendered a compilation to the bench and argued that it was not an isolated instance and that Khan “instigated’’ people on social media.
Khan has been in India since he was 2 years old, for the last 42 years, said Dhond having studied here, worked here, married and having a child in India. He should be heard, Dhond argued. The State said an FIR is registered against Khan.
Dhond said but neither has the actor been summon nor called for any probe and all offences including disobedience of orders and unlawful assembly are bailable offences. The actor was passing by and was curious to see the protesters as mentioned in the petition, Dhond submitted.
“I(Khan) have at the moment no film in hand. Have nothing to do with those who organised the protest. The HC can take an undertaking that I (Khan) have no part in the protest. Before I (Khan) could even reach the site there was a police bandobast…’’ Dhond submitted.
The ASG questioned the veracity of Khan’s claim over how he landed at the protest spot saying “It is a misleading statement. That out of curiosity he went there to check…He is part of the protest."
Singh said the actor is a US citizen and the Centre is within its power to expel him. The Centre “requires no foundational basis to expel a foreigner from the India,’’ said Singh.
“Hence there is no question of granting any protection. He takes all benefit as citizen of US and as your lordship just said Article 19 doesn’t apply to OCI. The (FRRO) has taken a decision to remove a foreigner. It is the Centre’s discretion. A visa too doesn’t mean a foreigner has all the rights to enter India.”
“If you read the petition the impression given is that…he was curious… but see he has given an interview…” Singh submitted. The HC sought a reply from the Centre. “It is better that you (Centre) respond. Khan will have a chance to file a rejoinder. We can then decide the matter," said the bench.
The bench remarked, “This case is purely distinguisshable…He has on his OCI registration said he is “unemployed."
The Judges said to Khan, “Why don’t you accept India citizenship. You work and live here. You make films here. You are a celebrity. Why don’t you apply for Indian citizenship…You have to give a categorical undertaking that you will not participate in any such protest as you are an OCI and these are not available to OCI card holders."
Dhond tendered the undertaking and the Chief Justice said, “If this kind of undertaking comes, you have to tender one with an unconditional apology…You (Khan) have everything and recognition pan India. Your (Khan’s) one statement would have decisive impact (on fans)."
The CJ Tripathi and Justice Sethna orally said, “It is least expected. You (Khan) are a responsible person. Literate and highly educated. you come from a responsible family. You have a great following. Since childhood you are in India. And the country has never raised such an issue against you in the past…you cannot behave or be placed on par with Indian citizens…’’ The bench on seeing the Centre’s compilation said, “You cannot say, ‘I was a novice and had no idea."
Dhond sought a copy of the compilation, saying they cannot tender fresh material across the bar.
The CJ said, “Inadvertently if you had participated then there should be regret on oath. You (Khan) had no role at all in the SIR. Whatever statement you have made. You should make an unconditional apology. We will record in the order."
The ASG said, “This undertaking and apology is by a foreigner as an OCI holder falls within definition of a foreigner. This is not merely a question of participation in a protest
The CJ at one point said smilingly, Khan has lived here for so long that he “forgot that perhaps you are an OCI". Power of govt to expel a foreigner is absolute court has held
The ASG Singh said, "A foreigner has no right to stay in India Or remain in India."
OCI card holder doesn’t alter the situation
"OCI card holder is not a citizen of India." The bench orally said to the ASG "That the Centre has unfettered power (to remove a foreigner) we agree. But this is a case of a dispute..." and the CJ said "Vasudeva Kutumbakam and smiling said once apology is tendered perhaps the Centre would be "magnanimous".
HC CJ recorded that Khan has tendered an unconditional apology and posting the matter to December 7 at 3pm said in the end to Khan’s counsel, "you must tell your client
that filing an apology doesn’t mean it is a green signal to say or do anything...You can go to the USA and cast your vote and participate in protests there... It is a very serious matter."
Imran Khan’s legal team also comprised Kunal Vajani, Zulfiquar Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik.
Imran Khan’s petition against 'Leave India' notice: Key exchange in the hearing
ASG Anil Singh (for FRRO):
- Even without foundational facts, the Centre can tell him (Khan, as a foreigner) to leave India, even if there is a valid visa.
- The Centre has an unfettered right and facts are not needed. That’s a different thing.
- Khan is a foreigner, a US citizen. An OCI, not an Indian citizen.
- The Centre has unfettered power (under the Immigration and Foreigners Act).
- That you have unfettered power we agree. But LIN was issued under these circumstances (of being present at a protest). If these circumstances go, your outcome or actions could be different.
- He (Khan) has been here for many years. Since childhood. We have to follow Vasudev kutumbakam.
- Someday you may say this man must remain in India.
- Once he tenders an apology, magnanimity may be shown.
- OCI are at the mercy of the sovereign county. They have no right at all to stay here and criticise the country and its policies.
- You must tell your client. By filing an apology doesn’t mean a green signal.
- Hopefully his apology and undertaking will persuade the FRRO to take a different view.
- I had no intent, as can be seen from my limited remarks to the media on 10.10.2026. I have never made any demands and have categorically stated that I am no one to make any demands. I was present there to see why the freedom of movement was being restricted and why people’s voices were being oppressed and suppressed.
- I have utmost love and respect for this great nation. I have, to a great extent and in my limited personal capacity, contributed substantially through the furnishing of taxes and the creation of jobs for several persons.
- There will be no participation by me in any protests in the future.

Judge dismisses Trump's lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday book
- Published
A US judge has thrown out President Donald Trump's $10bn (£7.4bn) lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, ruling the suit was "grasping at straws".
Trump had sued the media outlet's parent company Dow Jones and its leader Rupert Murdoch last year after it reported on a letter allegedly written by Trump to disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein as part of a birthday book in 2003, before Epstein was charged with sex crimes.
Trump has denied writing or signing the letter, which included suggestive language and a drawing of the outline of a woman's body.
Judge Darrin Gayles threw out the case, finding the suit runs counter to the First Amendment, which protects freedom of the press.
Gayles had already once dismissed the defamation lawsuit, which sought $20 billion in damages. Trump's team refiled the suit seeking $10 billion, and this time, the judge threw out the case "with prejudice," meaning the suit cannot be filed again.
The news outlet's story about Epstein's 50th birthday book, external - and the letter with Trump's name - came as the Trump administration battled intense bipartisan criticism over the summer for its handling of Epstein documents.
Trump had said the newspaper had slandered him and violated libel laws in publishing the article.
In his 20-page ruling, Gayles noted the paper's "thoughtful and detailed investigation" that led to the story and said the lawsuit was "grasping at straws" to "manufacture flaws" in their work.
The judge wrote that Trump's legal team did not prove that the defendants made defamatory statements with "actual malice", which the law requires be proven.
Actual malice is high bar to meet, as it requires proof that the defendant knew the defamatory statement was false or acted with reckless disregard for whether it was true or not.
Trump alleged that the letter obtained and released by the Journal, which features his signature at the bottom, was "fake" and that the defendants devised the story in order to defame him.
Trump's legal team had argued that because Trump denied writing the letter when contacted by the Journal, the paper should have "disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story", Gayles wrote.
"But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment," Gayles wrote.
If that were the law, he wrote, then "any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press—a result that flies in the face of the 'American privilege to speak one's mind'".
According to the Wall Street Journal story, a letter bearing Trump's name "contained several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker".
It reportedly contained a joking reference that "enigmas never age" and allegedly ended with the words: "A pal is a wonderful thing. Happy Birthday - and may every day be another wonderful secret".

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
- Published
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.
Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.
On Tuesday, Nigeria confirmed a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda to Abuja. Nigeria is the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East and Central Africa.
Ugandan health officials say the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
The health ministry stressed she did not have symptoms while transiting through Uganda and only developed them after arriving in Abuja.

Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.
In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.
Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.
The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.
Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.
Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.
“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.
In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.
Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

Russia ramps up disinformation war on UK with propaganda claiming Britain is ‘ungovernable and defenceless’
Exclusive: Putin’s campaign to erode trust and cause chaos has reached staggering levels amid Britain’s support for Ukraine and Russia’s closer relations with Donald Trump

Russia’s disinformation war on the UK has reached new highs as Kremlin-backed media seek to sow chaos amongst Britons and ramp up attacks on their “main adversary”, experts warn.
In the past six months, state-affiliated media have pushed hundreds of thousands of stories on social media portraying Britain as ungovernable, defenceless, and a legitimate Russian target, The Independent can reveal.
Analysis by risk intelligence firm Osavul, which tracks global hybrid threats and supplies technology to Nato, shows such media output rose by around 15 per cent in September, when it produced around 40,365 stories about the UK, while similar levels of disinformation pushed in October.
False claims that the UK bombed the city of Voronezh with storm shadow missiles, that British police were threatening to arrest people for using air conditioners, and that Andy Burnham was “powerless to stop the UK's collapse” are among several posts seen by The Independent.
Osavul said the aim was “to leave British readers with a lower opinion of their own state, and readers abroad with the sense that Britain is not a serious power”.
Experts said the threat of disinformation has become far greater because of Donald Trump’s closer relationship with Russia, and Britain’s strong support for Ukraine, meaning the UK is viewed as an enemy.
They warn Russia’s ability to share disinformation has also been turbocharged by artificial intelligence, which allows for faster, cheaper, and more effective campaigns.
Vladimir Putin critic and anti-corruption campaigner Sir Bill Browder said the campaigns “had very big success” in the UK and warned that without government action, it could “get exponentially worse”.
He told The Independent: “I don't think we've even begun to see how AI will be used in this whole thing.”
Osavul analysed Russian state-affiliated actors, state-owned media outlets, state agencies, government officials, and reportedly state-affiliated outlets and channels with a combined audience of 1.37bn.
Other posts included claims that were wildly exaggerated, such as warning of widespread power cuts and an energy crisis in Britain after UK media reported warnings that there could be blackouts this winter. They claimed Mr Burnham’s “priorities included Nato, Ukraine, and support for pubs, rather than concern for energy”.
Following his resignation, Sir Keir Starmer’s tenure was described as being “marred by a rampage by gangs that carried out the sexual exploitation of children” – a reference to criticism of the government’s handling of a probe into grooming gangs.
Analysis found 1,019 messages from 172 accounts Osavul classifies as “high risk for information manipulation” around Sir Keir’s resignation and the collapse of his Labour government, which garnered 93,548 engagements.
Another common claim is that the UK is preparing to attack Russia. Posts describe the UK as “deliberately opting for an escalation”, with the clearest case of outright disinformation falsely stating that Nato had conducted missile strikes on Russia from the London Underground. This came after UK forces took over a disused tube platform to simulate such operations in the event of an attack.
A report about Iran-linked hackers shutting down a small power plant in July became a story about British energy systems being vulnerable to hostile actors. It drew 337 messages from 117 high-risk accounts and received 1.89m views between 22 and 26 August.
The government said there was never a risk to the wider grid, but this was absent from every version sampled, with Osavul saying it “is the clearest case of a true event being reframed to produce fear of state weakness”.
It added: “The sheer volume means that for anyone searching in English for news about Britain's politics, security or constitutional future, a meaningful share of what they find has been shaped by Moscow.”
Sir Bill called for more regulation on social media and said there was “no question” that the UK government had the power to do this.
Last month, the prime minister unveiled plans for a new National Centre for Information Defence to tackle Russian information warfare, saying Britain had been subjected to an “industrial-scale assault” by hostile states.
But Mr Browder urged more radical change. He said: “Enough is enough. We've sat around and watched all this stuff go on for a long time. We know it exists. We know it has absolutely vicious effects on our democracy and our society, and we should stop this from happening. We have the ability to stop it; it just requires some brave policy-making.”
Keir Giles, a senior consulting fellow at the Chatham House policy institute, said Russia was trying to create an environment in which it could deceive Britons.
“It means playing both sides against the middle a lot of the time, like the Brexit referendum, where it was not just a campaign to boost the Brexit vote; it was actually stirring, using an emotive issue to set people against each other,” he said.
“Russia gets the best result by constantly working in the background to change attitudes, change perceptions, and through doing that, change the political stance of the target country.”
He said: “The reason why the UK has come to the forefront as the primary adversary at the moment is because the United States is no longer in that role. When you have a leadership group in the US that is determined to play along with Russian objectives, it becomes harder to describe them as your main adversary.”
Former British diplomat Andy Pryce, a fellow of the defence and security think tank Rusi, said analysis showed that state-media conversations about the UK being an adversary “dramatically increased after the Trump administration sat down with the Russian government in Riyadh in February 2025.
“If you're an authoritarian government, you usually need a foreign enemy to point to... The UK is reflected as an enemy more.”
Former Tory defence minister and ex-Army captain Tobias Ellwood said the disinformation threat to the UK was “huge” and had dramatically increased because of social media.
“The priority now has to be national security, and therefore the fact that social media is absolutely front and centre of our adversaries' efforts to sow societal discord [requires] a wider discussion and debate about it to be able to immediately remove falsehoods from the narrative,” he said.
Shadow national security minister Alicia Kearns, who has specialised in Russian disinformation, said: “The threat from disinformation is significant within our societies because it's a low-entry, easy, and cheap method to undermine confidence in governments, and that's ultimately what the Russians are focusing on.”
Ms Kearns said it was crucial to have more education in schools and to teach people to think critically and challenge information and for the government to counter disinformation during major incidents that Russia might seek to take advantage of.
A government spokesperson said its new national information centre would “strengthen the UK’s ability to detect, attribute and disrupt hostile information attacks from foreign adversaries that pose a threat to our national interests and security”.
“We will work alongside intelligence agencies, law enforcement and social media companies to ensure the UK has the defensive capability necessary to combat information warfare and build national resilience,” they added.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

Nearly 40% of patients seeking neurological care at the casualty in NIMHANS are patients, with as many as 705 cases reported every month. As the number of patients requiring emergency neurological care remains a concern, a hub-and-spoke model linking NIMHANS with the Karnataka Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Institute (KMCRI) in Hubballi is helping extend specialised stroke treatment to northern Karnataka.
The initiative aims to ensure that patients receive prompt assessment and treatment closer to home, particularly during the critical first few hours after a stroke. KMCRI manages around 100 to 120 stroke patients a month under the collaborative model, with teleconsultation and coordinated treatment protocols helping doctors make time-sensitive decisions. World Stroke Day is observed on October 29.
Girish B. Kulkarni, professor of Neurology and head of the stroke unit at NIMHANS, said early recognition of symptoms, rapid transportation to a stroke-ready hospital and timely treatment were essential to improving outcomes.
‘Every Minute Counts’
“This year’s theme, ‘Every Minute Counts’, highlights the importance of recognising stroke symptoms early and ensuring that patients reach hospitals that are equipped to provide appropriate treatment without delay,” he said.
Dr. Kulkarni said around 1,700 patients attended the neurological casualty services at NIMHANS every month, of whom 705 were stroke patients. The institute administers intravenous thrombolysis to around five to eight patients and performs about five to nine endovascular thrombectomies every month.
To northern districts
Under the hub-and-spoke model, NIMHANS serves as the central specialised centre, while KMCRI in Hubballi is developing its capacity to evaluate and treat acute stroke patients in the region. Teleconsultation and structured coordination between the institutions help doctors assess patients and initiate appropriate treatment without waiting for a transfer to Bengaluru.
Amruth, professor and head of the Department of Neurology at KMCRI, said the centre was managing an average of 100 to 120 stroke cases a month.
“Through structured coordination and teleconsultation mechanisms with NIMHANS, patients arriving at our centre receive immediate medical management and targeted interventions,” he said.
The model is particularly relevant for patients in northern Karnataka, for whom travelling to Bengaluru during a medical emergency can consume valuable time. Stroke treatment is highly time-sensitive, and delays in diagnosis and intervention can increase the risk of death or long-term disability.
The KMCRI spoke centre has begun evaluating stroke patients and providing intravenous thrombolysis. A dual-plane digital subtraction angiography (DSA) machine has also been installed at the centre, with endovascular thrombectomy services expected to be introduced soon, Dr. Amruth said.
Thrombolysis involves administering clot-dissolving medication to eligible patients with an ischaemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain is blocked. Endovascular thrombectomy is a procedure in which doctors remove a clot from a blocked blood vessel using specialised equipment. The choice of treatment depends on the type of stroke, imaging findings, the time since symptom onset and the patient’s clinical condition, Dr. Kulkarni said.
‘BE FAST’
Dr. Kulkarni said improving public awareness was the first step in reducing delays in stroke treatment. He said the acronym BE FAST can help people recognise the signs of a stroke: B for sudden loss of balance, E for eye or vision disturbances, F for facial drooping, A for arm weakness, and S for speech difficulties. The final letter, T, underscores the need to seek timely medical help and act immediately.
Sudden onset of any of these symptoms should prompt immediate medical attention. Patients should not wait to see whether the symptoms improve or attempt to manage them at home. They should recognise the warning signs and seek emergency medical attention immediately rather than wait for symptoms to subside, he added.

Think twice before putting your gaming console inside a cabinet
Cabinets are a great way to keep your game console hot, which is terrible for it.
One of the reasons often cited for the failure of the original Xbox in Japan is that the console (and its original bulky controller) was too big for many Japanese homes. Now, there was more to it, such as a lack of the genres and franchises Japanese gamers preferred. But this highlights an important point that space matters; some modern consoles could be an awkward fit if you're living in a cramped studio apartment.
Even in the West, gamers often need to optimize the space around their TV to make it livable for everyone in the home. Aside from comfort, you might be worried about style, aiming for a sleek, minimalist look. And while it may seem like a great idea on the surface, you certainly shouldn't jam any of the latest consoles into a cabinet in your entertainment center.
That might seem counterintuitive, since AV gear is often what those cabinets are for. But doing so could hamper your console's performance or shorten its lifespan. That's a potentially expensive mistake with memory prices inflating console costs by hundreds of dollars.
The dangers of stuffing your console in a cabinet
The primary concern here is heat. A modern console like the PlayStation 5 is a far more power-hungry device than your Blu-ray player or cable box. It's rendering real-time 3D graphics and physics, and the hardware necessary to power that consumes a lot of energy. During a game, the standard PS5 can consume up to 220W, a figure roughly matched by the Xbox Series X. Conversely, even Panasonic's relatively high-end UB820 Blu-ray player isn't going to hit any more than 32W.
Consoles have fans to expel heat and vents to take in cold air, but this can't flow well when the system is in a cabinet. The hot air can end up trapped, while it might not have enough room to draw in new air, so it cycles the same hot air. When your console is surrounded by heat like this, it forces the fans to work harder to maintain a safe internal temperature. Your system also might scale back performance to reduce heat production. Under extreme conditions, prolonged heat can trigger visual glitches or force the console to temporarily shut down to avoid damaging its components.
Closely related to this is the issue of dust. Although a cabinet can block some material from getting in, it also make it harder for particles to escape. As with any device, a thick enough layer will trap heat by reducing airflow out of vents or how much air can be taken in. This leads to the same problems and can reduce the lifespan of your console.
What you can do to keep consoles running cool
For proper ventilation, Sony recommends leaving about 4 inches (about 10 centimeters) of clearance around a PlayStation. Microsoft is a little more aggressive with the Xbox, proposing 4 to 6 inches (up to 15 centimeters) on all sides. Nintendo simply advises docking the Switch 2 in an "open, ventilated area."
The same principles apply to PC-based systems too, such as the ASUS ROG Ally X or Valve Steam Machine. While every system takes in and expels air at different places, a trapped space is never good. You should also avoid putting controllers, game cases, books or similar items on top of a console, as that will block its vents. Don't keep your console near a heat source, either.
If space is at a premium, some airflow is better than nothing. Remember that the PS5 and Xbox Series consoles can both be placed vertically or horizontally, so experiment with what fits into your setup. You might even consider aiming a small fan toward the console to help air circulate. It's also a good idea to periodically dust the outside of your console using a microfiber cloth and can of compressed air. If you use canned air, be sure to hold it level and several inches away from your hardware. Otherwise, you might spray liquids onto circuitry.
None of this is too complicated. Rather, console makers don't put it front-and-center in their instructions, which they probably should. Gaming hardware has come a long way since people were jamming the 9W NES on a shelf to play Super Mario Bros and Zelda.

Zverev becomes deserved world number one - but sense of discomfort remains
- Published
Before this year, Alexander Zverev was, for many, the best male player never to have won a Grand Slam.
He will end 2026 as a two-time major champion and deserved world number one.
The 29-year-old has become the oldest man in more than 50 years to become world number one for the first time, with victories at the French Open and US Open providing the springboard.
Diagnosed with type 1 diabetes aged four, his overdue Grand Slam breakthrough was a reward for persistence and intense hard work.
However, the new standard-bearer for men's tennis has been accused of physical abuse by two former partners, and been the subject of a major independent investigation by the sport.
How 10 days with Nadal changed on-court approach
At the start of this year, Zverev was already an Olympic champion, two-time winner of the season-ending ATP Finals and a former world number two who had appeared in three Grand Slam finals.
The most excruciating of those was the 2020 US Open final, in which he led Dominic Thiem by two sets to love but lost in a fifth-set tie-break after serving two double faults as his opponent began to cramp.
The inability to play with the same freedom and attacking intent that is often on show in big matches on the ATP Tour had become a perennial problem.
This year would be different, he promised himself. He would hit the ball with more speed, take greater risk and employ more variety in rallies.
The impetus stemmed from the 10 days he spent with Rafael and Toni Nadal in Mallorca in July 2025.
"I wanted to see and then hear a new vision of what tennis in their mind looks like - and how my tennis, in their mind, looks like," Zverev explained.
"Rafa, for example, played against me for 10 years. So now, as a spectator and also as an opponent, he can probably give you the best advice anybody can, because he knows what it's like to be on the court with me."
There were still moments of extreme anxiety, including cramping in June's French Open final against Flavio Cobolli.
But this time Zverev made no mistake in the deciding set, winning it 6-1 to claim his long-awaited first major trophy.
Zverev's on-court success is a family affair. His father, Alex Sr, has been a near-constant presence in the coaching box, while older brother Mischa has joined him since his retirement from playing.
That particular relationship has come full circle, as Zverev was once a toddler sitting by the side of the court as Mischa practised with Andy Murray as a junior.
Zverev has said his relationship with his father works so well as they spend "zero time together" off court.
"The big difference with my parents is that they never forced me to do anything," Zverev once recalled.
"They wanted me to play different sports so they didn't have to coach me. They always told me 'why don't you play football, or field hockey?' as that was the sport I loved.
"They are very smart. They've been through it. They've been tennis players themselves."
Not only is Zverev now the French and US Open champion, but he was also runner-up at Wimbledon, where he played his best tennis of the year.
He was aggressive and daring in a four-set defeat by Jannik Sinner on Centre Court, and will need to take a leaf out of the same book in future meetings with both the Italian and Carlos Alcaraz.
The German has lost 10 matches in a row to Sinner, and if he and Alcaraz are fit for the start of next season, Zverev's challenge will be to make 2027 a three-way rivalry for the major titles.
A polarising world number one
Zverev has previously been the subject of serious allegations.
In October 2020, his ex-partner Olga Sharypova accused him of physical violence and controlling behaviour.
Zverev maintained his innocence from the start and described the allegations as baseless.
There were no legal proceedings, but the ATP Tour opened a major investigation that was carried out by third-party investigators.
It found "insufficient evidence to substantiate published allegations of abuse".
"Based on a lack of reliable evidence and eyewitness reports, in addition to conflicting statements by Sharypova, Zverev and other interviewees, the investigation was unable to substantiate the allegations of abuse," the ATP said in January 2023.
A director of safeguarding was subsequently appointed, and this year a new safeguarding programme was launched to introduce a "clear, global framework for preventing and responding to abuse, including cases of harassment, bullying, domestic violence and other forms of misconduct".
In October 2023, Zverev was issued with a penalty order and fined 450,000 euros (£392,000) by a German court for bodily harm against another ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea.
Zverev denied the claims and contested the order, with a public trial taking place in Berlin in May 2024.
A week into the process, the court terminated the proceedings before a verdict could be reached, and told the BBC there had been a settlement between Zverev and Patea.
"The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence," the court said.
"One decisive factor for the court decision was that the witness [Zverev's ex-partner] has expressed her wish to end the trial."
Zverev reached the French Open final on the day the settlement was announced. Having spoken earlier in the tournament about the trial being a chance to prove his innocence, he was asked whether he had any regrets about settling before that was possible.
"That's what dropping the case is. That is innocence," he argued.
"They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day. I don't know what translations you have, but that's what it means.
"Done. We move on. I never ever want to hear another question about the subject again. That goes out to everybody."
Patea has not publicly commented on the settlement.
Zverev was heckled by spectators in 2025 at the Australian Open and Munich Open over the allegations.
In 2022, he was given an eight-week suspended ban by the ATP Tour after being found guilty of a 'major offence' for smashing his racquet into the umpire's chair four times after losing a doubles match at the Mexican Open.
Zverev, who was thrown out of the tournament in Acapulco for unsportsmanlike behaviour, was incensed by a line call that went against him and partner Marcelo Melo in a deciding tie-break.
He swore at umpire Alessandro Germani and accused him of destroying the whole match. One of his four angry swipes at the chair nearly caught the umpire on the foot.
Zverev later apologised and said it was "difficult to put into words" how much he regretted his behaviour.
The ban was never imposed, as Zverev avoided being fined for 'disrespectful or aggressive behaviour, or verbal or physical abuse' in the 12 months following the incident.

The picture posted by Goyal was also used by several other politicians, including Rajya Sabha MPs Satnam Singh Sandhu and Sujeet Kumar. They also posted images of the same crowd from different angles.
